I read this kinetic visual novel years ago (probably around the time it was published) and absolutely loved it. Honestly, it probably heavily contributed to my interest in visual novels. I think this was the second visual novel I'd ever read, because it was free and I still wasn't sure if I'd like VNs at the time.
While it is a short visual novel, I didn't ever feel like the story was being rushed and nor did it feel unfinished.
It's quite well-written and uses language commonly known from the early 1900s. (Admittedly, if someone isn't familiar with some of the terminology, they might have to look it up. It might also be difficult for those whose first language isn't English.)
The artwork is great and impressive. There is also bonus art in the extras menu, including concept art and guest art.
The story is interesting and bittersweet. It can cause the reader to feel empathy toward both characters, as some scenes are quite emotional.
There is also implications of the female character being queer, as she talks about another woman in an affectionate, loving way.
I definitely recommend this visual novel to those who enjoy the genre. I also recommend Dysfunctional Systems, a non-kinetic VN series by the same developer.

The gunplay is OK, and there is ample quests/objective points to be discovered and looted.  If you're a completionist, can look past the glaring graphical bugs that have not been fixed since day 1, and want a casual shooter with a story that takes its self too seriously, then buy this.

Far Cry 4 offers an open world, that contains a lot of things you can do out of the story, there are enemie outposts, extra-missions etc. If you want a pause from the main story, you can just take over some outposts e.g. You won't get bored so fast.
The controls are almost the same as its forerunner, but i like the controls in Far Cry 3 a bit more, it's a bit easier. But they are not bad. The gameplay is well done like in FC3, you can either shot all of your enemies down, or go sneaky beaky like and kill them one by one, hopefully without being noticed by the enemies. The gameplay is very open, you can do whatever you want, as long as you complete your Mission.
The graphics are perfect. It's just awesome to look over the map, it's beautiful. You can take a bunch of beautiful screenshots, if you want to!
The game is great, you can play it for a long time without getting bored. I dislike some little things, but its still a great game. If you like the Far Cry Series, you should buy it. But i have to recommend Far Cry 3 a lot more.

Graphics is very good, it is smooth, and the AI is pretty well balanced, and the issues below have been addressed.
1) (Fixed Issue) The accuracy count literally "forgets" all except your current round for kills, but keeps ALL of the shots fired.  By the time the player gets past round 5 or so, the "accuracy" count drops below 20% because you've shot ~70 times overall, but the kills for the current round only is about 10. Big oversight in the stat counters.  EDIT: Also, just thought of another reason the "accuracy" count is broken. "Accuracy" in any other game means "average chance a shot fired HIT an enemy," but here it means enemies Killed. Enemies with armor can take 2 "hits" if hit from the wrong side.
All in all, this game counts accuracy as: "number of enemies killed (last round only) divided by the number of shots fired (for the entire match)."
2) (Rebalanced and tweaked points/difficulty, fixed) This is the main reason for not recommending, there is no way to save upgrades between matches AND you can't upgrade between rounds either. I.E. Any coins spent on upgrades are forgotten the next time the player loses.  If you can collect coins at all and spend them before a match, WHY forget the upgrades after the match is done?
3) I know this is a very simple game, but the planes mode makes me cringe.

This free to play kinetic visual novel by Dischan Media features a small boy who got lost in the Moors after losing his horse and accidentally stumbles across a female fiend(demon with horns and pointy ears) imprisoned for centuries within a magic circle inside a burnt out ruined building. With no way for the fiend to leave the magic circle, the fiend made an offer for the boy to stay with her for the day and to exchange stories with each other in return for roasting the boy's collected chestnuts. Feeling fascinated rather than afraid of the fiend, the boy decided to stay with the fiend and as the day draws to a close, the boy gradually develops a friendship with the fiend.
The plot is written as a fantasy dramedy and has a nice happy ending. It has nice artwork in the character sprites, backgrounds and CGs and nice BGM which match the various different moments in the game that is also included as free MP3 and FLAC files with the game(My favourite BGM are Politely Honest when the boy is seeing the fiend for the first time, Bleeding in the promo video and middle part of the visual novel and Stella during the happy ending moment in the game). The DLC has a nice and attractive Thank You CG artwork featuring the fiend for supporting the developer. Recommended for those who like a short fantasy visual novel with a nice happy ending as a free to play game with optional DLC.

Video:
Plot/Overview:  Spell words, defeat the monsters, collect gold, and get to the top of the tower. This is a port of the andriod/iOS version of the game, with the ads and monitization removed.
Menus:  The menus are laid out pretty simple, seperate sliders for music and sound.  As well as lots of resolution choices, all the way up to 4k.  The shop is where the RPG elements come in, you buy permanent upgrades for your wizard, these range from staves and robes, to hats and extra bag space.
Music/Sound: The music is nice, but gets repetitive after a while.  The sounds are cartoony, mostly popping noises.
Gameplay:  The gameplay loop is that you're given 10 random letters on each level, and you must spell words with at least 3 letters.  The more letters, the more damage you do.  Enemies attack based on a timer that is represented in the middle of the screen.
There are two main ways to unlock upgrades, clearing higher levels of the tower and earning stars for replaying levels and completing the challenge.  The gold you earn for clearing levels and defeating monsters is used to buy and upgrade unlocked equipment.  Most monsters can have a resistance and weakness to certain elements, which is where the difficulty can come in, if you bring the wrong weapon for a boss, you'll lose.  The game will make you replay levels for gold however unless you're really lucky.  As well as every 8 hours you're given a chest with your choice of one of three things, usually gold and two comsumables.
Controls:  The controls as simple, use the keyboard to type the words out, and press enter to attack.  The menus are completely mouse driven.  There is also controller support but I feel it will hinder a game based around typing.
TLDR
Pros:
Simple gameplay loop that is enjoyable.
Progression is thought out.
Learn new words
Fairly well done port
Profanity can be used.
Cons:
Profanity can be used.
Music and sound effects end up being annoying after a while
Sometimes you get too many vowels
Lack of variety in monsters

Okay, so, initially I gave this game a negative review, but I've since started to appreciate it more.
It's basically exactly what it says in the description, just a little cute game where you shoot stuff in space. At first I was somewhat irked at the fact that the playing field is restricted to the player (i.e. not Asteroids-style, where you can fly off the screen on the right side and come out on the left side), but after further examination, that mechanic is actually fine within the context of the game, since it forces you to prioritize on what powerups to chase after, for example.
The fact that you can unlock ships with different stats, and the fairly wide selection of weapon powerups (spreadshot, grenade, 'flame', laser etc.) gives this some more play and as much depth as it needs to keep you coming back.
I'd totally recommend this game for the price, especially in comparison to a lot of other Steam games in this price range that seem like they didn't have half as much effort put into it as this one.

Panzer Corps is a gem of a hexbased wargame. It's my own personal sit back and command game, so relaxing yet also challenging.
In Vanilla Panzer corps you control the wehrmacht fighting from Poland to the end of the war in various scenarios. Each scenario has two methods of victory, Marginal Victoy and Decisive Victory. You should strive to obtain Decisive victories since it will allow you to access different scenarios to overthrow history and eventually invade the United States.
Controls are super easy, left mouse button is all you need, what you really need to get familiar with is mechanics. I will not pretend I know every single mechanic in the game (i.e. just learned today that it might be better to obtain Marginal Victories to get more Prestige) and may get some wrong, but it is fairly simple for the most part (although I wish the game would make a better effort to tell you these less obvious mechanics). Your only income is Prestige which you use to purchase new units, ungrades new units, overstrenght you units and replace your troops.
Overstrengthing your units occurs when you give one of your unit one more health than the base 10 that every unit has. Every unit can reach to five stars of veterancy which means you can overstrength your units from 10 health to 15. This doesn't sound like a big deal, but a 15 health Tiger Tank is almost impossible to kill (already that 10 health Tigers are a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥ same with 15 health infantry, aircraft, tankdestroyers etc.
You have two options to replenish your troops, elite replacements which cost more prestige but allow your troops to retain their Veterancy stars so as to over strength and green replacements which is cheaper to replenish your troops but experience is lost.
So you find yourself having to learn to economise your Prestige and learn when/when not to overstength, upgrade and/or replenish
The amount of units is crazy, nearly all tank, fighter aircraft, strategic bombers, tactical bombers, AT (self propelled or otherwise), troops, artillary etc. is depicted in games. 90% of scenarios are ground based, but there are some with naval scenarios. However, you cannot buy ''core'' (core refers to units that you purchase that carry over from scenario to scenario) naval units.
Now, personnally I find Vanilla objectives to be less than stellar, no real variety. All offensive scenarios Decisive Victories are Control all objective cities with X turns remaining i.e. if you have 20 turns, you have to capture all objective with 6 turns remaining, meaning by turn 14 if you want a decisive victory. Marginal Victories are capture all objective cities within X turns, keepin with the 20 turns example, capture all objectives by, including, turn 20. The DLCs fix this lack of variety offering differnt methods of obtaining MV and DV.
I've purchased every single piece of DLC and I'd adivse to hold off from them if you don't really want to go beyond Vanilla (i.e. you're satisfied just playing Vanilla campagin). The only reason I'm giving this advice is that is can be quite costly to purchase all the DLC, so make sure you really want more of Panzer Corps than what Vanilla offers.
If you do want more to the base game I'd say you can't really go wrong with any of the DLC, personally here's my favorites:
1. The German grand campaign
2. Allied Corps/ Allied grand campaign
3. Soviet Corps
4. Sea Lion (haven't gone too deep in this one yet)
5. Africa Corps
Asthetic wise, sounds are pretty solid, tanks shots, damage to enemy units, bombing, machine gun fire etc. are all really good. The worst sound imho is truck movement that perhaps can be better. Graphics are not AAA but I find PC has the greatest graphics out of all the wargames I've ever played Ofc this is all subjective but I really find PC has some really great graphics.
In the end, PC offers a really great remake of classic Panzer General and is a no-brainer pick up for veteran and casual wargamers.

Took a little while for me to get into this but once I played more of the tutorial battles I started to like this game more and more. At first, it seems quite slow and cumbersome. The graphics aren't great and moving pixelated squares around may not seem exciting. However, once you play the 5th tutorial battle you are right in the middle of a full-on battle and trying desperately to counter the AI. The difficulty level is quite high and single player is a challenge. Your army gets stretched as you go across the map and you have to make quick decisions on where to reinforce, and how many units to move where. On a tactical level this game is very good.
Battles move along quickly with fast fighting, and it is very easy to load up a game in your campaign and play a game or two after work. There is not much strategic planning as there is no base building, no allocating resources over wide areas, and no planning on a grand map. All the strategic decisions are made as you play your battles with units carrying over into your next battle, and new units being made available before each battle.
It is quite a simple design but the battle mechanics are very good, and with even the early battles being a challenge it really keeps you engaged. The campaign DLCs add a lot of content as well. Recommended for wargamers, and especially so in the frequent Steam sales. 8.5/10

If you haven't tried playing this game after the 0.3 update, then you should take a look!
The frustratingly long build times and short play times have been revamped. The timers have been greatly reduced for resource collection and army healing.
I find myself easily engaging in 10 battles a play session (45 minutes) now while rotating healed troops in and out of my lineup. The troops that are wounded will be healed by the time I complete the battle so it allows for lengthy playtimes if you like.
I must say that I do not love the building proximatey buffs (ie you have a church and a tavern next to your barracks that gives you +2 attack). I like the concept, but I find it strategically forces me to arrange my towns in a certain way.
The map size has also been reduced in 0.3, but I suspect this has something to do with making it compatible with iOS and Android. I doubted tablets could handle that size of  map anyways.
All in all 0.3 takes a lot of the bad things about the game and fixes them, all the while keeping what was already good about the game.

The Sexy Brutale is the first game I have ever 100% completed with all the collectables and that is saying alot as I don't useally finish singleplayer games in the first place. At first I was put off by the title but after only seeing about the first five minutes of gameplay I knew I was going to love it.
The Sexy Brutale is an original puzzle game about stoping a string of murders that take place in a mansion. The game takes place over the course of one day with diffrent murders taking place all over the mansion. As you stop and save guests from these horrific muders you unlock more of the mansion allowing you to explore/save more guests. The games main feature is a time rewind mechanic that can be compared to The Legend of Zelda: Majora's mask. There two types of collectables to find one thats kind of scattered about and one that useally takes a bit more thinking to find.
The Sexy Brutale's art and music are absolutely terrific! I've had some graffical glitches when moving from room to room sometimes but it quickly fixes and it didn't ruin the expearience at all for me. THE MUSIC ROCKS! It's kind of hard to explain but I enjoyed it and there is even a couple of times when the music working in tandum with the story and scenery gave me chills.
The story is probably one of the weakest but also one of the strongest parts of The Sexy Brutale. The locations and guests of the mansion are very original and the way they set the lore up really the guests and locations together. Now the over arching story of The Sexy Brutale is beautiful but they leave most of the story devlopments till the end of the game wich gave me a feeling of an abrupt ending but it was a powerful ending and I think I shall always remember it unlike some generic ending. After you finish you can go back and collect all the collectables wich I enjoyed and there is a bit more story after you get all of one of the collectables.
In conclusion I truely love this game. The music and art are original and in conjunction with the story can give you
chills. The story is not overall well paced but that lets it pack a punch at the end that will personally stick with me as a gamer. The puzzles can be simple or tough depending on if you miss things or just how good you are at logical thinking.
If you really want this game you should try it and get it. If your not sure I would watch about the first five minutes and then get it on sale.
I finished the game in about 9.5 hours after geting all the collectables and 100% completing the game but for 9.5 hours I feel that I got what I payed and about double worth in good memories and experances.
I rate The Sexy Brutale a 9.5/10

NOTE: This is a sale game, for sure. For reasons I'll go into below, I really can't justify the full £15 price tag, but it is absolutely worth playing and supporting otherwise.
The Sexy Brutale is a cunning murder mystery wrapped in cabaret drapings, set in an elegant casino mansion that positively oozes with style and decedance. You play a silent priest, Lafcadio Boone, who sees his friends and fellow guests murdered in macabre and beautiful fashion, and must then make use of Majora's Mask style time looping to prevent these grizzly crimes.
Myself, and many others I'm sure, were drawn to The Sexy Brutale by its aesthetic. Like any house of vice and splendor should be, The Sexy Brutale boasts a gorgeous art style filled with warped paintings, haunting statues, and a colourful menagerie of fun characters. The graphical fidelity is pretty tame, which isn't an issue since the excellent art style carries the visual factor excellently on its own. The music is similarily fantastic, with some great jazzy swing tunes throughout the mansion, and some tracks even boast alluring and weirdly haunting vocals to boot. It's a shame then that the rest of the game's sound design is so lacking. Environmental sounds don't really have the satisfying effect the rest of the game's atmosphere deserves, and footsteps (as well as a few other noises) are obnxiously loud. Cranking the music volume up to full helps alleviate this, but it doesn't change the fact that so many of these wonderfully orchestrated death traps are punctuated with what seem to be bog standard stock sound effects from shoddy radio dramas.
This, unfortunately isn't the only area where the game falls flat. I went in expecting devious puzzles and machinations to match the game's glorious set dressing, but was sorely dissapointed by what I ended up with. To put it bluntly, the game is painfully easy. Each of the guests is killed in a shocking and gruesome manner, ways that leave you expecting a Rube Goldberg machine level of complexity behind what leads to the deed itself. Instead, it seems the staff of The Sexy Brutale couldn't manage anything beyond moving an object to a different room, or flicking a switch; seriously, I solved a lot of these puzzles by complete accident. You shadow guests until the moment of their demise, then restart the day and throw an obvious spanner in the works, and its never a satisfying solution. The first puzzle after the tutorial is a prime example.
Puzzles lack any twist or change in mechanics to dupe you, or make you think twice about what you're doing. You do unlock more 'Mask Powers' by saving the guests, but they feel criminally underused and many aren't particularily inventive (
).The gameplay as a whole is just underwhelming.
It isn't just the puzzles either, getting around the mansion itself is nothing more than a chore. The layout is confusing, and filled with seemingly random contrivances that stop you from easily navigating the place; on several occasions I had to spend a frustrating amount of time backtracking and following long, linear paths to get back to an area, constantly being met with roadblocks. You're left feeling frustrated and bored, rather than the feeling of accomplishment you'd get by finding shortcuts with the mask powers you unlock along the way. Add to this the fact that the game has a tendancy to glitch out and freeze for a few seconds whenever you enter a door (which is A LOT) and the whole experience is soured. The game has so many opportunities to give the player better ways to navigate, but all these tricks are missed. I wouldn't be surprised if this was to pad out the playtime, which was only around 6 hours for me. Short playtimes aren't a bad thing, but the content has to make up for it, which it simply doesn't here. There are a bunch of collectables to find which do unlock a few more secrects and background lore, but for me, the gameplay wasn't attractive enough to merit searching for them instead of just googling the info. Don't expect a fun treasure hunt to enhance the gameplay either; these collectables are mostly just found in the environment, which basically equates to examining everything you can as you go.
It's tragic that the gamplay is such a letdown, because as I've said, the presentation is terrific; what makes it worse is that the story buried beneath it all is equally wonderful. The Sexy Brutale keeps you hooked through the turgid gameplay with its mystery and allure. Who's behind this devious plot? Who is the mysterious blood-soaked woman who urges you to proceed? What is the source of the supernatural and magical elements at play in this glamorous casino mansion? Unlike the puzzles, all of these questions have satisfying conclusions, and the final stages of the game's plot are genuinely thrilling, and even emotional. Sadly this doesn'y permeate through the rest of the game. Though wonderfully designed, the guests and staff of The Sexy Brutale are rather flat and unmemorable, with most of their actual character seeming to be locked in a game's lore 'brochure'. You do get some fun conversations between the guests, but it's too little too late. By the time you've moved on to the next guest in need of saving, the previous ones are already forgotton. You can still hear their scheduled deaths from anywhere in the mansion as you progress, but you'd be hard-pressed to actually care, which is a frightful shame and another of the game's missed opportunities. Again, this is doubly tragic because of how well the game wraps up, and it pains me to think how much more emotional it could have been if the guests were given more time to flourish. As great as the final act is, it also comes a bit out of nowhere. The game was over before I knew it, and it feels like there should have been more hints seeded throughout the game to really let the player explore the mystery for themselves. It's still a great story with some good thematics, but that story seems to be absent for most of the game.
To summarise, The Sexy Brutal is a game that desperately needed another good few months, if not a year of extra development. The game constantly teases you each time you restart the clock, 'Saturday', but Sunday never comes. It makes me wonder if the game was cut short in production? A few more days to explore would have allowed players to become much more attached to and familiar with the characters and mansion, allowed for more difficult puzzles to present themselves as the game progressed, and would have given ample opportunity for some more clues to the final act to be hidden around the mansion. Instead, this feels like the proof of concept for a larger, more satisfying work. And if that game is ever released, you can sign me right up, and thats why I still feel happy to recommend the game, but only at a sale price. It's a game full of charm, flair, and intruige, all dolled up with sultry penache, but one that leaves a lot to be desired when it comes to substance. Quite fittingly for its decadent setting, it's very much the gaming equivilent to a one night stand. You'll enjoy youself and might even revisit it one day, but it's not one you'll be falling for; that said, I'll be spending a while pondering what might have been. If only...
P.S. If you finish the game, I can't recommend Steam user Skirlasvoud's breakdown and analysis of the plot enough, fantastic stuff.
Don't read until you've finished though, because there are of course HEAVY spoilers, and the plot itself is certainly worth experiencing.

The Sexy Brutale got quite a lot of praise when it got released, so I had a lot of expectations of it. Which was, perhaps, a bit of a disservice to my experience with the game. The premise is very intriguing - you are locked in the events of one day, happening in a bizarre casino, where all guests are getting murdered one by one by the staff, until the day repeats again from the start with, seemingly, only you being able to change anything. As such, main gameplay usually consists of you seeing someone get murdered, trying to untangle what led to that and then preventing said murder. At least, that's the intent.
The reality is, sadly, a bit simpler than that. The "challenge" of the game is set up mechanically by basically saying that you can only restart day from the beginning, you can only restart at one of several clocks you have to activate and synchronize with, you cannot be in the same room with any other character (their mask will try to kill you) and you cannot keep any items but 3 special ones when you reset, but you keep all the knowledge (codes, secrets, map markers, people positions at specific point in time, etc). Which sets it up as a Hitman meets Groundhog Day type of deal, except, you always deal with the complex situation of the game that all guests are getting murdered one after the other quickly one step at a time, and most of all solutions are one or two step only. To the point, where I solved more than a half of all murders first try without ever seeing how they will unfold.
It's not bad, that the game is intuitive, of course, in fact, most people, including myself, will enjoy that. But it also then has moments where you have no clue what game even expects of you, and it also, in the end, feels like a great concept with some great ideas, but ultimately done "Good", instead of "Great". Mind you, I loved playing it, and I definitely recommend anyone, especially with any liking to the mystery/detective stories plots, to give it a go. But I feel that such a rare take on an adventure game deserves an even better project. So hey, maybe The Sexy Brutale will be a much needed inspiration for someone.

So, it's occurred to me that I've had this game for a long time (and played it for more hours than it even shows here) and yet I've never done a review of it as I usually do for favorite games.  'Bout bloody time I did.
So, Dungeons of Dredmor... where to begin?  It's hard to really talk about all of the aspects of the game because there are SO MANY of them.  This is likely to be one of the first things you notice about Dredmor:  The sheer ridiculous amount of content, particularly once you have the expansions installed (and I highly recommend all three).  Character creation for example... even just the base game has 35 "skills" to pick from, with the number being just under 50 with the expansions installed.  And these skills are really skill SETS.  You choose 7 of them when you create your character (any combination is fine), and once you're in the game, each of these will start at their base skill.  When you level-up, in addition to getting a boost to your prime stats (more on that later) you also go into the big skill list, and you choose one of the seven to rank up.  Each rank in each set offers you something new... some fun new active ability, some wonky passive, some stats... in my experience, there really arent any "duds" among the skillsets here, and levelling up is always very satisfying.
And the skills are VARIED.  There's some crazy stuff here.  Some of them are fairly basic... for example, sword skills, or crafting.  But then you get to Dredmor's general comedic weirdness.  For example, one of my favorites is the Bankster set.  Right from the start, this one gives you an ability called "High Interest Loan".  Use it, and a big pile of money drops at your feet.  Sounds good, right?  Well, it has a fair chance of then also hitting you with a "Bankster debuff", of which there are about 7 types.  ALL of them drain money from you in some fashion, with one of them lasting indefinitely until you either run out or the effect is removed.  Now it doesnt seem so good, yeah?  Well, that's where the rank 2 ability, "Dump Toxic Assets", comes in.  You can take any Bankster debuffs you have at the moment, turn them into poison-based damage, and fling them at your enemy.  As with any skills in the game, these have cooldowns, so using this set PROPERLY (as most of the abilities in the set can debuff you) requires that you time your skill usage correctly, and that you understand what they do.   Skills and spells in the game are like that:  Some of them get complicated in an interesting way, and they often tend to be fairly creative in how they behave.  I mean, really, when was the last time a game let you kill a giant angry carrot by having a bad credit score at it?   Things get even more interesting when these skill sets combine, and with so many, there's TONS of ways to synergize.
Items are pretty similar:  Very creative, very diverse, very useful.  And this game LOVES it's items.  You'll get a ton of them.  WAY too many.  You have a large inventory, but you'll run out of space fast.  From things like food/drink (heal HP/MP) to potions or mushrooms to crafting equipment or much crazier stuff, the game has about a kersquillion items.  The best part is, most of them are actually USEFUL to you.
And that's good, because the game REALLY expects you to be using them.  While the combat, at it's core, may be simple (walk towards a monster to strike them, and of course you have your spells and such) the game likes to throw alot of monsters at you.  Sometimes a HUGE amount, in what are known as "Monster Zoos"... big rooms where every single freaking tile has a monster on it.  You could get anywhere from 50 to 150 monsters in one zoo; zoos are effectively the "boss fights" of the game (complete with unique music) and there's one on each floor (but you dont know where!) except the first.  Beyond that, sometimes you get elite monsters, the occaisional monster from a couple floors up, and of course monsters have various stats and abilities, some getting rather unpleasant indeed.
Which relates to one issue that some players may run into is that, yes, while the game may be accessible in some ways, it can get pretty darn tough.  I've seen plenty of players hit their first zoo and just get utterly splattered (and then try it a few more times, getting splattered even worse); traditional roguelikes dont exactly teach you to deal with 120 enemies (many of them with ranged spells or goofy abilities) all at the same time!  Yet the game expects you to do this on EVERY floor.  This is where all of those items and skills come in though... beating really tough encounters in this game, zoos or otherwise, is almost like solving a puzzle, carefully figuring out how to use all the stuff available to you to defeat it; you cant just beat everything over the head and do nothing else.  The good thing is that the game pretty much ALWAYS gives you the tools (there are a sqillion items lying around for a reason...) you just need to figure out how they can be used to get past a given situation.  It can get complicated.  Not to mention the way your stats work.  You have 6 primary stats, and 19 secondary ones.  Primary stats can affect secondary ones, but more than that, this means that there's LOTS of possible stats that can appear on equipment (or on buffs/debuffs).  Building your character well means understanding what all of these do.  In addition, there's ALSO like 16 damage types.  For players such as myself that love min-maxing and dealing with stats in these games, well, this game does it VERY well.  But for others this may be a major turnoff.
However, this IS a roguelike... one way or another, there are so very, very many ways to die, yet one issue is that this is a LONG game.  Each floor is huuuuuuuuuuuge, and in the base game, there are 10 of them (with expansions, there are 15, as well as special side areas).  And there's about a gazillion things to do.  A full run-through of the game takes quite a long time.  This isnt exactly new for this genre, but it's very worth mentioning.   You have the ability to save & quit at absolutely any time though.  But it can be very frustrating to do something like get aaaaaaallllllll the way to Lord Dredmor (who is NOT a pushover) and then die to him.  All that time it took to get there... lost in one moment of SPLAT.   The game will never kill you in ways that are genuinely unfair, but that of course never stops frustration in a case like that.   Accessible though the game may be, it really is best suited to roguelike fans that are more than used to things like that happening.
If you can get past that bit though.... this is an absolutely fantastic game.  I've played so many roguelikes, but this one is by far my favorite. It has it's small issues... but there's so very much going for it that it's way more than worth those minor quibbles.  Also it's got a really good sense of humor.
Highly recommended.

Most of the things I wanted to say have already been said in the review section, but after two playthroughs (one for the story and challenge, one for assorted achievements) I feel like giving my two cents nonetheless.
In the very likely case you don't want to read the wall of text below, my overall opinion is that while this game doesn't suck, it's also very much “meh”.
If you want to play a Thief game, go play the old ones! I recommend the second :)
If you want a modern, triple A spiritual successor to the Thief series that also allows for some really fun action gameplay, go play Dishonored.
Thief 2014 is not wasted money, but definitely money that could have been spent better.
Gameplay.
The stealth gameplay is there and it's not bad. Sure, now you can see the alert status of enemies, but on the other hand I feel like their AI has been slightly improved: for example, they react to doors being opened\closed.
The parkour stuff is really fun in theory, but you're limited to the places that the game decides for you (and conveniently color-codes for you). As a lot of other people pointed out, Thief I and II did this in a much more fun and creative way with the old rope arrows, fifteen years ago.
There's a lot of potential for action gameplay and lots of upgrades, if you're into that; although it's kinda dull.
Focus mode is basically Batman detective mode and conveniently highlights all the important things for you. It feels like cheating and it's kinda sad it was put in to begin with, but it can be safely ignored.
There are also several action sequences and even QTEs. You can close your eyes when they come up, I guess.
Level design.
You could easily get lost in the old Thief games. The levels were huge and in order to figure out where your objective(s) was you could only rely on a minimalistic map, plus whatever hints you could find. In this game, on the other hand, you have an objective marker and a real-time minimap. The streamlining is also pretty noticeable: there's always a direction that's the correct one and in order to progress you have to keep moving in that direction; often times the game is even so kind as to close off parts of the level once you've reached a certain point.
Since I'm on the topic of level design, this might be a good moment to mention how dark this game is. Not dark as in “it's night”, dark as in “there is no concept of brightness in this universe”: most things are black, grey or brown, any other color is actually a bleak shade of whatever that color is supposed to be. This has the double effect of making every level look the same and being pretty tiring on the eyes (in my experience, at least).
Enemies.
There are quite literally two enemies in this game. The standard human guard, and the freaks. The freaks are... the freaks. They all look the same and only appear a bunch of times, but at least they're pretty creepy and sneaking around them is slightly different. On the other hand, officers of the City Watch, Graven mob and random thugs are visually undistinguishable from each other unless you're actually in their face, and their “personalities” are the same: they all repeat the same lines constantly, relentlessly, until you know them by heart.
In a game like Thief you need a decently varied array of enemies, both for gameplay purposes and to make the universe more engaging.
Open world.
Thief is an open world game. There's a (supposedly) sprawling city which you need to move through in order to reach the starting points of the game's chapters; and which you can explore to discover all its secrets. At first you're going to be awestruck by how big it is: so full of alternate routes, so full of secrets to find... but all that excitement is going to quickly disappear around the second time you're sneaking through the long path you're forced to take in order to get where you need to get, while you're trying to make sense of the map (spoiler: you'll never be able to make sense of the map). And you'll have to do this again, and again, and again.
If all of this sounds familiar, congratulations, you've played Thief III! Except the City in the previous game wasn't as confusing, if I recall correctly.
These are mostly minor nitpicks. You can safely stop reading here.
The plot.
In the old games the plot was some kind of creepy big conspiracy that Garrett stumbles upon because he's always where he isn't supposed to be; and it slowly built up level by level. Here they try really hard to make it extremely personal from the very beginning, but they do so using a character that's barely introduced and a world whose only inhabitants are idiot clones who spend their time wondering what's in the sloop.
The plot is also at the same time predictably clichè and ridiculously vague. “Oh no, the bad guy wants to use the vaguely defined plot device to do... something! Oh no, now a new bad guy wants to use the vaguely defined plot device to do something else!”.
Continuity
I can tell they decided to ignore
because they thought burricks, treebeasts, haunts , automatons etc... weren't bleak enough for this modern triple A masterpiece of bleakness. The Pagans with their hilarious broken English and their creepy wood witch vibe are gone. The holier-than-thou, priests-turned-engineers Hammerites are gone. The Builder and the Trickster are gone. So how do you deal with making a sequel\reboot to a series while at the same time not wanting to use that series' lore, but wanting to keep the main character? Simple: you set it sometime in the future and make it so Garrett isn't actually Garrett, but another guy named Garrett who looks very similar to Garrett and is also an incredibly skilled thief, also has a fence who is coincidentally named Basso... you get the idea. And this is not a complete reboot, mind you, it's officially a future version of the old Thief world. You can check
to read more about it, because you sure as hell won't get more info by playing the game.
Long story short, you can probably guess that I'm very salty about the complicated stupidity of this game's continuity and lore.

Would I recommend this game?  Yes, but just barely.  6.5/10
I was a fan of the earlier games, especially Thief 3.  And while this is definitely a thief game, its attempt at being noob-friendly and story-driven detract from an otherwise good stealth game.
PROS
-stunning graphics with crisp textures, detailed environments, and good lighting
-tons of exploration
-stats on all levels that are accessible at any point in the game
-customizable difficulty and hud elements
-"collectible" loot sets
-bonus mission achievements
-player skill and equipment improvements
-aerial takedowns
-unlike predecessors, can only jump when effective, so as not to create noise from failed jumps
-"swooping" is fun and useful
CONS
-expansive but linear missions that don't allow backtracking to find all secrets. forced replay?
-tedious but somewhat infrequent quick-time events
-inexplicably inconsistent and limited saving leaves you frequently either unable to return to a specific part of a mission or redoing long sections because of one screw-up
-unusual sound positioning causes some sounds (especially dialogue) to seem like they're closer than they are
-occasional crashing
-guard NPCs sometimes get stuck in place from loads, interrupted conversations, or disturbances
-consolitis buy/sell interface
-boss fights and action sequences that have no place in a thief game
-the amount of clutter and environmental detail makes the focus mechanic a necessity

Although I did not really like the older thief games (mainly because of the controls) I am a fan of this one.
This sentence already says much about the thief reboot. It cannot be seen as a sequel or prequel, because it is by no means like the older thief games. Those who played the older games may notice a few characters, who already appeared in older games, but after all it is a new game with little up to no connections to the outstanding older works.
So the question is, is it able to reach or even beat the older games?
Well apart from obvious points as better graphics and better controls it is simply different. New 'interactive' controls (button mashing, quick time events) got introduced, an optional minimap and a slowly discovered map replace the tactical maps at the beginning of each mission, but most important close combat with sword got removed and made the game a whole lot more demanding and less forgiving, when it comes down to stealth mistakes.
The AI is more or less good and the story is quite interesting.
The first person view was one of the best ones I ever got to enjoy and even beats many Bethesda games in terms of feeling realistic.
Summary:
For quite a good price you get a brilliant game with thief (4). It's immerse and when played with a controller it feels as interactive as possible with current controllers.
I can only recommend this often underestimated first person stealth games to all who love stealth, first person and beeing a thief hiding in shadows.

Florensia is a great little game, but it's a dated experience. It won't appeal to the majority of the Steam community because most are used to more modern MMORPGs. The new Florensia developers seem enthusiastic and poised to handle any potential server issues, though, and new content is apparently in the works.

The limited inventory space and slow walking speed can be frustrating, and the cash shop will alleviate those inconveniences, but you can get by without spending money. I recommend Florensia if you want to play a free game with some friends for a weekend or two. There are better MMORPGs out there, and Florensia is outclassed even by some of its comtempories, but if you're interested enough to be sifting through the forums and reviews, you should give it a shot.

Two Digits must be the most boring and sadistic game I have ever played. I honestly remember homework assignments that were more fun. Just imagine solving 250 identical number problems, while listening to the same elevator music on a loop! The same exact puzzle, again and again. Two hundred and fifty times. If that's not Hell, I don't know what is. Granted, you get nine different numbers each time, but the strategy to solving the puzzle is always the same. Eventually, the process becomes automatic and almost mindless as you load a problem, look for familiar patterns, select the right numbers, and start the next puzzle, all the while wondering what you are doing with your life... Depending on the numbers, you can literally do five problems in under five minutes. I can see Two Digits as a simple mobile game to kill some time (it certainly looks like one), but it just doesn't hold up on PC, because even finding the level where you left off is a chore.

3rd person MOBAs have hard time to grab the market, and this one will not be an exception.
tldr: Game-play mechanics are padded with various complications for the sake of "feel different and strategic" while in reality it is quite brain dead and bullet spongy game. No proper matchmaking, character balance is way off. Shooting and killing is not much of the fun. Game requires separate registration and supplied with separate launcher (Why god, why?). F2P wise game is fine, heroes are unlockable in sane amount of time.
=============
Game is objective based, no creep waves, no items. Your team (you play 5v5) have 3 points to control and enemy have the same. Each point periodically generate "energy" which you collect. Upon gathering 100 of energy your Guardian (huge animal sitting at your base) is awaking and attack enemy guardian. Your team is supposed to help him with this task and destroy enemy guardian's weak point. If you fail to do so - zero damage is done  otherwise it receive 1 wound. Whoever score 3 wounds first - win.
To help you with energy gathering and point protection you can summon a creature on each point and it will auto-collect energy and provide various utility (heal, vision etc). You can only summon on your points, and creatures are stationary, basically it plays role of tower in traditional MOBA terms.
Beside control points energy also gained from players kills and creature kills (10 energy per kill).
Map is pretty compact which result in extremely chaotic running in between points shouting left and right. Game visuals don't help much with structuring the game, quite often it is hard to figure out are you winning or losing. Special effect galore will make sure  your eyes start bleeding and begging for mercy.
Characters are nicely animated and colorful, Currently there is 19 in total with 5 of them in f2p rotation. Classical holy-trinity role split: Tank, DPS and Support.  Each hero has 4 abilities + ultimate and all can sprint. Movement is WASD controlled.
Kills and captures give you exp, you level up and can upgrade your skills. Each skill can be upgraded twice, and each time you need to choose one upgrade option from two available similar to HOTS.
Max level is 10 and you will hit it in no time, no idea about who designed exp curve but you maxed out in the middle of the match and after each team fight you get like 1-2 levels. Also Ultimate doesn't feel strong but it could be for better.
Balance is one of the worst I've ever dealt with. Most of the heroes move fast and have plenty of mobility, means all hit scan heroes have immense advantage over projectile one. But not only this, often projectiles usually have slow travel speed and long shooting animation. Needless to say they do not compensated with bonus damage. For some reason they added dodge mechanic into the game which allow you to  move like 0.5 meter to the side, again utterly useless in 99% of situations. Overall combat dosn't strike me as something polished and thought trough.
The game gives you strong feeling that it was created like patchwork blanket, random ideas were thrown into without much cohesion. We have super fast gameplay? Lets give level-up choices to the player which he has no time to read about. Also we can copy-paste Bastion from Overwatch but not an quick skill summary. Summoned Creature provides vision? But only one invisible hero who can't do much anyway. Complex control point mechanic and push condition? 99% of it is either unused or can be thrown out of the game with none of gameplay affected (well it can shorten tutorial by a lot tho).
If teams are equal games turns into  stalemate and there is no mechanic to break it. We played 30 mins of boring attack/defend as none of the team was able to wound guardian, Game ended only due to some players get tired of it and left.
There is no Roshan or strong ultimates or scaling damage with time to bring game to conclusion. To win you need a successful push into enemy base. If your team is not organized well - your can do push forever.

I'm gonna get the negatives I had with this game out of the way first, because there's only a few things I had issues with.
1. My framerate randomly dropped for no reason I could think of, it would only drop for 10 seconds or so, but a drop is a drop and caused issues with trying to navigate the rooms.
2. Sometimes I would *repeatedly* click on doors to move through to another room and he just wouldn't go and stood there for 15 seconds before moving through, as sometimes it froze (before he moved through) and sometimes he just stood there and time ticked by, frustrating.
3. I *frequently* had rooms that just didn't load, I would go through a door to find a black room with some candles lit, couldn't see anything else and had to wait up to 30 seconds for a room to load, which ate up my time.
(Yes my PC can handle this game, so I am not sure why these things were happening)
Other than that, I really did enjoy this game! The ending was not one I expected, and seeing as I usually can somewhat predict endings, being surprised by an ending is something I really enjoy! The graphics, and overall idea of the game, are great, and although the above issues annoyed me quite often, they didn't completely ruin my enjoyment of the game! I loved reading little pieces of info about random environment features, and running around trying to work out what to do to progress and save guests.
I heartily recommend this game, it isn't really a long one, but for the price, I really would suggest you give it a go! Even if you're not fond of puzzles, I am positive you can probably follow some guides and still really enjoy what's going on, as the story is a good one!

I can't really describe much about the sexy brutale without giving away it's best parts. I can however, say that the sexy brutale is an adventure game that is a mix between Ghost Trick and Majora's Mask. Game takes place during a single day and much like Majora's Mask, there's a time limit. However, you can get around this time limit by using an item that repeats the day. There are several people you need to save from getting visciously murdered by solving different puzzles. The answers to these puzzles are found by following each victim through their routine. Of course, I put it this way then the game doesn't sound that enticing. What I can say is that The Sexy Brutale has a beautiful art style that never fails to catch your attention and imagination, the soundtrack is fantastic with this jazzy vibe that makes the game's surreal world to feel more vibrant and alive. Each character has his or her own routine where you learn about their past, present and grimm future and it never fails to be entertaining. What's more important for this game is the overall plot, which I won't spoil but basically holds your interest through the entire thing and pays off with one of the best endings in videogame history.

It's a gorgeous Thursday morning. You're up earlier than usual, with a spring in your step and a song in your heart. You're daily commute lies along the District Light Rail, an overground train through the outskirts of London. Perhaps not the most spectacular view, but certainly a step up from the 'scenic' grey of the underground. You've arrived a few minutes before the train is scheduled, giving you time to glance around the station.
You see a few people standing, arms crossed, seemingly scowling at the thin air in front of them. You can't empathize their gloomy mood; it's too nice a day. Far in the distance you see the train stop at the station before yours, but with only a few people at this station, you make no rush to stake out a spot.
You realize your error much too late as the coming train pulls into the station. From end-to-end the rail is packed with people, and none are getting off. They've staked their spot to take them all the way back into London, with you stuck in the station until the next one comes. Of course, it is only the one train, right? Surely this one is only packed because of the rush hour commute. Your mood sours only a little as the train takes off without you, but your spirits are lifted by the rays of sunshine washing over the land....
Several hours later, as you stand white knuckled and dripping with sweat, you pray this train will finally have some space. Your boss has called numerous times to angrily inquire as to your tardiness, and you fear your job may well be on the line if you don't show up soon. The station is now full of grumbling, groaning, greasy, grumpy Gus', and you bitterly realize you're just another one of the bunch. As you push back all the people clambering to the front of the line, you hear a horrified wail from the near end of the station. Your heart sinks rapidly as the approaching train audibly rolls into the stop, carrying with it what must be the entire London populus.
The station, now eerily quiet collectively holds it's breath, hoping, praying that there is space for them on that train. The doors open, and to your surprise, the entire station politely lets off the passengers. Well, just the one passenger, actually. A lone man, who upon exiting the train notices the unsettling silence that has enveloped the station. He clears his way slowly through the throng of people who watch as he goes by, eventually reaching the exit and leaving them behind.
A shout from the back of "IT'S MINE!" breaks the deadlock, and suddenly you and everyone else are clambering to make your way onto the train. The passengers already aboard are terrified, the train itself begins to violently rock back and forth from the wave of people crashing into it. Alarms blare in the din of it all, set off by the dislodging of the train from the tracks, but no one seems to care. It's not about getting to work, or making it to the restaurant for your date, or getting home before the kids set fire to everything. It's about getting on the train.
A loud bang echoes from nearby, and screams soon follow suit. An elderly man, clearly fed up with public transit system set up, begins to open fire with a handgun. You seem him blindly firing into the crowd, hitting men, women, children, all like fish in a barrel. Time seems to slow down as you watch the carnage unfold, people dying right in front of you, family trees uprooted with a single bullet. You try to turn and run, but you can't peel yourself away from the carnage and terror that has taken place. As you take one last look at the shooter, you find yourself staring straight into his eyes as he pulls the trigger. And as the blood drips down your forhead, you notice just how pretty the sun looks when tinted with red on this goreous Thursday morning.
So for all of you hotshot's who think this is just another game, remember: This is what happens when you let your stations get overcrowded. 10/10

Juniper's Knot is a small kinetic visual novel developed by the same people who made Dysfunctional Systems, another VN I quite enjoyed. Given that this was free and also rather short, I decided to see what their first venture into VNs were like. Much like Dysfunctional Systems, the story is written with a rather intricate hand, and the art is superb and complements the tone of the VN. Despite being short, they managed to pack a bunch into this story without compromising execution and pacing, something that I really appreciate.
The story is centered on a female fiend and a human boy who happens to chance upon her after he got lost. They are never given a name (I will refer to them as Fiend and Boy, respectively) but their personalities are developed quickly and concisely. Immediately, based off of their dialogue style, you can tell when Fiend is speaking or when Boy is speaking, and you can also tell their ages as well as their personalities without much effort. There is even some world building, which is incorporated into the VN as the characters telling stories about their lives. This all leads into a tightly written story that, while linear, gives a strong sense of depth despite the shortened length of the VN.
Art and music help to enhance scenes further, especially with art that both accentuates aspects of a character as well as subtly indicates a trait. Music is never boring to listen to, and its quite pleasing to loop. Dischan has a good grasp on sound design as well, as music will fade away into other sound effects to help immerse the reader into the world, such as the crackling of fire. I also want to emphasize the UI in the game, as Dischan has some of the more stylish and interesting menu screens that I've seen in VNs.
If you want to see what Dischan is capable of producing and don't want to place money down for Dysfunctional Systems, I recommend playing this first. Not only does it offer one of the better stories from the free VNs on Steam, but it does it in a package that is highly polished with great art and music.

Dungeons of Dredmor is overrated. I'm not sure why it is, but one thing's for sure: It's sure offset as hell.
The gameplay itself is average compared to other dungeon crawlers, except for the fact that the game is almost impossible to play without taking the tutorial first. RPGs are usually easy to learn to play on your own, but DoD just flat-out crosses the line. To give you an idea, it takes you about 8 seconds to simply place a goddamn item in your inventory. There's an option for a quick place, but it barely makes a difference.
The camera is offset to the point where it's risky to just move down. The GUI is in the way of almost the entire bottom screen, and there are no options to move it somewhere else or even just lower the size.
Don't even get me started on the graphics. The graphics are as if Doom and Oregon Trail II had a baby and then proceeded to puke all over it. Maybe that's an exaggeration, but the screen is blurry, it's hard to make out what the monsters even are, and the main character. Ugh! Why did the developers make his eyebrows the size of the Titanic?
Overall, I rate Dungeons of Dredmor a 4/10.

Nope, you get to fear walking down in this game because you ui blocks anything below you so you will never know what's there until you walk headlong into it.
- game has little annoyances that slow it down into a slog, like constantly having to pick things up manually (yes there is an auto option for pickups but its lackluster) or having to watch your screen like a hawk for traps because even though your character  can see them, he will happily walk into them like an idiot if you are not paying close attention.

- THERE is a RIGHT way to build your character, and if you built them any other way you cannot win! At least not fairly.
The final boss has only one real weakness so I hope you chose one of the skills at the start that let you capitalize on that, else your dead. Restart and try again from the beginning chump.

You click on the numbers to change them green or orange, and your green numbers are added in one column, and your orange numbers are added up in another column. I could tell the difficulty was ramping up, but that's beside the point. Even if I could go up through number 250, I wouldn't want to. It just gets old. I could do Sudoku all day (I actually have on jury duty once, waiting to see if I was called to be a juror), and there's a certain charm to doing long algebraic equations and functions and all that stuff, as I recall from school/college, but here, you are just adding numbers to make them equal. The basic premise behind two digits is solving the equation
[Sum of (Ai*Ci) from 1 to n] = 0, Ai e {-1,0,1}, Ci e [1,99]
for non-trivial solution (e.g. Ai = 0 for every i).
As can be shown, this problem is non-polynomial, as each additional number triples the search space.
Therefore, a general solution is likely nonexistant.
This is not a math game, this is a guessing game.

The premise behind The Sexy Brutale is that your character is locked in a mansion during a masquerade party where all the guests are being murdered.  He's stuck in a time loop and has to keep repeating the day of the party until he manages to save all of the guests. It's an interesting premise, and the game does many things very well. It's a gorgeous looking game with a very fitting and expressive art style that really sets the tone for an extravagant aristocrat's casino/mansion. It's animated well and the sound compliments the setting perfectly. So why the negative review?
Frankly, the game is trivially easy. Although the mansion is nominally a large, open world to explore, in practice the game is divided into a number of discrete "levels" in the sense that you must save the guests one at a time in a particular order before the game will let you enter a new part of the mansion. Once you do move on to a new area you'll very rarely have any reason to return to an old one. Thus, you only ever have one puzzle at a time to solve, and the pieces you need to solve that puzzle will always be nearby. Compounding this problem is the fact that every interactable object in the game is painted with a bright fluorescent circle, so there's no possible way you can overlook an important item. It's literally possible (and happened to me) that you can accidentally prevent several murders just by aimlessly wandering around and clicking when you see a glowing circle, without even understanding what it is you're doing or why that particular circle stops the murder.
Perhaps my disappointment has more to do with my own expectations than anything the developers did wrong -- I was expecting something along the lines of the classic Maniac Mansion. At any rate, it seems the devs don't trust players to be able to figure anything out on their own and felt they had to spoon-feed the solutions to the puzzles.
Bottom Line: The Sexy Brutale is worth picking up on sale if you're interested in a very well-presented kind of interactive cartoon. Just don't expect a meaty puzzle-solving/exploration game.

Entropy Rising is a neat first person puzzle game.  The player is to manipulate water, acid, lava and stone orbs and use them to clear obstacles or activate scales, acidity meters and temperature meters which in turn open doors and passageways to progress in the game.  This is achieved by using a gun that can push-pull nearby orbs, and can also  create a gravity bubble that you can move at will.  If you mess things up, or get killed, you can rewind time on the fly and take another approach.
While visuals are not at all breathtaking and there's absolutely no back story to the game, this is not an impediment to enjoy the cleverly designed levels puzzles. There are 33 levels and some user-created ones you can download from the workshop, as well as create and publish your own, if you dare.
Steam achievements are included. Most are easy, some require exploration because they involve secret areas or activating certain gameplay  elements. Others are plain difficult since they require speedrunning the levels while collecting items and clear the level without dying nor using the rewind feature, all at the same time.
If you are into first person puzzle games, this is worth playing.
Fun and challenging puzzle game, worth the price.

I played the entire game and after considering it a while, I don't think that I can recommend it.  It has a bit of a Portal feel, but without any story and none of the humor.  What's important here though are the puzzles and the mechanics.  The game looks pretty good but I found very few of the puzzles to be interesting from a problem solving perspective.  I think I spent about 10 times as much time simply trying to nudge things into exactly the right spot than I did trying to figure out how the puzzles needed to be solved.
Even that maybe wouldn't have bothered me too much if the mechanics weren't so terribly annoying.  So you have the ability to move an acid ball from lets say 1 meter away.  Guess exactly what distance you start taking damage from an acid ball at?  You guessed it, exactly the same distance.  So every single time you need to move one of these things you have to rush in, push it as fast as you can, and get out again.  It's so annoying and serves no purpose that I can see.   And it's not like this is something you have to do once or twice.  It's more like this is how you spend most your time in the game.
The one pretty cool mechanic of being able to go back in time whenever and as much as you want doesn't really serve any purpose except to fix mistakes.  It's not as if you can cleverly do something, go back in time, and end up changing where things were.  Everything goes back in time exactly how it was.  So, if you were super careful you would never need this ability.  Now with the crazy annoying mechanics it is super important, but then if you use it you won't get the achievment  for not using it at the end of each level.  It's kind of a slap in the face when you have to be so careful at every step to avoid the many game mechanic based pitfalls.
I will say that I was happy with the final level and the ending.  Still, I feel like I got much more frustration from this game than I got enjoyment.

Mini Metro is a realy simple but fun game to play.
In the game you have certain 'points' on the map, that can look like a circle, square, triangle etc. Those 'points' represent metro stations. From time to time smaller icons like a circle, square, triangle etc. appear next to these metro stations.
Those smaller icons respresent a traveler who would like to go to another metro station. For example, a smaller triangle on a circle metro station, would like to take the metro to a traingle metro station. If the traveler steps in, it will not go out until it reaches a triangle station. But it will step over on a different line if it can reach such a station faster.
When you start you will just have a few metro stations, and a few lines. Every week you get more lines / locomotives / carrages or tunnels. Somethimes you will get a choice if you want for example a new line, or a new locomotive.
You also have different maps to play, that are named like cities, like London, Paris, Hong Kong.
Also in the game you only use the left mouse buttons, that is everything.
I would say a great game if you would like a simple strategy game, but you also start a new map very soon. Becasue you get 'game over' eventualy.

I have to say, this game has no relation to a series of games total war. On a wave of the success of games-farms Sega decided to grab a piece of the pie, but that Sega did not the best way. This is yet another clone of clash of clans with a slightly modified concept. The main drawback of the game is that after a certain time, you will encounter the impossibility of further development without investing real money, with these funds, which you can buy a whole series of games total war.

'Two Sums' would have been slightly more accurate a title.  It looks simple take a great of numbers and find a way to make two identical sums.  That's the whole experience summed up and not much changes along the way.  Complementing the 250 included puzzles is the ability to generate random ones but even after solving just twenty there wasn't much desire to continue.
Controls would have benefited from putting the grouping colors on the left/right mouse buttons and a faster reset time.  These feel like carry overs from a mobile port that only had touch controls.

Overall, I'd have to say that I don't recommend this game.  It doesn't feel so much like a puzzle as it does math homework.  One of the worst features was the poorly organized difficulty and sense of progression.  Honestly, at the earlier part of the game, I felt like the solutions were harder to discover, though that probably had something to do with me working out the best manner of solving the puzzles in this game.  One of the best things a puzzle game of this nature can do is work up to harder puzzles so the player gets time to adjust to the sort of mindset they need to play the game and then become challenged the further they get.  However, several late-game puzzles were incredibly simplistic, especially the last set of puzzles with the multiples of 3.  It was not uncommon for me to merely add 2 or 3 numbers to match a number that was already listed in the puzzle, such as 5, 37, and 41 for 83.
The strategy I found myself using in the game was not to add up the numbers to see what totals I'd get and try to find other numbers that were close to or equal to that sum.  Instead I looked at the numbers and would look for patterns in how much difference there was between the numbers.  For instance, say the 9 numbers listed were: 1, 7, 15, 20, 25, 28, 40, 49, and 71.  With a 1 and 7 on there, if I find two numbers that have either a gap of 1, 7, or 8 that will solve the puzzle.  15, 20, and 25 all have gaps of 5, but I can't make a 5 anywhere else.  What works though is taking 20 and 28 for 48, which is only 1 off from 49.  Adding up simpler numbers like that and looking for smaller increments and differences is much easier than trying to add up numbers that get into the hundreds.
Much easier to realize that 73 and 75 are two apart, 41 and 42 are one apart, and 67 and 70 are three apart so you take the two smaller numbers from the one and two apart category and add it to the bigger number from the three apart to match the other set.  73+41+70=184 & 75+42+67=184  Not sure if that translates well typed out, but that style of thinking makes the puzzles much easier; at least it did for me.
I played the game through for the achievements, but I've done my math homework.  I want to actually play some games now.

Entropy Rising is a first person puzzle game. Playing through it you can tell it is heavily influenced by Portal and Braid, and possibly other puzzle games. I really enjoyed the puzzle aspect of this game, however I give it a cautious recommendation as it suffers from some presentation and pacing issues.
This is a first person puzzle game with several very interesting mechanics, which the game does tie in nicely together. If gravity fields and time rewinding sound fun to you, this game has them, and more! One of the main items in the games are orbs with different properties - water orbs extinguishes fire/ lava, dirt balls can be used on scales that generate power to open doors, etc. One unique thing I enjoyed was the momentum - you can grab orbs (they're heavy feeling in the game!) and roll them like bowling balls! Which means practice makes perfect and sometimes you can miss completely. Really reminded me of bowling but with huge, heavier orbs. The time travel mechanic kind of serves as a rewind/ save myself from death mechanic, and actually works as intended in this game - I haven't noticed any discrepancies so far.
There's also replay value in the form of: a 3-star rating system for time and the times you use rewind, as well as some secrets to find will be interesting to speedrunners and secret hunters.
Here are some reasons I didn't enjoy the game as much as I'd hoped, even with the interesting mechanics and combinations of these mechanics. The pacing was somewhat strange to me, and it felt like there was no particular ordering or progression. The game does introduce mechanics one by one, but apart from the rooms/ levels getting larger, I didn't particularly feel like the puzzle difficulty was making any meaningful progression. But the fact that I have this expectation may be due to the Portal games.
Another problem I had was that for the gravity field gun, there was always a lag and it may or may not work even though I'm sure I shot the gun at a correct place theoretically. This led to me restarting some long parts of the levels from scratch, and felt like more of a chore. Also the gravity field made things so blurry sometimes. If this was improved I think I'd have a better experience.
Recommended if you are a fan of pure puzzle games and enjoy playing around in large puzzle chambers, with a variety of mechanics. However the puzzles get sluggish, making some parts of the game feel like a chore. I give this game a cautious recommendation.

There is no fun to be had in this game. Not a single bit. No satisfaction to be gained, no immersion to accumulate, nothing worth experiencing. Joyless. Dead.
It's interesting because it's a high-profile game. A lot of work has gone into it. I think it's an excellent example of what what's wrong with major title game development. This is product. It's not art, it's not designed to make a statement -- it's designed to be as bland and marketable as possible. It is completely generic. It might as well be called "Action Video Game". There isn't anything you won't have seen before many times -- it feels like took as many bits from other popular games as they could and shoved them into a machine which mushed them together and sucked all the individuality and interest out of them.
Let's cover the good things first, because there aren't many. It looks nice. The Unreal engine is very competently implemented, and the Mac port which I played has many thoughtful little features (like disabling notifications).
That is it. There is nothing else I say to compliment this game.
The original Thief: The Dark Project is one of my all time favourite games. So much fun. Sure, it had its flaws but it was bursting with life, with personality. So much thought and care had gone into it. It was completely immersive, kinda hard and a privilege to play. It's safe to say that nothing of the original has survived.
You reprise the role of Garrett: Master Thief, but you'll tire of him pretty quickly. Before, he was a likable scoundrel, a master of his craft. The sort of guy who'd sneak an apple off from the table by a guard and slink off munching it. New Garrett is insufferably banal - he'd have been much better as a silent protagonist because every time I heard him I mentally disassocaited myself. And the master thief? He's now spends his time rummaging through hovels stealing mugs and scissors from poor people. Oh good, I found a bracelet in a drain. I stole a pair of scissors from squalid flat. This goblet that the beggar sitting opposite can't even be bothered with? I'll have that. It all goes into the enormous invisible bag of loot I'm presumably lugging along with me, full of hand mirrors and picture frames. You don't even get to fence them, they turn into cash instantly. Forget eyes on the prize, Garret's going for candlesticks now.
They've tried to make him into Batman, but didn't take on board that the main appeal of playing as Batman is that YOU GET TO BE BATMAN. Garrett is not Batman, no matter how gruff he is or how many time he reminds you that he's wearing leather (he will do that a lot).
The game combines elements from other popular titles such as Dishonoured, Batman, Assassin's Creed, Tomb Raider & Mirror's Edge resulting in something not nearly as good as any of them.
At every turn this game gives the impression that the makes had an incredibly strict script they want the player to follow. You will do this thing, now you will do this. Now you will go here. Now you will jump. Now you will climb a rope. Now you will think this thing. There's no sense of free will. There's no fun. It's horrible. Bad level design, terrible writing/story, awful acting, banal main character, frustrating gameplay, 0/10 avoid like the plague.

It is MTG alright. It's free and it's fun. I want to give this game a thumbs up, because how do you not thumbs up a free game. There are some frusterating factors though.
The Cons -
As many have commented, the card selection from expansions is not complete. The AI gets the cards for some reason, so they have been programmed into the game. Then why aren't they availible to receive from a pack of that expansion? There's no explination to this and it makes no sense. Why allow us to use for example the card "corrupt" during the AI story mode, then not have it in the origins card set? (When I first started playing I was so excited to see the old school cards I grew up with that it was dissapointing to say the least, when I discovered that hardly any of the cards I wanted to build decks out of had been added to the packs). Why even have them in the game in any form then, if we can't receive the cards and use them in our decks?
Ladder Ranking in multiplayer is done poorly IMO. Virtually every game I've ever played with a ladder ranking system will "save" your top rank that you achieved during the ladder session. Even if you drop some ranks later during the season. Your not punished by any means and posted at a lower rank than you earned through the season. This game does NOT save your high rank for the season. Let's say you made it to rank 25 around the halfway point of the season. Then have a lot of crashes, mana shorts, and general bad luck and you wind up dropping to rank 12 by the end of the season. Then this game posts you Rank at 12 permanently on your profile wall. As a permanent reminder every time you log in that you were screwed out of your high score. This is so frusterating to me, it's almost a deal breaker to want ot play this game anymore. I can't log in without it showing me the♥♥♥♥♥♥poor BS rank for the season that's just not true. Dev's you didn't do this aspect well at all.
Stability issues and crash/freeze will happen. That's a fact. It doesn't matter how good your computer is.
If your oppenent crashes during a duel, (which happens a lot) then the game turns them into an AI and you have to keep fighting it out. Only the duel takes at least twice as long now, because there is no timer during AI fights. And everytime the AI casts a spell it stays in your face until you click on the card. This will happen a lot at the very start of the match as it loads. I generally concede instantly since I wanted to duel a human being. If I wanted to play the AI I would be in solo play, not multiplayer mode.
Unfortunately what's worse, is that conceding against an AI during multiplayer mode still punishes your rank score. This will frusterate you a lot if you actually want to rank up and feel like you've gotten somewhere. Then the season will end and post your score as crud, because it kept turning your opponents into AI that you didn't want to fight. And you were punished by saying "no I don't want to fight the AI. Please restart a new match against a human."
Pros -
It's Magic the Gathering!
It's Free to Play!
The tuturials on game mechanics are very well done!
Gold to purchase packs can be gained fairly quickly by playing mutliplayer. Way faster than HS!
Note for Devs -
Please focus on fixing the server stability as a priority, not adding more content.
Please think about the the ranking system end of season scores, especially since you punish us for quitting against an AI we shouldn't be fighting during multiplayer mode.
Please don't put cards into the story mode that you are not going to add to packs. Seriously.
Thanks for your time ~ Jandar
