Excellent game with a few significant (but manageable) flaws. The art style, the music, the setting, are incredible. It's loads of fun to run around stalking people through the casino day after day, watching the set-up to the murders, which are spectacularly horrifying if you actually take the time to just watch, knowing that something is about to happen. If you haven't solved the puzzle of how to save them, people WILL die, in a horrible fashion. It's quite a surreal experience.
Now, that leads me to the flaws. I strongly recommend that if you have a controller to hook up, USE IT. Not because this is an action game, but because the keyboard/mouse control setup is awkward (press SHIFT to spy through a door then press X to stop spying, wtf?!), can't be rebound, and can actively hinder your understanding of the game controls. For instance, you have control over time in this game. If you're at a clock, you can move time ahead to 4pm or 8pm. And while I had thought that you could also reset the time to 12pm, the start of the game's day, it frustrated me to no end because there was no option to do this at the clock where you can change the time to 4pm or 8pm. So I wasted an awful lot of time in the game because I would try something to stop a murder, it wouldn't work, I would know right away that it didn't work but there was still plenty of time left in the day afterward and I couldn't just tell the day to reset so I could try again right away. Turns out, the option to reset the day is an actual button you press, not an option in the in-game interactable clocks, and I never pressed that button while using keyboard and mouse because there was nothing but a visual button on the screen that didn't say anything about what it did, so I never pressed it. After a few sessions, I plugged in my controller to try that out instead and discovered this button within a few minutes because the button on the screen that had been labeled "F1" now said "LT" so my brain now needed to know what left trigger did, whereas it being F1 was just so generic that it never even registered as a thing that could do something.
Furthermore, the way you use your inventory items is really unintuitive. It took me a rather a long tiime to figure out how to set other clocks as spawn points because you need to use your pocketwatch on them to do that. The Achievement Hunters had even more problems figuring this out. It's not difficult, it's just not implemented well so it's easy to overlook. You have one active item, it's displayed on your screen- it'll be whatever you last picked up unless you switch to something else. You can rotate through your items on hand by pressing one of the two buttons displayed near the item on your screen. Using an item on something requires pressing a completely different button than interacting with the thing normally- you press X to interact with a clock but Y to use an item on it.
Also, there is at least one puzzle which can be solved via looking at information in the map, after you have acquired the item which gives you that information. You have to press SPACE in the map to open this information, and I never realized you could do this until watching Achievement Hunters play this game after I finished it. I picked up the item which gives you the information, but had no idea what it was and instead solved the puzzle via just running around for an excessive amount of time using trial-and-error of trying items in various places until finally something worked.
And once you realize that sort of thing, this game possibly becomes too easy. I never had that problem while playing through it, I found most of the puzzles to be reasonably challenging to the point where I had to check guides to see how to advance at points, but if I had had a better grasp of the controls I don't think I would have needed to do that. If you watch the Achievement Hunters videos, they actually solve puzzles far too quickly without even fully realizing what they're trying to stop. And that's no way to play this game.
So, in a nutshell: use a controller rather than bad keyboard/mouse controls; F1/LT is your reset the day button; use inventory items with a different button than normal interact and scroll through them using the two buttons displayed next to the item; and just take your time and watch what's going on to best enjoy the game's atmosphere.

Having played this game for a few hours over the past couple of weeks, I can honestly say that I'm very impressed with it! Admittedly, I probably need some more practice with the game... but despite this the game is easy to pick up and play, but harder to master! I'd describe the game as "fast, frantic, and fun"! The dev has been updating it plenty in the week since release, and I can honestly say that compared to what it was like before, it's a much better game (not that the game was bad to begin with).
There are 4 different game modes with lots of options to choose from for each mode, and each mode offers something different; Arcade is your basic "horde mode", which you can play solo or with a friend; Deathmatch is a mode in which 4 players (bot or human) blow the crap out of each other; Powershift is deathmatch, except each match gives everyone a different modification to your tank, such as lasers, high speed, and even tiny tanks! There are other modifications, but I'll leave the rest for you to discover. The last mode, Juggernaut is essentially a King of The Hill mode, where you defend the centre point from your opponents in order to become the Juggernaut, and blow up your enemies! Each game mode has multiple power-ups that appear on the field (a couple specific to a particular mode), and all of them make use of the 50 maps that the game has, all of which have different features.
I have no hesitation in recommending the game to people who are into this sort of game, or even those looking for a fun local multiplayer game. The only thing that it is missing is network play, but that's not a strike against it. There is also the fact that the game needs at least one gamepad if you want to have additional human players, but that's just something to note, rather than anything against it; this game would be perfect with you and your mate(s) sitting on the couch blasting away at each other, or at the enemy tanks in the co op mode. One addition that has come to me just now is the addition of a map editor, which would allow people to create their own maps, but maybe that would be better for a sequel instead.
Ultimately, this game is one you can have a lot of fun with, regardless of if it's yourself, or with your friends, and for the price, it offers a lot of fun and challenging gameplay for the money!

Well... what can I say? I have over 400 hours put into this game and I still love it. If that's not enough proof, look at my achievements, certainly I wouldn't be playing this game to just get the achievements to prove a point.
Instead of the usual from what is said from many other reviews, I would like to point out what I liked about the game.
1. Skill Diversity: You can pick any 7 skills out of the ones presented before you. Truthfully based on my 400+ hour experience, any build is viable but killing Dredmor himself is entirely something else. Not all skills will/may be used and even a skill at their first level may be good enough throughout the whole game.
2. Loot/item diversity: There is a lot, and I mean A LOT, of items in this game. Most for crafting and some really good equipment. If you're the kind of guy that likes to hoard up on items for use later, this is your game.
3. Simple, yet addictive: When you start the game it's probably one of the hardest things to go forward from. You're weak, you're level 1, you might not have a weapon or enough food. But whatever the case once you get the hang of it you just can't stop playing, especially when you find a new and better weapon to use or a skill that's so freaking awesome.
4. Music/sound/animation: To complement with the game it has music. It's got sounds including voices. And they even had the time to animate pretty much all the attacks in the game. This ain't no ASCII nethack ( no offense to them really). Enjoy it while you can.
5. You can mod it: You may need an expertise to help you on this but nevertheless you can mod this game and make your own skills, skill portraits, attacks, and what not. There are literally thousands of mods out there, find one you like, load it up and play it.
Now this game isn't all perfect. There have been a number of glitches, annoyances, and bugs, can be game breaking, beneficial, and unfair, included in this game and have never been fixed. Some of them include game crashes, walking through enemies, mulitple turns, steam cloud issues (i only had this happen once and found out the problem), infrequent slowdowns on animations, and game loading issues. The bad bugs don't happen as often as you think and the good bugs are game breaking so I don't want to talk about how to do them.
Overall I really highly recommend this game. Don't be put off by the graphics, or let alone the innumerable number of stats you have to read. Once you play the game you'll find it to be quite appeasing, especially the countless number of jokes and references it makes to real life and fictional media. It's one of the running gags in the game. A very prime example would be the portrait you see on the bottom of the screen so go take a minute to look at the images for this game. It pays homage to the Wolfenstein games and your character gets more bloody the lower his/her hp, just like in Wolfenstein. Are you a Star Wars fan? The character Mace Windu has a sword named after him in this game called Mace of Windu. Not a Star Wars fan huh... what about Star Trek? Weld a Lirpa and destroy your enemies with its fantastically high attack power.
There's so much reference it makes to the outside, try to spot them all. That alone should be enough to keep you intrigued about the game.
10/10 EXTREMELY HIGHLY RECOMMENDED for roguelike lovers.

Normally I like to finish a game before I review it, but since this game is super cheap during the Steam WInter Sale, I wanted to go ahead and give a brief review while it's still on sale.
Is Hunted a great game?  No.  It is fairly medoicre, however I do think it is worth the $1.24 that it is selling for right now.
It kind of feels like I am playing an over the shoulder 3rd person version of Diablo, just not as good as Diablo.  The levels are quite detailed and interesting giving an open world feel, but is actually linear except for when you stumble onto secret areas.  There aren't a ton of secret areas (so far) but the secret areas are more than just a room too, and are actually a bit more interesting than the main game.  The secret areas actually seem to give the world more life than the main game does.  There are also some minor secret areas that require either the barbarian or the archer to open and if you don't happen to be running that character it's a little wonky figuring out how you are able to open them.  Thankfully, the minor secrets don't hide anything important, just the occasional weapon rack or potions.
I don't find the banter between the two main chracters to be all that annoying and overall makes them feel a tad more realistic to me.
As far as technical game play goes, there are occasionally graphic glitches that show up where it is clear two textures or meshes don't merge together very well, but nothing glaring or annoying.  Thankfully, for the first 3rd of the game I haven't run into my biggest pet peeve in games, clipping issues.  The characters are able to move around easily without getting snagged on invisible objects, etc.  The environment feels fairly immersive eventhough the occassional NPC you may encounter doesn't.
For $1.24, my expectations were fairly loose and I do feel that  Hunted: The Demon's Forge is enjoyable enough for such a low price.
If this game were buggy and such, I'd give a thumbs down immediately, but Hunted is stable with little to no issues and the gameplay, main characters and graphics/atmosphere I'll give it a thumbs up for it's sale price.
ADDITIONAL:  Uopn a little more playing, I noticed a bit more depth to the game which has made the cheap price I paid a bit more worth it.  Special abilities and how they look when used are pretty cool.  Meeting certain achievements, usually through kill types or finding things, gives added abilities or increased power.  nifty.

Mini Metro is by far one of my favourite games. You're given the challenge of building a metro system that successfully links people to the destinations of their choices without overwhelming the network or resulting in waiting too long at any one station. It's remarkably zen but also remarkably challenging... and I can't help but love to play this game!
I particularly love the daily challenges which provide their own constraints but which can only be attempted once.
Simple yet challenging, if you like puzzle games, check this one out.

The minimalist design is really beautiful, and the simple gameplay lends itself to trying a lot of strategies. Stations are represented as one of a number of shapes with passengers looking to be routed to a different shape, so lines need to be designed to effectively carry people around the network. This abstraction nicely mirrors the real world, with circles equivalent to commuter stops, squares as central hubs, and unique shapes representing individual points of interest. Somehow this game succeeds at being simultaneously relaxing and stressful as hell.

Fantastic strategy fun. Brings a lot more depth, frustration, satisfaction, and excitement than first appears. The early game goals/achievements of 200 passengers felt too easy, but I'm still learning how to design efficient models of transportation to break the 2000 passenger milestones of the endgame, and other players in the Steam community report numbers up to 3000 and beyond!
Deceptively Simple and engaging, Simply a good game.

Bit Blaster XL is your classic arcade-style shooter game in which you control an overhead view of a "spaceship" and have to stay as long as possible without dying to the enemies, falling off the map, colliding with asteroids, or whatever you can seem to die to. It's actually quite enjoyable for me and allows me to reminisce in the times that everyone would hang out at Nickel City or the arcade and play games on the big machines together.
Essentially, what you want to do is start it up, and change whether you prefer auto fire or not. This 100% depends on your play preference as the auto fire will help you get started but to really grasp the higher levels and be able to take on various power boosts (one specific one I can think of that uses a lot of ammo is the laser, which is extremely helpful especially over 30,000 score.) There are minimal settings, which allow for very smooth and fun at the same time gameplay for everyone of all ages.
There are achievement, and trading cards. The achievements are hard enough to get that you will have to genuinely work for them over just being given them for logging in. Many people will get discouraged by the large amount of score you need but please don't! It's not as hard as it seems and after a few hours of working on your skills I guarentee that you will be able to start getting some of the higher level rockets and achievements.
It's very cheap, for a modern day game. It provides tons of fun, especially offline. And with no in app purchases, pay to win features, and no multiplayer even, you can just wind down or relax after a long day and play some Bit Blaster XL. End verdict? Yes. Definitely. For the short price and amount of enjoyment I've gotten over 2 accounts, I can say that I would be willing to pay for it over and over again.
It recalled up the memories of my childhood.

It's pretty fun for what it is. A timekiller at best, really. The game itself is fun, but it just feels a little lacking. I think the main thing I found lacking is the upgrades, there are quite a lot of them, but only about ~20% are actually worth anything. There are a lot of really superficial upgrades that are mostly worthless or overpriced, not to mention a lot of the upgrades should really be passive, but instead require further spending during a mining year. I can understand the drill requiring a rig upgrade to be able to go through rocks, but purchasing the speed upgrade for your rigs is ridiculous, that should be a passive upgrade. Then most of the workshop upgrades are useless, really the only ones worth getting are the dowser upgrades.
Then there's the AI. On normal, they're pretty stupid, and will rarely make earnings anywhere near yours if you play well. But then, on expert, it's completely rigged against you. The first few digs you only get a month or half a year to mine oil, which barely allows you to get a few thousand dollars in earnings. However, your opponents will be making 10-20k in earnings, completely eclipsing you in the early game on expert, which only screws you over later on. The AI in general just needs a complete overhaul for balance.

The only reason I am recommending this game is because it is in beta right now and, despite the problems, it has potential. What problems? Crashing isn't really a problem, because when it does happen you lose nothing and it is very easy to get right back into the game because it is constantly running your scenario somewhere up there in the cloud.
-Gold is a problem, not a solution. I have no idea how to get it. It is far easier to spend than get, so don't spend it, but then what is the point in having it.
-Resources, in general, are a problem. Everything gets gathered so slowly you can't do anything without spending gold, which, when you do, you run out quickly and then can't do anything because you can't get gold. Either increase the yeild of basic level resource gathering facilities (because it costs way too much to upgrade them) or reduce the time it takes to gather the resources themselves. When you do have renewable resources like cattle and sheep, you can skin them for hides or sell them for 'honour,' but they don't let you keep a couple of them in order to keep the herd alive. Nope, they cut them all up and then you have to buy more cattle with the swiftly dwindling resources you no longer have.
-Getting good units is a problem, because whenever you have a single type of unit of quality, like longsword knights, you can't make anymore. You can make other knights, but they cost gold and you can't get gold so you shouldn't spend it. You could craft units, but that takes a ridiculous amount of silver and hides, and as previously noted, resources like silver and hides take absolutely forever to gather in.
-I have found that when you harvest something the results of the harvest can change dramatically. I have harvested all my wheat fields at once, but somehow get less per field than if I had done it one at a time. Ostensibly, the reason is that you don't have enough workers to get the full yield out of the wheat fields if harvested all at once. Then why did I sow all the wheat fields at once? And if we are going for reality, why don't we harvest wheat in the autumn and increase the yield to cover the year?
-I have gathered wood from deadwood piled up on shore in odd places. The store of the deadwood when you click on it says 100. When you gather the wood though, you get 50 and the deadwood disappears.
-Fishing takes longer than harvesting wheat. And fishing should replenish itself if you spread out and slow down your efforts. It does not, however, replenish itself.
-Battles can be quite maddening. The good news is you never completely lose a unit unless you delete its training facility  or disband it. Mission difficulty seems to increase with your rank, but your troops don't really keep up because it costs so freaking much of the resources you can't gather fast enough or gold which you don't get just to upgrade training facilities in order to upgrade the unit, which has experience points from battling you can't use unless you do upgrade the training facility. So, as you continue along, you start to lose a lot of battles because your troops just can't keep pace. I'm losing about half now.
-the Total War folks do put out codes to redeem in the game for free resources, which points out they are aware of how ridiculous it is to grow/gather your own stuff, but they seem to think that giving them out as 'single-use' codes is a good idea, so that only one person can use the code and then it is no good for whoever else is next. There are millions of gamers out there and I'm not tuned in to Facebook at all hours of the day, so I have given up on getting a code. Ever.
That's a lot of complaining, but I do like the game. The persistent timeline is cool, I don't have to be playing for everyone to keep on working. All this having been said they have a lot of good stuff going on in the game and I am eager to see it developed further in its gameplay and in ways to play, like tablets. This is definitely better than the Total War Battles: Shogun.

A good concept, but hampered by its Free-to-Play model.
The Good:
I love the art style, and the music is passable. The hexagon-based simple city building has promise. I like the variation of the seasons, and that they actually have gameplay effects. I like how terrain, especially access to water, affects resource gathering. I like how terrain will change—grass will spread, trees will regrow. Combat is simple, but fun. A good mix of units, and there is room for effective tactics (and not just spamming orders buttons) to change the outcome of a battle.
The Bad:
I do not like the running-clock mechanism; it makes the game feel like FarmVille or other FtP “FaceBook games.” Construction takes no appreciable time at all, but gathering resources hours or even days without forking over cash for in-game currency. Some of these times work (e.g. about 20 minutes to fully refresh an army after a defeat or pyric victory), others don’t (hours of quarrying for a measly 20 stone). So, really, what I don’t like is that it is free-to-play.
The Ugly:
I think if they had kept the core of the game (the map, the combat model, terrain modification, hex-based town construction, seasonal variation), but instead reworked it as a stand-a-lone game WITHOUT the FtP model and constantly running clock, this could have been a solid “midrange” or “light” game. If seasons were “turns,” and certain things (planting, harvesting, etc.) could only be done during particular seasons, the game would be much more enjoyable to just sit an play—instead play for about an hour or less then log out and come back in 12 hours or so. Such a game would necessitate a complete reworking of the way resources were handled, but a price-point of $30-40 would have made such a game a must-buy for me. As it is, I’ll fiddle until I get bored of the grind, then shelve it—and they likely won’t have made any money off of me.

Entropy Rising is a unique game. Sure it takes its inspiration from Braid and Portal, but it has taken the good parts of both those games and come up with a fresh idea.
This game has a mixture of clever puzzles, interesting environments and it does a really good job of giving the world a sense if weight and gravity as you interact with it. I am enjoying my time with this game currently, it has a few minor negative points. Those points and my gameplay are featured below.

Entropy Rising is a first-person puzzle game where your identity and purpose are unknown!  At the beginning of the game, you descend from the heavens. It literally appears as so as you play as a pink, luminous orb that gently floats and guides you to your objective. It’s your job to jump from platform to platform without fail; even if mistakes were made, the game introduces a rewind mechanism which is activated by holding down the right mouse button. Despite having this option available, each level has a three-star challenge: one for simply completing the puzzle, two for completing it at the recommended set time, and finally by finishing the course without ever using the rewind ability (meaning not dying). So for those of you who are perfectionists or achievement hunters, this is will be more than enough of a challenge.
The game slowly introduces players to more gimmicky items such as the “Grabber Gun”, which can grab and navigate elemental components such as water or concrete spheres to designated points. Shortly after, you receive an upgraded version of the gun called the “Gravi Gun”, which allows the player to form a gravity bubble around more hostile spheres. Hostile spheres includes those made of lava, in which you can hover them slowly to their rightful place. However, this can only be done in certain areas of a level so there are limitations. After learning the ropes, you’ll encounter strange machinery such as the Thermodynamic Machine, which requires a specific temperature before allowing you to move forward. That’s accomplished either by using the Gravi Gun to transport lava spheres to increase temperature level, or simply using the Grabber Gun on water spheres to cool down lava. These game elements and items all come together to make the the game not only entertaining but also to add a problem-solving aspect to the title that’s not hard to grasp for first-time players, yet adds a good amount of challenge for skilled platforming players.

Entropy Rising is very good with providing tips and advice in the shape of computer monitors. Like all puzzle games, you must first learn to crawl before walking and this game instructs the player in a smooth manner. It doesn’t become too overwhelming but supplies enough challenge to make the player think. The visuals are simple and aren’t too extravagant, however, it isn’t an aspect that takes the entertainment out of the game.

This isn't terrible, and there are some genuinely good missions in it, but ultimately it becomes less fun the more you play it. I'm quite close to the end, but I don't care about finishing the game anymore. I have been doing a fair number of side missions, but still: 20 hours in, and I don't care about what's going on. It's full of clichés, such as the empty wheelchair rolling towards you in the corridor of the haunted mental asylum (seriously), and other games do everything here better. Get Dishonored and its Brigmore Witches DLC instead.
A big problem is the city that connects everything. Familiarity breeds contempt, and you often have a lot of ground to cover to get from NPC to NPC which leaves the big feeling both big and small at the same time. You start to wish that some of the side mission characters might reward you with a fast travel option to other points on the map, given that you can't earn useful items from that work. Instead, we are forced to walk everywhere through a city that's bizarrely lacking interconnection. Often, you need to find an exact window to let you through into another city section. It is torturously stubborn when you're trying to get from A to B, and worse because of the completely unnecessary amount of loading points. Even with an SSD, this is still irritating. You'll quickly learn to hate the identical animations for squeezing through a tight space and the QTE to move the same fallen beam, and the "Hold X, now tap X repeatedly" thing for windows (which I could forgive if it was ever about a subtle movement to avoid being heard, but you will never be heard).
This tediousness feeds into everything. I was playing for a long time wondering when I'd finally get a razor to steal paintings, or a wirecutter to disable traps, when Googling the problem finally told me that only one trader in the entire city sells those. This is one of many things in this dreary game that just makes you think, "♥♥♥♥ you, Eidos".
Many reviews allege that the graphics are great, a viewpoint with which I strongly disagree. Animations, modelling and textures are pretty basic and old-fashioned. Swinging censers wreathed in smoke simply move their smoke field with them. Graphics settings appear to do very little to help or hurt the framerate, which is bizarrely low considering the lack of demand here (I have a 4GB Nvidia card, and it cannot keep the rate above 60fps at 1080p).

Where many Visual Novels as of late rely heavily on archetypal "moe" characterization, in tandem with, admittedly, impressive "cutesy" artstyle, this sort of story this game depicts is something that is much more than most of the Visual Novels of recent release here in Steam. This was a sort of passion project by the once defunct Dischan (they were dispersed some time ago, but had since convalesced and are now active once more only recently). The artwork, music, sound direction, and the general literary acumen, is simply gorgeous--and their quality is even more accentuated by the fact that this project was made in the span of just under a MONTH.
The premise of the story revolves around two individuals--and the duality between them will be that for the entirety of the story. Yes; there exist only two characters, with several other characters only merely being mentioned in utterance, and not actually shown--but disregard that, the two main characters is the fulcrum of the story. Their personalities, interactions, and histories, is--quite literally--the entirety of the story. Yet, this visual novel delivers it in such magnificent execution that it simply fazed me in awe the first time reading it. The dearth of characters is readily compensated by how much detail went into these two characters.
The ambience is quite bleak, being set in a desolate place, where a vestige of what once stood a town now lies a menagerie of ruins and moorish land, where much of the flora and trees have since withered; scraps and swaths of stone and dirt laminate the cold, unearthed pavement. The narration delves deep into detail about the surroundings, and it is also clearly illustrated in the artwork. You immediately feel this sort of wistful, melancholy at the ambience--the sort of feeling of one of the main characters know all too well. The destitution of the land is palpable.
Now, it is actually the execution of the narration what sold me on this story. We enter the story in First Person--as in, we see the thoughts of the Main Character, and we are intimately greeted by the emotions they feel at any given time. Now, in the story, it actually switches between perspectives--from the Fiend, to the Boy, and back to the Fiend once more. Ahem; apologies from not denoting this earlier, but the Fiend and the Boy are the story's sole characters.
The story itself is wonderfully crafted. It explores themes of racial disparity, of trust and hope, and of sullen and haunting past lives. The story, and I say this utmostly confident, executes each theme and blends them seamlessly with one another.
A truly good read, and it doesn't take much time too. I implore you to at least give the novel a few minutes of your time. This is simply too good of a free, indie novel to pass off as just another piece of fodder in Steam's endless catalogue of Visual Novels.

For £3.99 (well, -20% for me for launch discount!), this game is actually really fun. Sadly I don't have anyone to play it with though...

*10/10 would explode again.

Full Disclosure: I did receive the game for free for testing purposes. However, the details of that exchange are important. I found Ballistic Tanks during its development and thought it looked so incredible that I wanted to be involved. As a fellow game developer I saw what promise the game had and knew I would be passing by a real gem if I did not. Kirk did not approach me for a review or ask me to do this.
Things I like:
-The game is gorgeous. Kirk really has a way with movement and everything in the game moves and reacts so incredibly well. It's a lot of fun to look at while playing.
-The mechanics are a lot of fun. It's been a while since a good arena tank game has been available. Tank games really never get old, and Kirk has made sure there are plenty of new mechanics to freshen up this long-standing genre. I really recommend playing with bullet time, as the coolness factor goes way up. Also, playing as a Boss tank is SO AMAZING.
-Playing with people is great. It's a really good party game, and the game comes alive with others in the room.
-Kirk didn't forget solo players, and put a really challenging 1-2 player Arcade mode in. I would love to play this on an old arcade cabinet as it's got the look and feel down.
Things I don't like:
-This game screams for online multiplayer. I would probably never turn it off if there was an option to play online with other people. The bots are well made but there's nothing like humans.
-Some of the cannon sounds are a little small. They could really be improved with some bass, especially the boss shots. Really easy to address, though.
-Sometimes there are minor collision errors. Does not affect gameplay very much, but it does affect the game feeling.
Overall, for the price this is an incredible gem. If you have a party planned or are a fan of the Tank Arena genre, you will really enjoy this. It's been a real pleasure watching it go from beautiful gifs to a finished product.

Visuals and sound design wise the game is absolutely stellar, but it’s squandered by extremely simple gameplay that doesn't really evolve meaningfully beyond the initial time repeat shtick, despite the advertised "bizarre mask powers".
Puzzles are too easy and most of the new mechanics you accrue throughout the game are unimaginative and lackluster, usually context based "press a button to activate door / gadget" type abilities rather than something letting you naturally manipulate the environment. The game even automatically chooses the mask ability you have to use for each situation when it becomes available, not that it would be hard to guess anyway.
For example the glass shattering and lock-picking powers are perfectly identical in how they’re used and only serve to open different types of “locks”. The architect insight power is left completely unused in puzzles and only serves to unlock more optional lore, again through contextual button press that you randomly get when walking through certain areas. Even the increased hearing ability that you can actually use everywhere and lets you keep track of people outside the rooms you occupy isn’t really used that way very much, only notably during segments where you peek through a keyhole and you guessed it, use a contextual button prompt yet again to make otherwise unheard dialogue visible. I’d wager it was originally intended to allow circumventing occupied rooms more easily (you lose if you’re in a room with someone else for too long), but the death timer is extremely lenient and you can just run through occupied areas every time, even straight through the masks that start chasing you. No need to hide in closets either, as they only grant higher visibility of the room compared to keyhole peeking.
The progression is linear and puzzles encompass only their own set new area the vast majority of the time, and even after the mansion slowly opens up there's really no cases where you have to run from wildly different areas of the map to gather clues or gadgets to prevent a murder. Pretty much each puzzle and its solution is isolated to the new area you just unlocked, save for one where you just have to manipulate 4 very obvious switches. The last power you get that lets you use an otherwise clever
ends up being left completely unused despite perfectly lending itself for a grander mansion wide puzzle, and only helps speeding up a completely optional collectible hunt.
The story is merely decent, it’s not bad but nothing mindblowing either, and being a mystery game the lack of awesome moments where everything "just connects" and suddenly makes sense lefts a lackluster aftertaste.

Honestly my new favourite game.
The best way I can describe this game is by saying it's a reverse hitman. Instead of killing people without being seen try to save them from their demise by indirectly messing with their routine before it's to late and time resets. If you enter a room with people in it, time will stop and their masks will become sentient and chase you until you leave the room which is why you should avoid being seen. The premise instantly got me hooked.
The entire atmosphere is amazing, the visuals are simple but neat, the mansion itself is designed nicely and it rarely gets confusing despite there being a number of rooms. The music is also topnotch. Often it's a track that is as long as the entire day is and the music gets intense right as your target is about to die. You could be anywhere in the mansion and you'd still know that things are getting urgent.
The puzzles rarely feel unfair. They are challenging but not too hard, often if you dont know what to do it helps to explore the mansion as new info can be revealed by spying on some of the characters. For example, in one chapter you have to name a password and you find out what the password is by spying on a character conversing with another one.
The only problem I had is that this game is technically poorly optimised. My PC meets this games standards and yet theres some dips in the framerate here and there. Theres also this annoying problem where when you want to enter a room the game has to process that for a second, which will result in you waiting in front of the door for a second and then entering it. It'll feel like you didn't press the button right. Often these hicc-ups are connected with the framedrops. These problems are inconveniences at worst though and never made me miss a prompt. Generally the timing in this game is quite forgiving.
Overall I'd say this game is a solid 9/10. I paid 10 bucks for it but I'd gladly pay 20 too.

Being a very short visual novel as it is, Juniper's Knot managed to harness the limited time it has to tell an extraordinarily beautiful story. And it costs nothing.
Usually it is harder to actually grade a short visual novel as I can not know for certain if the story is good because it is short or the story is good because it is actually good. For Juniper's Knot, I think it is the latter. It tells the story of only two characters, changing perspective between each other, and it paints the relationship and their respective personalities directly to the mind of the reader. It is written so that you can sympathize with both characters even considering how contrast their characteristics are. It is easy to tell that they planned the story really well.
I actually got goose bumps in a good percentage of my run of the game. They managed to put little details as sound effects and every BGM fit perfectly to the scene and they are beautiful. The sound of the waves and fire crackling are especialy good. I did not notice any BGM being overly used. Maybe because it is short, but it is a good thing nevertheless.
As I said above, Juniper's Knot is a treasure. Not because it is a free game but because it got the quality other Visual Novels seems to lack, especially indie ones. It is very short and can be played through in under five minutes if you want to. I am very interested in the back story of both the characters and chances are I will buy it if they were ever to release it. All in all, there are really nothing bad to say about the game as the developer team really did a good job here.
I notice that there are blank entries to the arts in the extra menu after I finished the game. It might be a clue that the developer is going to update or release a continuation/backstory to Juniper's Knot.
The best free visual novel on steam <3

The pacing was swell enough that it kept me reading. It was nice to see both characters get some time to be in the spotlight and see their perspectives as they tell each other stories and information about themselves. The solution to the issue at heart of the tale was clever, and very symbolic.
My only complaint is for something so short you'd expect the writing to be on point. It sometimes dragged on in points that were not that important to the overall plot.
Definitely recommend, especially if you got the time and are in the right mood for a light read.

Ostensibly taking place around the late nineteenth century,
is the story of a fiend, or demon, who is trapped where she is in a crumbling building. However, a boy, who has been lost on travels, comes across the place and encounters the fiend. Without much else to do, he settles in for a little while and they exchange stories and learn about each other.
This game is a kinetic novel, a type of visual novel with no branching storylines nor any choices. It can be played through as fast as the player can read it. I would estimate that a complete play-through should take no more than an hour.
The game itself was originally released in 2012, but only made its way to Steam in August 2017. Considering the short length of the game, I generally found it to be a nice, little gem.
To start off, the art in the game is very good. There is not much of it because the game is so short, but what is in the game is quite professional looking. The music is also a very nice addition.
The main purpose of any visual novel is the story and writing. The game features a minimalist cast, only two characters. However, I found that the two characters are well-written and both get a decent amount of development in the short span of the game. The same praises can go for the writing in general. While it does not have the deepest plot, I thought it was a satisfying experience.
In conclusion, this short kinetic novel is not a bad way to spend about an hour. The art is great and the story is nice. I would recommend this to those looking for a short visual novel. Plus, the free price cannot be beaten.

The negative reviews for this game are laughable... I read a lot of people complaining about AI and the cards you start with. First off if you think the AI is too difficult you probably have never played MTG before... If you think the AI is too easy(which it is), play real people...
As for the cards you start with, If you cant build an at least competetive deck with all the cards you get from finishing the story modes for all the sets. You probably are just bad at magic... Youre not going to be able to build the most unique of decks with them but you should definitely be able to be competetive untill rank 20+, Even at 20+ theres still not that many elite deck combinations, but this is standard. Theres not that many different elite decks in real life standard.
Another gripe i see in the reviews is the shuffle system. This one is legitimate... kind of. It certainly can be very frustrating when you get no mana in your hand and mulligan 3 times with no mana in any hand... BUT this is a card game, its supposed to be random. Mana shuffling in real life is great but how can you expect that to be a thing in a video game.
The last thing i see people really complaining about is the crashes and disconnects. Im sure people are not lying about this, Yet in 150+ hours ive had like 2 crashes and never been disconnected during an online match.
Overall for a free game, Magic: Duels is great way to get your magic fix if youre ok with playing standard format. Could it be better? Oh god yes... None of the problems in this game are bad enough to warrant a negative review for a free game though.

Dungeons of Dredmor is a fantastic game if you haven't played any "real" roguelike games like Nethack, ADOM or Crawl and would like to make the entrance as smoothly as possible. Dredmor is hard, has permadeath (as an option!) and is procedural. Artwork is whimsical, silly and everything is covered in humor. There are jokes in item, skill and creature descriptions, in the lore and... everywhere! Tongue in cheek you seek the lord of the dungeon and try to slay him using skilltrees like Mathemagic and Communism with all sorts of weird DIY-gear from plastic arrows to tin hats.
All this might fall a bit short for those that know the genre by heart and seek both complexity and difficulty. Both exist here too but not in a sense where you want to spend hours thinking "what should I wear" and how can I survive this situation.

Note: my play time doesn't reflect my countless playthroughs. I can't even fathom the hours I've poured into this on rainy days.
PROS:
* As roguelike as roguelike can get. Sometimes RNG will bite you in the butt, but sometimes the dice are nice. For the most part though, it's pretty forgiving, at least early on. Most of the time it's just a matter of picking a couple skills that can reliably get you through the first few floors, and by that time you'll have enough levels (and lucky loot) to keep on climbing.
* Maintains an upbeat, quirky, and tastefully humorous tone in the music, dialog and flavor text, all of which belie the treacheries of the Dungeons.
* Mods galore! More rooms in floors, more classes with unique effects that are (usually) balanced, check out the Steam Workshop and see if anything tickles your fancy, there's plenty to choose from.
CONS:
* Very bulky crafting system, with an equally bulky UI to go with it. More often than not, you're better off praying to RNGesus than trying to amass the skill levels and materials for some recipe you found. Ironically, the game itself makes fun of how bulky its crafting system is, one joke I did not smile at.
Overall, if you like roguelikes even in the slightest, this is a must-have in your library. Get it, play it on hard with perma-death, get really far, die, get frustrated, shut it off, then come back because you *know* you want some more of that sweet Dredmor punishment.

Have you ever wondered what it would be like to have a Rogue-like developed by a team of roughly 10 people who grew up in the mid 90s and were raised entirely by Doom and The Secret of Monkey Island? Of course you don't, that's pretty weird.
Fortunately it exists and it is probably one of the best "true" rogue-like games made in the past 10 years.
Dungeons of Dredmor is a Roguelike Fantasy RPG with several pop culture references from the 90s up to the 2010s.
If you are unsure of what a
, it's a gameplay style based on the 1980 release "Rogue". In a nutshell, you are given
life to complete the entire game, any death results in a save wipe or a sentence back to the start of the game. As such the game itself is relatively shorter than other RPGs, maybe 2-3 hours with experienced players.
In the more traditional rogue-likes, like this game, you move in a square based grid and take turns with the enemies to either pick up one of the 20 or so types of cheeses, find new gear to equip, or die horribly to one of the many monsters in your way.
Controls to this game are rather simple, move in a grid based map with WASD and use the mouse to interact with objects next to the player. However,
. It sounds nice at first, but as far as I know you cannot cancel any mouse movement queues. So if you are suddenly ambushed, you have to take a good 3 turns just to move to the spot you clicked. Which is very bad.
Long story short, this is a
difficult game for newcomers to rogue-likes or even intermediate players who understand most of the things.
If you really like the concept of this game and must play it first rather than others, thankfully you can lower the difficulty and disable permanent deaths. And it doesn't even make fun of you for it!
I highly recommend the tutorial even if you know what you're doing, it's humorous and gives you a good idea of how to play (character numbers good, hp good, damage bad).

PROS:
+great storyline

+decent dialog/bantering
CONS: (serious flaws)
- gamebreaking bugs
- non-replayability
- no restart (developer FAIL)
- abilites lack flavor and limitations
Being an original Dungeons and Dragons fan, I enjoyed the dungeon crawling and mix of outdoor scenery.  HOWEVER, their was a crippling lack choices in this game that make this game irritating beyond measure.
1. 6 abilites to choose from, but only have buttons for 4?
2. AI will fail to pick up potions/heath or Mana, crippling their use.
3. Once you start a game, you cannot restart ? !!! That's right, you actually have to go into your game folder and delete every trace of the saved games - if you don't like your spell build and want to restart mid-game, well, sucks to be you because you CAN'T.  Want OLD SCHOOL hard mode, well you have to finished every side quest with no clue as to where they are, and your glowing wisps (directional hints) will send you astray, and if you hit the wrong button, oops, well you have to complete the entire game ALL OVER AGAIN, first !!!
4. Once you spend your "very limited" crystals on spells, there won't be any more, so you better choose right the first time.
5. Adventurers collect gold drops - apparently for no reason at all, this is NOT a RPG as one might expect, its uber-linear,
6. Dangles a giant Ogre in the face of the player, which you never get to fight.  End of the game, simply makes no sense.
7. Hope you like sticking like a bug to flypaper, becuase you get glued to every cover wall you get close to as if you were wearing armor made of magnets.
8. The aiming mechanics are "aweful" okay, worse than that, they're entirely  horrendeous.
If you like 3rd person camera man - not actually in the game / duck and hide gameplay, they this is for you.  The Developers should have fixed the glaring "RESTART NEW GAME" feature, but failed to do so, sending it down its dark dreary path of despair and unplayability.  This game had so much potential ~ yet was handicapped by its own designers.  DEV's, here's a word of advice, a player should be free to restart a new game at any time - instead of being shackled to a single play-through. AND - give gamers choice of Third  or First person - to appease both crowds (and you can actually see what you are aiming at!)
Unfortunately, I had to give this game a NEGATIVE: because of its start game function failings and lack of aiming and camera angles & player models that will actually block your line of sight - which is the main form of combat for an archer, silly Dev's.

I’m going to begin by saying that I understand some people with specific tastes may legitimately dislike this game, and they are entitled to their opinion and I respect that.  But I also believe some of the excessive negativity that surrounds this game is exacerbated by an overly vocal group of “Debbie Downers.”  At the time of writing this: the data shows that more than two-out-of-three people who took time to review this game enjoyed it; but there are mostly negative reviews as the “most helpful” on the store page.  So it seems the people who disliked the game
want you to know about it, even though there is evidence that suggests that there are more people who liked it than who didn’t. And so this review may receive a load of critique by those who refuse to respect my opinion even though I’m able to respect theirs, but that is OK.  All I know for sure is that: I liked
.
Is this game different from the early installments of the
franchise? Yes.  It has no doubt been modernized to appeal to a wider audience of gamers and not just the hardcore stealth fans (i.e.: it is easier).  Still, if you take the time to set up a custom difficulty, you can remove much of the “hand-holding” and make the game quite punishing.  Nevertheless, I can empathize with everyone who was let down by this game being too mainstream by default and not staying true to the established traditions.
is semi-linear, undoubtedly, especially during the individual levels; although there is a decent amount of freedom to explore The City.  The thing is: you certainly won’t get stuck spending 3 hours lost in the sewers like you may have in the older games.
is far less enigmatic than the earlier installments.  Some long term fans are upset by this, and you may be too— and that is your prerogative.  That said, there are also a lot of people who don’t want to spend a whole evening of gameplay being lost on one level in one game, especially if they only have a limited amount of hours of free time in which to play games.
So it is true that this game is quite different than the early editions in the franchise.  It does hold your hand in the default state (although you can turn off most assistance in the options and difficulty settings).  And it is rather linear.  You have every right to dislike that and dislike this game.  But maybe you are one of the many gamers who just wants to relax and play a game for a few hours after working all day.  Maybe you are looking to go on an intriguing adventure, want to be told a story, and don’t feel like getting lost or frustrated on the way.  Well then maybe you should give
a try.
I felt the most captivating aspect of the game was the stellar atmosphere of the gameworld.  The ambiance is mysterious, violent, dark, and mystifying.  The high production value of the graphics and soundscape went a long way to reinforce the air of quality inherent to the game’s atmosphere.  Moreover, even if many other aspects failed, I thought the ambiance of the game stayed true to the established traditions of the franchise.
The narrative isn’t the most riveting piece of writing to grace the realm of video games, but it is mildly interesting and serves to give some purpose to the gameplay.  The gameplay itself is fun.  With the custom difficulty settings you really can take the driver’s seat in determining how casual or grueling of an experience you want.  The controls are smooth and intuitive, and there aren’t any painful flaws that will cause you to accidentally be spotted.
There are plenty of collectibles, secrets, and achievements if you are into that kind of thing.  There are also a large amount of sidequests which can really open up and expand the game if you choose to pursue them.
is a pretty fun game, but certainly isn’t a masterpiece.  It is quite mainstream, and definitely has stepped out from the hardcore stealth realm of the earlier editions in the franchise.  If you just want to play a nice atmospheric game with a high production value and have some fun, you can definitely find that here.  If you want traditional hardcore
gameplay, you may be disappointed— although you may also want to consider trying the custom difficulty before you blindly dismiss it. It has some flaws and minor annoyances, but overall it can be a rather enjoyable experience. Regardless, this is definitely the type of game where you are going to have to determine your own preferences and decide if you want to try it or not.  All I know for sure is that: I liked
.

This is a surprisingly addictive little puzzler. You must connect randomly generated train stations with rail networks, and keep the stations from over-crowding by shipping passengers from place to place.
Where this game really shines is with it's minimalist design. This game could be held up in design schools across the world as a fine example of how clever design can make or break a game. In this case, make it. It's minimalist, but it's so intuitive that you don't even really need to think about the interface. You can concentrate on the game.
However... after four hours of gameplay I've unlocked all the maps, and I wonder about the game's longevity.
I can see myself coming back to this frequently - but the WOW factor is probably going to wear off now that I don't have a particular goal... and that's what this game is missing. A purpose.
Playing the game for its own ends is all well and good... but once I ran out of tangible goals, I really found myself wondering what was next.  Sure, I can play each map over and over, but I've *done* everything.  There are other game modes (endless, which seems like a waste of time, and extreme, which I'll probably try later) but once you've unlocked all the maps, there doesn't seem to be a 'hook' anymore.
This is a great game. I recommend it. It's a delight to play, and is beautifully designed... but I'm not sure there's enough of it. Get it, definitely... but wait for it to go on sale.

Growing up, the Thief games were some of my favourite. Even today I still hold them close to my heart. From the distant call of the Horn of Quintus,  to the ambient terror of the Shalebridge Cradle and everything in between, there was never a dull moment. It was a magical feeling that I rarely got with other games, that within minutes of loading the game I would be hooked for hours. So upon hearing the announcement in 2009 of 'Thi4f,' naturally I was extremely excited. So I waited...
and waited...
and waited.
Then came the announcement that broke the hearts of many a diehard Thief fan. Stephen Russell (the voice of the original Garrett) would not be returning. It was like being 5 years old and having your favourite teddy bear torn apart in front of you. Yet I still held somewhat high hopes for the game.
This hope was short lived. I bought the game, and loaded it up. The Hammers that I had grown to hate, yet love were gone. The Trickster and Builder were non-existant, the Pagans and Keepers all but vanished.
I didn't even hear a single mention of the word taffer.
That magical feeling I got with the original trilogy was no longer there. Thief was no longer Thief. After 3 hours of playing, I knew this wasn't the game that I'd grown to love as a young'n. Saddened, I put the game back on its digital shelf, where to this day it gathers e-dust.
TL;DR, diehard Thief fan becomes saddened upon playing this taffin' piece of non-canonical nonsense.

______________________________________________________________________________
Synopsis
The Sexy Brutale  is a stealth game with time travel and environmental powers, you basically see a murder happen and , with the aid of timetravel and mask powes, you'll  have to try and save the victim(s), both to unveil and advance  the plot and obtain new powers.
Pros:
✓ Great soundtrack: something i always persistently seek in videogames  is great music, like in the horror genere, music have an heavy impact on gameplay, and usually really makes the difference between an ok game and a masterpiece, i really love me some good tunes in my videogames, and i think this is something you strongly need to achieve a good gaming experience, The Sexy Brutale has it and left me pretty satisfied about it.
✓ Interesting gameplay: you'll have to peep in a keyhole, see the murder happen, tail suspects, eavesdrop conversations, timetravel with your pocketwatch, use and obtain new masks powers that give you advantages like : seeing ghosts, increased earing, shatter glass with your voice ecc..
✓ Easy on the eyes: The game is pretty, every room of the mansion is really well done, majestic, full of interesting details and never boring.
✓ Interesting diverse cast of characters : you got diversity and no one result flat out boring, gotta love the creative ways they get killed too,not really alot of character development ( we're gonna cover this better later) but they still end up being diverse, characteristic and all around interesting.
Cons:
✘ The game is too short: don't get me wrong, the game is good, so good that it will keep you glued to your screen until you finish it, sadly i completed the game in about 7/8 hours, you can get something more by trying to get all the last 4 achievements and cards, but still not alot of hours/usage you can get out of this one, it definitely left me wanting more, not really satisfied.
✘ Insignificant character developement: You witness their homicide, go back in time, prevent it, they give you their thanks and masks and that's it, you're given a quick image of the characters and very little development, you just know each others as old friends and they thank you for saving their life, you'll move on and pass to the next one, that's it. I'm aware of the fact it make sense in light of  the timetravel plot, but still i wasn't pleased about it.
✘ The name: There is nothing of "Sexy" in the Sexy Brutale ( aside from some statues and that hot soundtrack and a couple of naked statues, still this one is nitpicking at best) kinda misleading title.
✘ Too Easy: The puzzles are beautifully done, i like all the creative ways  the roster of characters dies, but puzzles are too easy to solve and answers tend to ,usually, lie there, highlighted.
✘ Disappointing Ending: Alright so, I found myself really enjoying the game, so much i end up finishing it up ( wiith only 4 achievements left to complete) in one single night without resting, i was really enjoying the game and it kept me interested, glued to the screen playing all night, wich is extremely good, but, i'm not gonna lie, i was pretty disappointed with the ending, since the start  i was waiting for some sick bad guy/s to reveal him/themselves and give that special flavour to the story you were waiting since the start when you asked yourself " how is this intrigue gonna end? why is the staff murdering everyone, what is the motif, is this gonna be something mystical, supernatural, are we gonna get some sick unexpected plot twist that is gonna leave us mouths open? are we gonna get some clarity about how they do this and why? I bet there is something really meaningful about the choice on the diverse and interesting way these characters are getting brutally killed" ... sadly no, turns out the big plot twist was pretty simple and kinda lame
at least this is what i felt when it came to it.
______________________________________________________________________________
Overall a well crafted game  but i'm not really sure i would  have bought it if i knew about the short duration and the blandess of the ending ,still, sometime you have just  take the risk, try and see.
i don't feel like i'd go back if i could because it still was worth the experience,
I chose to be positive cause the game was still good and the soundtrack was  remarkably good,
at least a 7.5/10 in my book.

OH. MY. GOD.
I am so incredibly torn up right now.
I just finished the entire game and I cannot describe the immense complex love/hate relationship I have right now with it.
Though, to be entirely right out of the gate, it's more a hate than love mix.
First of all, I love the story, the aesthetic, the snappy, jazzy yet omminous music and the overall visual presentation.
I'm immediately sad to say that the bad stuff, which I'll get to in a sec, progressively made it more and more impossible for me to fully enjoy the above-mentioned good stuff.
That said, here are the things I did not enjoy during my playthrough.
The game starts off strong by throwing you in a mystery-rich premise.
You're in a mansion with masked people everywhere you look, from guests to the party staff, and some unknown individual entity informs you right from the get go that you have to prevent the staff from murdering the guests.
You use a pocketwatch to turn back time up to 12 hours, so you can observe how each murder is commited and how you can prevent the situation from escalating.
Great concept! Love the idea of solving murders before they've been commited.
Reminds me a bit of the Minority Report movie.
But you know what I don't love? A universe that doesn't make sense within it's own rules.
Now, to be fair, in the end, the game kind of gives you an explanation why some stuff doesn't make sense.
But I find that a bare excuse after shoveling through so many guesses and chances and weird solutions to murders.
I can't really go into detail due to spoilers, but yeah, imagine finding a victim's body with a knife stuck in his back, a bullet in his skull and a glass in his hand with poisonous residu, and then finding out he was murdered with black magic even though that possibility has never been introduced beforehand.
It's just misleading and kind of detracts from the fun of solving a murder, because from that point on, anything is possible.
And again to be fair, this is not with all murders. Some are actually really fun and make you go "Ahhhh, yeah, of course, how did I not think of that!" in the end.
There were also uniquely designed other aspects that blocked my progress for no good reason (in my opinion).
Like when I completed an objective in an area and tried to leave the area, only to find the connecting door (to the previous area) blocked.
But what I didn't know was that somewhere in the entire area, an almost unnoticable trapdoor unlocked for me to use.
Because.... you know... what's more fun than completing an objective followed up by searching 30 minutes for a small unannounced exit! :D
I know it sounds like small stuff, but in my opinion, the Sexy Brutale has a loooot of these small elements which make the game feel less and less fluent and more like a chore to dig through.
It definitely tries SO hard to be this polished, tight, fun, rubix cube, but some coloured squares on the cube are just torquise, instead of blue, or pink/purple'ish, instead of red, and, as a player, you're often left wondering... "wait... is this red? or... purple... .... wait... no... what?".
And to be frank, if a puzzle fails to provide you with all the necessary information, tools and pieces needed to complete it, it is not a good puzzle.
So, unless you can see yourself not getting frustrated by such minor yet numerous confusing elements in a puzzle game, I would advice a very sad pass for this one...

- Fantastic art style

- Very diverse gameplay, with the way the leveling works you can play the same character multiple completely different ways (I main Mozu, and I can either play a scrappy little damage slinger, a support ally, or a ranged defender)
- You choose your character before jumping in to a match, meaning you'll always get to play who you want (but you can always change when you join if you change your mind)
- Easy to learn, after only 4 hours in game i jumped in to a match against other players and was able to get 10 kills with only 1 death, with decent efficiency to boot
- Generous business model, you can buy all of the characters (and most of the skins) with the in-game currency, and several of the characters are priced low enough that you can unlock them after just a couple hours of gameplay
- Stable; most new f2p games I've played are riddled with bugs; so far the only bug i've experienced in this is that you can't change your in-game icon yet
- Lots of updates planned; the developers seem to have a very strong passion for this game (they actually worked on it with no pay for a time, because they cared so deeply about it) though i suppose we'll see how that pans out
Cons:
- Limited game types; this may or may not change as content updates are released
- Playing against bots is limited to an extremely easy difficulty and only one map
???:
- No option yet for custom matches that I'm aware of; though I've never played with a crew
Please don't compare it to Overwatch (which is a great game in its own right but it's fundamentally different)

After looking for a good TBS game in the WW2 genre and being overwhelmed by the choices available, I chose to stick to something tried and true. I played PG 3d and 'Scorched earth' years ago and wanted something not too simplistic but not requiring a college text to learn. I found the perfect balance in Panzer Corps, a game I have been unashamedly addicted to since the beginning of the year.
For older gamers like myself that prefer turn-based games that have strategic/tactical depth and an immersive experience, PC is a near-perfect fit. I've slogged my way through the stock campaign as well as 90% of the DLC available. I've spent almost 1k hours loving this game and I haven't even touched the modding community's offerings yet!
For people with an above average understanding of WW2 history, armies, equipment, and tactics this game is a pleasant dream come true. However, some of my complaints are the lack of simple features:
a- Animations could be improved to show tank treads moving, truck wheels turning, soldiers marching, etc. 2D terrain appears dated, could use simple enhancements like trees swaying in the wind, water moving, waves on beaches splashing.
b- There could be more differentiation between tactical styles for different armies (I've found that using the same style of play works the same for Germans, Soviets, or Americans),
c- Units on high ground (hills, mountains, forts) should have stronger attack/defense benefits,
d- Comprehensive GC includes many what-if scenarios....but WHY isn't the Pacific war ever included in the official DLC?? I mean c'mon, its not that hard to model the USMC/USN taking on the Japanese across islands, the Phillipines, Okinawa, and a what-if invasion of mainland Japan. The UK's defense of Burma and India, China, etc...all ignored!!!
e- modding could be a little more easier / user-friendly
Overall, and excellent addiction that fans of WW2 TBS will enjoy;  just be sure to have lots of time available!

REVIEW
As many reviews here suggest, this game shows a clear descendance from Panzer General (for those who remember that venerable series).  Those older still, will recognize the style as the computerized form of SPI games or Avalon HIll's Squad Leader Series =  Boardgames with cardboard maps and real dice, so absorbing that shouts and hand slamming could punctuate play, with teams of players hanging on every die roll - cursing and posturing at foul or fair fortune.
I love this game, so for those who want the perspective of a fan, I will put up the main things that I respctfully still find some fault with - and later why those didn;t keep me from acquiring and enjoying the title.
Problems
1)
This game brings all that good stuff back I mention in the first para.. but obviously with the ease and greater detail possible only in a computerized instance.  While Panzer Corps is every bit as addictive as I remember those old games being this comes at a price as multiplayer is only asynchronous PBEM and only 1v1.  A shame, even if it is understandable with the limited objectives of the designers, this should not keep serious players from considering this title if they have the necessary green.  And that's another thing...
2)
At the time of thie writing, the regular price for this aging title is simply too high, with all the DLCs and the base game still costing $140 US when not on sale.  You need those DLCs to play the grand campaign which is by far the queen of the chessboard of experiences of the title, and would leave a big hollow place in one's game world not to have.  We purchased a few copies of this while on a 70% sale so the total bundle amounted to around the price of a regular Triple A title.  Thats for a title that is 5 years old, even if it IS a huge title in terms of content and an incredible amount of work is contained in it.  Many people probably don't care about large segments of that body of work... regardless of the depth it may add to the game experience.
3)
Repetition of scenario format and victory conditions makes some people go 'spla' and it can be a bit annoying at times since other means of accomplishing a scenario objective clearly offer themselves, and any afficianado of WW2 can think of dozens of objectives in history that could be modeled easily enough.
Benefits
1)
Library.  The detalied library of all the equipment provided in the game is an amazing resource and is accompanied by enlargeable diagrams.
2)
This highlights a lot of the ways in which the game models supply, fuel, and replacement.  It feels right, and the various equipment and formations feel properly weighted because of that research as well as clearly, a great deal of playtesting.
3)
There are few bugs.  No show stoppers.  Weird.  (heh !)
4)
WHen its on sale its a good value.  Many many units, and plenty of diversity.
5)
Granular control and difficulty settings.
6)
Not a computer hog, and while it is fun to look at, its no eye candy maven.  If you are looking for something to throw tri-sli at, you've taken a wrong turn somewhere...  (Hah ha ha ha!)
7)
If you leave it set to reasonable variation of results (die roll), there will be those times you WILL be grumpy and cry out loud... put your face in your palm, and reel so far back... "that you can clutch a fringe or two of the windy past" when we rolled real dice, and shouted "GODDA--- uhhhh ---NICE!"
Buy it on sale. but do get it if watching a playthrough makes you want to watch another one.  :)  ~'Crazy Uncle' Al

This is a surprisingly addictive little puzzler. You must connect randomly generated train stations with rail networks, and keep the stations from over-crowding by shipping passengers from place to place.
Where this game really shines is with it's minimalist design. This game could be held up in design schools across the world as a fine example of how clever design can make or break a game. In this case, make it. It's minimalist, but it's so intuitive that you don't even really need to think about the interface. You can concentrate on the game.
However... after four hours of gameplay I've unlocked all the maps, and I wonder about the game's longevity.
I can see myself coming back to this frequently - but the WOW factor is probably going to wear off now that I don't have a particular goal... and that's what this game is missing. A purpose.
Playing the game for its own ends is all well and good... but once I ran out of tangible goals, I really found myself wondering what was next.  Sure, I can play each map over and over, but I've *done* everything.  There are other game modes (endless, which seems like a waste of time, and extreme, which I'll probably try later) but once you've unlocked all the maps, there doesn't seem to be a 'hook' anymore.
This is a great game. I recommend it. It's a delight to play, and is beautifully designed... but I'm not sure there's enough of it. Get it, definitely... but wait for it to go on sale.

First thing, if you can't play this game (seriously, can't you Google search the errors you get? Usually, there's a fix somewhere, for almost everything) and are negativating the reviews, honestly, don't do that, there's a patch that fix it, so you'll be able to play the game on Windows 7 forward (I play it on Win10 without a problem). So please, stop blaming the game for your lack of care for playing it. The reviews are mixed because people can't simply look for a fix, that you basically just copy to the game's folder and there it is, play it to your heart content.
Now, to the actual review:
Manhunt is one of that few games that even though it's pretty repetitive, it's still fun as hell. The story is pretty simple and the game don't really take time deepening it, but still entertaining, and it's a gameplay that don't give you much time to think about it.
A gameplay which, by the way, is really good, following the stealth genre for most of the time, but sometimes you can just take a gun and Rambo around (even though I warn you, Cash is human and will die fast, and also the aim is not that great).
Voice acting is not really bad but nothing special, exception is Starkweather's, his voice apparently got more attention since you'll hear it for most of the game.
The difficulty of the game could be higher, actually, 'cause the AI is really dumb. Seriously, there are moments that I was almost angry at how stupid they are. You're hiding in a little shadowy corner and a guy is looking for you. He walks around and looks, about 1~2 meters away, directly at the corner you're hiding. He's close enough to even hear your breath, but no, he don't see you and simply walks back like. Or you shoot a guy, they start chasing you, you hide and they don't find you. Just wait some seconds (or minutes, not sure) and they will completely forgot that there's a guy dead on the middle of the street and simply go back to their "daily activities". It's kinda frustrating, but funny as hell too.
Also, a point that I'd like to say, but it's more based on personal opinion, is that the game is much more fun on Hard difficult. See, when you play on Normal, there's a radar that tells you where the enemies are and if they're aware of your presence, while on Hard, there's no radar at all, so you have to follow the sounds (the music changes when they're alert so it's pretty easy to know) and well, trust your stealth instincts. If you don't know if there's someone coming from the next corridor, get on the wall and check before putting your head in danger, or make some noise to see if the area is clear, making sure to hide right after. So I think you got my point, a good part of the fun is lost when you have the radar, but it's  basically my opinion.
So, I give it a 8/10, specially considering when it was released. It's a very good and fun experience, worth the money (and the time looking for a patch cof cof). Just ignore the reviews, look for the fix while downloading this great game and enjoy it!

The thing about Dredmor is that, on the surface, it's really just an average roguelike, intended to ease people into the genre by featuring colorful graphics and easy controls (with mouse support!).
But Dredmor actually does have a few things going for it:
- Workshop support.
- Witty Dialogue.
- Skill Trees (most roguelikes only have a class system, with each only having one specific ability that you're allowed to build on).
- Actually being a roguelike, in spite of its goal of easing people into the system.
Dredmor's Skills are on a build-as-you-want-it basis, so you can take a magic skill tree and pair it with a warrior skill tree with some (possibly disastrous) degree of efficiency. And with every update adding a few more skills, you can technically play a lot of classes without having to play the same combo ever again.
It's also actually a roguelike, compared to "roguelikes" like Binding of Isaac (don't get me wrong, that's a fun game, but it's not a roguelike as some people claim it to be), Enter the Gungeon, and so on and so forth.
Of course, it wins on Gaslamp's sharp wit department. You might end up chuckling at least once at all the referential humor the game boasts.
