I recommend it, but only because it's a good time-waster – not because it's all that great.
Two Digits involves clicking 9 numbers with the goal of equalizing their values.  It basically depends on mathematics and interval recognition, and if you are good at these two skills you can beat this game in a few hours.
The problem with the game is that there isn't really any difficulty curve.  Some early levels can take 10 minutes to complete as you struggle to determine which numbers can yield the solution; meanwhile, several of the later levels can be completed in a few seconds, clicking two numbers which obviously add up to a third number on the board.  There was a stretch of 20 or so levels in the middle that consisted of me going "these two numbers are 10 apart, these are 20 apart, these are 30 apart.  Done."  Then, there was another stretch of 5 or 10 in the late game that functioned the same way.
There was never a moment where I needed all 9 numbers to solve the level, and that's kind of a problem.  Early puzzles should be solvable with 2-4 numbers, but later levels ought to use 7, 8, or even all 9 numbers to solve.  There's no real complexity that prevents you from solving the problem; no brain-wracking moment that stresses you out for thirty minutes.  The only thing that prevented me from finishing it faster was eye fatigue from just staring at 9 numbers over and over.
So, I don't like the game very much, but I'm satisfied with my purchase and I do recommend it.  After all, it IS a good way to pass a few hours, which is what I wanted.  And perhaps it will present challenges to those people who aren't arithmetically inclined.  To the rest of us, though, it's too simplistic, and doesn't have a difficulty curve.

I love a good murder mystery, but
is not a murder mystery.
Disclaimer: I only played the first half hour of the game, the tutorial level.  Later, when deciding what game to play of an evening, I considered
for a moment and already it felt like a chore to go back to it.  I elected to refund.
The premise is interesting: a
-style setup in which you relive the same time period over and over, searching for a way to change the situation.  Sounds cool on paper, right?
For me, the reality was an exercise in repetitious frustration, as failing again and again (and again) is integral to the design.  You gather a snippet or two of information, the majority of which is useless, and run out of time when the murder is committed (possibly right in front of you ... again, there is no actual mystery involved).  Then you start over and look elsewhere and fail again, then start over again until you find the one critical element that you can arbitrarily change, and as soon as you find it, the level is over.  Then it's immediately back to failing in a new set of circumstances.  This is not what I would describe as enjoyable.
There is no intrigue, no motivation, no deduction.  Gameplay is a brute force accumulation of character movements and prop manipulation.  Repeat and accumulate until something works.
On PC I found the controls counterintuitive, coarse, and annoying.  The simple act of walking through a door feels clumsy and time consuming.  This was clearly made to be played with a controller from a couch; prompts are huge on the screen and inputs are few and slow to respond.
Maybe I'm being too harsh, but this was not what I expected or hoped for.  Perhaps I was biased right from the title screen, because I find "Electro Swing" music grating and obnoxious.  Maybe I would have loved the game if the music was appropriate for the high society setting.  Sadly, we'll never know.

Update for my FAVOURITE GAME EVER - March 2016:
I've played Thief 2014 for 88 hours as of today, and it seems like I'm not going to stop anytime soon. Best stealth game I've ever played.
Honestly, how can people judge a game after less than 1 hour of gameplay? LOL?
I especially enjoy this game because you got every freedom you can imagine, hardly any restrictions, and even I discover new things every time I play. The gameplay is very dynamic, and the gameplay got highly improved in comparison to Thief 1, 2 and 3.
The story's alright, the graphics are great, the music rocks and I enjoy especially the whole atmosphere. It's this gloomy silence I miss in many games, which are way too colorful and loud for my personal taste. However I admit that most people in the game annoyed me, but Basso. He's my favourite character.
((Personally I highly agree with Garrett's attitude of "Leave me alone and let me do my own thing."))
There are so many different way to achieve something, so many ways to go somewhere, you won't get bored. The side quests are plenty and very entertaining to play!
I play Thief 2014 in a very peaceful way, as I agree that quietly sneaking in somewhere is much more challenging than creating an ankle-deep pool of blood.
Once you take out a guard with your blackjack, he'll stay that way until the end of the chapter, so there's no need at all to kill anybody.
Play the game on Master with everything turned off but focus ability. Great fun ^^
I really enjoy the collection display! My favourites are the city heritage plaques.
10/10, simple as that.
IMPORTANT:
This game is not for the impatient! If you're impatient, short tempered and have a short attention span, go play something else.
If you just want to run through a level instead of really using your brain, imagination and your environment for looking for hidden loot, go play something else.
This game is neither for the aggressiv ones! If you love to stab, slash and shoot people instead of sneaking past them, go play something else.
That's the reason my friends don't play it. They say themselves they're way too impatient and trigger-happy for Thief 2014. Fair enough!
I actually think this game is aimed at a slightly older audience, around 25+.

After 25 days of playing Thief, 160+ hours, 4 finished games (with all available DLC) there are only 3 words:
BEST GAMES EVER

First, I'll address the issues a lot of people have been bringing up about this game:
This has been announced as being addressed later; as this game was a dual-platform release on PC and XBox by a development team that at various times ran out of funding, limiting it to 60fps across the board let them get it shipped sooner.
I play on a 180Hz Acer Predator monitor in many games, I appreciate high-refresh-rate gameplay, but it's really impossible to notice in this particular game due to a combination of the art style and gameplay. As others have said, many competitive-oriented brawlers (like Smash Bros and Street Fighter series) have been limited to 60fps, and it's accepted there. Don't approach this as an OverWatch FPS MOBA competitor, but more of a 3D brawler MOBA.
Seriously, grow up. Over 80% of folks have that aspect ratio in the latest
and that doesn't even touch on how that is
standard for TV. AKA: XBox.
For competitive-oriented games, preventing aspect ratios from granting advantages has become more and more common; OverWatch does this as well, you can either 'zoom in' or 'letterbox/pillarbox' your screen to 16:9 aspect ratio, but you'll never, ever see more than someone on a 16:9 aspect ratio screen there either.
Please stop playing on a potato.
My
has 8GB of RAM, ten years ago. RAM is cheap, and if you have less than 8GB of RAM you're seriously crippling your computers performance in a lot of ways. At
it's the single best upgrade you can make to a computer today.
See above regarding money issues. Perfect World Entertainment footed the bill to see this game released, so yes their launcher with Champions Online, Star Trek Online, Neverwinter, etc is visible briefly and requires an extra click or two to actually launch the game.
When it came down to either "Don't release Gigantic" or "Release with the Arc Launcher" I'm very glad they chose to go with the Arc Launcher so this game didn't get cancelled before release.
Have you played any other game when it first came out?
Also, make sure you play the actual PvP mode not just PvE. PvE is limited to a single map at this time, while PvP modes have a LOT more maps.
As said, approach this as a brawler like Smash Bros or Guild Wars 2 that happens to be 5v5 and in 3D. Gameplay is a combination of dashing around and brief fights, and the game focusses entirely on objectives so it's very possible to end up with a very high score despite having 'negative' K:D ratio. If your team wounds the enemy monster, even if you team-wipe every single time, you win.
This is an entire game built around the type of complex multi-objective layered gameplay of the HanaMura map in Heroes of the Storm, so it's balanced around that level of complexity. Generally you'll end up deciding between
summons to either give yourself places to recover faster from after team fights if you're tougher, or
summons if you want to prevent the enemy from approaching from certain directions. Unlike in some games, the 'walls' it places are very effective at locking down escape routes, with your own team able to move through them as they lower when you touch them.
For most characters, when you're starting, just use the 'auto build' skill selections, worry about learning the gameplay and finding some characters you enjoy first, then go back and learn various characters in more depth later. Most of them can very EXTREMELY widely depending on the approach to skills you take, such as the 'Bastion' like
which defaults to a very rushdown-like build but can be taken into an extremely tanky/sniper build as one obvious example.
Surprisingly good. While some characters are weak or very situational so they rarely if ever get chosen on most maps, they all seem to have a purpose and many times what's weak for one person is overwhelming for another. While some such as HK-206 are broadly useful and usable, others such as Griselma are not, but nothing is poisonously bad to choose currently.
This is a game that offers a very different take on the MOBA-like genre which is very fun, and works excellently in 3D, with the different characters very noticable at range and all very unique, noisy, and entertaining. It runs very well, very smoothly, and I hope grows well with time.
The art direction and choice of "empowerment" roles for your heroes lost me.

This is a mostly elegant puzzler that has you constructing stylized light rail lines in big cities and avoiding overcrowding at your stations for as long as possible. There's not much else to it other than daily challenges with leaderboards, a mode that makes all your tracks permanent and a mode that disables terminal overcrowding. It's kind of like if
was a survival game.
There's a couple problems that don't kneecap the game, but are still worth noting. The music is automatically generated from train movement and passenger sounds, which might get grating after a while. Stations pop up seemingly randomly enough, and end-of-week upgrades are determined randomly enough, that games are as much up to chance as they are up to your on-the-spot problem solving ability. At higher levels of play, the game becomes more about micromanagement than triage and strategic planning; "train warping" and "ghost lines" are terms often used to describe skills that are essential to earning high leaderboard positions and some achievements, but woefully immersion-breaking for a transit game. I still recommend this - I can see it being something you play while you're commuting yourself. Bonus points for having a night mode too.

"Wait, Auckland doesn't have a..."
"Oh. OH. I SEE THE JOKE HERE."
Brought the game on the strength of that joke alone. However, the game is strong enough on its own merits that I'm very pleased with my purchase. On endless, you've got a fantastic idle game you can fiddle with while listening to a podcast, trying to up your efficiency. On normal, you've got an intriguing puzzle that requires your constant attention, analysis and problem-solving skills [along with the occasional gamble] as you try and make sure that the people flow so as to not get left standing on a station to the point where their complaints get you shut down.
As a side note, I like to imagine that this represents the complete anarchy of people who're waiting on a station platform for too long. An hour is fine, but when they're waiting for a whole day to get to work, they're probably going to start burning things to get your attention.
The way you draw 'lines' in both the sense of a metro and in the sense of them being literal lines is a kinaesthetic pleasure. The visual and auditory senses combine to create a meditative yet active and engaging mood. Fantastic work on that sound, by the way. Very few games combine what's happening in the game with the sound the player hears that well. You can see from screenshots, too, the aesthetic appeal of the game. If you don't get some amount of pleasure just from looking at the game, then you might want to check whether or not you actually want to buy it.
In normal [which in some ways feels like 'survival', at the end of each week you get an upgrade to your system. These vary from map to map [In Cairo your trains only hold four passengers, in another of the maps you can get fast bullet trains] but you always get another train of some description which you can plop on an existing line or use as the basis of a new one. After accepting this, you get the choice between one of two additional upgrades, both of which you'll sorely need. Perhaps you need another two bridges to complete some loops, or another car to double the capacity of a train, maybe a fourth line so that you can make each more efficient. Whichever you choose, you may within moments regret your bad, stupid choice, because there's now a station on that one little island you've been looking at, wondering how soon you'll need more bridges to access. Now you have to redo a track or two to free up a bridge to make a line that reaches it. And a line it shall be, because although loops are generally more efficient, you just can't do it with that track if you want it to cover where you need it to cover.
Thus is the loop of the game. Meet demand. Watch demand rise. Panic. Meet demand.
If I must provide some outright negatives, I'll say that the game does what I might call a shoddy job at teaching you the basic controls. The tooltips telling you how to play only pop up once, so if you missed them, good luck. You can fiddle around a bit and make peace with losing a couple of games prematurely in order to work it all out, but some things it doesn't even seem to tell you [at least in enough detail you you'd understand it at first], like the fact you can click in the middle of a line between two stations and drag it to another station to add it to the link. A basic tool at your disposal, though not indespensible, the alternative way to perform the action is more time consuming, which gets in the way of the main appeal of this game, which is its creative flow.
That being said, all in all, this is a fantastic minimalist piece of logical art. The couple of issues I had learning the game at first were all resolved within the first hour, and I've had a great time since  then. It's fresh, and even after you understand it, the occasional curveball always keeps it interesting, as does the pursuit of perfection.

is a platformer that is reminiscent of old-school games like
, mainly by the gameplay revolving around killing enemies by throwing objects and corpses at enemies (she also has a sword which is mainly good for killing smaller enemies). In the case of enemy corpses some of them have different attacks when used (like archers firing arrows down on enemies, or firewitches throwing out waves of fire) which allow you to deal with large groups or tough enemies easily. The bosses are generally simple but can do massive damage, so it boils down to finding out when it’s safe to attack them (with one boss being more of a puzzle instead of a straight fight). There is also a leveling system but it mainly exists to keep the player on even terms with the game, but it does mean it is possible to farm levels if the player feels they need to.
Graphics are decent for 16-bit fare, with bosses having a different style of animation when compared to everything else (skeletal animation vs. sprites). Sound and music are nothing too special, they do their job without becoming overly grating. Keyboard controls work well and are rebind-able, with controller support being an option. In terms of stability the game ran at 60 FPS on my old laptop without much problem, and I’ve had a few crashes but nothing that outright stopped me from finishing the game.
After finishing the game once you unlock several New Game Plus modes, all of which must be beaten to access the true final boss (think
but larger in scope). Each mode adds or changes something that fundamentally alters how that mode is played; Bat Princess for example makes it so only bats can be damaged by your sword, which forces you to approach large enemy encounters more strategically. Meanwhile, Naturist Princess becomes more of a stealth variation in which you have no sword and lower health but can make most enemies peaceful, so you can run by them unharmed. Most of the modes also include a double jump which can allow you to bypass certain sections of the stages entirely, which can break up the tedium.
While each mode presents their own challenge I feel this is both the game’s biggest strength and weakness. The main issues I felt were that apart from padding out the game’s length, I also felt some modes were more varied than others; Drunk Princess is the weakest in terms of variety, as apart from the screen moving effect and stronger enemies it isn’t that different from the main mode. The difficulty can also vary significantly between each mode: Angry Princess is the first mode you unlock and can easily be the one of the most aggravating, while Naturist Princess (the second to last mode you unlock) is by far the easiest overall.
All of that said though, I did enjoy the game. It does have a generally fast pace and tries to avoid overly cheap deaths like many old video games were guilty of doing back in the 90s. However, the over-saturation of New Game Plus modes did put a damper on the overall enjoyment. Because of that I can’t truly recommend it, but it’s still far from the worst I’ve played.

Two Digits is a combination of maths and puzzle game. At each level, you have 9 numbers listed and you must select with one colour one to four numbers and then another one to 4 numbers with another colour, knowing the sum of the numbers in each colour must be equal.
I was initially very attracted to the idea because I love little puzzles that require a lot of thinking, but for once, I found this one too difficult.
However, I will not give a negative review because I think some players may enjoy this game but it depends on the degree of challenge expected. I used a guide for 75% of the 250 levels because I could not do without, and because I didn’t even have fun anymore.
From the same publisher Cleverweek, I preferred the game Tenrow for example, I found it more enjoyable despite an increasing level of difficulty.
Anyway, I recommend Two Digits to players who really love the challenge of mental arithmetic and have the patience to spend a lot of time thinking on every level.

Two Digits est un petit jeu de calcul mental. A chaque niveau, 9 chiffres vous sont listés et vous devez sélectionner d’une couleur un à 4 chiffres puis d’une autre un à 4 autres chiffres en sachant que la somme des uns doit être égale à la somme des autres.
J’ai été au départ très attirée par le concept puisque j’adore tous les petits puzzles qui demandent un bon niveau de réflexion mais pour le coup, j’ai trouvé celui-ci bien trop difficile.
Pour autant, je ne vais pas donner un avis négatif puisque je pense que certains joueurs peuvent apprécier ce jeu mais que cela dépend du degré de challenge attendu. Pour ma part, sur les 250 niveaux, j’ai utilisé un guide pour 75% d’entre eux parce que je n’y arrivais pas sans et surtout parce que le jeu ne me paraissait même plus amusant.
Du même éditeur Cleverweek, j’ai par exemple préféré le jeu Tenrow que j’ai trouvé beaucoup plus fun jusqu’au bout malgré un niveau de difficulté croissant.
En tout cas, je ne recommande Two Digits qu’aux joueurs qui aiment vraiment le challenge du calcul mental et qui ont la patience de passer pas mal de temps à réfléchir à chaque niveau.

I'm not sure this is a game I can recommend.

But for replay value I can't suggest anyone buys it - it'll last you until you finish it (which likely won't take too long once you figure out how it works - the tutorial could use some video or pictures. More instruction than the one or two sentences it consists of), but for a challenging game Three Digits is tougher and better as a game.
I think the main problem is, it doesn't innovate enough. When you figure out how it works there's not a lot beyond whatever random numbers the game gives you, there are no additional challenges or tools at your disposal and when you have over a hundred levels there needs to be more variety than the same three-by-three grid of random numbers.

Really fun game if you love math. Achievements are unlocked automatically just by beating levels, which makes me wish they had thought of some more complicated achievements such as beating a level within a certain time or using certain quantities of numbers in your solution.

Usually I make funny reviews but this game definitely deserves a serious one.
Part of the reason why I enjoy this game is because its atmosphere resonates with me (dark, smokey, mysterious, depressing) but I also enjoy it because it's just a ton of fun.
It has the kind of immersive, depressive atmosphere that makes you dream about running along the rooftops of a broken city bathed in moonlight, while also being a load of fun at the same time. The game gives you the options to turn off every single bit of the HUD, which is exactly what I did at the start, not only making the game more difficult but also making it that much more immersive.
You don't have any gimmicks either, unlike in other stealth games. The only tools you have, and the only tools you need, are your ingenuity and your short range shadow-dash. That's it. There are a few special powers you can use, although like I said, they are not gimmicky at all, and only provide minor bonuses to situational awareness and combat ability. No teleports, no sticky cams; nothing of that nature. The main thing you need is your head. That's it.
You also have specialized arrows, but they aren't needed at all. They are strong, but expensive. Use them when you get tired of having to be smart, but don't expect them to last. You have an especially limited supply of the stronger arrows (you can only carry 3 of the explsoive arrows without DLC.)
Patience is a big thing as well. If you are patient enough, you can get by anything, while also incidentally eavesdropping, allowing you to find out where hidden treasures and hidden paths are. Thief won't reward you for sprinting through every shadow. Take your time, look around, listen, and be patient. Take in the atmosphere and you'll be rewarded for it; if not by hearing a treasure's location, then at least you'll find the coin directly under your nose.
Thief is definitely one of the best modern stealth games and, as an owner of the previous games in the series, far surpasses them in every way. Garrett is a far more animated and identifiable character (not to mention he's hot, no homo  tho) the gameplay is very well refined and very great fun for intelligent and patient people, and the world is an absolute blast to get lost in.
Buy this game, crank up some Depressive Metal, and get playing.

Today, Dungeons of Dredmor (DoD) completes five years, and still remains a great introduction to the classic style of Roguelike, while it offers a great deal of challenge to veterans of the genre.
DoD features character building, with a wide range of skills to choose; easy to understand mechanics; great dose of humor, with a lot of references to movies and games; a fantastic soundtrack (the best of this kind of game, IMHO); Steam Workshop support for mods and backup on Steam Cloud (despite the store page not show this feature). The gameplay it's slow paced, ideal for a strategic approach instead of an action-oriented one, and demands patience from the player.
The biggest bless and curse of this game, at the same time, it's the loot fest at every level. When you start playing, you'll certainly spend a decent part of your playthrough managing your loot on your tiny inventory (remember to use Shift+left click to pick up  and drop items with more ease). Thankfully, the "Conquest of the Wizardlands" DLC adds the Pocket Dimension - a place where you can store unlimited amounts of loot. By the way, this game is so cheap that you should buy the complete package for a better experience.
Last but not least, I strongly recommend you to activate the OpenGL on the launch options to achieve a smoother experience, avoiding crashes caused by memory leak, while it enable the Steam Overlay. To do this, simply right click Dungeons of Dredmor in your Steam library -> Properties -> Set launch options -> type in -opengl -> press ok.

This is by far one of, if not the, best roguelikes. It's got all the staples; permadeath (optional), difficulty levels, dungeon crawling, randomised level layouts, and different skills that let you customise your build. The skills aren't the typical RPG '+1' stat boosts, they're actually interesting and unique, and they combine with skills from other trees to make a huge variety of ways to approach the game. And you have just one objective; get to floor 10 (or 15 with the DLC enabled) and kill Lord Dredmor.
It's challenging, but not essentially impossible like so many roguelikes. Because it's turn-based and offers plenty of different skills, there's plenty of ways to tackle this one. I love that the weapons, trinkets and armour (of which there are many) are static and not procedurally generated. This means you can go hunting for a particular item you need for your build or to deal with a given type of enemy. And when you come across that super rare, super powerful weapon...
An amazingly good game. On top of it all, the game has a great sense of humour. Sure, it's a little rough around the edges. I'd love a bit more variety in the level randomisation. But as they're an indie developer I'm happy to cut them some slack. And it's so cheap; just give it a shot!

As a long time player of Overwatch, Smite, HOTS, Strike Of Kings and having a dabble with unreal tournament and quake in their golden years, I have to say this game is nothing like those, it presents a new formula which seems to be a culmination of a million and one different sources.
Pros
The graphics for this game are crisp and the colours are intense and vibrant with an art style thats a perfect mixture of borderlands cell shading, shadow of the colossus and ICO.
The games themselves can be fast or slow depending on the teams played with and the map played on and how these change over the match, i have had 5 minute fragathon matches and big drawn out moba like 30-45 min matches.
The maps themselves are greatly balanced and SPOILER ALERT change over the course of the match as the guardians clash together changing the arenas entirely, sometimes making them smaller or making them more open with greater ambush potential
The scoring system although barebones is different from the average hero shooter/moba in that it focuses on k/d/a and this new thing called an efficiency rating, this really peaks my interest and gives players a good look into who is pulling their weight in a team although it would be nice to see how this is calculated.
Cons
The game is locked at 60 fps yes, this is a problem for the FPS monsters (of which seems to be the richer pc master races guys amongst us) it will be a problem for some but for others who are just here for fun it wont matter too much.
The lack of a competitive ranked match system is something that is concerning as this game has had a troubled past and it would be beneficial for them to push an esports formula, although i know that market is pretty saturated.
The microtransaction formula is a little on the steep side making it aa bit too heavy of a grind fest for the free to play players who dont purchase the packs. As a note for the devs I would beg you dont pull a paladins and overcomplicate the pack buying but instead put on regular sales and make some featured packs just to entice players to come back.
Overall I would give this game a solid 8/10 its a well balanced hero shooter moba that rips up the rulebook and instead makes a whole new concept not yet seen in this genre, it will be fantastic to be playing this game as it grows out of obscurity and into fame.

I really like the premise of this game, however simple [and I'm not all about mindless violence in games like Killing Floor or Hatred]. This is one of those early kinds of stealth games that really do better than most stealth games today, except for those like Dishonored. But the flaws weren't NEARLY as prevalent as they are in this PC port.
The controls are alright, actually: the game goes out of its way to instruct you on every action you can take, the very first chance you have to take said action. But very early on, you'll need to download and install three fixes; three files you'll add to the game's folder to make a gate of all things open up. It won't even open up for the enemy unless you use these fixes, and I'm sure they remedy a few other issues I've had the pleasure of not having to experience. After that, the game is relatively enjoyable.
BUT THE ENEMY A,I. IS SO BAD D:
I mean, they do their job if they see you, yeah, sure. But, being a game about stealth, you're encouraged to take that gameplay route. But a lot of times--and I mean a LOT of times--you're almost forced to make noise just so the enemies come your way. And this is because...get ready... They have trouble turning. They really suck at turning any number of degrees, in any direction. They just kind of shimmy their legs around and shuffle, whistling and being even more annoying, if waiting on their butts isn't irritating enough for you. You're being forced not to play the game for a length of time, and so, take me for example: I'd get so tired of waiting [for this absurd reason in this stealth game], that I'd just ram myself into a dude that refused to move, and wrecked him with my bat. I'd do this more times than I'd like...
Wanting to play through the rest of this game, but I don't see myself doing it. And I'm a very patient person.

Here is my little (first time play) review of Turmoil in romanian language:

Turmoil is a 2-D, omniscient business-simulation, taking place during the brink of the 20th Century, where you take the role of one of four people who are considered rivals of each other, each trying to make their gains through the profitable oil industry (OIL RUSH!!!). The main goal of the game is to procure enough profits through the discovery of oil pools, harvesting that oil, and selling them to two companies at certain times in order to reap the most profit.
There are two gamemodes: Campaign and Single Game.
Campaign is.... campaign. You play through the story of the game and to the end.
Single Game is basically
round of the game as similar in the campaign, but you can decide what is in this one round and what isn't.
The game itself is played most like a pathway game, where you have to build pipes in different patterns to get the most oil from a certain pool. One such example would be if there's a large oil pool and you have two oil towers sharing the pool together through the complex (or simple) connection of their pipelines. In addition, according to the tags, this game IS a strategy game because players can buy upgrades that better support their harvesting of oil or overcome obstacles that may come their way, and there are two companies (will discuss that later on).
Speaking of obstacles, as you progress in the campaign (yes, there is a campaign) of the game, you will be placed in a different region every time it is completed. As such, there are four regions in the game as follows (the names I made up, hopefully clear enough): Grassland, Desert, Forest, and Winter Wonderland (the Snow area). Each and every one of these regions has their own obstacles listed below:
Nothing.
Rocks requiring a drill to bypass, plus diamonds requiring a mole to dig up in order to bypass (and get the diamond itself).
Gas pools that can unfortunately speed up the fill time of each oil tower, increasing the likelihood of oil spills.
Temperature problems that require thermals.
More precisely, other obstacles include the use of a two-industry problem and, of course, oil spills.
With the two-industry problem, there are two businesses during each round of the campaign, a Left and a Right business. Each business has a certain pricing per barrel of oil that continues to fluctuate, thus making Turmoil a strategy game because players have to decide which business they want to sell their oil to. Do they want to sell their oil to the Left purchasing at $0.20 per oil barrel, or the Right purchasing at $1.40 per oil barrel? Furthermore, this system becomes more and more intense as you get to later parts of the game because you'll basically be going back and forth repeatedly while focusing on digging oil, selling oil, and continuously trying to find the oil.
With oil spills, each oil tower has a gauge, and when it fills, a timer shows up. That timer indicates when the tower is about to spill oil, and when that happens, you lose profits (so don't let it happen).
Every round, you, as an oil profiteer, are able to purchase upgrades for your oil production, as well as bribe people to support your own gains. In addition, every round you need to decide what piece of land you want to take for your oil mining operations and you DO HAVE TO THINK CAREFULLY! If you don't, you'll likely end up with a horrible drilling spot, which isn't fun.
Also, every round you'll be able to auction for a portion of the Mayor's stock, and the goal of the game is to not only have the most cash, but with that cash win the most of the Mayor's stock, basically whoever is the new Mayor wins the game.
Personally, this game is great. As simple as it is, it's very creative, very fun, and can be addicting after finishing the campaign (might play it again). The game mechanics and strategy-esque style of the game makes it fun and worth the price, the style of the game is very clever, and the left-right system of playing with selling the oil is enjoyable. This is a hard game to recommend. I bought this early by the sole virtue of Jim Sterling's review. Long story short: I was oversold on it. It's still a very good game, but Mr. Sterling had me expecting something outstanding, something that would stick with me, and The Sexy Brutale didn't do that.
Short story long: This is a groundhog-day/adventure-puzzle game where you watch murders most foul, then suss out how to prevent them. The Sexy Brutale has well-polished art and sound design that emphasize wealthy excess, and most of the puzzles are clever without being difficult. These virtues are pretty much enough to make it a decent game, but the real deciding factor of its lasting quality rests on its ambitiously thoughtful narrative. Without giving anything away, the endgame revelations will either work for you, or they won't. While I appreciated the effort that went into making the story impactful, I wasn't impacted.
My bottom line rests on an unfortunately useless platitude: Your mileage may vary. So, should you get this game? Sure, roll the dice, but maybe do it on a sale.

"Wait, Auckland doesn't have a..."
"Oh. OH. I SEE THE JOKE HERE."
Brought the game on the strength of that joke alone. However, the game is strong enough on its own merits that I'm very pleased with my purchase. On endless, you've got a fantastic idle game you can fiddle with while listening to a podcast, trying to up your efficiency. On normal, you've got an intriguing puzzle that requires your constant attention, analysis and problem-solving skills [along with the occasional gamble] as you try and make sure that the people flow so as to not get left standing on a station to the point where their complaints get you shut down.
As a side note, I like to imagine that this represents the complete anarchy of people who're waiting on a station platform for too long. An hour is fine, but when they're waiting for a whole day to get to work, they're probably going to start burning things to get your attention.
The way you draw 'lines' in both the sense of a metro and in the sense of them being literal lines is a kinaesthetic pleasure. The visual and auditory senses combine to create a meditative yet active and engaging mood. Fantastic work on that sound, by the way. Very few games combine what's happening in the game with the sound the player hears that well. You can see from screenshots, too, the aesthetic appeal of the game. If you don't get some amount of pleasure just from looking at the game, then you might want to check whether or not you actually want to buy it.
In normal [which in some ways feels like 'survival', at the end of each week you get an upgrade to your system. These vary from map to map [In Cairo your trains only hold four passengers, in another of the maps you can get fast bullet trains] but you always get another train of some description which you can plop on an existing line or use as the basis of a new one. After accepting this, you get the choice between one of two additional upgrades, both of which you'll sorely need. Perhaps you need another two bridges to complete some loops, or another car to double the capacity of a train, maybe a fourth line so that you can make each more efficient. Whichever you choose, you may within moments regret your bad, stupid choice, because there's now a station on that one little island you've been looking at, wondering how soon you'll need more bridges to access. Now you have to redo a track or two to free up a bridge to make a line that reaches it. And a line it shall be, because although loops are generally more efficient, you just can't do it with that track if you want it to cover where you need it to cover.
Thus is the loop of the game. Meet demand. Watch demand rise. Panic. Meet demand.
If I must provide some outright negatives, I'll say that the game does what I might call a shoddy job at teaching you the basic controls. The tooltips telling you how to play only pop up once, so if you missed them, good luck. You can fiddle around a bit and make peace with losing a couple of games prematurely in order to work it all out, but some things it doesn't even seem to tell you [at least in enough detail you you'd understand it at first], like the fact you can click in the middle of a line between two stations and drag it to another station to add it to the link. A basic tool at your disposal, though not indespensible, the alternative way to perform the action is more time consuming, which gets in the way of the main appeal of this game, which is its creative flow.
That being said, all in all, this is a fantastic minimalist piece of logical art. The couple of issues I had learning the game at first were all resolved within the first hour, and I've had a great time since  then. It's fresh, and even after you understand it, the occasional curveball always keeps it interesting, as does the pursuit of perfection.

Although I've played it a fair bit over the past few days, I can't fully recommend Mini Metro.
It uses the theme of a subway and subway map, but the experience of drawing subway lines doesn't feel close to that.
New nodes pop up sort of randomly and every day the subway gets a little busier, until a single station gets overcrowded. The mechanics, such as not being able to cross your own tracks, except at a station, and the fact that every train *must* stop at each connected station, make it hard to recreate traditional subway lay-outs, such as local vs. express trains.
In the end, Instead of a making a system that's easily navigable, you're optimising it for mathematical constraints, and often end up with a sytem that's incredibly gerrymandered and Kafkaesque, rather than something a sane person would want to navigate.
The result is that  during too few moments do you feel that you're running a public transport system, even in the abstract. It ends up a, somewhat interesting, puzzler where you're trying to optimise for mathematical constraints with a little "transport sauce" poured over it.
Although the various maps have their own little quirks, almost none of them display true character, nor do the differences affect gameplay much, with possibly the exception of Osaka, where you get the use of "Shinkansen" trains. As a result, as it is, Metro Mini hardly makes a difference  playing London, Sao Paulo or any other city. You could just as well be playing on some randomly-generated map.
All-in-all: an abstract puzzler with some limited appeal, but best avoided if you want some semblance of realism.
Overall: 5/10
The designers should've either gone for more realism, or ditch all the references to real-life and keep it a fully abstract puzzler. Now fans of neither genre get what they could have had.

I cannot currently recommend nor ever recommend this game. (You don't have to read the review just look how much i wrote for whats good and what's bad)
THE GOOD
I can say Total War Battles: kingdom greatly improves Total Wars' world building aspect. Cities can be built with walls, stables, barracks, churches, housing and slums tailoring to the landscape, albiet with severe building restrictions, but is a breath of fresh air. unforntunately that is all i can say that is good about this game. If you see people giving positive reviews, it is because of the world building and possibly because their patronage to Total War blinds them.
THE BAD
Total War Battles: Kingdom completely tosses out its beloved combat system, something that was quite renown in the industry and the hallmark of the Total war franchaise. I can see that they wanted to change the battle system because of its length it adds to the game, but what they have here is a joke. Virtually no strategy, each players units in a row and cannot flank another player's unit but charge straight ahead and ranged units must manually target unit squads, but they share a cooldown for this with all of the other ranged units, you probably have to play the game to understand.  Every battle missions gives you 8 xp for each of your units, and their upgrades to gain a skill or gain a rank is 200xp, generally speaking.
After every battle a player has to heal their units which costs about 1-4 gold depending on how much damage you take or wait 15 minutes or so. Paying the gold doesn't seem so bad because a player recieves 100 gold for starting but there is no real way of recouping gold unless you are lucky enough to find a gold ore deposit which gives you 2-4 gold. Gold is also used to speed things up such as filing in a dam, which takes 12hrs for 3 gold. While constructing buildings takes 10s, demolishing buildings takes 5hrs or 3 gold. Mining Stone takes  2 hrs or 3 gold. Needless to say, your debts catch up with you.
It is clear that the game was designed for IOS and ANDROID from the get go, and is designed with the smartphone game logic of inconvenience, that is waiting hours to do an action or pay real world money.
VERDICT
Don't get the game, I'll say it at the top, I'll say it at the bottom.
NOTES
To be fair, I only played about 1-2hrs of this game, the game could pick up, but I severely doubt it. I have played only  Total War Medieval I, Total War Medieval II, and Total War: Empire and am lacking the full spectrum of the Total War franchaise but I have loved what I played.

I really liked the original Thief. I was bad at it, and it was really hard, but it was GOOOOOOOOOD, and the challenge made it satisfying. I'm not one to compare reboots to the original, because I support the sentiment that a reboot should have a unique feel and it strikes me as a bit overly-sentimental when they try to make it as close to the source material as possible, like they're trying too hard to relive the glory days, so my opinions on this game are, overall, how the game stands on its own, but when the game tries to be like the The Dark Project, of course I have to compare it to the standard it's aiming for.
Thief does try to recreate the feeling of the original game, while also introducing modern gameplay mechanics, a new story, and more things to steal. However, it fails at almost everything it tries. It can't capture the essence of the original when it tries to, because it has no concept of what made The Dark Project enjoyable. In contrast, it's incapable of forming its own unique identity because most of the new ideas clash with the misdirected nostalgia. The writing is terrible, the voice acting is painfully average and uninspired, every new gameplay mechanic feels more like a tryhard gimmick, and you're tripping over loot to the point of it being an inconvenience and a distraction. Stealing things can be fun when you're required to be sneaky, but amazingly, stealth is rarely a factor since most of the loot is found in completely unoccupied rooms. That being said, when it's done right, it feels great. I really liked the instances of watching guard movment and carefully timing my steps to remain unseen to get that shiny object on the other side of the room, it's just a shame that these moments are so scarce in a game that should be built around this very idea.
Old ideas like listening to guards converse from around the corner are insultingly simplified to the point of no longer serving the intended purpose. Whereas the original Thief had realistic conversations that were usually interesting and occasionally informative, the guards in new Thief sound less like actual peers discussing current events and more like robots conveying conveniently useful information to the player, or at least it pretends to be, but most of their not-so-subtle hints are obvious and redundant. But it's not just the written script that makes NPC's feel hollow: the artificial intelligence is absolutely non-existant and seems to have accidentally been replaced by a dementia simulator, considering the only people in real-life I've ever seen act so absent-minded and apathetic to their surroundings were in a god damned nursing home.
Why does he keep the most valuable loot instead of selling it if he's a career thief? Because if he sold it, the player wouldn't get to have a collection of shiny things neatly displayed around your dim safehouse for you to stare at. Logical inconsistencies like this are abundant because everything in the game feels like it was designed for the PLAYER instead of the CHARACTER. Windows with scratch marks tell you where to climb, metal grates on the wall exist only for you to use your hook on, and many  paths seem to have been built specifically for a thief that's trying to avoid confrontation in a busy room. You don't feel like you're exploring a city or large buildings because their design is too linear to feel organic and convincing, the maps are so obviously intended to guide the player toward the objective so it's impossible to imagine anyone actually living in these spaces. Developers may try to convince you that it's a design choice, but it's really just an excuse for a lack of effort; claiming otherwise is saying you can't have fun exploring a detailed map, which was half the fun of the original.
With video game budgets constantly growing, it's flabbergasting to me that a game from 1998 can be more detailed, open, immersive, and be better written than a AAA title from 2014. It's trying to be way too many genres at once, and it doesn't really nail any of them, so you wind up getting a misguided array of half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥assets from better games. You MIGHT enjoy this game if you're into other modern blockbusters like Dishonored, but I can't honestly recommend it to anyone because it holds your hand so tightly that it comes across as insulting and offensive.

This game is simple enough. Old-school platform jumping game that feels right at home with anything from the SNES/Super Famicom, Genesis/MegaDrive, or TurboGrafx/PC Engine era. It plays like a cross between Super Mario Bros 2/ Doki Doki Panic and Castlevania. You throw things at the baddies, or whack them with your sword to drop them, then pick them up and throw them at other enemies. You can bounce off the heads of some enemies, while others hurt you. Don't touch enemies, spikes, or hazards. Whack torches to gain health pickups.
The controls are okay but not excellent, which, I suppose is typical for the kinds of games I'm comparing it to, but compared to the really good games of that time, it is somewhat lacking. For the record, I'm using an XBox 360 gamepad.
The soundtrack is excellent, easily up to SNES-par, but the sound effects are okay-but-not-great (notice a theme here?). The protagonist makes a lot of low-fi noise, but I suppose you can turn it down if it's bothering you.
The graphics are a mixed bag; the sprites are very colourful, but not very detailed most of the time. I'd give them a Genesis rank. The level designs are not very colourful, but they are SNES-level detailed, some with some effects in the background, and even have an active effect on the player, with icy patches, watercourses that push you back, and so on. The character designs are of TurboGrafx vintage; lots of anime boobies everywhere. It's not evocative, it's not racy, it's not offensive, it's actually just silly, and a bit comical, which is good because it keeps you laughing at that instead of raging at the terrible level design.
Oh that level design. Whomever was responsible for the level design needs to be dragged out into the street and flogged. There are lots of "gotcha" tricks and just plain mean enemy placement choices that would be fine if you could see it coming and avoid it, but most of the time you can't. Almost evey level has a section where there are bottomless pits with enemies flying at you that make this NES-era Castlevania enthusiast boil with ineffectual gamer-rage. There are a lot of moving or disappearing platforms over spike pits that force you to redo the entire section, or just die a slow, spikey death if you make even one mistake. I cannot understate how obnoxious the levels are.
The enemies are all varied, each with their own trick, which in turn, provides the player with said trick if they are used as a weapon (kind of the whole schtick of this game). The bosses are screen-filling monstrosities that each have a gimmick to defeating them. They all have tells to avoid being hit, though sometimes it's unclear what will damage you and what won't.
Overall, given the inexpensive cost of this game, I'll give it a pass, but just barely. It's not, and I mean NOT up to modern standards, even for a game of this kind, but if you want a hit of newstalgia, or if you are too young to remember the NES era, if you want to know what it was like, then this is worth checking out, but do yourself a favour and wait for a sale.

Five stage old-school platformer where the damsel in distress is actually the main character's father, the king. Amazing Princess Sarah feels a lot like Super Mario Bros. 2 / Doki Doki Panic; you can pick up and throw neutral objects like clocks (aka turnips) and enemies themselves to use as weapons. You can also jump on a bunch of the game's enemies without issue (the fire elementals have flaming heads, fire hurts), and the platforming feels super smooth and fast-paced throughout.
First playthrough is decent, with learning how the stages are laid out and the patterns the bosses have. After that you get SIX more playthroughs to look forward to before you finally take down Lilith, and each one has its own flavor to it:
Other than the effects on Sarah and the enemy difficulty nothing changed. Enemies always in the same places, level layouts exactly the same, bosses behaved exactly the same. Rather repetitive after the first couple of runs, variety or not, and is pretty weak in attempting game longevity.
Still a fun title in the end, nice to play a platformer that has some Mario Bros. 2 feel to it, and it's nice to play as the princess and not her hero for a change. Worth picking up!

Welcome to the Robot Maid Review of... Amazing Princess Sarah.
Amazing Princess Sarah is a decently fun action platformer game created Haruneko Entertainment. I've played Akane the Kunoichi on XBOX 360 and finished that game 100% and I thought I may enjoy this game as well, since I actually did 100% Akane the Kunoichi.
The game is decently long, but it's filled with a bit of artificial longevity. The way the game works is that you go through the main campaign and then it pretty much throws you back to the beginning of the game, tells you there's a new rule or implacable enemy or some other caveat has been added, then asks you to play the game through its entirety again with that rule.
For sake of simplicity (and because I actually haven't done the NG+ system too much), this opinion is only for first playthrough.
So my opinion is... It's not a bad game. It's taken up 2 hours of my life and I didn't regret it at all. I think that with the way the game is, $4.99 may be a little much, but any sale on this game ever would make it a decent buy.
This has been a Robot Maid Review. Thank you for reading.

Mini Metro is a minimalistic, strategic puzzle game which will have you design a subway in areas such as London, Paris, New York etc. Your objective is to transport passengers to their designated stations by connecting stations together drawing lines. You have complete control of which stations you want to connect to which, but what makes it good is you have limited resources. You can only have a certain amount of trains and lines so you need to be strategic, plan ahead and make the most efficient routes for the trains. The game is very simple, clean, well designed and polished, and it's got great background music. One criticism I have is there isn't really much of a tutorial, which will leave you a bit clueless the first time you play it. However, a great minimalistic game that is very enjoyable.

Mini metro is an absolutely fantastic game. The first thing to say about it is that it is so elegant. It's clean and not overcrowded with features or unnecersary complexity. Yet there is still time for a few cool features - such as the ability to output .gifs of your game.
It's also highly additcive and can be played for hours. This is because there are many cities and three game modes (normal, endless, and extreme). To unlock cities you need to complete milestones in normal mode (eg. transport 1000 passengers) and to unlock cities in extreme mode you need to complete even tougher challenges (eg. transport 1000 passengers using only 1 tunnel, transport 1600 passengers with no more than 1 locomotive per line).
In normal mode you can move lines to respond to new stations, in extreme mode they are fixed. In normal and extreme mode you recieve investment (eg. a new line, tunnels, trains or carriages - you can choose) at the end of each week and you loose as soon as a station overcrowds. In endless mode you recieve investment based on efficiency milestones and stations do not overcrowd.
This game is 100% worth the money.

New rule for Eidos Montreal before proceeding with anything else like this: hire new writers. Especially applies when you're creating a new title in one of the most beloved and creative storytelling franchises in videogaming history.
It's tragic, so very tragic, that they focused on the wrong thing. The graphics are great. The stealthing around is pretty good. But these are incidental. These aren't what made the Thief games so incredibly, stomach-knottingly, deliciously, terrifyingly immersive. Even now, playing The Dark Project, you can look past the now-somewhat-awful graphics - because the story and the world-building is so damn good, and sinister, and sometimes absolutely petrifying.
You had one job, Eidos Montreal. Instead, you base the game a century after all the others and largely threw that world away - but then brought in all the familiar names, and....oh, I can't go on, it's like trying to criticize the plotting of an Uwe Boll film. Nothing makes much sense. That's unforgiveable.
Don't be fooled by those lovely graphics, Thiefers. Their allure won't last for long, and then you'll be wincing at a tone-deaf, cack-handed, Dan-Browned travesty of a game series you love. The story is tripe. The way it's told seems badly translated, but not in that lovably insane JRPG way you'll happily put up with for foreign titles. It's rendered in English by people with no apparent flair for dialogue, no sense of plotting continuity, no eye for the little details that bring digital worlds alive - including expansive arenas you can sneak around - everything's cramped in a way that upsets gameplay - and if that's because the graphics were too good to handle big arenas, well, scale back on the graphical detail. Dishonored managed just fine, guys. We'd be fine with less pretty as long as it all worked.
This was horribly disappointing - and avoidable. In trying to reinvent everything (weirdly, pointlessly), it looks like they threw out 95% of what worked. The previous 3 games laid the world out in detail, with plenty of themes to continue to explore. This game's script should have been a no-brainer. Instead, this game is hollow, bland and painfully clumsy - the Star Wars prequel film of stealth games.
Verdict: would willingly ram lockpicks into my own eyes instead of playing this again.

One of the better roguelikes on Steam. With all of the DLCs loaded, there are literally dozens of different skill trees that you can pick for a new character. Not to say that all of them are equally useful (because they're not), and it's entirely possible to cherry-pick an overpowered build - which, if you ask me, is perfectly alright: let people play how they want to. It makes hitting the 'random' button during character creation more exciting.
The game's sense of humor will either totally pull you in or will totally put you off. Every skill, enemy, and item you find in the dungeon will have a description that's punny, a meta-reference to something else, and/or just silly. Personally, I love it, but I could see some people taking the game's lack of seriousness as a point against it.
Levelling up almost always provides new skills and abilities that significantly improve your hero, so you really feel like you're getting more powerful - it's not just 'your mana bolt is now 1% stronger.'
There are negatives/things that bother me:
- There are only about a dozen different monster types. Going deeper in the dungeon will just unlock the same monsters with new color schemes.
- By default, everything moves wayyyy too slowly. Hit the '+' key at least once when starting out so you don't have to spend hours watching your character amble along through the dungeon.
- Inventory management is a total pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Even with the Wizardland DLC (which I highly recommend), which gives you your very own dimension to store all the crafting junk you come across, you'll still find yourself constantly running out of room because you've picked up a dozen types of cheese, a bar's worth of different types of booze, masses of mushrooms, crossbow bolts made out of six different materials of four different qualities (not even including one-off bolt types!), potions, throwing weapons, wands, etc., etc., etc. Get used to hearing "Your inventory is full!"
- The game's too long, and yet there are options to make it even longer! By default, there are 10 levels of the dungeon. At around dungeon level 5 or 6, your character will probably be strong enough that anything outside of massive monster zoos or a crazy mini-boss monster won't pose much (if any) threat. However, to be able to keep up with the power curve, you're going to have to grind through the levels anyway. With the DLCs, you have the option of expanding the dungeon to 15 levels, as well as having a virtually unlimited amount of wizarding worlds to explore - I would highly recommend NOT doing so.
- While there's an option 'no time to grind', which makes the dungeon smaller (yet having a roughly equal XP curve), which I totally recommend playing with, do note that by choosing this option, you significantly alter the balance of loot - specifically, any crafting class will find it more difficult, since you'll run into significantly less materials.
- Dredmor himself has been balanced against the twink builds. This means that it's possible to have a character that can clear out the entire dungeon but still be unable to actually win the game. Especially classes that are forced to go toe-to-toe with the big man himself - bring massive amounts of dodge and counter or you may as well just go home.
All those things are real problems with the game. However, I've sunk 120 hours into this game and have won it at all difficulties (with permadeath), so I obviously think that the game is well worth playing, despite its warts.

Puzzle-wise, The Sexy Brutale is a little lacklustre. Perhaps only half of the few puzzles are good; the rest I blindly fumbled through. However, the story and environment make up for it (and this comment comes from someone who usually doesn't care about story and environment).
In The Sexy Brutale, you play as priest Lafcadio Boone, who runs around a giant mansion, witnessing the murders of guests at a party, and rewinding time to stop their deaths. The whole game takes place over the course of a single Saturday from 12 noon to 12 midnight, though time rewinds back to noon once you hit midnight.
The direct comparison would of course be to
, as both games revolve around the same premise. However, while
has you stop the murder *while* it's happening, The Sexy Brutale has you stop the murder *before* it happens. It forces you to do this by disallowing you from being in the same room as another character, so you can never directly affect things in the room.
Another key difference is that this is a more isometric view, and you have free movement (as opposed to in Ghost Trick, where you can only move between cores). You also don't have any special ghost-powers. This makes for slightly-less-good puzzles in The Sexy Brutale, unfortunately.
The environment in The Sexy Brutale is superb, however. Since the whole mansion is a single setting, you can observe evidence of other victims' deaths while you're working on saving a different victim. For instance, one of the first victims you save dies from a gunshot at ~3:45. (His death, along with any other deaths you've prevented, resets when you reset the day.) No matter where you are in the mansion, assuming you haven't managed to save said victim, you'll hear that gunshot. You'll also hear a bell go off just before 7:00 (that's another victim), and some glass breaking at 4:15. This happens on every iteration of the day you're in. And indeed, the people in the mansion do react to these sounds, adding to the immersion.
Another way the game plays with the time-looping mechanic is with the soundtrack. The same ~6 minutes of soundtrack play throughout each iteration of the whole day. While the soundtrack changes with the room you're in, it's undeniable that it feels very much like you're playing through the day again and again, but trying to accomplish a different goal each time. Further, the soundtrack accompanies the murders well.
The controls, unfortunately, are a little weird for keyboard and mouse, and unfortunately aren't remappable. I don't know how good the game plays with a controller, but you may find it more comfortable using a controller instead. Regardless, this is a minor quibble I quickly got used to; the constant key-prompts helped, too.
Without spoiling too much of either game, I should also note that the story in The Sexy Brutale isn't as intricate as that of Ghost Trick, and nor are the puzzles; if I had to recommend only one of the two, it would be Ghost Trick hands-down. Nevertheless, both games told the stories they wanted to tell well, and The Sexy Brutale has a more immersive world than that of Ghost Trick.
Point is, The Sexy Brutale is a good game in its own right. It may not be great puzzle-wise, and it may not surpass Ghost Trick in terms of story intricacy, but its world is very well-made and is enough to carry it through from "just OK" to "pretty good". Get this first if you like a neat story with a good environment, and if you feel like the "stop the murder from happening" type of puzzle felt fresh, feel absolutely free to buy Ghost Trick as well (on Nintendo DS or iOS).

This was a wonderful game, with tons of charm, uniqueness, and sharp gameplay while it lasted.  I'd recommend this when heavily on sale, as I 100%'d the game in 7.6 hours, and there's only marginal replay value as each murder is easy enough to solve once you figure out what needs doing.  The puzzles were in my opinion just the right amount of difficulty.  I spent some time on some, but always knew I had the tools in front of me to solve it.  The time pressure is minimal since the day is fairly quick and easy enough to jump to later points in the day, so unlike other time-loop games you're never really waiting around for anything to happen.  The story is also very intriguing, moving at a nice pace and revealing little details about the people and the mansion itself.
The big thing that makes this a heavy sale recommendation is really just the length.  With only 7 murders (including one pretty much tutorial murder and an "epilogue" murder with a fair amount of hand holding), there's just not a lot of content to burn through.  A successor to this game could be incredible of it either doubled the amount of murders or expanded the individual murders to have more moving parts.  At the end of the day though too much risks overstaying its welcome, and the game definitely doesn't waste your time, each murder is unique and full of charm.  I would recommend this for a heavy discount sale and keep an eye out for any sequels as they're sure to be a gem!

This is difficult to say, since I was an absolute fan of SSI's Steel Panthers and later of Panzer General (of which Panzer Corps claims to be the offspring and evolution), but Panzer Korps falls short of its promises.
I was so excited by the prospect of playing again one of my favourite war games of all time that I bought the whole bundle (admittedly on offer). Not only I enjoyed the original game, but I also contributed to it by creating several community maps since I am a military history buff.
If you played the older titles the interface looks immediately familiar and you can jump straight into the game. The graphics haven't greatly changed either, and although I don't mind the retro-look as I don't play this kind of games for the visual effects, something a little more refined wouldn't have hurt.
The main problems with Panzer Corps are the game balance and the map design. Most scenarios are won or lost in the first few turns if you can (or most often can't) take control of some "chokepoints" (mostly fortified towns held by overly-strong A/T units). Any delay will inevitably lead to failure. Since most available routes pass through the chokepoints you'll have to fight at a disadvantage. Problem is in most scenarios the A/T units in built-up areas are way too strong and can stop any armour you throw at them. Infantry would be a good option in these circumstances IF it could be moved fast enough, but most of it will lag behind. So you'll need a lucky hit that knocks out the opposition before you take too much damage or lose too much time. And it often really comes down to that, a lucky hit.
During WWII both tanks and A/T evolved in time, with one or the other (usually the tanks) gaining the upper hand as circumstances went, but in Panzer Corps you'll find your expensive armoured units shot to pieces by oddly powerful cheaper units.
There is very little in Panzer Corps which wasn't already in Panzer General while the scenarios are a lot less balanced. Ultimately a disappointing game, though one I relly really wish had turned out better.
---------- Read further if interested in more details and response to comments in thread -----------
In response to comments I'll expand my critique of the game for those interested.
The main problem of Panzer Corps is that it changed its scope from a tactical game (such as were Steel Panzers and Panzer General) to a strategic one. This in itself could be a good thing but it is only half implemented.
The scale (not necessarily the actual size) of the maps is much larger, encompassing entire countries, BUT the units fighting on them (and their combat values) are still tactical units. So, for example, you may happen to attack Paris with a couple of panzers, which is plainly absurd, facing a couple of A/T units. In tactical combat a decent A/T unit at close quarters could easily knock out a few tanks. However, the game has the ambition of being played at strategic level (hence the Grand Campaigns scenarios) so the units shown on the map should necessarily be strategic units, ie Panzer Regiments or larger formations.
Panzer Divisions were COMBINED ARMS units, their strength being the mix of Motorized Infantry (Panzer Grenadieren), Tanks and Artillery, plus fast recce units (motorcycles and armoured  halftracks). On the other hand there were no A/T divisions in any army at the beginning of WWII. Germans never set up any such units for the whole course of the war as they were deemed too expensive. Soviets set up A/T artillery divisions only in 1943.
So the game places on the same level tactical A/T units and strategic armoured ones, thus the unbalance. This is why the A/T units are very cheap in comparison. The game is basically an hybrid and doesn't quite succeed in either the tactical challenge (where Steel Panzers excelled) or the strategic one, as manoeuvre is overly hampered by chokepoints.
In the end this is just a game. You may like it or not and anyone is entitled to his own views. I am happy to have a civilised exchange of opinion, but I find Cuqueen remarks about my military knowledge insulting and showing poor manners.

Two poorly dressed mercenaries attempt to make some money, fail an intelligence test, fight their way past hordes of demons despite the constant distraction of jiggling breasts, a shiny bald head, various phobias, and personality disorders, but in the end, still make no money.
It's actually not a terrible game, despite the metacritic score. The current Steam score of around 70% is more fair, I think. And considering its current single-digit price, it's hard not to recommend if it interests you at all.
I've only played a few other Inxile games, but they seem to follow a trend: full of heart, mostly-competent technical/artistic merit, but gameplay mechanics balance done by a middle school kid.
Granted, it only affects perhaps 20% of the game, but they tend to be the bigger fights, so it can be annoying. Annoyances include:
- pixel-perfect aiming, but they give you a circle aiming reticle
- enemies tend to move erratically, which is not great combined with the above, plus arrow travel time
- a number of enemies have stun-lock or juggling attacks, at which point the only defense is to hope to get lucky with a dodge (no i-frames), or simply use a potion.
- "challenge" tends to be of the formula: spawn lots of enemies, spawn the strongest enemies, surround the player. Pretty ham-fisted.
- a few times, goes for one of the worst action game cardinal sins: unlimited respawning enemies.
- literally pitch-black areas sometimes. Gamma adjust option doesn't work; no fix for this, as far as I can tell. Only light source tends to be lighting your weapon on fire, which goes out after you use it too much (at least as E'lara, the elf). Seriously stupid idea.
- AI companion seems to go out of their way to deliberately block your path and shots, and even seems to mock you with various voice lines.
, once you know how to deal with these, it's not so bad, as the two characters are given plenty of skills to use. Your AI-controlled partner seems to have pools of health and mana, so equipping them with skills is actually quite helpful. The infinite spawn segments aren't so great though, depending on the skills you have equipped and the difficulty level. Playing this game on the harder difficulties seems like masochism.
It may sound like there's a lot of negative points, but if the game description and screenshots interest you at all, you'll probably like the game just fine. It's just that the gameplay mostly seems to feel like trying to exploit the enemy AI's dumb behavior rather than out-skilling it. Then again, sometimes it can be fun and powerful-feeling to mow down a bunch of enemies.
Good points include:
- decently long campaign for an action game; took me about 15 hours.
- decent replayability; can play through with (or freely switch between) two characters, use different skills, or even the different character/weapon skins (more on that below). Plenty of stuff to look out for, which can improve abilities.
- Fairly entertaining banter between the two mercs that reminds of Gimli and Legolas from the LOTR movies.
- Surprisingly meaty side quest treasure hunts that are a lot like the newer Tomb Raider side areas, but possibly even bigger. Probably one of the best parts of the game.
Final note: This game uses/used GameSpy for multiplayer and DLC redemption. GameSpy was shut down, and so this game has no official multiplayer support, nor can you redeem the pre-order DLC codes if you bought them. However, there are some work-arounds for multiplayer, although they look like a pain. It's also possible to download an existing save that has the DLC enabled, if you wish to play as Seraphine or use one of the other skins. Check the forums for more info.

I really like this game. There might be some games with significantly higher budgets that have received even more polish, but there is still a lot of good stuff in here. Hunted is neither a full-fledged action game nor RPG, it's a genre mix with a rather well done duo of protagonists. Made with co-op in mind, the game still works very well solo. One way or the other, I find the 2 main characters well written. They have a constant back and forth with remarks which are relevant to the story or are simply funny. There aren't really many games that pull off this principle as good.
I usually play as the elf, because it's lots of fun to just run around and shoot all the various monsters which try to overrun the team. Maybe it's not very deep, but it sure is entertaining. The story is nothing groundbreaking, but it's there and it's certainly serviceable. It doesn't steal the show from the 2 PCs and it doesn't have to.
Most levels have secrets and optional quests (some spanning almost the whole game) besides the main path and they are the first sign that this game is a little bit more than I expected it to be at first glance. It doesn't loose speed throughout the campaign and there are even multiple endings, which is a nice payoff, showing one was right for believing in this game.
It's too bad this game isn't a hit, because I would have loved to play a sequel. I'm sure E'lara and Caddoc would be quite impressive on Unreal 4 or something like that.
