When push comes to shove this is a small game by an independent developer which I got on sale for less than $2. One might think that voids my right to have any criticism at all. No because time is also invested and that's even more important than money.
Amazing Princess Sarah is a platformer with a few pretty good ideas to it that ultimately spits in all their faces. An EXP system lets our cantaloupe-chested heroine get stronger and have more HP. Although you have a sword it's far more beneficial to pick up objects or fallen enemies to throw. This is the game's primary mechanic and it works great because different downed enemies have different behaviors when thrown. The ogres slow you down, limit your jumping but do loads of damage. Bats fly far and fast when thrown. Elementals send a magic wave left and right. Succubi clear the screen. And there are enough different enemies to warrant some varied playthough for the raw-fighting areas.
The platforming is average, which would no doubt drive most players crazy. I can't count the number of times a bat or stray arrow knocked me off a cliff but it'd be somewhere between Castlevania 1 and Whomp`Em. But lives are infinite and checkpoints are fairly frequent (often just before and just after a brutal area) so the frustration is far less than it would've been in the early console era.
Graphics-wise the game is good enough. That titlescreen is beautiful and truthfully foretells the fanservice level. While the monsters themselves are generic flair they're well-made. There's only so many ways you can design a skeleton or zombie after all. I will give the bosses some flack though since most of them just look out-of-place. I understand that sprites that huge could be a problem but each time I saw one I was reminded of an old flash game I tried to make once where I was very lazy with the enemies.
When you beat the game it implores you to try Newgame+ to see the true ending. Upon entering Newgame+ you find a game mode selection with most of the options locked. I think there was 7 or so total. You can view the descriptions of the modes and they do things like warp the screen, give you time limits, have a ghost haunt you (that behaves like a regular Boo enemy). It seems like a pretty good way to advance the gameplay experience. Beat the game twice, get the true ending and final boss and then for those challenge-lovers you can try the harder game modes, possibly for other rewards...
Except that's not how it works. You actually need to beat ALL modes to get the true ending. I tried mode 2 (haunted) for a bit but had other things to do so I put it up for a while. Then while I was telling a friend about the game he explained that he saw a youtube video of it and told me not to bother going for the true ending. I did my own research and found a video with the final battle and true ending in it and I was actually stunned for a bit. You do all that work for a meh boss fight and the lamest ending ever? Seriously, ANY endings to a game I've seen in the past I'd say 15 years is more fulfilling than that. Had I sunk the time into getting that ending, I would've been furious. I was expecting at least another art piece on par with the titlescreen or even some fun credits music but there's not even end credits.
There's so many things that could've fixed this. Art of the king and his daughter. Maybe something showing or saying that the kingdom was being rebuilt since from what the intro tells us the denizens of hell were apparently made it all the way to the throne room. Maybe jack the absurd comedy up a notch and have Sarah pick up the whole castle and carry it farther away from the demon's realm.
But it really feels like the developer just stopped caring about his own project. That anyone who played it that far was rewarded solely by the challenge and not any hope of a decent conclusion. And that feeling, that knowing that NOTHING of value awaits me challenging those harder modes makes me not care either. I won't say I want my money back because $2 was fair for that gaming experience. But if I'd played through even one newgame+ mode I would've wanted my TIME back.

Mini Metro is a minimalistic, strategic puzzle game which will have you design a subway in areas such as London, Paris, New York etc. Your objective is to transport passengers to their designated stations by connecting stations together drawing lines. You have complete control of which stations you want to connect to which, but what makes it good is you have limited resources. You can only have a certain amount of trains and lines so you need to be strategic, plan ahead and make the most efficient routes for the trains. The game is very simple, clean, well designed and polished, and it's got great background music. One criticism I have is there isn't really much of a tutorial, which will leave you a bit clueless the first time you play it. However, a great minimalistic game that is very enjoyable.

Mini metro is an absolutely fantastic game. The first thing to say about it is that it is so elegant. It's clean and not overcrowded with features or unnecersary complexity. Yet there is still time for a few cool features - such as the ability to output .gifs of your game.
It's also highly additcive and can be played for hours. This is because there are many cities and three game modes (normal, endless, and extreme). To unlock cities you need to complete milestones in normal mode (eg. transport 1000 passengers) and to unlock cities in extreme mode you need to complete even tougher challenges (eg. transport 1000 passengers using only 1 tunnel, transport 1600 passengers with no more than 1 locomotive per line).
In normal mode you can move lines to respond to new stations, in extreme mode they are fixed. In normal and extreme mode you recieve investment (eg. a new line, tunnels, trains or carriages - you can choose) at the end of each week and you loose as soon as a station overcrowds. In endless mode you recieve investment based on efficiency milestones and stations do not overcrowd.
This game is 100% worth the money.

Many smaller, simpler games often fail because they have difficulty managing to stay challenging with a relatively simple premise--but this isn't one of those. This is one of those games that have the great combination of 'easy to learn, hard to master' going and manages to keep on your toes.
The idea is simple, drill for oil and sell it. But with that simple premise you still have a lot of things that keep you always challenged:
Do you sell low and not worry about overflow or storage? If you choose to stockpile, you might run out of time and not get to sell the oil at all.
You never know where the oil is, so how much will you invest in exploring for oil? If you don't, you might lose thousands of dollars in oil, but you might also waste thousands of dollars fruitlessly searching for oil that isn't there.
How much money will you save for making important game winning purchases later in the game? (Won't get into that too much because, spoilers). If you save it all, you're going to miss out on important upgrades, but you could lose out on important things later on if you don't have any left.

From what I've played so far, it's a very simplistic game, but that's not specifically why I wouldn't recommend it.
1. There are a LOT of levels. Normally, I'm not one to complain about too much content, but the additional levels do not add anything of value on top of normal game play. 250 levels is too many to justify individual selection and 'progress'. Levels should indicate a distinct progression: new mechanisms, bigger puzzles, etc. Levels here mean nothing in terms of playstyle. An example of what good level progression would be HexCells, where new worlds either introduce a new mechanic, or increase the difficulty of the puzzles. In Two Digits, the progression means nothing.
2. Poor PC porting. To anybody who has played this game or watched the trailers or screen shots, it's obvious this game was developed with touch screen in mind. If a game that is made on a different platform is ported to a new platform, the controls (or at least the options for controls) should reflect the new platform. In this case, it was minimally done. I see potential for left/right clicking to switch between states, but it was never addressed.
In my opinion, calling this a puzzle is a bit of a stretch. At the very least, it has puzzle elements, but this plays more like a math education game than your standard puzzle. For an educational game, it wouldn't be that bad (I could see a style of this game being extended to other operations and potentially being a great tool for educators), but as a puzzle game on Steam, it might be hitting the wrong core demographic. The concept's not bad, but I think the execution could be better.

I'm personally baffled by the positive reviews for this game. I guess there are just a lot of simple people out there.
When you brainstorm ideas for making a game, some you keep and some you throw out because they don't go anywhere. This game idea should've been thrown out.
Here's the idea behind this game: You have nine numbers. Pick two groups of those numbers that add up to the same amount. That's it. The gameplay does not get any deeper. Level 1 is literally the same as level 100, just with different numbers. With good game ideas, you find the gameplay expanding as the game goes on. This is just rote repetition. I can't imagine anyone enjoying it. If you do, you have an exciting career ahead of you as a cashier.
Some reviews say this game is educational, which I also don't understand. I'm not sure what these people could be learning. Did they not know how to tell if two numbers are equal before playing this? That could be it.
Bottom line, if you are 8 and need to practice your addition, or if you want to get into accounting for the thrills, buy this game. Otherwise, steer clear.

This game fails to make use of the source material in any meaningful way. It is almost like the development team were given just the name Thief as the title, Garret as the protagonist and Basso as the fence and told to make a game about stealing stuff in early industrial revolution generic grey steampunk city. Maybe they didn't get usage rights for anything else, because thats what it feels like.
Garrets character is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ised from the word go. Gone is the aloof, cynical, selfish, anti-hero that only acts on other people behalf when it suits him, when there is no other option, or for revenge. Instead we are given a flat boring character that essentially denounces all of Garrets traits that the first game made us painstakingly aware of. All within the tutorial. What ever happened to 'I only work alone'. Adding to that the Keepers taught Garret to be invisible in a crowd in order to document history, but not interfere. Garret corrupted the teachings by using them  to be a stealthy thief. But in this game everyone seems to know who you are, even the 'Thief-Take General' (*rolls eyes). If the original Garret was in this situation, he would have just left. Why take unessisary risks.
The original games were setup as an unrestricted world puzzle where you felt that your own ingenuity, quick(slow) action and sensory feedback  allowed you to complete missions with a smug sense of statisfaction. This game is an pre-determined obstacle course for the player, complete with '90's sidescroller loot-that is impossible to get untill you know how-and has no earthly reason for being there'. There are points in the game where you try and not follow the pre-determined path because it is too risky, only to find it is the only way. Usually leading to a forced action cut scene where.... YOU GET CAUGHT.... In a game called... Thief. This doesn't just happen once, but all the time, followed by hell being raised as you try to scramble and escape along a new pre-determined path. I know that game designers need to up the ante, but this is just cliche at this point.
All in all this game would have been great as a prequel. Garret having freshly left the Keepers in order to persue a life of burglary of the wealthy and undeserving for his own gain. Working with people he initially trusts, who then betray him or die on the job. Hell... they could have even kept the main story elements intact. Maybe then we could have seen where Garrets dark personality came from in the first game and why he is behaving like such a noob in this one. But unfortunatly the games story line is irrevocably terrible.
Ultimatly game play and graphics are slightly above average. The inability to even try pay lip service to the original brings it down to a 4/10. Don't bother. Go play the originals. If you can't stand bad graphics get the story arc of Youtube.
What is with the obsession with The Claw!! Seriously I had Jim Carrey in my head every time they said it.
Edit: A note for Steven Gallagher. Head Narrative Director. Garret is not against killing 'without thought or good reason', he's not a conscientious assasin. Garret's rationale is that killing is messy, noisy and gets you caught. Again, would have been fine under it's own brand. The game probably would not have tanked.

I had high hopes upon loading this game for the first time given the sheer brilliance of the original games - this was quickly dashed as the linear, closed, languid environment was set before my eyes.  The graphics are nice, yes, but where is the ambiance?  Where is the quirkiness or the eccentricity of the townspeople and guards?  Where is the magic, the factions, the religious zealotry that I grew to love about the believable and engrossing world that encompasses everything about Thief?  Nowhere.  They have now decided that these things should be stripped out in place of a boring, lazy version of the game that simply takes less time and imagination to create.  I cannot recommend a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ization of such an amazing series of games.

Amazing Princess Sarah is a well made platformer with a pretty good difficulty curve. Sarah fights enemies the Super Mario Bros. 2 way: you mainly kill your enemies by picking up items -- or already slain enemies -- and throwing them at your foes. If you time it well, you can get cascade reactions where you kill multiple foes with a single throw.
The (forgettable) story is told without words through simple cutscenes. The same style is used to introduce the bosses.
Where Sarah is frustrating, is in the level design. Even for a game in the platformer genre, there is a LOT of backtracking here as you mainly fight your way to a switch, flip it, then backtrack to a previously locked wall/passage and continue.
Enemies respawn throughout so you are always in danger, luckily save points occur frequent and are mostly well placed so you don't have to repeat particularly difficult sections too often.
Most annoyingly, flying enemies and enemy projectiles go through walls, and as you'll be spending a lot of time passing through narrow corridors next to other sections you've either already visited or will visit next, there are a lot of cheap hits as a result. Luckily there are also sections where you can just dodge or kill enemies without worrying about cheap hits too much.
Overall the experience is a good one. A well made game and worth the (low) price.

This game is made of all of the worst and most annoying jumping puzzles from every other platform game (I got to level 3 before realizing I'd rather be doing anything else).  There are a lot of moving/disappearing platforms with instant death as the consequence, and they are made worse by bats that are constantly flying across the screen, and also by a quirk of the engine that doesn't preserve your momentum:  if you are on a moving platform and you jump, you are suddenly going straight up.  Also, using your melee attack while jumping feels awkward.  Really everything about the jumping could use some work.
There is a cool mechanic where you kill enemies and throw dead bodies at more enemies.  Indeed, its necessary even, because your melee attack doesnt do much against harder enemies.  Unfortunatey you don't get much room to play with it; you are constantly dealing with whatever ridiculous terrain problem they have you doing.
Health power ups are rare and disappear in about 2 seconds.  Some puzzles nearly require throwable objects to complete, but throwable objects don't respawn.  Deadly falling spikes are not rare and do respawn rather briskly.
The gameplay seems to be designed around playing for a very small amount of time and then dying, and then repeating that about a thousand times.  Sometimes the game is a lot of fun when you are traveling from the end of one puzzle to the beginning of another.

I haven't played a game like this ever. You read about the horror and injustice of war, but when you have to guide playable characters through hell, it's a whole different story (or stories). The atmosphere in this war of mine has a grey, black and white them, to depict the gruelling depression and drain on the humans trapped in a warzone. Hunt for food, water, warm your shelter, fight off raiders, scavenge fo food, etc. TWOM is a 2D sidescroller with beautiful graphics for a game made by an indie studio. In built workshop and modding support allow you to create your characters and scenarios. Want to put your favoruite fictional characters in a warlike scenario? Done. Want to see who'll die if you put your family in a warzone? Done.
I had fun playing with the fictional cast of "Life Is Strange", since I was morbidly curious about what might happen if war struck the continental US. A country whose populace hasn't seen war on its land since the 19th century. Even though the game is designed with Eastern Europe in mind. The sidescroller formate helps the suspension of disbelief.
TWOM doesn't hold back the harsheness of war, disease, hygiene, illness, death, depravity, starvation, fatigue, depression, total societal collapse are just some of the things that  you have to deal with.
You can only scavenge at night, so that the snipers don't get you. Events in the background, such as the weather, Payable Characters who've been sent to help other survivors, raiders and so on are decided by a RNG system.
Scavenging for food, bandages and medicine is very difficult, All the place where food is readily available are either dangerous or run by old people. So, do you endanger your life, or do you let the old and the weak starve and die?
My advice for playing this game is:
Don't accept children (it's harsh, I know) unless you have enough food and meds to last days.
Don't forget the clock when you're scavenging, otherwise you'll have to return in the morning which takes longerand is more hazardous.
Don't forget that you're sick and sleepy need food, bandages and rest. Always have a healthy and well-rested person guard the house while you're scavenging.
Don't face hostile people head-on, even if you're armed, you're alone, they aren't wounds and disease are almost a death sentence.
Thirst and rest are more important than food, but don't let your people starve either.
Make sure your house is warm, other wise you'll die from the cold.
And most of all don't forget to let your family die.
Everybody dies, have a nice day.

This game is just...damn. Simply amazing. It takes place in a war zone however you don't play as the soldier. You play as the victims of the war. The game is all about survival and decisions. You must decide what you must do first. You must decide if you're going to take on the heavily armed military base for canned food, medicine, weapons and materials OR if you're going to go to the supermarket to hopefully find some food or materials. The game is mostly on choosing where to go and how you are going to do it. The combat system is a bit hard to learn at first but once you know it you're good to go. There are numerous survivors and you get them randomly (unless you make your own story which allows you to pick your survivors. Now you may think that this game sounds easy but it's not. You get hungry everyday. You can get sick. You need to be warm. There will be bandits raiding your base from time to time. There is a phase in the game where it will be winter. There is a phase in the game where there are daily bandit raids. You need to go out every night to scavenge. Your survivors need to sleep. They need to be happy. If your character gets sad, they get depressed. If they are depressed, then they become broken. They can now kill themselves. That is the game. You can easily tell the game is an anti-war game. It makes you do decisions to protect the ones you love and who you are with and how you will go beyond the horizon to do what it takes to survive.
I myself got sad when my scavenger died at around Day 30. It was Marko. It was my mistake why he died. He was shot trying to loot the rest if the military base as I've looted it before. I actually became sad that my scavenger was now dead. I know that my one of my other survivors can become the scavenger but it just wasn't the same. After Marko died, I usually just stayed in my base as I had unlimited food (I had the trap where you put 1 food and get two food in return...profit).
I also had weapons like 3 assault rifles, 2 shotguns, 1 sniper, numerous knives and etc. My base was maxed out on security with that alarm door and all boarded up. I also relied on the trader that comes every 3 days to trade. I still felt sad that Marko was now gone. The game ended around Day 45. I was happy. I felt relieved that the war was over. Even if it's a game, it makes you feel like you really are one of the survivors. This is how impacting this game is. This is how amazing this game is.

This one is a definite no.
As others have said there's no online anymore, but we had tunggle set up to use the LAN so I'll consider that a minor issue just mentioning it incase it's more of a problem for others.
Even though there's magic, ranged and melee characters are basically stuck in one role. The warriors crossbow sucks, and the elfs melee equally so. Expect to stay in the one role if you're playing that class. There are set points (purple crystals) that you can switch characters. The magic largely sucks too, there are 3 unique spells for each class then 3 they share. During my time playing there were only 2 worth using and the others are just pointless wastes of mana. The warrior only gets 3 different weapon types: Sword which is fastest and weakest, axe which is middle ground, and club which is highest damage but slow. The speed makes more of a difference in my opinion so again 90% of the game with a sword made the combat have almost no variation to it.
The systems are super clunky. The enchanted weapons have set amounts of charges, so they'll do really high damage for about a single fight then usually drop to worse damage than unenchanted items. The shields have durability which gets eaten away very quickly with blocking making them feel like they're made of cardboard. Some shields have armor stats with them and there's a single slot for armor (a pauldron of all things) but the game gives no indication of what armor is worth and it seems to make very little difference. Magic can only be leveled at special white cricles but since magic is so bad it feels pointless to limit leveling it up. There are collectables that feel like a chore, like deathstones that gives background story but since you'll care so little about the story these are pointless, people you can save which serve the same purpose, and gold. That's right gold is a freaking collectable! We were picking it up hoping it would help us when we got to buy something but no, it doesn't do anything it, just fills up a bar in your menu. Also you can only hold at most 3 of every potion type, this means you'll constantly alternate between having almost none to being surrounded by potions you can't pick up and have to leave behind to go through the next gate. There are also executions in this game but they are also worthless. The only people you can execute are basically dead anyway, so doing the execution would just waste time when you could've just hit them one more time. This is especially true if you're using a slow weapon.
The graphics aren't great. The voice acting isn't either. The dialog is terrible, rather than two mercenary partners they end up sounding like 2 people who are forced to be together by some common goal. They say maybe 3 mildly funny things through the entire story. You'll also constantly pass people standing off the the side talking to themselves in a loop of dialog which adds nothing to the game and gets pretty annoying half way through. The story is trash *Spoilers* Some dragon hunter gets corrupted by sleg (the child of soylent green and mercury), leads some orcs to war and you stop him, bad ending if you drink sleg during any of the survival fights, good if you don't.
Lastly, the game is painfully linear. I'm fine with linear games, especially ones that focus on story, but this game basically pushed you through it. Constant sections that are a few feet long at best. There was always a tiny ledge you couldn't climb after you jumped or a door it wouldn't let you go through again that would stop you from back tracking even the slightest bit. The result makes you feel like you're just passing through a bunch of ready checks since you can't proceed through them without your partner there and they're LITTERED throughout every map. This discouraged any attempt to explore since you could rarely go anywhere off the path. The rare exception was the 4 "Puzzles" and these are puzzles in the loosest sense. They usually consist of finding something to open a door than solving how to open the door. Then they would end with a skeleton fight. Completing the first 3 lets you do the 4th one and doing the 4th gives each character a weapon. Excluding bosses there are only 3 types of enemies, orcs (wargoth); minotaurs; and skeletons. The orcs would use bows and had one special one that used magic but mostly all enemies are just melee of slight variations (Armor/no armor, sheild/no shield, duel wielding). The boss fights are terrible too, for example one is a spider you just run from until you reach a balista and shoot a rock so it falls on it, and you're done.
P.S. this game glitches too. The last boss involves pushing down pillars that heal him whenever he tries to use them. We could easily have done this but it took about 4-5 tries because the game refused to let me push them down. Some animations bug. I tried pushing a cart and my character looked sideways instead so it didn't give me the push button mash prompt. When I finished a melee chain I would sometimes teleport to the other side of the enemy I was fighting. The most common glitch was with the door based ready checks. One person lifts the door and the other goes and helps lift it the rest of the way, but maybe 30-40% of the time one of us would move into position like we were going to lift it but wouldn't, then they'd just stand like that for a while until they set the door back down and we could try again.
All in all this game isn't worth it in my opinion. I got it on sale and only payed $3 for 2 copies of the game, but there are so many problems with it it's ridiculous. You won't be missing anything if you skip this one.

I just read some of the reviews for this game and i just have to say most of them are not quite fair.
First the pay to win argument
Many players seem to think it is a pay to win system but that is not the whole truth.
I have not spent a single cent at this game, just played the daily quests each third day and evolved my decks in the long turn. My latest Deck was in the PVP ranking around rank 37 without having more than one generation cleared....
The real task in this game is not building the absolutely optimized deck, no you just try to build the best of what you have and if you ask me that's much closer to the true Magic feeling than playing in the usual magic store. When I started Magic the gathering I had no billions of dollars to spend for card so I had to play with the cards I got, not the cards I bought on the Internet to fulfill already optimized deck lists made by professional players!!!
Instead it makes me proud to defeat players with unlimited resources who buy their cards and have every planeswalker you can get ;)
In my opinion its quite clever of the game makers to limit the number of the same rares and mythic rares because it provides a larger diversity of different deck types and inhibits the extreme decks which are just build around a single card.
=>This tries to PREVENT pay to win!!!
To all the players who say the computer is too hard..... realy? Would you go to a magic store, play against a random guy and complain his deck is to good??? Go on, modify your deck and try it again!
This game is designed for the multiplayer! You build your decks and test them against players all around the world! Not just the two decks of your best friend...
If you ask me the multiplayer is by far the best magic online multiplayer i have seen and all in all it works quite well.
Sure there are bugs sometimes but the turn based magic system (card stack, instant etc.) is just excellent for everyone who wants to learn the rules. Sure you will lose your first battles but there is no punishment for this, and every victory brings you closer to more cards to enlarge your library.
Oh, in addition there is a new generation every 4th month and last but not least: IT IS FREE TO PLAY, and if you read my post I hope you will follow my argumentation that it is also FREE TO WIN! (if you learn how to play and improve your skill ;)

I still remember as if it were yesterday the feeling of excitement when first playing the classic wargame
over 20 years ago on my first ever Windows desktop. The idea of a war game on a pc was quite new back then – previously, war games were played at a table, on a cardboard map, using countless units (or counters) to be placed and moved over the map's hexagons according to a set of rules which was often so complex that one needed a couple of days to read, study and memorize them before you could actually start playing.
, released in 1994 by Strategic Simulations, changed all that for me, and for several years the turn-based wargame became my favorite genre on the pc: the games didn't need the graphical horse power of the earliest 3D-games and their expensive dedicated cards, since the focus rested almost exclusively on the strategic, operational or tactical gameplay. While the genre stayed quite popular (although in its own niche) throughout the 90's, I lost interest after a couple of years, with so many graphically more pleasant titles grabbing my attention. And truth to be told: the iconic
series didn't seem to have got a proper continuation after 2000, so I let it go.
That is untill I stumbled upon a copy of this game in a sale, only a month or so ago.
was first released in 2011 by Slitherine (who do a mighty good job to keep the turn-based wargame alive and kicking), having been developed by The Lordz Games Studio. I didn't expect that this kind of game, essentially representing an historical armed conflict in a highly abstract way, would still be able to grab my attention as thoroughly and as intensely as it did. Don't make any mistake:
is a classical turn-based wargame in every possible sense. It doesn't try to be up-to-date by having fancy graphics, nor does it intend to appeal to the masses by making the genre less intricate (some would call it difficult to grasp). On the contrary: this game takes the original
as its starting point and pays openly hommage to it by using identical game mechanics and even progression as the main campaign unfolds.
And it is exactly in that progression where one of these games main strengths lies.
, in its base form as released in 2011, contains 26 scenario's or combat maps, most of them (but not all!) based upon an historical campaign during the Second World War. Most of these are well-known, such as the German invasions of Poland, the Low Countries & France or the Soviet-Union or the desperate efforts by the German Wehrmacht to withstand the tide of ever growing enemy operations towards the Reich. These scenario's can be played on their own (either as the Germans or from an allied perspective), but in truth the game begs to be played in the campaign-mode, where every single scenario leads to a next one in a quite widely branching campaign. This campaign has always to be played from a German perspective, and the progress you make though the campaign (which route you can take), depends on your results in any given scenario. Do particularily well in the Low Countries and France, and you might even get an early opportunity to invade England – yes, there are several "what if" scenario's as well!
But the fun goes much further – and deeper – than that. You start the first scenario with a rather small group of "core units": several basic infantry & artillery units, some poorly equipped early Panzers and a couple of Messerschmitt fighter-squadrons. As you take enemy victory points and win scenario's as convincingly as possible, you earn "prestige" – the in-game currency – which you can use to either call for reinforcements during a scenario (which come pretty expensive), for upgrading existing units with better equipment in-between scenario's, or to order new units for your core force. This game-embracing mechanic adds a very rewarding strategic element to the game: how do you build, maintain and upgrade your core force? Do you pour lots of prestige points into an air force, hoping that one day you'll have to batte it out against the Royal Air Force, or do you play it more safely and postpone investments until better tanks become available for those Panzer divisions? But even then, some sort of air defence is badly needed, so why not ordering a couple of 88-mm AA guns which can double as very powerful aint-tank guns as well?
And there's even more: as units fight, deal and take damage, they are rewarded with combat experience – a unit can gain up to five stars, and in doing so becomes ever more powerful. It can even be made "overstrength" for each star of experience it has in-between scenario's, making it very useful as the spearhead in an armored attack, for example. As units fight and stay in play through the campaign, they also get "leaders", who offer an ever greater bonus to the unit they command. An elite, 5-star unit with a couple of leaders attached to it, becomes something to cherish – which makes one hesitate: should I use it in the first line of attack/defense, and risk losing it? It is choices like this which make the campaign so extremely addicting: I have replayed it over and over again, trying to get as powerful and well-balanced an army as possible, ready for the ultimate (and hard to reach!!) series of scenario's which put the German Wehrmacht before the almost impossible task to invade and effectively conquer the U.S.
Sadly, all of these wonderful ideas would immediately become irrelevant if the actual combat mechanics were badly executed. After all, this is an hexagonal wargame, where one has to position and move dozens of units on a map.
happily delivers in this department as well: the combat mechanics are very easy to grasp, more dificult to master (but there are a ton of difficulty options, so everyone can tailor the game to suit his or her needs) and quite complex underneath (as they should be, since all sort of parameters including weather and terrain are included into the mix). There are some points of criticism here: some maps are a tad too small for the forces being deployed, which makes large-scale operational decisions almost irrelevant as the outcome will be determined mostly by the correct (and rather traditional) use of infantry, artillery, armored units and airforce. Truly daring and original tactis are not always feasible – but then, neither were they during the war itself, so, what's the complaining all about?
I want to state very clearly that I only played the base game for this review, and none of the huge amount of extra content which was released since. This additional content multiplies the amount of available scenario's by more than ten, adds a gigantic Grand Campaign as well as campaigns for the Afrika Korps, the U.S and Soviet armies. I will certainly try them out in the future, but they are not necessary to enjoy the base game, which is perfectly complete by itself. Three of the "dlc's" sold on Steam are actually stand-alone expansion packs (or rather new games using the same engine), so if you'd come upon a good sale for the entire package you'd be certain to make a great bargain.

I found Dungeons of Dredmor somewhat compelling, but every time I would play, I would get sucked in for several hours as I traipsed through level after level systematically destroying everything, only to get wiped out by one stupid play. I eventually decided I was wasting too much time with it and not enjoying it any more, so I uninstalled it. I found it frustrating that I couldn't min-max *everything* because some crafting recipes are pretty much always not available to you. I liked the skill system and that you can choose several rather than just rolling up one of seven different classes or whatever, and some of the descriptions were entertaining, but ultimately my problem with roguelikes is that they often end up as the video game equivalent of road hypnosis -- you spend hours and hours playing them and then you slip up once and you're toast. Or maybe I'm just playing them wrong?

I've decided to go ahead and give this game a thumbs up, but mostly because I knew what I was getting when I bought this game. This IS the first Thief game I've played, and yes, I do have some idea why this game is so different from the earlier games. But, differences aside, I do enjoy playing this game. And so, thumbs up it is.
For starters, I like the overall feel to the game. The plot is in-depth enough to keep you interested without being obnoxious to the gameplay, and there's enough choice within the game to keep things interesting. It's certainly not the best game out there, but it certainly isn't a waste of money. With that said, I would NOT pay full price for it. For what the game is lacking, and for the number of little bugs, $30 is a bit ridiculous.
The biggest cons for me are:
* If I have to watch one more cut scene where the audio is a full 3 seconds ahead of the video... ugh.
* For a game about a thief, you'd think the stealing items part would be a bit less, um, pointless.
* Too many chapters of the game are way too easy. It's annoying to discover that you've been sneaking around a building for half an hour, only to get to the exit without encountering a single obstacle. What's the fun in that?

Having played all 3 Thief original games, I was really looking forward to play with Garrett in modern graphics.
I liked The City's ambient, photography and music. But that really is all that will keep you from giving up on the game.
The main reason for this is that the story is so boring. The first games had excellent and somewhat funny dialogues, along with factions such as the Hammerites and the Pagans that gave such depth to the original games.
And I was expecting to encounter them again in this game, but they were not included because this game is set several decades after the first 3 games. So, obviously, Garrett is not the same person, but a "descendant".
Still, even if we overlook that fact, the Garrett in this game is not at all engaging and one reason for that is its monotonous voice acting.
It is fun to play but it is not as engaging as Dishonored, for example. Tomb Raider, made by the same studio, is a fine example of an excellent reboot. Thief, on the other hand, left me disappointed as a reboot and does not make me excited for the next Thief installment. Still, I recommend you to play this game because there is such a draught on stealth-based games nowadays.

* UPDATED WITH SOLUTION *
Make sure it's working on your computer before buy it. I have i7 3770, 16 GB ram and GTX 970 (Windows 10). It crashes randomly without an error message. I tried many things that suggested but no solution. I really wanted to play it but under these circumstance I can not. Also it is a shame developers haven't fix this because when I searched about this problem I saw that the problem isn't new, people are complaining about random crashes since game released.
* UPDATE * (Thanks to Poio Diablo IX from Grid 2 Steam Forum):
Click Search (next to your start menu) and search for "Services", Desktop app.
There search for "Touch Keyboard and Handwriting Panel" and stop the service. Done.
If you don't want to do this every time, right click to the service > properties > startup type: disabled
I'm continuing the game and to inform other players, I will keep this review.
So far, it's not great but a good game.

Do you love math? I don't mean in an abstract yes-this-concept-appeals-to-me sense, I mean do you love adding and subtracting♥♥♥♥♥♥ If you can honestly answer yes, then Two Digits might very well be a game for you. The premise is as simple as you can get: You get nine numbers, and you have to pick two sets of numbers that equal each other when added. That might mean finding two numbers that add up to a third, or that might mean summing dozens of combinations until you hit upon one that works. It's a great game for taxing your brain, because you need to work out systems to identify potential equals. Looking for numbers one digit apart or ones that sum to others will save you a lot of headaches, so if you're good at coming up with math shortcuts, you'll be well prepared for this.
That's it. Literally it. You have several hundred puzzles of what I just described. There are no additional systems, gimmicks, unlocks, or features. The art style is clean and clear, and there's some pleasant background music to facilitate your puzzling. That is very, very much it. Two Digits lacks the sort of depth that something like Sudoku or Picross offers, but if you want straight math brain-teasers, that's exactly what you'll get. Honestly I can only really recommend the game to people that really really want that, so for unapologetic mathophiles it's a solid puzzler.

Hunted: The Demon’s Forge is a linear third-person adventure game featuring sword & shield combat combined with cover-based archery sections. Production values are high – voice-acting, music, and graphics quality (Unreal 3) are good – but can’t make up for how boring the game becomes. Travel by corridor, enter an arena, fight a horde of enemies, rinse, repeat. There are a few side-dungeons and puzzles which add much-needed variety (and are well-designed). The story is your standard snarky-adventurers-battle-orcs affair, but it never goes into too much depth, almost as though it’s only there as an excuse for the gameplay. Never a good sign. Oh, and if bikini warriors are something you like, one of the player-characters easily qualifies. If that’s the kind of thing that annoys you, well, prepare to be annoyed.
Designed to be “king of co-op games,” co-op unfortunately doesn’t work since Gamespy was shut down. I’ve read in the forums that third-party apps will still enable cooperative play, but this seems hit-or-miss, and I haven’t tested it myself. Played solo, the campaign works well enough; your companion has plenty of health (though not invincible), and if powers are used consistently, the combat is easy. There is one tomb that bugs unless you play as the elf (
), and you can only switch between characters at specified points, and not at will (something that other co-op games manage without trouble). Magic feels a little cumbersome to use. Select the desired power using numbers 1-4 on your keyboard, and press Q to use the selected power. Why not have the number keys also use the power? It’s an extra key-stroke that isn’t appreciated in the heat of combat. There’s a rudimentary skill set and level-up system, but I collected so many points that upgrading was never something I thought much about.
Hunted: The Demon’s Forge is easily a $20 game if everything works as advertised. That it is for sale at a list price of $5 indicates to me that Bethesda is aware of the issues but can’t be bothered to fix them, so the game is sold at a perpetual 75% discount. Worth a purchase IF you can get the co-op to work. For most of us, though, the time of Hunted: The Demon’s Forge has passed, and it’s not worth the asking price. Get it as cheap as possible if it tempts you, but be prepared to quickly move on to something else.

Some games manage to slip under the radar, barely noticed because they are low profile or poorly marketed. Such is the case of Hunted: The Demon's Forge. Totally slipped under my radar not even doing a blip in passing. I discovered it only during a Steam sale and then a bunch of reasons pushed me to buy it. First, it was cheap, second it features one of my all time favorite video game female voice actress and then there was curiosity because the whole thing was developed by Brian Fargo's company inXile (and no, the skimpy outfit of the female protagonist was not a factor... well, barely).
For those who don't know him, Brian Fargo is the mind behind the Wasteland franchise (most notably the recent Wasteland 2) and the original Fallout games (1 and 2). So when you relate Brian Fargo and PC games the first thing that comes to mind is "serious isometric hardcore RPG stuff".
How does Hunted: The Demon's Forge fits in this conception? In absolutely no way. Not even close. It's not a RPG (despite featuring a skill tree) and although it could be in some regard qualified as "hardcore" it's certainly not isometric... nor serious. The closest description could be third person hack and slash/shooter with a RPG-ish veneer and a side of puzzles.
But what it is above all is a fun way to spend time.
The game is designed to be played in co-op, although it can perfectly be played in single player with little fuss with an AI handling of your partner OK although not terrific. Additionally to the main story, there are secret objectives, detours that can be found by going sideways. These involve puzzles, sometimes relatively hard ones;  and generally feature rewards that even if not necessary to complete the game can help.
Hunted is a simple but fun game. Sure it won't gain any GOTY award nor be remembered as a major game 10 years from now but it makes for a fun diversion. And being fun is always a good thing for a game...

I’ve greatly enjoyed my time in this game. I even happened to start playing just as the devs released an anniversary update which added some characters and locations!
This War of Mine infuses story into its very mechanics, and for that it should be (and is) lauded. The immersion ran deep as I was learning the game: a risky attempt at theft would leave a character wounded, with bandages only to be found in dangerous areas. I listened behind a door as a soldier offered a woman food for sex. When she refused, he became violent, but not before I burst through the door and provided egress for the woman, risking my own head as he shot at us both. I had to make the hard choice to rob an elderly couple in their home. The man followed me around but never attacked, just begged me to stop. When I returned a few days later, they had both vanished. I understood that I killed them by raiding their food and medicine stores.
As I played more and became more comfortable with the game, it became easier and the strife seemed less real, even on the hardest difficulty. I never found justification to build an herbal workshop. What’s interesting, though, is that I may have built differently depending on the cast I chose to start with.
That’s because of how much goes into the characters you play as: varying available inventory slots make them better or worse at scavenging, most characters are addicted to a certain product such as coffee or cigs, and each has an ability or special reason to use them. Bruno is a terrible scavenger but a good cook, using less resources to prepare our food. He’s also a sensitive prat and he’s no good at making others feel better. Katia is a reporter who’s expert at trading, rewarding me for bringing the right items to the right people. (a huge early-game bonus can be had for trading meds with the son and his sick father) Pavle’s a fast runner and someone else is very strong, or sneaky; that particular sneaky character makes quick work of a house of hostiles. On the subject, it’s also an optional-violence game, so that’s great to see.
There’s even an option to import pictures and create characters of your own; I recently finished a rewarding run using some of my closest friends.
It will make you feel. It will challenge your mind and show you, in a unique way, what can happen when a civilized community – like yours or mine – goes without food for a month.

*Disclaimer: The game is still relatively new and this review is subject to change.
Line of Sight, is it a good free to play FPS game? Yes. The core of the game is fluid and there's a nice balance of weaponry ranging from fast paced SMGS, all around ARs, long-con snipers to suppressive machine guns.
There's a huge layer of custimization to be done, so much so that you can actually call one of your character set ups or weapon load outs truly 'yours'.
The game is fast paced and rewards those who become adept with their own personal arsenal. Switching between 3 different load outs each respawn gives a lot of options for players who have never experienced a loadout system in most modern shooters.
There are multiple servers too which caters for different geographics allowing for most people to be able to play without too much of a ping issue.
The ability to try out gear and weapons before even buying them is also a welcome change to modern FPS. Not only that but the training mode is very neat ranging from close range targets, clusters, far range targets, targets behind different types of materials, etc. Very innovative.
However, there are problems with this game.
Whilst the daily/weekly/monthly quest system is a nice way to earn bonus in game currency, the overall supply stemming from games is honestly - too little. Permanent weapons cost upwards of 144k-210k in game currency and for the casual players, this is quite a startling sum to swallow. When you're only making a couple hundred (depending on performance)  every match, I can see why newcomers feel this sense of P2W even though the balance of the earlier weapons are right up there with the higher level unlocks.
Another thing of concern for some folks is the somewhat clunkiness of the character movement (or maybe this is just me playing from OCE), the game feels extremely 'grounded' despite all the cool special skills that allow you to blink or speed up like in MOBAs. If you're used to wall jumping, jet packs and whatnot from the later CoDs or Titanfall games I'm sorry but this is 100% a boots on ground type of game.
Overall, I still think this is a good game to check out if you're looking for a free to play FPS, just don't expect anything groundbreaking.

Pros:
-Not P2W. A level 1 can kill a level 25 if they're skilled.
-Lag doesn't seem to be a thing. Even people with terrible ping seemed to be keeping up with the rest of the team.
-Weapon choice. There are a lot of different guns available that are (mostly) viable options.
Cons:
-Match balancing (there is none). Just seems to throw you in to a match that has an opening.
-Character models need their hitboxes fixed. I've killed and been killed by people who were definately not in my "Line of Sight"
-Spawns. If you have an enemy team overwhelming your spawning area, theres nothing to do. You can try to fight your way out, but chances are you're stuck till the end of the match.
-Map Size vs player count. Some maps are far too small to accomedate 16+ players, and yet that's what happens, often with you spawning in the middle of a firefight.
Overall, I'm a bit underwhelmed with the current status of the game. While they completely nailed a few aspects of the game, it feels like they've completely missed other (crucial) elements. There are other reviews which go into more detail, but I thought I'd throw in my two cents.

I was one of those who really, really wanted to like this game.  Unfortunately, given what the game actually is, I can't recommend it.
What I liked about The Sexy Brutale has already been covered in depth by others: the artwork and the atmosphere are quite beautiful (I especially liked the combination gasmask/playing card idea for the staff).  The characters have good backstories which keep them from becoming two-dimensional.  The brochure, which contains information and backstory for the hotel and updates as you play, is an excellent idea.  The dialogue is passable and appropriate for the characters.  A shadowy, chained figure waiting for his cards is something I find very intriguing.
And there the list of positives ends.  I will list the negatives in order of importance.
The first negative aspect of the game is the name itself, "The Sexy Brutale."  While I don't necessarily agree that use of the word "sexy" will lead prospective gamers to expect sex, I still think it was a mistake.  You simply don't find casinos or hotels with the word "sexy" in the name.  In fact, you don't find any high-end establishments where the word "sexy" is featured.  It doesn't need to be.  "The Brutale" by itself is a superior name, and it's not even my first choice.
Secondly, this has been referred to as a puzzle game, but the actual puzzles presented to the player are so simple that it's tempting to call them pseudo-puzzles.  All too often the object needed to solve the problem and save the guest is laying in the open for no apparent reason.  I assumed (incorrectly) that the puzzles would become more complex as the game progressed, and more than once found myself overthinking the problem; the solutions are uniformly unsatisfying because they are so simple, and sometimes that simplicity makes them seem downright unrealistic.  Guests can only be killed in a specific time and place, so that saving them can be as easy as keeping the staff away from the appointed place during the appointed time.  If you're expecting the target to be chased through the hallways by a determined killer, you will be disappointed.  Once the initial murder is foiled, the game considers the guest in question perfectly safe. Furthermore, foiling the murder usually comes down to using a single quest item one time.  There are no intricate problems to untangle.
Lastly, the ending is absolutely abysmal.  "It was all a dream" kind of abysmal.  There was a period of time, maybe in the late 90's, when every other horror movie ended with the revelation that the main character had multiple personalities, and none of what you just watched actually happened.  The Sexy Brutale's storyline ends with a silent, wet fart.  The reveal is the definition of anticlimax, where the original sin of the antagonist and the premise of the entire game are shown to be incredibly mundane and well-traveled.  It also accidentally destroys the backstory (as revealed through dialogue) of the protagonist, Lafcadio Boone, without any explanation, so that the lack of originality is exacerbated by sloppiness.
The Sexy Brutale could have been saved by better puzzles and a decent story.  As it stands, it isn't worth anything close to the asking price.

Turmoil is a lovely, stylish and surprisingly strategic little game, throwing players into a heated competition for oil where timing and decision-making is of paramount importance.
Turmoil revolves around the simple principle of extracting and selling oil for profit.  The tutorial is concise and swiftly guides players' way around the game's mechanics.  Players start a level by auctioning on a plot of land, then proceed to drill for oil with an initial budget of $2,000.  The player is tasked with the task of drilling to the correct depth to find oil deposits underground and carefully managing their investments to maximise profits.
Oil can be sold to either the two aptly named businesses on the left and right side of the screen, these two stores buy oil at constantly fluctuating prices, prompting the player to keep an eye on the screen.  I found myself constantly monitoring the two stores to make sure I could sell my oil for a fair price, simultaneously making sure that the oil reserves had not run dry or if I had bought enough horses to shuttle away the oil from the rig.  Neglecting the oil accumulated in the rig will lead to a spillage, costing the player a hefty fine.
The player has until the end of an in-game year to gain as much profit as possible, which will be compared with the 3 other AI competitors.  The cycle continues as players begin to earn enough money to afford upgrades to improve their efficiency, such as increasing the capacity of drilling rigs, storage silos and the oil carriages, or speeding up the dowsers.  These upgrades are all situational and players will find that some unlocks, while being faster, can impact their economy.  A great way to ensure the full and proper usage of all the tools provided to the player.
The game's mechanics are unique because the player's success can be determined by timing.  Players who use their time wisely and effectively will be rewarded.
Although the NPC's are each given names and their own tone, the game's focus is clearly not on the story and a good story simply isn't needed for these types of games.  In fact, the addition of a story would probably be far-fetched and wouldn't benefit the game.
Turmoil is set during the events of the oil rush, typically portrayed to be set in the "wild west".  The game has a witty sense of humour and provides players with a comical, tongue-in-cheek approach to the oil rush.  The visuals are a perfect fit for the game and all of this is backed by the game's soothing soundtrack.  Without being over-ambitious, Turmoil brings a unique, light-hearted style to the table.
+Exceptional style
+Enjoyable pacing
+Innovative game mechanics, properly executed
+Poses as a realistic challenge for the player
+Thorough tutorial and adequate player guidance
+A fitting price tag
-No story (arguable)
-Can sometimes be extremely punishing (arguable)
-Can only be played in short bursts as gameplay can get repetitive after a while

Well it’s been a while since this came out and now I will write what I have to say on it. Like its real time predecessor total war battles shogun the game is different in nature to other total war titles. However for this version the gameplay was split. In battles shogun you had to build buildings and train troops during the battles which behaved in a similar format. Your troops would mindlessly march across the hex based map and the only thing you could do to them was switch lanes. At this point not counting the pay to accelerate system in place there are a lot of gameplay problems with the game. unlike total war battles shogun the management and battles are split up. In this version  you have a hex based grid where you build villages that take forever to gather resources and also require player interaction to do so. The battles are summed up with your troops mindlessly go towards the enemy with a few player interactions in charging and ability’s to break up the boring aspect of battles. Now the part that really pisses me off and arguably breaks the game is the difficulty system. The game scales difficulty based on how powerful your army is and the game was designed with the logic “hey let’s make the AI more powerful than you all the time to make the game challenging.” The problem with that logic is that you get to a point where the AI is so powerful it takes any fun that’s left out of the game. Worse is that when the AI is weaker than you there is no reward for winning. The ridiculous difficulty is seen with the raiders that attack your villages every so often. Now for some reason raiders are not scaled with your army for difficulty. Instead they are scaled with the number of regions under your control. So I have 4 regions and am facing armies that have troops that are so powerful that I can only get through one line of troops with all 3 lines of my troops filled.(there are 3 lines in total for both sides and apparently the AI can get reinforcements) Raiders steal your resources and destroy your buildings so you have to get rid of them. If you can’t defeat them in battle you have to pay them silver (one of the resources in the game) the problem there is that the raiders demand ludicrous amounts of silver in the last case they demanded over 4000 silver which drained days (and I mean real world days) worth of resource gathering. That’s not mentioning the yearly droughts that dry up the rivers over halfway up the map, and the pay to accelerate system that is in place. It’s worth noting that this is a beta and I do hope that many of these problems get fixed but until they do I cannot recommend this game to anyone.

A grand tactical, turned-based war game with roots in hex based board games from the good old days.  The very simple mechanics provide a very tactical feel--the type of unit and the order in which they move and shoot is a core concept:  the game rewards good combined arms tactics (as does real life)--that keeps the game moving without being bogged down in tactical details (other titles provide that fix).  You also get a strategy game since you must decide on what battles to fight, and based on prestige gained in your battles, what equipment to buy or upgrade or overstrength, where to deploy to start and then plan a course of action.  This provides a role playing aspect as you must decide on how to build your core and then grow your units in experience by earning awards via combat efficiency and potentially gaining a hero that then provides additional tactical benefits to the unit.  It has another what if aspect when building the core:  do I go armor heavy and win with tanks or dominate with air power disregarding that artillery is the king of battle or use recon or airborne or engineers or other options to explore or replay trying a completely different mix (seapower is used but not as part of your core with the capital ships all historically named--that is awesome).  You can be rewarded with some Special Experience units that add to you core and provide extra assets that come in very handy when used properly.
The scale of the maps and the number of units always gives you room to manuever (some reviews disagree):  it is another key concept.  The base game requires you to move out and take your objectives (some have said that is a detractor--but good tactics can overcome this issue and you may need every turn to get that decisive victory).  The DLCs allow some flexibility by providing an adjustment to ease the hurried feeling.  The situations in the scenarios (maps) are always interesting and contain solid historical and actual geographic elements plus at times actual units or leaders for the particular battle.  The DLC's add some very challenging tactical twists using very innovative objectives.  The DLC's also provide some surprises both as tactical problems or a very special reinforcement to your core (some very powerful units with perhaps a potential flaw) and some rewards for good battlefield management via captured equipment (a very nice touch).
It is just fun and addicting: you ALWAYS want to play just one more turn and that will get you in serious trouble with the significant other!  I played Panzer General (and some other titles in the 5 Star series) and this game has taken the original concept far beyond that great start.  The DLCs push the limits even more.  Bravo Zulu Matrix and Slitherine!

Dungeons of Dredmor is a roguelike. For those of us who are not elite(ist) gamers, just think of it as a hard hack-and-slash game with procedurally generated content and very real risk of permanent death which forces you to start over (a little wiser each time)
My initial impression of this game was a very positive one. It's very easy to get into, has a lot of skills to choose from for character creation (implying lots of replayability, but I was wrong) and it covers everything with a layer of clever tongue-in-cheek humor (like witty pop culture references? this game has lots!)
However after playing this game on a netbook for over 80 hours, properly experiencing it in all its glory, I stand corrected enough to say that I would not recommend this game to someone else looking to derive some fun out of their play sessions, unless their entertainment consists in dying over and over unfairly...case in which I probably still wouldn't recommend this game because it simply isn't that good all things considered.
First off, a major technical issue. This game is built poorly, seemingly by dwarven plasticsmiths (those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s) It's a little 2D game with sprites that have 2 animations each. Still it actively takes 600MB of RAM, reserving even more than that. On my 2GB RAM netbook I can forget running this and a browser at the same time.
Shame, because it looks like exactly the type of game to be played on a netbook/tablet, and not on a proper desktop configuration like the game demands. It also personally annoys me as this seems to be a problem with more and more lazy pixel-style indie games: games that look like they were made 20 years ago demand 4GB RAM and 1GB VRAM. What the hell?
Onto the gameplay itself. It's balls hard. Not in a good way as it seemed on first glance. It's unfairly and frustratingly hard. It's unfair because while you have an ample amount of skills to choose from, only a few are actually effective (give you a high likelyhood of winning the game) while others are downright useless. The same goes for weapons (don't use crossbows unless you like taking 4x longer than a character with his bare hands to win the game). This wouldn't be so bad, as every such game has some strategies that work better than others, but this game in particular is very stingy with its descriptions of mechanics. Without reading a guide, you will frequently encounter weapons and abilities whose actual effects are very underwhelming compared to what their descriptions would have you believe. You pretty much have to read a guide before diving into the game, or you'll frequently wonder "what does THAT mean" when finding, say, an artifact or another with a typical description like "The honorable poodles - it is studded with cheese crust and decorated with high quality tin"
Once that's out of the way, and you finally have a good understanding of the game mechanics that let you create an effective character with a fair chance of winning...you will run into another problem. Basically, once you figure out how to not die, everything all the way up until the final boss becomes one relatively simple, mindless, long-winded repetitive grind. And the final boss? FUBAR, because even many good builds won't scratch that guy (hints:
). A situation in which 99% of the game play is mindless faceroll, and that 1% (final boss) has the shot of taking it all away because of RNG is not fun (again, unless you're a difficulty fetishist). I also have to ask myself why they even made the game with 51 skills to choose from when less than 15 of those are actually going to let you win the game.
Could it be that in spite of first impressions, this is not that good of a game?

Enter the dungeon, collect loot, slay the monsters, and die ridiculous deaths.  Dungeons of Dredmor is one of the most accessible rougelikes on the market, but don’t take it for granted.  This is a punishing, difficult game.
You start the game by selecting the skills your well-eyebrowed hero will use.  There are your normal RPG expectations, like Swords, Armor expertise, etc.  But then you get down to skills like Battle Geology, Necronomicomics, or Egyptian Magic.  Pick Vampirism, and you’ll sparkle like a bad actor in Twilight.  All these ridiculous and funny skills are useful in their own way, but its up to you to combine them in useful ways to ensure you can survive the depths of this dungeon.
Each randomly-generated floor of the dungeon is chock-full of monsters, traps, food to eat (which replenishes your health), alcohol to drink (which replenishes your magic), and most importantly, loot.  You’ll come across a sword that does existential damage (it may or may not damage enemies if, in fact, they do not exist) or a set of rubber pants that prevents conflaguatory and aetheric damage.  There are so many different stats to keep track of, points to weigh against one another, but it is not overwhelming.  Everything is clearly presented, and the random seeding will rarely give you useless stuff as you go deeper and deeper.
You can play this game entirely with the mouse, though keyboard shortcus and movement make it a lot easier.  You can either play with Permadeath (one life, no mistakes) or turn that off and play a little more casually.  I started with permadeath, but after losing a couple characters 3-4 hours in, I turned it off so I’d be able to rewind only 5 minutes instead of multiple hours.  This game is punishing, and sometimes can feel a little unfair as you run into things you had no idea would be coming, which you had no chance to prepare for.
The humor in this game is top notch.  From pop culture references to simple gags and dad-joke level puns, there is hardly anything in this game that takes itself seriously.
I did manage to reach Dreadmor, and I stabbed him a few times, but the power of his attacks are so far beyond anything else in the dungeon, he killed me in a few hits, even with every buff I could give myself.  I think I might never actually beat him.  Some things are meant to stay unfinished.
Dungeons of Dredmor has two paid expansion packs and one free one, if more ridiculous skills and bad puns are your cup of tea.  This was a fun game, with just enough depth to keep me interested but not enough to drown me.  This is a kiddie pool Rougelike.  Guess that makes me a gaming toddler.

I haven't played a game like this ever. You read about the horror and injustice of war, but when you have to guide playable characters through hell, it's a whole different story (or stories). The atmosphere in this war of mine has a grey, black and white them, to depict the gruelling depression and drain on the humans trapped in a warzone. Hunt for food, water, warm your shelter, fight off raiders, scavenge fo food, etc. TWOM is a 2D sidescroller with beautiful graphics for a game made by an indie studio. In built workshop and modding support allow you to create your characters and scenarios. Want to put your favoruite fictional characters in a warlike scenario? Done. Want to see who'll die if you put your family in a warzone? Done.
I had fun playing with the fictional cast of "Life Is Strange", since I was morbidly curious about what might happen if war struck the continental US. A country whose populace hasn't seen war on its land since the 19th century. Even though the game is designed with Eastern Europe in mind. The sidescroller formate helps the suspension of disbelief.
TWOM doesn't hold back the harsheness of war, disease, hygiene, illness, death, depravity, starvation, fatigue, depression, total societal collapse are just some of the things that  you have to deal with.
You can only scavenge at night, so that the snipers don't get you. Events in the background, such as the weather, Payable Characters who've been sent to help other survivors, raiders and so on are decided by a RNG system.
Scavenging for food, bandages and medicine is very difficult, All the place where food is readily available are either dangerous or run by old people. So, do you endanger your life, or do you let the old and the weak starve and die?
My advice for playing this game is:
Don't accept children (it's harsh, I know) unless you have enough food and meds to last days.
Don't forget the clock when you're scavenging, otherwise you'll have to return in the morning which takes longerand is more hazardous.
Don't forget that you're sick and sleepy need food, bandages and rest. Always have a healthy and well-rested person guard the house while you're scavenging.
Don't face hostile people head-on, even if you're armed, you're alone, they aren't wounds and disease are almost a death sentence.
Thirst and rest are more important than food, but don't let your people starve either.
Make sure your house is warm, other wise you'll die from the cold.
And most of all don't forget to let your family die.
Everybody dies, have a nice day.

Secondly, this thing is an unoptimized mess. So you need to pick a number to be in bucket 1 or bucket 2 to make them match. Logically, right click = bucket 1, left click = bucket 2? Nope. This is a tablet game so you press a number twice to get it to bucket 2. So ok, I play this on my windows tablet and it glitches out where you can't scroll down on the level screen after using it for a bit, forcing a restart every once in awhile. For the Steam achievements, they don't unlock until you restart the game.
Bottom line is that the game is ok, but as a PC gamer you just can't support lazy, overpriced ports like this or it will be all we get. If you like puzzle games, I suggest some alternative choices (some of which are also ports - but aren't lazy messes like this game), like Hexcells, Strata, Cubot, Unium, etc.
Just as good as going back to elementary school and being scolded for not finishing my homework on time.

This game is just...damn. Simply amazing. It takes place in a war zone however you don't play as the soldier. You play as the victims of the war. The game is all about survival and decisions. You must decide what you must do first. You must decide if you're going to take on the heavily armed military base for canned food, medicine, weapons and materials OR if you're going to go to the supermarket to hopefully find some food or materials. The game is mostly on choosing where to go and how you are going to do it. The combat system is a bit hard to learn at first but once you know it you're good to go. There are numerous survivors and you get them randomly (unless you make your own story which allows you to pick your survivors. Now you may think that this game sounds easy but it's not. You get hungry everyday. You can get sick. You need to be warm. There will be bandits raiding your base from time to time. There is a phase in the game where it will be winter. There is a phase in the game where there are daily bandit raids. You need to go out every night to scavenge. Your survivors need to sleep. They need to be happy. If your character gets sad, they get depressed. If they are depressed, then they become broken. They can now kill themselves. That is the game. You can easily tell the game is an anti-war game. It makes you do decisions to protect the ones you love and who you are with and how you will go beyond the horizon to do what it takes to survive.
I myself got sad when my scavenger died at around Day 30. It was Marko. It was my mistake why he died. He was shot trying to loot the rest if the military base as I've looted it before. I actually became sad that my scavenger was now dead. I know that my one of my other survivors can become the scavenger but it just wasn't the same. After Marko died, I usually just stayed in my base as I had unlimited food (I had the trap where you put 1 food and get two food in return...profit).
I also had weapons like 3 assault rifles, 2 shotguns, 1 sniper, numerous knives and etc. My base was maxed out on security with that alarm door and all boarded up. I also relied on the trader that comes every 3 days to trade. I still felt sad that Marko was now gone. The game ended around Day 45. I was happy. I felt relieved that the war was over. Even if it's a game, it makes you feel like you really are one of the survivors. This is how impacting this game is. This is how amazing this game is.

The Good:
This is a very beautiful game. The graphics are very pleasing for the characters and the architecture. The level designers should be given top marks. There are lots of secrets to explore and find along with plenty of change of scenery and triggers along the way so that each enemy encounter is different, and exciting. The Bad:
Who ever did the lightning did a terrible job, there are huge areas of the game that have zero lighting at all so you just bump against walls and hope you find your way through, even with gamma turned all the way to the top. There is an a ton of bugs that I encountered in my 2-3 hour play time which was mostly pertaining to my companion not staying with me and getting stuck on terrain or other parts.. and just stood there.  The ranged combat system is working nicely except the DPI is set to super low and it's very hard to get a viable headshot if you are manually shooting. The melee combat system is pretty much useless because blocking is nearly impossible due to no lock on system or it does not allow you to back pedal while blocking to reposition for proper blocking. The design is great, the graphics are great, the level design is great.

Hunted: The Demon’s Forge is a fun Co-op play. Online is dead (RIP GameSpy), but playing over LAN works pretty well. I really enjoyed that mechanic, giving you options in each battle. Granted one character is far better at ranged, and the other is a tank in melee. The enemies drop weapons for loot. You can carry three weapons at any given time as well as a shield, and armor. Each weapon has a few few basic stats, damage, durability, and item quality. Each character has weapon and battle magic powers wich can be leveled up, I wish this system was a little more in depth. The foes you encounter are your standard LOTR variety with different names. During the campaign you retrieve gold wich unlocks resources that you can use in Crucible mode. Crucible is basically a user created Horde Mode. It adds to the replay value, and is a fairly decent level creator. I only wish it was possible to share your levels over Steam. The music is really on point with some of your standard medieval gothic tracks, think of the soundtrack from Conan the Barbarian and you get the idea. Overall this a great game for a husband & wife co-op team, and alot of fun to play.
You can also replace your save file with one that unlocks all the pre-order content.
