This is one of those games I wish I could give a neutral rating to but since I can't, I'm giving it a thumbs down. This game has great ratings, so you can read many other reviews on why PC is a good game. It does many things right - a neat branching scenario structure, solid foundation and some good voice overs to introduce the scenarios. For me, thats not enough and thus I'm going to explain why I don't think it's good enough to get a thumbs up.
Simply put, PC is a remake of the old Panzer General games. And after playing this for 20 hours and playing those, I still think they're better games for one main reason: the Panzer Corps scenarios are usually very flawed.
Panzer Corps makes the mistake of having too many units on too small of a map. There is little to no room for manuever. Thus the game is more puzzle-based than it is tactical. It's just a matter of figuring out that at "x" chokepoint I need 3 infantry, 1 arty and a tank to bust through. Once I know that, it's a matter of going to the next chokepoint. The time frames are always very tight, which rewards perfect unit usage and not necessarily good tactics. Seriously, whether you win or lose in any given map is often decided by your first half dozen combat results - if they're very favorable you're golden. If not, you're probably totally screwed.
There are two types of battles - you're on the offense and you're on the defense. If you're on the offense, the AI is going to just sit back and let you come to them. There's no ebb and flow here - it's all a matter of finding the "right" way to knock down yet another brick wall. After playing a number of these scenarios, I felt like the Allies trying to fight through the German hedgerows - frustratingly slow, brute-force combat tactics because you can't manuever. It gets old, fast.
If you're on defense, you can expect overwhelming odds since the AI isn't as effective as a human. So those scenarios are gamed up to present a challenge in numbers since the AI can't do it otherwise. They were, in a nutshell, disappointing.
There are other issues as well. I find the map to be muddled and not attractive. It's a wargame, I know, and it doesn't need to be beautiful. But I'd personally rather have counters than the muddled color scheme presented here. The branching campaign is pretty neat but has some real issues - for instance, if do well enough as Germany and you're going to presented with an almost unwinable scenario in the USA. Do slightly worse and delay the US invasion by two years and you'll have a far more winnable scenario. That's just bad design. Sea power has almost no part in the game as well, so it's all ground and air combat. Combined arms need not apply in most scenarios.
But it all goes back to scenario design - too many units, too small maps, no manuever and thus no imagination. I found them constricting. So why would I advocate paying for Panzer Corps (and don't get me started on the absurd DLC prices) when the old Panzer General II does it better? I can't. I'd rather play PG than PC and therefore PC gets the thumbs down. For those who are interested in the genre, I recommend Order of Battle: Pacific. It's a very similar game with larger maps, more fluid combat, combined arms and the maps aren't as muddled. To me it's a far superior game and easily worth the price difference.

I have been playing strategy games for almost 25 years. I love them. I am not an expert, but I am not bad at all.
It is extremely uncommon for me not to find any flaws in a game. There is always something wrong.
I have been thinking about buying this for a long time, because I have bought some games before, and just after that I have lost my motivation to play them.
But now, after 11 hours of intensive playing I think, that this game is PERFECT. I am really amazed how everything has been thought out. UI is extremely useful, intuitive, and everything, what you would expect, is shown in the right place.
AI is amazing. Many times, I just wanted to rush and moved my artillery (or support units) ahead into a theoretically safe area. And every time some AI units jumped in and slayed them like little kittens. AI behaves almost exactly like a human. It will exploit all your weaknesses. All of them. No regret, no remorse.
I have skipped built in campaigns and have bought Grand Campaign '39. And, if you think, that conquering Poland is piece of cake, you are SO WRONG. 7 hours of playing and I have just came into the third scenario. Campaign is thought out very well. The map is not 100% accurate, but it does include all the terrain features that you would expect, type of units (lots of Polish infantry, but not a match for Wermacht, lots of AT guns, and great Polish cavalry), and strategic objectives of that time (ie. bridges in Northern Poland). It also features successful Polish counter offensive near Bzura river - in that scenario you really need to be careful with every move you make. I live in Gdansk, former Danzig, the place where IIWW broke out, so I know what I am talking about.
Tutorial is just great and very informative. It doesn't treat you like a child trying to learn you how to click with your mouse. It focuses on the most important stuff.
If I had the opportunity, I would come back in time and SLAP my past-me in the face. Just for thinking too much.
Well, I don't have an access to a time machine, but don't do the same mistake... because the future-you could have...
Do you remember, what I said at the beginning? It is extremely uncommon for me not to find any flaws in a game. This is the first time. Panzer Corps has no flaws at all.
Just buy it. If you love strategy games, this would be AT LEAST one of the best games you would ever play.

Panzer Corps is a fun and accessible war-game. I know, I know hexes are scary but don’t let that deter you too much. If you can put up with a little sparsity in its presentation Panzer Corps is an engaging and expansive strategy game.
The base campaign sees you taking control of the German army during WW2 and you will visit most of the fronts in the European war. The game also uses a semi dynamic campaign which will give you access to new missions depending on your performance.
It also features my favorite thing in strategy games, persistent units. througout the campaign your units will gain experience and perks that in the end can have a big effect on your units survivability. It almost goes without saying that your dead units will stay dead. A more personalized core force might have been even better but what is there is engaging and fun.
In the end Panzer Corps is fun and easy get started in and I reccommend it to anyone who likes a bit more challenge in their strategy games without going full Hearts of iron. The only thing I can really say against it is that it might be a tad over priced without a sale and that its simple presentation makes the ipad version more attractive than the PC.

Ball of Wonder is an Arkanoid style game.
This clone is set in the wonderful world of circus, and has some improvements that add a little bit of interesting to the formula.
The pad could be move it using the keyboard or mouse. I prefer the second one because it's easier to control it.
There are nine types of power-up, and three slots to collect them. So you can activate them pressing 1-2-3 keys depending of the situation. These power-ups are very similar to the original ones and they haven't surprised me.
There are different objectives in each stage too. Sometimes you must destroy everything, sometimes gather points, pop-up balloons... and there are some dark levels where its very difficult to find the last few blocks. This fact offers a little of variety and breaks the routine.
The game seems a port from portable devices and in my opinion it fits better there and it also offers a co-op mode to share the experience with some friend.
Does the world need another Arknoid style game? May be not but this is a cheap decent clone of the classic with some nice features that it looks like interesting.
Buy it if you are a fan of this kind of games.
The game has achievements and trading cards.

More of the same from Ubisoft. It's difficult not to compare this to Far Cry 3 that was released two years proir. It is still an open sandbox environment that offeres repetative mission types and collectables that encourage you to scour the map in search of them but not much has been added in this new entry to the series.
You play as Ajay Ghale, a son that has travelled to Kyrat to spread the ashes of his mother. Just like the previous major title in the series the land is under the control of a war lord, Pegan Min, although he is not as compelling as Far Cry 3's Vaas. The opening cutscene introduces the player to the world of Kyrat. As nice as the game's cutscenes look they often feel overly long and unskipable. As they are always from the point of veiw of the player character they are very boring after the first couple and the camera sways as simulate the character looking around a room but it is distracting as this only happens in cutscenes. Characters tend spew pages of dialogue while either sitting or standing right infront of the playing locking their dead eyes with the screen. Ajay is quickly drafted into helping the rebellion named The Golden Path against Pegan Min and even though Ajay is not a soldier he is all too happy to pick up a rifle and start slaughtering enemies one fortress at a time.
Story missions tend to involve travelling to a location and killing all enemies or sneaking around to steal an item or assassinate a target. Side missions are a mix of common mission types such as attacking, stealing or protecting convoys, hunting specific animals, rescuing hostages and assassinating targets without being detected. The Golden Path has no clear leader and the two contenders have differeng opinions on how they should fight. This results in them sometimes offering different objectives during missions. The game makes a big deal out of these choices but they ultimatley mean nothing until the final mission when the same two options are available regardless of past decisions.
Controls are the same as the previous installment with only the driving being adjusted. By default it is set to use the left analog stick of the contoller to steer and adjust the speed both forward and in reverse. With the vehicle controls bound completely to the one stick you can now shoot in any direction while driving but the twists and turns in the road are difficult to cope with if you're not looking forwards. To compensate for this is an auto drive feature that can be activated any time and the car will stick to the road and drive to the current waypoint. Controls for driving can be changed back to normal in the options.
Gunplay is still the same. You can carry up to four weapons and a knife for melee attacks and stealth takedowns. You can also carry grenades, molotovs, C4 and mines but some of these are only unlocked after purchasing them from the arms dealer in towns and outposts. Enemies can still spot you from far away and different types will react by hiding behind cover or rushing to take you out. stealth takedowns are always an option and bodies can be picked up and moved to prevent guards from noticing your intusion. However one guard can still walk around oblivious to the fact that his commrades have all disappeared.
The parachute and wingsuit return to make falling from a hight or jumping off towers less dangerous however you need to slowdown fully after opening the parchute before making contact with the ground otherwise you'll be instantly killed. It is not as forgiving as games like Just Cause 2. Running across the map can sometimes be quicker than driving but you do run the risk of being attacked by enemies or wild animals. The frequency of animal attacks is lower than Far Cry 3 but they are just as dangerous. Simply sprinting past a Rhino will spook it and when they start charging then you will usually end up dying. The animals can be skinned to upgrade weapon holsters and other items which is recommended to be done early in the game so that you can carry more ammo and weapons. One new addition to the game is the grappling hook which allows you to climb the side of certain cliffs and swing between platforms. These are nice little additions but finding the anchor points can sometimes be difficult.
Far Cry 3 found a comfortable style of gameplay that the developers are reluctant to alter. The gunplay is easy and once you have your favourite loadout of weapons you can be unstopable. The stealth sections still frustrat when you're forced into them without weapons but it is greatly rewarding to clear out an outpost without being detected. Collectables will appeal to the completionist type of players but other than money and experience there is little reason to find them all. The previous game at least rewarded the player with a more powerful melee weapon but Far Cry 4 has no such reward. If Far Cry 3 impressed you and you want to play more then this should entertain you. The story is not great but the gameplay is fun although unevolved from the previous entry in the series.

Played before it came onto Steam, so my hours on here aren't a real representation of my time spent playing.
However, none of it's really inspired me to come back. I was hoping that with a Steam release they would do away with their own clunky, unecessary client. However, that was not the case, as it still forces you to install "Arc" upon first start up.
Developers, the beauty of Steam is that there are more than three games. Please stop making your own client to seem more official. They're often horribly designed and annoying.
As for the actual game, it's meh. There aren't enough characters to lock them out if someone else has already picked them, such as League or Dota. So if you only have a few characters that you enjoy playing, well that sucks. Not to mention the grind to unlock other characters is much too long. If the gameplay was more satisfying, perhaps it'd be worth it.
Instead of towers, you have energy pools or whatever, that allow you to summon three different creatures that fill different roles. However, you can summon over what someone else has picked, so there's really no tactical rhyme or reason for any of it, because there's no punishment for picking the wrong creature in the wrong spot. Also, if you're team isn't doing well, you're pretty much going to lose. To win the game, you have to kill enemy players and get objectives to charge up your guardian, so it will attack the other one, allowing you to deal damage to it. But if you're losing every fight and objective, well that sucks, looks like you're losing the game because there's nothing you can do as an individual.
The art style is interesting, and I enjoy some of them, although it's clear where others took their inspiration. (cough cough Bastion cough).
Either way, there are other games I'd rather invest my time and energy into. An interesting base, and maybe it will grow into a better game, but right now I can't really recommend it.

Every once in a while there is a new Moba/HeroShooter, that comes into the world of gaming and mostly it is more or less just a different artstyle that differs it from other competitors. BUT, there are also new entries that trying to make a change in this rusty used genre, the latest one is named "Gigantic" and I will give you a little peak why it is different, but feels so familiar.. in a good way.
First of all, Gigantic is a 3rd-person Free-2-Play Action-Moba, so in terms of gameplay, a faster version of games like LoL or DotA where you look over the shoulder of ther character you play, to give you a hint what the hell it is.
The goal in this fast paced 15 min matches is to defeat the enemy guardian, the active inhibitor or base in other Mobas. To do so, you need to fill up a gauge where the first team who just gets 100 points, is able to damage the enemy's guardian. You gain those points by killing your enemies, or placing your own or defeating enemy's creatures on specific points on the map. Once in a while the creatures are creating those points by themselves. The guardian at the end has 3 lifebars, which needs to be destroyed to win this game.
So in short, gain 100 points, attack the guardian of your enemy and take his 3 lifes to win.
It's as simple as that.
With a control you know from Palladin, Smite and other games which Gigantic is sharing his more action oriented gameplay, you get this familar feeling, you played those games before. Which in most cases feels boring after a day or two, so you move on or go back to old games you played.
But the mixture of the objective style gameplay from mobas, with his unusal use of mobs as creatures, which serve as towers, and the shooter like experience of most of the classes, you get tactical freedom in terms of how you get the needed points, while staying a fast paced and action-packed game.
In terms of champions you have 19 different champions, which the usual roles, like Tank, DD and Support. Important is, the skill system, where you need to pick two different paths for each skill, which 2 tiers, to change the champs the way you need them in the game, also there are no items you equip in this game. Anyway, in my opinion its good, cause otherwise it would slow the game more than someone could wish for.
True you know most of the different roles and their playstyle, but because of the very fast movement, where you can get to every place on the map in a few seconds, you cant play your for example support like you are used to. Furthermore, most champs do have a little twist, which makes it slightly a new experience.
After 5 hours, well I can say Gigantic has the potential to be a very good game and can finds its own niche to exist next to all the other competitive games. Before I get into this, I should say this is a fun game. But a review is a decision to tell people whether or not you would reccommend it. And I don't.
Good things:
1) It works. There's no real hiccups, the UI is a little clunky but functional, and it has yet to crash (which is more than I can say for some other card-based video games I play).
2) You can get every card for free if you're up to the grind.
3) The aesthetic is what you'd expect from Wizards, with top-notch art and fitting music.
Less than good things:
1) The free-to-play model isn't strictly bad if it's done right, and it's not strictly done wrong here, but, strictly speaking, unless you're willing to drop a few dollars on some booster packs, you're going to have an extremely slow, difficult start until you start getting better cards.
2) The free cards you get at the beginning are garbage. You'll have a hard time beating even the easy AI without some luck. It lets up after you start unlocking cards and building better decks, though.
Opposite of good things:
1) You can unlock every card basically for free, if you can put up with the garbage starting cards and grinding a maximum of 400 coins (not even 3 boosters) every day for about a year.
2) The final story missions in each chapter are almost unwinnable without an extreme amount of luck. Enemy decks are way better than yours, and you'll end up having to restart just to get a good starting hand most of the time. Let alone those games (most of them) where you spend 5 turns being mana-starved, playing 1 card at a time until you're top-decking, barely holding your opponent back, only to draw 5 lands in a row.
3) The UI is frustratingly slow and clunky, revolving around a timer that players can stop manually in order to play cards without risk of their turns running out, or that will randomly stop itself for no apparent reason, or will seemingly skip past phases and pauses the player wants to take.

Dungeons of Dredmor ended up being the gateway roguelike for a lot of people on Steam. The ASCII tiles of NetHack and ADOM aren't the best place to start for everyone, but the goofy classes and antics of Dredmor's bushy-eyebrowed heroes are an easy sell. It straddles an important line between more mainstream adaptations of the concept and the originators, where neophytes can find easy access and veterans can find a new take on old ideas. And while it may not be perfect in a lot of ways, it passes the main test of being something you can play for way, way too long.
Dredmor is really a traditional, grid-based, turn-based, everything-random roguelike dressed up in some handsome(ish) graphics and modern(ish) sensibilities. The only story you get is that you're a hero, and you're descending into the titular dungeons to whack the equally-titular Lord Dredmor. There's a thick layer of nerd humor over the whole package that runs more than skin-deep, as it even informs the class and stat systems with entries like Mathemagic and Caddishness. Luckily it's not the aggravating metahumor of something like Retro City Rampage, and is actually quite snappy and clever for the most part.
The aforementioned class system is probably the big draw of DoD, for newbies and veterans alike. Each character you roll gets seven skill sets to choose from a list of dozens, including everything from sword and shield skills to veganism and communism. Every time you level up, you can unlock another skill from one of your sets, allowing you to knock out one tree with half a dozen levels or diversify as you see fit. Sets tend to be eclectic mixes of active skills and passive bonuses, with some being demonstratively better than others but all of them interesting and worth a try.
Outside of the skill system, there's admittedly not a lot of innovation to be found here. You wander the dungeon, grab loot, kill monsters, and so on. There are shrines to pray to, gods to appease, vending machines to shake, traps to disarm, levers to pull, and plenty of things to die to. Unlike the roguelikes of yore, however, death tends not to come all that swiftly in Dredmor. It's pretty easy to keep your stats and gear up with the challenge presented by enemies if you're cleaning out the floors, to the point that by floor three or so, nothing's going to kill you outside of a room completely packed with monsters. Your demise is more likely to come via attrition, by small mistakes adding up to run you out of healing items and eventually health.
This ties into the main problem with Dredmor, the fact that individual runs can get pretty boring after a point. Unlike most roguelikes, the early game is when you need to pay attention to your skills and your loot. Once you get your rhythm locked in, levels start to blend together. The slow default move speed and animations drag things out a bit longer than they should, and your inventory and crafting windows really could have used another pass on usability. For as many steps forward that Dredmor takes as a modern roguelike, it has a couple feet planted firmly in the past.
All that said, I was able to sink 30 hours into the game before I grew well and truly tired of it. And those were an enjoyable 30 hours of looting, smashing, and giggling at the goofy jokes. The odds aren't good that you'll face down Lord Dredmor before boredom claims your character but on the way there, you'll get to charm diggles and make omelettes and wear a magic traffic cone on your head. Dredmor will go a lot farther with those new to the roguelike genre, but there is undeniably something for everyone, at least while it stays fresh.

Be warned. This game is hard.
If you are a namby pamby elf, this game is not for you.
Give it a finger and it won't take your arm, it will take your entire family tree.
However, it is also fair.
Get used to the phrase "YASD" which stands for "Yet Another Stupid Death".
When you die, it is your fault. Maybe you didn't pay attention to where you were going and stepped on a trap. Maybe you underestimated your opponent and didn't realise you had to run before it was too late. Keep your escape routes open and weigh up risk/reward before doing anything.
You are one step away from death at any and every point in the game.
The challenge is overcoming the dungeon, but also yourself. Those rash impulses that overtake body and mind as victory looms every closer. When you finally see your prey, the Lord Dredmor and bloodlust over runs your mind, hunger for the suffering of the one who put you through so much to get here, fight it! Your hatred and thirst are his greatest weapons, though his array of spells aren't to be sniffed at.
Becoming complacent is akin to suicide in this game.
All of that aside though, if you're looking for a challenge, it's a good intro to the rogue like genre and I got 300 hours out of it, for my £3, so it's a great value proposition. Be careful and you should be fine, once you learn the tricks.

This was a great game. It's bursting with style and personality. I loved the art direction, the easthetic is great and the characters are well-designed. Dem paintings, too. Freaky. The music was great, too, I found myself humming some of the tunes to myself when I was away from the game. Most of all, the story was great. I always love a story that brings a tear to my eye at the end.
The game isn't without its flaws, though:
The puzzles are astonishingly simple. I was never really stumped, I even solved one of the puzzles by accident without even knowing how the person I saved was getting murdered.
There's also very little connectivity between each puzzles. You almost never use parts of older puzzles once you've solved them and the people you've saved once never become relevant again. That's a pretty big missed opportunity right there, since this game is heavily based upon time loops and such. This game could have been so much more.
Also: it's short! Outside of collecting all the playing cards, there's not much replay value.
Still, it's a pretty good game, I enjoyed it.

Having played the original Thief Dark Project (1998) and Metal Age (2000), this brought me back. It's the great stealthy "FPS" any old school Thief player knows and loves, but with updated graphics, some new features and skills (focus), and a deep immersive story line. They brought in new storyline characters, but kept Basso!

I was really excited for this when it was previewed at E3. That was a while ago. Even with the bits that seemed out of place (rooftop chases) it still was exciting to see a new Thief game coming out.
But...it's a little disappointing. As a Thief game.
It's not bad. It's a good stealth game, but it's not a good Thief game.
The graphics are nice, the stealthing is nice, the voice-acting is good, the animations are fluid but it's just not like the original games.
The story is generic, the writing is amateur, and it is somewhat linear even with a semi-open hub world you can explore. It does hold your hand with waypoints and the threat indicators, but there is a twist.
The game is FILLED with customization options. Not for the graphics, but there's a custom difficulty that allows you to change the game mechanics. If you want to you can completely turn off any sort of waypoint, health bar, threat indicator, and even turn off your light gem. It is nice to have some customization to change up what is your standard (somewhat) butchering series reboot.
It's in no way a bad game, but it's a bad Thief game. Go in cautiously.

the negativity at this games release hailed from people expecting something neither the dev-team nor the publisher of this glorious dungeon-crawler-pearl never promised. people expected another open-world-rpg ala Fallout or Eldar Scrolls.
people saw "Bethesda" and simply jumped to conclousions.
that out of way:
Hunted is an amazing game.
it's visual quality holds up pretty good, even today. the art-direction is more a dark/gritty type of fantasy which looks a) fantastic and b) gives this game a more mature touch. in some aspects the art-direction reminds me of Gears of War...yes sounds strange...
Talking about Gears of War -> Hunted is pretty much a fantasy version of said game with more rpg-elements and loot.
Combat feels great, no matter if you're takin cover and shooting enemies from a distance, blasting them with spells or hacking/blocking in melee range controls are always responsive and feel fluid. which is a good thing, cause apart from solving some simple puzzles or listening to great npc-dialogue you will be fighting most of the time.
Inspite of the end-of-days Gears of War setting Hunted does feel like a classic dungeon-crawler come to live.
But what sets this game realy apart from a simple action-game with steller production quality is the way the game is set up. Your basicaly never alone, the premise is two people and the game sticks with it. the great thing about this is that the AI doesn't suck, yes sometimes (realy seldom) there's a little path-finding issue, but in general you "feel" like playing with a another person, no matter if it's combat, exploring or a riddle your team is solving.
The story centers on those two and is actualy not that bad, it's not the grand scheme of things which is important, but their relationship. you will chuckly hearing some their pockin at each other, you will feel attached to both after some time. especialy when playing singelplayer this game provides an amazing expierience simply from the fact of your companion. i've never played a game where my ai-companion felt that much alive/real and that is taking never Bioware games into account.
Overall:
-still realy good visuals
-fantastic soundtrack, great voiceover (english)
-tight controls, polished combat
-an interesting story, which is more suited for mature players, both mainchars are not "heroes" and they show a real lack of empathie for anyone but themselves (which is a fantastic setup and i did love it, but not suited for minors)
-an interesting gameworld and a great sense of exploring/dungeoncrawling
-in general a great sense of polish and budget
-one of the best integrations of an Ai-companion
-creat two player co-op (but since game-spy is down you will have to read up on gettin co-op started)
way underrated simply cause people expected something completly diffrent than the dev always promised. Hunted is like  one of those great old-school arpgs, immersive stroy and gameplay but not sporting a open world setting.

Without a doubt this is the most under rated and polemic game Rockstar has ever made. I was never big into stealth games but this tittle has completely changed my mind on the genre. Is not to say it’s an easy game, it requires patience and it will take a while for you to get used to the mechanics, but once you do you’ll get immersed into a gritty world and you’ll be cornered into many terrifying moments.
Its very niche and it won’t be everybody’s cup of tea, hence why it has a small (But strong) following. But for a game that has a big controversy behind it is not tasteless or immature, in fact the topics the game deals with are done in a very credible way, and that keeps the plot engaging. Is not heavy in plot, but it has very fascinating plot elements and horrifying implications. It’s extremely well made and it saddens me that many of its strong elements are almost over shadowed by its strong violence. It’s truly not a game for the squeamish, it might be old, but it has aged pretty well and the executions that make this game get its reputation are brutal and cold.
The sound design is incredible, the use of dynamic music adds amazing depth to the experience and the enemy gangs have excellent voice acting that adds great characterization and back story to them, but doesn’t make them more likeable, after all, they are scum, just like you. This added with the level design and gameplay creates for a unique experience. You might be fighting other human beings, but they are stronger and outnumber you. Some levels demand the use of stealth and wits while others require you to go gun blazing. I’d argue the third person shooting is a bit dated, but with some practice I was able to pop down enemies and feel like an action film hero. This game demands dedication and doesn’t hold your hand, after all it’s from a very different era, which some will love and others dislike.
But more importantly the controls work amazing on a Keyboard. You can freely customize the controls and they were never an issue for me. It controls and plays like a charm, and I love it. It makes fantastic use of a keyboard and mouse, so this is in fact a very solid PC port (Now if only they were gentle enough to make it friendly on newer operative systems so you didn’t had to mess around for a product you just paid for).
And if that wasn’t enough, the game has some very good replay value, it has two difficulty settings, and the hardest setting only removes the enemy radar. So it’s very balanced difficulty wise, and any mistake you go through will be your fault. But being able to unlock concept art, cheats and extra game modes is something that makes playing through this game more rewarding. You’ll spend 40 hours and more trying to 100% it.
So, whether you’re buying this to revive the PS2/Xbox memories or to get into it for the first time, I heavily recommend it, especially if you are into stealth and subtle psychological horror.

This is a game that really makes me question the binary nature of reviews on Steam. This probably not a game I would recommend but that doesn't make it bad and I don't feel it deserves a thumbs down.
This is a game that you will probably only enjoy if you like Breakout clones. I haven't played much but the basic mechanics are straight forward: move a paddle back and forth bouncing a ball at bricks. What differentiates this from other Breakout clones is the fact that the ball has a small amount of gravity applied to it. Normally in Breakout the ball would just be an aimless floating object that went in one direction until it hit an obstacle. In Ball of Wonder we get something a little different; we get curvature. If you knock a ball too far to one side of the field, it will not bounce indefinitely until reaching the blocks as would normally happen in Breakout and is usually quite annoying to wait for. No, instead the ball will lose upward momentum and return to you in a reasonably timely fashion. This may not sound like much but in my opinion it's quite a big improvement over the normal mechanics. I only wish I could increase the gravity value just a tad, as the ball is still very floaty.
I don't see myself playing a lot of this, but I support the creator's outside-the-box thinking and would love to see what they might produce in the future.

7 hours played, version 1.2.6, Linux
7 hour Overall: Undecided. The graphics are pretty and the game has tremendous variety, complexity, and depth. But the AI and user interface need polish.
******
3 hours playing: it was interesting with pretty graphics and intriguing strategic elements.
Worlds of Magic is entertainig with strategic elements (portals, settlers, city development) similar to CaveWars and Age of Wonders III. The ability of units to stack on the strategic map makes tactical combat similar to the Heroes of Might & Magic series. So far the difficulty is on the easy side, but with only 3 hours I have yet to encounter anything besides neutral enemy armies.
Pros: Graphics are nice, animations smooth, MANY different player options. the magic system has great depth and adds strategic complexities. Solid gameplay and user interface.
Cons: A few minor bugs found; lacking campaign/story/quests/scenarios for single player. The high complexity probably makes the game unbalanced in some-way, although I haven't found anything yet which is clearly overpowered.
******
7 hours playing: So many tedioiusly easy battles with roaming neutral armies. The animations and user interface now seem too slow because I now know exactly what I want my units to be doing. [This game needs to shorten the animations, or allow issuing orders to groups of multiple units at the same time: E.g. tell all archers to shoot at a group of three selected enemies.]
Also it is starting to get annoying trying to figure out where they are coming from. It is difficult to track enemy movements across the map because neutral enemy armies are grey and blend into the map. If you aren't looking directly at an enemey during the enemy turn you can't see what has moved where. There is a button to alert you to spotted enemies, but after you click it once you can't cycle back to it.
Speaking of the map, there is no indication of the difficult of the random dungeons across the map without clicking on them individually. This could be fixed by indicating on the map the level of the highest level monster that might be there. It is tedious to click on all of them to determine which ones are too hard, and which are possible to defeat with your current armies.
There doesn't appear to be any way to zoom in or out without a mouse-wheel. The options don't appear to have the option to set an alternate key-binding for this important feature.
AI errors/exploits have become prominent. For example, teleporting unicorn riders next to enemy archers, and then enemy melee units next to the enemy archers choose to abandon the archers to their doom and move towards my other units (archers, druids, etc.) instead of attacking my unicorn riders right next to them and the enemy archers.
The developers clearly focused a lot of time into the rich diversity of units, unit attributes, and spells but some parts are lacking polish. Sometimes powerful random events appear without warning (e.g. fire drakes spawning near your first town). If something so drastic is about to occur there should be some kind of lead-up before hand that might hint that something is about ot happen, or some explanation of 'why' it happened.
Minor Bugs: Tutorial blocks access to the menu so you can't skip to next tutorial if/whenever you want to.

Before I get into this, I should say this is a fun game. But a review is a decision to tell people whether or not you would reccommend it. And I don't.
Good things:
1) It works. There's no real hiccups, the UI is a little clunky but functional, and it has yet to crash (which is more than I can say for some other card-based video games I play).
2) You can get every card for free if you're up to the grind.
3) The aesthetic is what you'd expect from Wizards, with top-notch art and fitting music.
Less than good things:
1) The free-to-play model isn't strictly bad if it's done right, and it's not strictly done wrong here, but, strictly speaking, unless you're willing to drop a few dollars on some booster packs, you're going to have an extremely slow, difficult start until you start getting better cards.
2) The free cards you get at the beginning are garbage. You'll have a hard time beating even the easy AI without some luck. It lets up after you start unlocking cards and building better decks, though.
Opposite of good things:
1) You can unlock every card basically for free, if you can put up with the garbage starting cards and grinding a maximum of 400 coins (not even 3 boosters) every day for about a year.
2) The final story missions in each chapter are almost unwinnable without an extreme amount of luck. Enemy decks are way better than yours, and you'll end up having to restart just to get a good starting hand most of the time. Let alone those games (most of them) where you spend 5 turns being mana-starved, playing 1 card at a time until you're top-decking, barely holding your opponent back, only to draw 5 lands in a row.
3) The UI is frustratingly slow and clunky, revolving around a timer that players can stop manually in order to play cards without risk of their turns running out, or that will randomly stop itself for no apparent reason, or will seemingly skip past phases and pauses the player wants to take.
So many deaths, so much lutefisk, not to mention a few thousand diggles. I like it!

Using the name of an established gaming series is already a task riddled with expectations. It is a difficult and often daunting task to replicate and improve a milestone of any genre.
Like the gentrification of your favourite suburb; Thief, as much of a title as it is a testament to the gameplay, has deducted the core values of the franchise and replaced them with shallow marketable features.
Any game focused on the design principles of 'stealth' would do so with intelligent level design, a player directed experience and tools that feel valued to their potential contexts. However I found a substantial lack of engagement in all these areas, both in my experience at home and while playing at a friend's house.
Although the game falls short on everything that should be expected of Thief, the nature of a purely market-orientated game gives rise to some impressive features. Features that I did enjoy, were the noise hazards, expanded options to tailor your gameplay experience, and the visuals.
They did an excellent job exploiting the first person medium; having you direct Garret's hands over containers, paintings and items of interest. This feature could be perceived as redundant, but it gave you some ephemeral agency in your role as a 'thief' and made you feel much more engaged in the action of stealing itself.
However this could not save the game for me. On every objective level, the game fails to deliver innovation relevant to it's title, legacy and to this era of gaming.
The common challanges that drive the appeal of stealth are replaced with linear environments, predictable enemies and uneccesary assistance in beforementioned challenges. Players will feel little agency in their navigation through the world, and any illusion of choice will always be broken from poor combat mechanics and a lackluster sandbox attempt.
This game would be worth the money for $20, but I feel there are many games out there with half the production size, but infinitely more in gameplay features. For this, my time with Thief was frustrating and in the personal space of my own home I felt uninclined to continue my gameplay experience.

The thing about Thief is it doesn't know what it wants to be.
And I'm gonna explain in my convoluted drawn out review style, enjoy the paragraphs.
This entry in the Thief game was hyped up a lot by Thief fans, stealth fans, and others (me for one) in general.
I never played the other Thief games, but everyone knows that they are critically acclaimed, and for good reason, however this entry, or Thief 4, is the black sheep.
When I mentioned Thief doesn't know what it wants to be, I meant it wasn't sure if it wanted to be an action game (from the bow and arrow bits), or a stealth game, if it wants to be a stealth game it's very clunky, and Garret feels like he's carrying an elephant, if it wants to be an action game, the fighting is easy and you get a lot of leeway for bow kills.
Honestly this deserves comparison to recent successful stealth titles, notably Deus Ex: Human Revolution, and Dishonored, especially since it feels like Thief drew a lot from Dishonored, but still ended up a boring game.
In both titles you could fight your way through to the target, or stealth your way to the target, either method worked great and felt really rock solid, in Thief it feels watered down.
The setting of the story is something of note as well, the devs mentioned Garret would not get involved with the current politics, rather just weave through it to serve his own needs. Yea uh...no, and its disappointing because a "spectator" point of view from Garret would have been great, but instead you gotta get involved to save your jailbait friend who got caught.
This game is a conundrum, I read all dev interviews, what they had planned, what they wanted to do, watched it at E3, hell I read about how they developed the bow which is the best part of this game, and somehow this game still falls flat.
The map and level design also fukken SUCKS. Stonemarket is a maze without the map, there are ledges and walkways that lead to dead ends and nowhere, there's load screens in places you don't want them, using windows to travel between places sounds easy but in reality its a hassle.
Levels are not too complicated at all, often with very simple pathing helped by the fact that the game feels the need to shoehorn you through it with the whole you-cant-come-back-to-this-area, making levels linear.
Edit: I want to add to my review, after giving this game a second shot and retrying it, I found it was just as bad as it was when I put it down.
There's cripplingly bad lag similar to what I saw with Watch_Dogs which made me question if Eidos can even goddamn code or do any QA, there's a bug where windows just don't open no matter how much you mash E after chapter 3.
But most of all I want to addon how I feel about this game after going a bit more indepth.
It sucks. The impact isn't there, combat is dull, stealth is dull, the fact you steal crap to buy stuff so you can...steal more is a derp moment, the goddamn QTE for opening windows riles me up, I still continue to question if this game wants to be stealth or action but it's a blend of both and ended up looking like some mutant experiment gone wrong.
This game feels like Dishonored, if you gutted it, sold the organs on the black market, and used the money to try and make it on a budget, simply put. No soul, little substance.
If you want to get into the Thief series specifically, skip Thief, get the previous entries instead and THEN this one, but on discount.
If you're interested in stealth games, skip Thief.

It's not very good, tbh, like a VERY short choose your own adventure game, but I see the core of a good game there. I can imagine a Depression Quest II made in RPG maker, or some Rouge-like procedurally generated isometric world, where you struggle to build up your self-worth, energy, while manitaining relationships, physical health, and surviving day to day.
So, I can imagine a good version of this game concept, but that's not why I recomend it. If that was all it had going for it, I'd give it a thumbs down. But you can't talk about the Depression Quest without grappling with the meta-narrative around it, and if you are in any capacity a gamer (e.g. someone who genuinely enjoys playing lots of games, and possible enjoys the company of other people who do so as well), you kinda need to grapple with it. Part of that process is actually playing it. Is it good? I don't think so. Could it have been? Potentially, sure. Does it merit the hate? It's not like it's some sh*t asset flip, no. Could The Quinnspiracy make a good game in the future? I can't be sure, but I truely believe she has the capacity for it at least.
Anyway, you can't beat the price, and you'll finish it in under an hour probably. Give it a go.

Pay to Win

Disadvantages:
1. The game seems to be purposely slow paced  (especially when it comes to equiping troops and leveling to 2nd rank), it's very likely for most to lose their patience and either buy gold or quit the game.
2. Nonsense restrictions, such as on crafting, which can be carried out only by one blacksmith at a time.
3. Gold buttons are everywhere, thus making it very likely to 'accidentally' spend even that little gold bars you got available from in-game leveling and battle quests.
4. Enemy AI on challenging and 'brutal' difficulty,  has often additional soldiers which do not appear on pre-battle info. In general it feels the AI is 'cheating' on certain battles.
5. The game is quite unbalanced when it comes to the gathering of resources. Insanely long cooldowns. As an example: gathering 20pcs of stone takes 2:30 hours... Upgrading structures consume an imposible amount of resources.
6. Crafting gear is expensive and exaustingly slow, it takes 5 crafting 'stages' and takes about 4 days to craft a simple bracelet.
7. There is no way to tell about the water level and flooding likeliness.
8. When I reached winter season, I found it so terribly boring, no crops and no forests. Trees yield way too little wood, by chopping 1500 pcs (first castle upgrade) you end up clearing everything around making the map desolate and cold, like Isenguard... Furthermore 'tracking beasts' on winter removes all the last (if any remained) forrest left on the now depressing looking map. In retrospective, I think I mismanaged awfully the resources, however it is actually not hard to do so and go off track.
9. The game fails to inform the player early on about building bonuses (forcing you around level 25-35 to demolish, rebuild and spent additional time and resources restructiring your cities). For example, I found out later in the game that you must build producers next to military buildings, it is rather vague how many residences you need to sustain a city and I had to count hexes to make out wood cutters range (tracking and wood cutting range is about 4-5 hexes).
10. Has some minor bugs and disconnects from server 2-3 times (on average) during a 6h period.
Advantages:
1. The game has very well polished graphics for a game of it's kind.
2. Battle and map zooms in, up to a great detail, very pleasant to the eye.
3. Terraforming (changing the flow of rivers etc) and the changing of seasons is quite nice.
4. Great variety of troops, however I'd like more detail on weaknesses and strengths of certain units.
5. I believe the game most probably might be much more playable on my tablet.
Conclusion:
There is lack of vital information about how things work and -alas- you got to discover them by yourself. It's very difficult to enjoy properly this game, you either must have got lots of time and patience or  spend a good deal of real cash. I'd prefer just paying a one time amount for it as a complete game, without the long resource 'cooldwns' and any other cash-involved transactions.
Suggestions :
Reduce the cost of construction and cooldowns, amplify the benefits of gamer commitment to the game. Alternatively give the posibility of a one time purchase into a 'premium' status (global reduced cooldowns, reduced crafting costs) with the guarantee of no more gold transactions.
Epilogue:
We choose to play a game in order to get entertained, enjoy some challenge and overall feel better at the end of the day. This game fails delivering such.

And I think that was the point. It’s a brazen, ghoulish celebration of violence and horror, as twisted and immoral as they get, and has no pretensions to be anything else. Almost holding you down and asking you “Is this really something you enjoy doing?” It may sound like I despise the game but I actually really enjoyed my time with it. No matter how raw it gets I was still very much engaged with it’s setting, story and tense if a bit dated stealth gameplay. I was drawn in and wanted to see more of what it had to offer and how it was going to end. I don't know if there can be a middle-ground of opinion with it. You'll likely either love it, or hate it. But for what it sets out to do, it does it admirably and with skillful craftsmanship. If that sounds like your jam well then have fun. You monster.

Far Cry 4 replaces FC3 as my favourite open world FPS game. The developers have managed to one-up the predecessor in all but story, which I felt a little disconnected with.
Even though there are still some significant flaws, I'm having a hard time being objective about it, because I love the core gameplay so much. It's like reviewing bacon, even if it's not perfect bacon, it's still flippin' BACON!
There's simply SO much to do throughout the campaign, and even though some would argue it all get repetitive at some point, I still enjoyed the 30+ hours I put into completing all the objectives and maxing out the 2 skill trees and getting all the uprades.
My complaints:
- The AI, it's acceptable for the most part , but mostly lemming style daft.
- The NPC's repetoire of dialogue is simply too thin. You'll hear them say the same few lines over and over and OVER. Even the local radio host aparently reruns the same 10 monologues to no end.
- You cannot have 2 active events simultaneously: I killed the driver of  a truck I was gonna hijack, but I hear gunshots and yelling behind me. It turns out to be a karma event where I was supposed to help the rebels kill a couple of soliders. I run 10 meters down the road towards the soldiers, crouch and snipe them - Tada! karma event complete. I turn around to get into the truck, but it has disappeard along with the dead bodies around it. Hrrrmpf!
- The boss fight in the last Shangri La was VERY frustrating to me. The infinitely spawning enemies do a good job in preventing you from hitting the boss at the exact time you're supposed to hit it, in order to keep it from spawning more enemies. Hated that part.
- Unskippable cutscenes / dialogues after a restart point.
Bottom line - Great FPS mechanics in a gorgeous open world bursting with activities you can complete using a plethora of vehicles and cool customizable weapons.  Even though the story might be a little thin, it has some very entertaining, colorful characters, presented by top notch voice actors.

Personal Rating: 7.5 of 10
Well, in general this is an awesome game. You can actually feel that the developers put in tonnes of effort to give you the old, dark and corrupted slum of city. I have not played any of the previous Thief title but this game gives me enough freedom to play and approach each quest. Thief is basically a semi open city game where you have to try to avoid being detected while achieving your goals.
The graphics is awesome specially when you maxed out your settings. However there is a serious performance issue after playing a while. There is a benchmark feature in the game and with maxed out setting I can get 50-60fps. The game is smooth for a while and after a mission or so it begins to lag terrible as if the game is trying to reload the texture for the location. The only work around I can find is to set graphics to the lowest possible. Even running on low texture will cause the lag issue. The background music only plays during encounters or certain event and you can only hear sound effects the other times which is excellent.
The story mission brings you to different locations and settings. Each mission feels really unique. The side quest are basically, well, item retrieving but there is a short story to accompany it. There aren't many side quests but in my opinion it is just right. As you progress, you will be able to purchase enhancement item, upgrade your equiptment and even skills. The game offers a selection of ammunitions that gives you more options to play the game. After each story mission, you are able to freely roam in the city completing side quests or simply finding loot. This process can be time consuming but it does give you a really great sense of completion as your collectibles loot are show cased in your hideout.
Apart from the performance issue, there are a couple more things that can be frustrating. The game allows quick save and load. But I do notice each time you reload, the enemies behaviour are reset. Example the guards are suppose patrol in certain pattern but instead they are teleport to a certain location and stationed there. There is also this particular guard in the city when you reload a quick save nearby, he will spin in a 'fasionable' manner while stationed. It is really difficult to approach him then because he will spot you (spinning 360). The city is divided into 2 region. Within each region the map is again divided into 2-3 areas. Now crossing between these areas will not cause the guards to respawn but moving across region will cause the guards respawn. This is extremely annoying and time consuming because you might need to travel between these area several time to complete side quests. And to travel between these areas, you might need to find the exit/entry point which could be an apartment, roof, blockage or door and there are no markers in the map and might be a little frustrating since you haven't memorize the entire map.
Now looking pass through all those set backs, Thief is a really great game and if you are a fan of first person stealth genre, you can give this game a chance.

Overall, the Sexy Brutale is definitely worth playing. It can probably be completed in about 5 hours, and has a great style, with art, music and theme coming together very well. However, for experienced puzzle solvers, or point'n'click veterans, the solutions to each mystery will seem somewhat shallow for the majority of the game.
The Groundhog Day comparisons are almost universal, and with good reason. However, I think it is also worth comparing The Sexy Brutale to both the N64 classic 'Majora's Mask' (you are locked in a timeloop, and each time you go through it, you progress a little bit forward; not to mention the theme of masks both games have) as well as the most recent 'Hitman' (similarly playing through the same space of time over and over, where instead of trying to make creative murder happen, you instead try to make that creative murder... not happen).
The game does have a few strikes against it. Its time mechanics are a bit underdeveloped (better time manipulation and/or access to fastforwarding are the primary concerns). The game has a tendency towards slightly simplistic puzzles (a 'complex' mode a la Hitmans Professional mode would be much appreciated, even if it might jar with some of the themes). The game also makes each 'case' very isolated from the rest of the mansion and the other victims (which makes the mansion feel less like the sprawling party it is clearly supposed to be). Finally, the game unfortunately saves some of the best concepts and ideas for the end (the 'Arm' idea have a LOT of design space in my view).
These shortcomings, however, are not nearly enough to make The Sexy Brutale a bad game, it merely keeps it from being an instant classic. The asking price is perfectly reasonable, but if you can get it on a sale, be sure to grab it immediately. Score (if you are into such a concept): 4/5

Panzer Corps Wehrmacht (PC) is a light, turn based (Igo-Ugo) strategy game and a reimplementation of the old school Panzer General (PG). If you liked PG you'll almost definitely enjoy PC and the opposite of course. The idea is simple. You start the second world war commanding part of the German army, starting from the invasion of Poland and decide its fate with possibilities ranging, depending on your performance, from its historical demise to a *minor spoiler*
.
All you have to do is move and fire your units in any order you desire. Simple enough, huh?
Sure, but in order to master the game, you have to grasp many subtle mechanisms. Panzer Corps features: a variety of terrain with unique characteristics, unit suppression, an interesting initiative system, unit retreat/surrender, a weather system, supply (albeit in an unrealistic form due to the lack of supply lines), entrenchment, zone of control, strategic redeployment and many more interesting elements.
Furthermore the game comes with many units that, besides chrome, offer many tactical opportunities. Will you plow the battlefield with slow moving King Tigers or blitz with Panther tanks? Will you dominate the skies with a combined fighters/dive bombers force or follow a fighter-bomber doctrine? Due to the many different unit types offered, the efficiency of combined arms really shines.
You are given command of a core force that you control through the entire game, in contrast to a couple of secondary/temporary units that are provided for a single scenario. This core force can be expanded by buying/upgrading units between or during the scenarios but, friendly note, don't try to figure the scale; units may represent divisions, corps, or even armies, depending on the scope of the scenario. In addition, every unit gains experience through combat and the dilemma of how to replace loses, through regular (inexperienced and cheap) or elite (battle-hardened and expensive) replacements, arises. This of course means I have to explain prestige as well...
Prestige (the game currency) depends on your performance on the scenario. That is the capture of objectives (primary/secondary) and the battle outcome (normal/decisive victory or defeat). A decisive victory may have to come many times through attrition which may cost in the long-run. Even more choices!
To begin with, the A.I. is relatively uninspired. It doesn't act terribly ahistorically or plain silly (besides two rare situations) but the difficulty of most scenarios comes through the numerical advantage of the enemy. Then we have the repetitive objectives, at least in Wehrmacht, "Capture all cities in X turns". A few people nag about the lack of replay value as well but I beg to differ. Besides the branching campaign and the multiplayer scenarios (can be played both online and hotseat) there are a lot mods at your disposal for free!
Another thing that bugged me is the fact that, although there is an option of a detailed battle sheet both before and after each combat, the game lacks detail both in the tutorial and the manual. This leaves those eager to dig deeper no option other than to go through many forum posts. For example artillery has a rate of fire stat that isn't mentioned anywhere in the game! Every basic piece of information is covered however and the interface, in most cases, is intuitive and elegant.
Finally, the realism issue arises. Due to its abstract nature this game is far from a simulation at a strategic level. The lack of many important details make it unrealistic at a tactical level as well. At its heart however every decision the player makes is realistic, in a sense that the same dilemmas arose to WW2 generals as well. Somehow, through the careful deduction from realism, this game manages to remain true, as much as a light wargame can, to the nature of the war.

This game has only been out for a little bit, but in how little time it's been here I can say that I have fallen in love with it already.
So, to give a good description, Games happen in a 5v5 format where both teams are working to kill the other teams guardian, however, the guardian can only be damaged when your own guardian rampages and holds the enemy's dwon to expose its weak spot. In order for your Gaurdian to rampage, you must give it energy, which is earned for getting kills and collecting it from special "nodes" on the battlefield.
These "nodes" are split equally between teams and can be defended by a variety of summoned creatures, but teams can steal energy from the others node after killing the creature belonging to that node.
Guardians have their own health and their health has been depleted, the team responsible wins the match
As far as balance goes, character stats are not balanced by their "class" as a characters "class" simply describes their general purpose. Instead character stats are based around the character's kit, Knossos, for example, unlike tanky characters in other games, exceeds in tanking damage and being HIGHLY mobile, but instead deals comparativly low damage to large groups with his basic attacks, instead opting to focus on one opponent, and really being at his most usefull when all of his abilities are not on cooldown.
I would recommend this game to those who enjoy MOBAs and team based shooters like Overwatch and Paladins, it just adds the tiniest things about how the game works that I just love, and that I have the feeling others will love too.

The original Manhunt is a very surreal game. It's almost practically forgotten about by most and only really brought up for it's political controvercy when it came out. It's a sadly overlooked game I think deserves more attention because of just how good it really was and how immersive of a game it is.
In Manhunt you don't play as a heroic character. You play as a convicted murderer sentenced to death, who is saved at the last moment by a sociopathic movie director. Who puts you into a walled off section of this ruined city called "Carcer City" which is essentially based on Detroit, to murder gang members and other undesirables while he films you doing it.
What the game does well that is strangely not talked about is how immersive it is. The world of Manhunt is not a pleasant one. You walk through long abandoned sections of a ruined city. And you're entirely alone throughout the game.The soundtrack to the game is also lots of ambient tracks that reflect how creepy and disturbing it all is. Every character in the game comes across as vicious and nasty, and it always feels like the main character is the most vicious of them all.
Thankfully the developers also understood exactly how to create a game like this. Manhunt is a well made stealth game (largely, I'll touch on that) where the main character is almost like a slasher villain. Inorder to kill enemies you must aquire weapons, and almost all of them are household objects. Plastic bags, bricks, shards of glass, almost anything you can find. And you get rewarded for killing enemies without being seen and for stalking them for a long period of time. It reminds me of Thief in terms of how it plays (having sound and light based stealth), except being focused on killing enemies. It is sick, sadistic, brutal, and paints a picture where there is no escape from the world you inhabit.
That being said it's not a perfect game. Later on in Manhunt parts of the game devolve into shooting sections that are frankly less interesting than the stealth sections. I think Rockstar added them in to inject variety but it comes off as unnecessary.
But that being said it's a fantastic game, and there isn't anything else quite like it. I think it should be played largely because it shows a different side to humanity than most people are willing to feature in games. But it isn't for the faint of heart. You play as the most dangerous animal, a hunter of man, and it's time to go to work.

I recently started getting back into magic after being inactive for around 15 years. However, other than standard tournaments, I don't have many opportunities to play against other players, so I figured I needed an online version of magic to practice. Magic duels is OK to get back into the mechanics and see what other people play, but other than that, it's a HUGE disappointment:
- Insane grind. buying boosters as a poor kid in the 90ies (p2w in its pure form) was more fun.
- Stupid deck restrictions: rares 2x, uncommons 3x (to keep serious players away or p2w low?)
- Strange format: not pure standard, balance seems off ( banned smuggler's copter still being played, too many cheap removal spells...)
- Terrible connectivity: connection losses all the time, dropped players get replaced by AI and most of the time, you have to beat the AI in order to not receive a loss, alt+tab is all it takes to get disconnected, possibly lots of room for exploits. Lags are so hard that often you can't hit the stop button to react to your opponent, which defeats the whole purpose of playing magic.
- No possibility to interact with other players: no chat, no trade, nothing. Which might be wise, because...
- The duels community equals the bottom of the magic community. You won't find many good matches, real magic fans are probablly somewhere else to be found. Often enough, playing a removal spell is all that it takes for your opponent to pull the plug and let the AI take over.... which surprisingly often leads to the AI coming back hard and winning a lost match... and then there are these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s just waiting everytime as long as the timer allows (playing a land after waiting for 1 minute) to make YOU unpatient and disconnect, giving them a default win.
- Always playing against the same decks. Right now: red burn, topters, green ramp, sphinx tutelage. boring.
- The campaigns are a joke. The way they try to tell stories is just unworthy of the magic universe. It's nothing but still images and written dialouge, combined with a muted 90ies-style render-cutscene at the end of each campaign. And the stories are just boring. It rather ruins the unvierse for me...
- Presentation is rudimentary at best. Graphics are just the cards, a boring table, generic FX like fireballs and lightnings... even tablets could do better. There is only 1 music track playing throughout the whole game and it will drive you insane after the 2nd loop.
I honestly can't find a reason to play this other than getting a very blury first impression of what magic the gathering is and that it's probably best to stay away from it lol. Do yourself a favor and play real magic or Xmage. I honestly can't understand the people giving this a thumps up. I am very sad not to recommend WoM in its current state (1.2.4). It had a lot of good ideas, sadly the product is crippled with flaws and bugs (and not only myrodants, the insectoid race in the game). UI is very clunky, lists are not exactly presented as list and are scroll fests (what good is an overview that show only 2 cities at a time? no troll in the game, so here they are?).
While artwork is gorgeous, translation to 3D models is very uneven. Music is decent while SFX are pretty awkward (smells like placeholder). Visual feedback when casting spell is present, although sometimes very discreet and as there is no sound to accompany the effect... Isometrical 3D also has counter-intuitive implementations (i.e. to select a unit on a mountain, you need to click at the base of square of the mountain, cities control zone visualisation is also affected by relief and is pretty confusing). Top-down map is present, but nearly no information is there (no armies, no resources) so its like totally useless. While the game seems to be fully in 3D, there is no way to rotate the camera (neither in strategic or tactical views) while this would already solve quite a few "visibility" issues.
There are also several bugs, most of them not game breaking but still ranging from slightly to very annoying.
The game feels so unfiinished and unpolished, yet I could go over it if the features in the game did work properly. Yet they don't. For example you have resources (typically minerals like adamantine or mithril) that are supposed to provide your troops with bonuses in the town owning them if you also have an alchemy guild. Does not work (or if it does, there is absolutely no visual feedback on that, numbers stay the same, unit skills screen don't show any modifier).
For a price tag nearly matching a triple A title, so many flaws, unimplemented or buggy features, this is not acceptable. After checking the forum, the resource bug was reported at least since March 15. At the time of this review (end August 15) such a major feature still hasn't been fixed despite a dev acknowledging the feedback at the time. And that is one of an overly long list of typos, missing text, placeholders, glitches and bugs that was indeed reported. I mean, it seems no one does any QA (except the users) or track and prioritize the bugs. Many of those reported stuff is easy fix - probably as fast as answering "thanks for the report we are working on it" like they do on their steam forum, but is still not done. It feels like the company is badly managed and organized and it shows in their product, despite all the heart artists, designers and some programmers must have put into this game. It already feels like WoM is a lost cause (even if some patches rolled out since official release, most visible and major issues are not fixed) like if the code was not documented either and they are lost into it now, scared to try to fix anything without breaking much more.
It is a shame. I would advice to only buy if you are really getting tired of playing MoM on Dosbox since more than a decade and don't care about money well spent. Even then you may end up frustrated and could consider the excellent Endless Legend or Age of Wonders 3 instead. Too bad, this game really was a promising remake of MoM with nice upgrades.
I reserve the right to edit or delete this negative review if Badlands actually release a patch that drastically and visibly improve WoM.

Thief is a good stealth game, in which the player impersonates "The Master Thief" himself. A good 50% of the game is about thieving, and these mechanics are very well shown in terms of gameplay. Nothing to tell about the graphics and audio: gorgeous, and if you own a good piece of hardware by ATI you can enjoy the many benefits of the Mantle technology. The other 50% of the game, however, is composed by its story, which is very different from Garrett's profession, although it requires a bit of thieving as well. If you like stealth games as a challenge, not worrying too much about their stories, then you'll enjoy Thief, buy it for a few bucks and have fun discovering how you can approach the different situations.
If you don't want to play it for the only sake of thieving though, be warned: very probably, you won't like it. At all. As I've said, this game is made of two parts: 50% story, 50% gameplay. From a good game, you might expect this two to be complementary. Here, they're not. Instead, we might say that for how they're developed within Thief, they might as well work flawlessly each one on their own. If this is not enough to convince you to leave your wallet where it stands, read on: the story is totally inconsistent, and not only it has nothing to do with Garret, his profession (except, maybe, for the beginning) or even the previous Thief games, but it doesn't even involve the player, nor it tries to get complex and dramatic, not even at the end. As a mainly good stories-seeking guy, I was hoping to find just that. And I was hugely disappointed.
BIRDS.

This game is a self-proclaimed successor to Master of Magic, but in the end it falls well short of the goal.
Initial setup was promising. Wizard selection/creation gave me hope, there were traits and various schools of magic to fiddle with. The mixed school selection was a nice touch. You can choose to go deep in fire, for example, and you pick up all sorts of fire-related spells from different disciplines. Or you could be a specialist in the summoning discipline that gets access to a variety of summons from the different elements. Planes? Not just Myrror here, but fire, water, shadow, and many more. Maybe too many if you enabled them all, but I liked the option.
Graphics are poor for a current release, especially on the city screen and world map. The world map in particular is a complete mess. Is that plot grassland, swamp, or something else? Couldn't tell you just by looking. Mountains have a strange, flat-topped appearance. Does terrain even matter? In addition to the low graphics quality, the city screen is non-intuitive, some areas you think should be clickable aren't, and some areas you must click are not in the place I would have thought.
The interface needs a lot of work. Strange combinations of right and left click options left me sometimes moving units across the map when I wanted to just select a stack. The menu on the lower right could be better explained. I didn't get a good feel for tactical combat since I rarely had opportunities for conflict in the games I played. The choice of some form of the d20 system seems tacked on and irrelevant.
Sounds are adequate. Nothing stood out, but I didn't have and jarring, out of place sounds either.
As an early access backer, I didn't really feel that feedback was acted on. I saw very little difference between the early access builds and the released product. The feeling I got was of an operation running out of time and/or money and shipping an incomplete product, unfortunately not an uncommon story these days. Yet one more disappointment, and reason to be hesitant of early access titles.

I can't see why this has so many positive reviews and so few negative ones.  Rather than being comparable to arcade classics like Asteroid and Space Invaders, it's a pretty average free-to-play mobile game, like an uninspired Tilt To Live clone, up on Steam for some reason.
The good:  Responsive, not buggy, there's a game here with an element of skill.  Graphics and sfx are simple, but appealing.  Seems well-programmed and highly compatible.  Occupies your attention if you need to kill time.
The bad:  Unoriginal.  Slow, dull start.  Awkward control scheme, without enjoyable movement physics (space-themed graphics, but drives like a car).  Success seems more based on randomness than skill, due to random power ups and enemies.  No real depth.  Skinner-box unlockables.  Music is an earworm that gets old fast.
Bottom line: It's not like it's crushingly terrible, and it's certainly not expensive, but why spend time playing this with so many other options?

From what I've played, this is a very, very good game, in a Beta-esque state. Some things do need to be tweaked and polished, but its fairly good so far.
Bigger issues:
-The UI in the menu is a bit cluttered and is a bit hard to navigate for a first time user. Some of the text is a bit small too, like the explaination of mods and the bonuses they provide.
-The gun noises are fairly loud, while the voices of the characters are very, very quiet.
-The climbing animations feel slow and clunky. If I was caught in the animation, I would most likely die, assuming the player shooting me isn't completely terrible. I usually circumvent it by jumping sideways or aiming then jumping over.
-The AI mode was really bad. 70% of the AI are completely brain dead, walking up to a corner and shooting extremely loud sniper rifles and missing completely. (Never landing a shot.) While the other 30% are dead-on snipers, shooting your head in a blink of an eye. It feels like it's not my fault that I died, but rather that the game is shutting me down after a 5 kill streak. Especially since I had 97 kills, and all of my 17 deaths were to an AI that shot 1 bullet and hit my head faster than I can react.
-On top of AI shutting you down, the AI usually get extremely aggressive and just spawn camps the enemy AI team. So what happens is just a lot of death at one side of the map.
-Experienced a weird glitch whenever I use this game's equivalent of an ACOG scope where after 1 kill, the entire scope goes black and I can't see through it. There was also a small red dot sight where the reticle was too large and blurry, so I couldn't see through it very well. After further playing, this also happend while using the default L96 scope. Is this an anti-camp thing, or a glitch?
-I'm not a fan of the Nut shot, but if there's a female equivalent, thats fine. Else, its a bit unbalanced for male characters to be a larger hitbox as well as having 2 one-hit kill hitboxes in exchange for like, +5 movement. (Guys have 80, Females have 75 or so.)
-Possibly allow some way for sidearms to get ammo or something? While you can just replace your primary gun when empty, there isn't much you can do about an empty sidearm, from what I've seen anyways. It forces you to reload and die when you could have swapped to a loaded sidearm.
-Maps I've played so far are almost claustrophobically small. I can usually see the enemies' spawn from my spawn. Snipers aren't really snipers in this situation and I typically see them used almost like a shotgun. Typically, the fights end up as spawn camping from both teams, since we can literally just shoot each other from spawn, more or less.
-I haven't been able to play Defense Mode at all, since matchmaking for it is dead and creating a lobby generates almost 0 interest in players. When I was finally able to get 2 other players in, it wouldn't let me start because I needed more players. Max in lobby is 8. Hopefully you don't need 8 to start a game. Really, you should just be able to start with just 2 and have the rest join in after, else its just a long waiting game.
