A very accessible rogue-like with enough depth, strategy and personality to stand above most of the rest. The simple graphics and combat of Dungeons of Dredmor obscure its incredible depth of design, functional mechanics and polishing, and it really is a fully fleshed out title. My fun in Dungeons of Dredmor comes from battling through hoards of monsters while interacting with the world, using traps, spells, crafting and more, all while exploring ever deeper.
There are plenty of little things that help this stand out and help to make it something more than most rogue-likes, but the central design philosophy of accessability and the respect it has for the classic elements that make rogue-like games so fun that make it very much worth my time and keep me coming back.
A plethora of additions and extra gameplay elements like crafting and landmines which would easily become an annoying chore or distraction in other games has been made completely optional and ignorable here, yet still adds lots of practicality to the game when you spend the time.
* The attention to enabling and supporting Steam Workshop content definitely deserves comment. It's been woven into the game perfectly and means sharing rooms, items, monsters and even things like insults and decorations is rewarding.
* The humour deserves mention. There are references to movies, old video games and culture not just spread throughout the world, but even in the U.I. and elsewhere.
It has been genuinely quite hard to find something to dislike about this game and the only things that are worth pointing out haven't really affected the fun I've had with this title, but they're here in the interest of a complete
review. The main drawback or limitation of the game is in the simple and, some would argue, boring combat. Fighting thousands of monsters in the same way, typically using the same specific skills and abilities can wear thin and unless you're willing to make some form of goal and targets, or story for yourself, reasons for playing can easily feel empty and flat.
* The tutorial is quick and simple, but also very lacking. There are a ton of gameplay elements and user interface mechanics that aren't covered anywhere and usually have to be searched for to learn about, or will simply be discovered by chance.
* Dredmor, the end-game boss can feel out of place and the ending can feel abrupt for some.
Presently available on Steam for £3.49/4.99€/$4.99 and with no real limit in replay value, Dungeons of Dredmor will take around 20 to 30 hours to complete a successful run, but reaching that run may take you 100 hours or more. As a
result, it's very fairly priced and good value for money even when not on sale, yet routinely goes on sale for -50% and -75% and is a must buy for anyone looking for an approachable rogue like.
The Complete version costs just 30% more, is available for £4.99/5.99€/$6.99. It is almost exclusively the better choice over the stand alone because it adds Conquest of the Wizardlands and the Realm of the Diggle Gods DLCs which add a total of 12 new Skill Trees, hundreds of new items, dungeon levels, monsters and mini-bosses and plenty more. Unless you don't expect to play more than a few hours or you're on a strict budget then there's no obvious reason not to grab the Complete pack.
* Don't forget to install and name
which is available for free.

The game is very simple: It's a sadistic version of "hide and go seek." The sleazy voyeur "gore porn" theme is pretty interesting. It does have some shortcomings, especially later in the game where the flawed gunplay mechanics become more prominent. If you don't mind the somewhat simple mechanics, it's actually a lot of fun.

Several years old now, Manhunt upon release created a seismic moral storm within the video-game world with the player assuming the role of a reprieved convict given a second chance, only by acting out in ever more extreme scenarios, the sadistically violent and perverted, murderous whims of a depraved psychotic sociopath.
While some may say 'a game is just a game' and that existential questions of the rights and wrongs of human behaviour  should have no bearing upon a mainstream product of entertainment for society, such a viewpoint is dangerously nihilistic and simply serves to shroud human consciousness in darkness. The mahatmas of India, who are beings beyond the mind, state unequivocally that the purpose of human existence is to love, and even people in the world who are considered to be at the extreme end of the cruellest still themselves do not want to suffer and do not want others to hurt them.
If the designers at Rockstar Games would attempt to sneer at the above by stating that criticising a game for lacking a healthy moral outlook is merely hollow sanctimonious preaching rather than an attempt to make the world a kinder place, then perhaps they should look inside and ask themselves what good is given to humanity buy this product? Violence in games is one thing and certainly can be stimulating and exciting. Yet, in a wargame even though one is killing, at least there is some justification for it in that whichever side you are on the soldier feels he is killing at least to right a wrong and therefore for a good purpose. However, this game revels in and celebrates killing purely for its own sake with the sole intention of inflicting pain also for its own sake. This attitude is neither healthy nor helpful for people to imbibe.
In addition, putting aside these fundamentally important questions, simply as a game, Manhunt is not just morally bankrupt but also poverty-stricken in terms of gameplay. Although the environments of dark streets and back alleys are atmospheric and immersive both visually and aurually, everything is made far too easy and the player is treated like a child and led by the hand, albeit simply to perform acts of killing which, although certainly distasteful, are largely bereft of any skill, and fundamentally vacuous and dull.
I read much of the press about this game for many years before I played it and now, having done so, although I can agree with the moral viewpoint taken by magazines such as the brilliant PC Gamer, I find it surprising that Manhunt's entirely uninspiring game-play managed to still get it a reasonably high review score. Well, erm, as you can see, dear reader, it certainly doesn't get high score from me.

Amazing game that always has me on the edge of my seat.
The developers did a heck of a job making sure you'll be engrossed in the game and story. Though I skip past a lot of the biographies and various texts, the visual aesthetics and sound really set a gritty tone that perfectly compliment the narrative they’re trying to set.
It’s also worth noting that since you’re only controlling a handful of characters (about 3 or 4), it’s a big deal when any one of them dies. I wouldn’t say that you become devastated because the game tells you that Marko’s wife and kids won’t see them again… If that sort of thing does it for you, awesome. But the pace and generally calming nature of the game makes it so that death FEELS like a significant blow to the player (more than just the loss of another useful tool to work your way to victory).
THAT BEING SAID: I wouldn’t recommend this game to someone whose favorite games are high paced shoot em ups. This is a game of strategy and patience. It requires tact and some aspect of risk/value assessment. If your favorite game is Broforce, and you only like games like that, then this may not be for you.
But for the gamer that wants to try something different and interesting, this is a MUST BUY.

You are in the Himalayan country of Kyrat and that is a place of myth, faith, secrets, lies, and beauty, and it's one of the best-realized locations I've ever explored in a video game. Kyrat is a colossal, dense, visually diverse place that feels lived in, torn up, and ancient. Far Cry 4 capitalizes on every available strength to make it an amazing open world for first-person action and adventure, while failing repeatedly in creating enjoyable characters within it.
Ajay Ghale, the American son of Kyrati freedom fighters, returns to his Himalayan birthplace to scatter his mother’s ashes, and becomes embroiled in his parents’ revolution. It’s a smart, human premise that justifies Ajay’s rampant warpath throughout Kyrat, but Ajay isn’t remotely as interesting as the things he does.
Liberating outposts is more challenging in Far Cry 4 than in its predecessor, and more satisfying as a result. Take the stealthy approach and you can disable alarms individually to prevent enemy reinforcements, and use bait to attract tigers, bears, and other animals to occupy the enemy’s attention. The hard counter to this is the Hunter, a new, silent enemy wielding a bow and capable of charming animals into fighting for him. He creates another unexpected variable that made me think even harder about how these excellent combat systems worked together. Plus, enemy forces sometimes attempt to reclaim their territory, challenging you to drop what you're doing and fend off waves of ruthless soldiers. This also  encourages you to take down specific strongholds that, when vanquished, cease the takeovers.
I really loved discovering every inch of Kyrat because it always presented compelling opportunities.
Far Cry 4’s competitive multiplayer does a marvelous job of capturing the freedom, scale, and surprises of its co-op and campaign. The 5v5 competitive multiplayer, called Far Cry Chronicles, sees two asymmetrical factions fighting in different ways, using the wide-open environments to their particular advantages.

never review games, so i guess you can take this with a grain of salt if you want, but this is something i would like to comment on. let me preface this with the fact i'm a depressed person. i know that depression is different for everyone who experiences it, but from my personal experience with it and the experiences of other people i know, this is my opinion.
many people have simply given it a bad review and not reccomended it, saying it's "boring", "not very personal", "barely a game", "the worst game", etc, but not many have really elaborated in a concise way. let's start with boring. i think, to some extent, i agree. it's not the fact that it's plain, it's the fact that it seems to be plain
it's about depression. that heavily plays into the stereotype that depression is like the color has been sucked out of your life and it's just monotonous grayscale. this game/visual novel seems to play into quite a few stereotypes like that.
the mechanics are kind of sh!t too. the game presents you with options, but some are unclickable because of your depression. for example, communicating with your girlfriend, who loves you and whom you love. depression is NOT an excuse for poor communication. now maybe, the idea was that you didn't want to worry her with your depression, which is a valid point to make. but
also, the game portrays depression in a very black and white way. if you go to the therapist, you start getting better. if you start meds, you get better. depression in real life isn't like that. medication doesn't help everyone, not to mention the fact that in the game, it's hard for the main character to psych themself up enough to go to therapy, when it isn't like for everyone. and sometimes depression comes back out of nowhere. i have plenty of really good days in a row, and then i'll have a day where i just want to sleep all day. and vice versa. clinical depression usually doesn't go away. it's a disease that people have to live with for most of their lives. so i think the game coud have made more of an effort to portray that idea.

After playing this for some time, and ignoring all other reviews so that I can play the game thoroughly enough to form my own opinion, I can say that the game is not just pay2win / progress.. it's also grow-old2win / progress.
PvP review:-
Do you want a chance to get to the top without putting in any money at all? you won't get it here.. why you ask? well for pvp you can call in "extras" like fire arrows or better melee power to even calling in another unit to help you out.. the catch is that it costs gold OR using up a bracelet which can be crafted... the downside is that the crafting takes 80 hours to produce and you're not guaranteed to get any bracelets at all.
Take for example an average outcome with "master crafting" (which is more expensive than normal crafting) you may get 5 bracelets in 80 hours, your top pvp opponent does not need this as he just pays 3 gold for his advantage each and every time.. that puts you in one of three camps.
1) pay2win the same as your opponent for an equal chance of winning (if you don't take stats into account).
2) use one of the bracelets it's taken you almost 4 days to make and get a win or two granting you a few places higher in the ranks.
or
3) save up a huge amount of bracelets so that you can get the advantage in pvp the same as the pay2win folk do 100% of the time.
This leaves you be one of 2 players, either Pay2win or grow-old2win (by which time no one will be playing anymore / game will be shut down).
You may enjoy this if you just want to attack AI and you only have about 5 - 10 minutes every 5 hours to play (as this game was very much aimed at the mobile market) or pay for everything, otherwise it's just frustrating, unfair and a complete grind.

Remember those browser games, where you build stuff, farm stuff, destroy other people's stuff and steal all their resources so you can repeat this again? Generally they are all the same. You can pay some extra bucks there to get extra income of in-game resources, finish construction of virtually same buildings instantly with a level number increasing next to their name somewhere, so you can spend another 10 minutes of your pathetic life playing a game that's not fun but you can at least ruin other people's fun?
This game tries to be something like that. I'm thinking so the very least, in a way when that awkward guy you have as an acquaintance does something strange, you try to be polite and not make fun of him. Which I'm not trying to be, as this game is not my ♥♥♥♥ing acquaintance and it sucks major♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Almost literally.
Okay, so here we have it. A F2P game with Total War in its name. A major AAA title you don't even have to pay for. Let's get to the gameplay!
You are the lord of some Britbong duchy/county whatever, turns out something happened to your daddy and some old regent dude is giving you a tutorial of doing things, which he was too wasted to do. You build a dam, which is the coolest goddamn part of the game, because there are water physics (!) then you get praised for clicking on something. Surely increased my self-worth.
Oh, and about clicking: you only need to use the left mouse button. Right click does nothing, it would be too hardcore for the game. It's obvious this was made with touchscreen in the mind.
Anyway, from first glance it looks fairly average but it gets worse: you need two hours to saturate a resource tile which gives you 20 wood/food/something or you can click on harvest all button, which does it for all the tiles eight hours and nets you half that much per tile. And the best part is: you need to manually collect all collected things by clicking on them. Then wait for it to grow out again. Which won't start until you collect the resources. Then once it grew out, you need to order them to start saturating it again. So much fun to be had! But wait, it gets even better: if you pay money, you don't even need to wait for all this fun, it happens instantly! And you should pay, because getting 10 resources is not even nearly enough, you need about 100 to build the silliest of buildings. Then upgrading it, of course, which costs even more.
That's about the management part, but worry not, there is
like in every proper game! And it even gets you resources, so you can have more fun faster! But not so fast. First the concept: there are different units, which is the gathering of soldiers. A battlefield can hold 9 units on each side. To create a unit, you need to build a corresponding building, which gives you one unit of the type you want. There are barracks, archery ranges and stables, for starters. When a building is finished, you are asked to pick one of 4 possible units to be linked to the building. Too bad, two of them are more powerful and you can only buy them for real money, so get your wallet ready! More advanced barracks housing knights are avalaible later in the game but I don't think a living human being played this game long enough to get that far. One unit consists about 16-18 men, so that's about 150 dudes fighting against 150 other, assuming there are no siege engines shooting an army, because they are substracted from the lineup and are shooting offscreen. This is the
I was promised, but it's okay, gotta give some suspension on disbelief. In Fall of the Samurai more people died in a single battle than in the entire war, historically.
The battle system is having the 9 units forming 3 rows and 3 columns, practically making a square. The first 3 lines charge each other and... you watch them fight. In the charging period you need to click once to get a charge bonus. Once a unit is beaten, the one behind them takes its place and starts fighting. There is no flanking if you have taken one of the columns, you just watch units 1v1 each other until one of them drops dead. Archers are worthless because there is a global cooldown on the fire order and at best they can kill 4 dudes from an idle unit before the frontline collapses. And you can never expect an archer unit to excel in melee.
For winning battles you get some resources, then you will wait 10-20 minutes for your injured units to heal. But fear not tovarich, you just need to pay and they are healed instantly.
Oh, and these are game-generated opponents of course. I have not met a way to play against other players besides inviting a friend to a duel, which is a waste of time. Basically: this is a f2p
game which expects you to pay money for its incompetent gameplay. I'm sure they have plans for multiplayer and whatnot, but I honestly feel sorry for programmers who have to work on this pile of unfun♥♥♥♥♥♥
tl;dr: The design is irredeemable♥♥♥♥♥♥ so do yourself a favour and don't install it. Even better; forget it ever existed

When there are so many shoot 'em up's on the market, it can be really hard to find one that leaves an impression so vividly in your memory. What better a game to do so than one about a fish with realistic biceps and a 10 second long memory span?
Let's face it, you already know what this game is about. You shoot stuff. However, this game is unlike many other shmups because you shoot stuff in high volume for very short amounts of time. 10 seconds to be exact. And then you get to pick one of three upgrades - within 10 seconds. And then that upgrade lasts (depending on the upgrade) for the next 10 seconds of shooting before it's gone. This mechanic not only ties you to your avatar - a fish with arms - using gameplay in a very clever and intuitive way, but it also gives for a fast paced, replayable, arcade-like game.
Aside from the main mechanics, the controls are responsive and simple, the upgrades are hilarious (sometimes infuriatingly so), the visuals are pleasing, and the music is the best culmination of 10 second long chiptune tracks that I've ever heard. I think the only thing that could improve this game is a 3DS port so I can bring it with me everywhere.

Despite
odd choice for a title, I've been keeping an eye on this game since it was first announced. I'm not a huge puzzle game guy, but I loved
time rewinding elements and it's not every day that you get to play a game with time travelling mechanics. I didn't have high expectations walking in, because of my disinterest in puzzle games. However, I was thoroughly impressed with this game, and was compelled enough to complete it in one sitting, something that is
for me to do. There's definitely some room for improvement, but I would be lying if I said I didn't have a great time playing this hidden gem.
First of all, this artstyle wasn't my cup of tea at first glance. Similar to my experience with
, I thought this game looked rather ugly based off of the screenshots. However, just like
, I was quite shocked by how good everything looked once I played it. The mansion itself oozes charm, with the different areas where you rescue the victims all being unique in different ways, which made the puzzles quite fun to watch when you completed them. All of the guests' appearances are just as varied as the areas are, with everyone looking interesting in their own way. However, the visuals are held back by some animation problems, namely when one of the guests starts singing and their mouth is out of sync with the music.
I wouldn't call this game
, as there are plenty of games that have used a time travelling mechanic well, however these games come out very rarely. This means that
is quite a breath of fresh air in the abundance of open world games that have plagued 2017. The game flows very nicely, and there wasn't a point where I felt something was dragged out for too long or way too short. As much fun as I had with this, the gameplay also showed quite a few glaring problems I had with this game. The controls, at least on PC, are awful. I constantly misclicked and nearly screwed up massively. There's also no way to change them, so I was stuck dealing with the poor controls for my entire playthrough. The puzzles, while they were pretty satisfying to complete, weren't very hard at all. I was able to save most, if not all of the guests on my first or second attempt, usually not knowing what I was doing. Despite all of this, the gameplay is still pretty solid in my opinion.
At the time of this review, I'm also playing through
, and I noticed a very interesting aspect found in both games. This aspect I'm referring to is how both games are great at hopping from being lighthearted and humorous to being dark and philosophical. I don't want to spoil the game, however I will say that
has nailed the tone down. When I started making some progress in the game, I noticed a few little details that seemed out of place, and I was concerned that it was due to a lack of polish. Luckily, all of my concerns were put to rest during the very satisfying finale to the game. Some might not like it, however I thought it was an appropriate way to conclude the game. The main story was interesting from start to finish, and I loved every second of it. The characters had a lot of depth to them, and there wasn't a single guest I was saving where I thought to myself, "Why do I have to save this guy? He's a total♥♥♥♥♥♥" If I really had any complaint here, I would've loved to see the game get even more in-depth with some of the characters. There were definitely some interesting things I noticed that could've been touched up on a little.
I'm a huge fan of Electro Swing music, and I enjoy playing jazz music. Seeing it in action here gave my ears an ♥♥♥♥♥♥, but I also loved how subtle the details in the music were. The music changes based off of what's currently happening in the area you're at, and that rush you feel when the music becomes increasingly hectic gave me a sense of dread I don't normally feel in soundtracks for any form of entertainment. Just do yourself a favor and listen to the music on Youtube. I don't need to say any more about that. There's no voice acting, but I didn't really mind because it would've probably been distracting and would've messed with some of the game's mechanics. The sound effects are also top-notch, as they're also very subtle and help play a part in signifying when a guest is killed. All the little audio details fit together nicely, and for a musician like myself, this type of interconnectivity is extremely satisfying and an absolute pleasure to listen to. Where the audio falls short, however, is in the transitions. Why? Well, there's no transition. Want to look at your map? BOOM. Sudden cut to different music. Enter a room with ghosts in it? Well, prepare for some horribly obnoxious earrape. I felt this killed the mood a little bit and removed any tension and suspense that was building up. If they spent some time adding some form of transition between pieces, then that buildup won't abruptly go away.
Although the game itself isn't very long, it stays consistently interesting and doesn't overstay its welcome. Because of this, I'm actually considering going back and 100%ing this game, something that I almost never do. I'll give this category some extra credit for being a fun game to 100%, despite it not being too difficult.
To conclude,
was a pleasant little surprise and it kept me entertained the whole time. The game lacks general polish, but otherwise you're looking at one of 2017's most underrated gems. If you're uncertain about it, then wait until a sale. Otherwise, your $20 will be well spent putting it towards this game.

The Sexy Brutale is one of the more unusual puzzle/adventure games I've played and I'm glad I did. There's something very original about it. Rather than giving you obvious missions, you find out how a guest is assassinated by tailing them, then you search the surrounding areas for clues and possible ways on how to prevent their death. It's a clever game about gathering information that will reward patient players.
I wouldn't exactly recommend The Sexy Brutale to people who search only for action or challenge. When you mess up and find yourself in the same room as a guest or staff member, their mask coming to life and chasing you may be eerie at first, but it's more of a slight inconvenience. While you are defenseless, It's not trying to be a horror game or an unforgiving struggle to survive. The game is also relatively short. 10 hours to 100% it isn't much. However...
Far more than the gameplay, its stylish morbidity, excellent jazz music, and storytelling compels. Said story is starting off very slowly and seems afraid to tell you too much at first. It's being so big and mysterious that you'll be wondering if it can possibly be worth it in the end. In my opinion it was, the payoff was very, very moving and satisfying for me. It completely made up for the short playtime I mentioned.
In summary: If you're looking for something unique, smart and emotional, The Sexy Brutale should be your pick.

A little background, I am both a big fan of the 'free to play' model as well as the Magic The Gathering card game.
I've been playing Magic for about four years now.
I've owned a few of the other digital game versions as well as having a few competitive decks in real life as well.
It's been no secret that many people have found the digital series to be pretty hit or miss. I don't know what Wizard's of The Coast does to miss the boat so hard. But I'll first put this review into a technical and then a business sense:
What works about the game:
-Bare bones, the game launches, plays, has a GUI and from what I've seen as of February, very little bugs. It's a smooth experience to start and once you get into the interface it's an enjoyable segue into the game.
-The music as always is top notch. I have yet to see anyone lodge a complaint against the music
-Fair art direction. The cards already have art that they have on file so it's hard to say that they really go out of their way with the art on the cards. However, the 3D cutscenes don't quite match the style of the cards and come off more as a Nickelodeon spinoff of Magic; which, depending on your preference, may be a good thing.
-The deck builder that everyone's been asking for is here. People complain about it not featuring a 'search by name' function. But I truly don't care. If you can remember the picture it takes all of about two seconds. And even if you unlock all the cards, it doesn't hurt to give your other options a browse while you flip to the card you want.
What doesn't work-
Now, before I get into the blemishes, it should be said that I generally enjoy the game but a review in my book is to tell people whether or not the product is worth investing in.
-The RNG. The point of the RNG being so poor is obviously an incentive to get you to buy more and more boosters. Hopefully with your own money. An easy way to observe this is to play the story mode decks. The 'challenge' often doesn't come from having a winnable deck and being forced to outthink your opponent's cards. It's redrawing, and restarting the duel over and over and over until you get a really good hand, (Hopefully with good draws afterward) and sometimes even then, some duels I found were almost impossible to win unless the opponent suffered from several bad draws.
-The Free To Pay model. Now, as I said, I love Free to Play. That's an awesome step forward with games with a competitive environment. I'll talk more about that in a second. But the problem here is that in the competitive side of the game, there's a huge incentive put on buying better cards than everyone else. Keep buy buy buying and hope your RNG gets you better cards than the other guy. A little RNG isn't bad, it keeps things interesting. However, when the incentive is to force the player to spend money when they would rather play with skill, then it's a waste of development time as you'll be seeing diminishing returns on your usage of those features.
What's just in the middle?
Well, between good and bad there's a few things that just sort of fall by the wayside.
-The free cards you earn are not very competitive.
Grinding for better cards can be fun. However, it shouldn't be done in the multiplayer against people with better cards, or at the very least not left to RNG boosters. Not neccessarily saying that the cards offered from the story should be perfectly competitive, but at least enough (if you've completed the whole story) to be able to play against starting level duelists.
-Lack of dynamic matchmaking
As far as I can tell, there's not really any matchmaking algorithms in place to match you with people at your skill level. You seem to be matched with just whoever happens to be playing. This results often in playing against other players with much better or much worse cards than you rather than someone who offers a challenge and a fun game.
-Lack of players
I don't know how many people actually play this game. But I'm judging that not a lot do from how long it can take to matchmake. I guess many people would just rather play the hard-format card game.
Ways to fix it really simply-
1.) First fix and probably most important: specifically two modes that I think will make the game even worth installing-
-Team battle: Basically, five players on each team (5v5) or (4v4) or (3v3) duel it out with premade competitive decks (similar to picking a hero in Dota, each deck has unique themes and abilities and once picked, can't be picked by the enemy team).
This is going to be the main draw of the game. Teams can use game chat to speak to eachother, and make tactical decisions. Suddenly there's a team dynamic, and it's even better than just playing 1v1 with a friend.
-Free battles: These are the current gametypes but reworked. #2 will talk about how to improve this mode. These are duels using decks that you've assembled yourself using the cards that are in the game. However, there can be certain rules applied:
Legacy, Modern, etc.
2.)Observe functioning Free to play systems: perhaps some of the best and most marketably viable free to play models are actually on Steam. Team Fortress and Dota 2 come with their own brand of users and you take them or leave them. Magic is much the same. However to make Magic work as an online game, all the content of the game needs to be free and readily available with balancing patches to control the meta game.
The reason why this works: players can spend more time on the game getting better, and more competitive with the game. Switching the content you want to buy to cosmetic, makes the game more worth playing.
3.) By switching the focus to cosmetic, people invest more time into the game. As they invest, they spend more. I hate to say it, but Dota found the magic formula. You spend X amount of hours and as X+fun=Financial investment.
Now you may say, but that still applies to this game! However, consider that because it's also pay to win RNG, you've got to face facts and admit that you've also got, X+fun-(loss x loss conditions)=fincancial investment. The greater the amount of losses, the less likely that user is to spend money on anything in the game. Nobody except a very small handful of people with huge egos will buy boosters just to compete in a pay to win game. It's very niche. The rest of the people willing to buy are hardcore magic fans who are already likely to just buy hard copies of cards.
Ultimately Wizards is in no financial trouble. However, they are walking away from a lot of money with this particular online game. By tweaking their approach by a bit, their financial rewards could be greater.
Players however, if you are a huge Magic fan then you'll love that the game is free to play, but may grow tired of the monotonous grinding for boosters and long loss streaks in attempts to get better cards with less frustrating outcomes.
If you're not a fan of Magic, but a fan of card games looking to install one on steam, then try it out.
If you're not a fan of Magic and can take or leave a card game, then pass. There are plenty of other, (better) free to play games out there.
If the game is updated to a state where it adresses some of its core issues, then I will happily update this review.

Long story short, the
that
delivered in 2014 works just fine as a standalone action stealth title, but it was bound from the start to take a walloping of criticism under the intense scrutiny of longtime IP fans thanks to the developers decision to deviate in numerous ways from the traditions of said series.
My initial negative reactions stemmed from features of the "Thief" difficulty setting, which allows the player to see a flash of light on valuables & even secret objects.  Focus Vision also has a certain easy-mode effect to it.  Visual cues are abundant in areas for accessibility, scalability, etc.  None of this is even noteworthy until viewed in light of the series; previous installments were notoriously tough due in part to how little help the player actually received.
That's the real story behind
.  It's a matter of modern gaming standards clashing with expectations borne of a long running series.  Account for how nostalgia tends to blur the lines a bit, and the backlash is utterly unsurprising.  Thankfully there
a difficulty setting that should satisfy even the most hardcore fan.  Higher difficulty settings remove all crutches & increase challenge.  I for one am satisfied with the experience!  I chose to complete one playthrough on the standard difficulty then move upwards; I might recommend fans skip straight to the harder settings.
There's plenty to reminisce over, too.  Like previous Thief games, this rewards being perceptive as well as eavesdropping on guards, merchants & commoners.  I had a couple of nostalgic moments, inspired by familiar architecture, garments, etc.  Most importantly, this  game still encourages stealth overall which is so gratifying.  My initial pessimism faded with exploration of Master/Custom difficulty & the Challenge Mode.  The point system in Challenge Mode & the Classic Thief Mods in Custom brings it back to
for me.
If you choose to use it, the Focus upgrade points can be earned with gold to enhance activities (combat, marksmanship, stealth, intuition, sensory perception & more).  One gripe I have is that the lockpicking mechanic, while a suitably "finesse" oriented minigame, just seems to simple here in a game that is all about thievery.
On the differences between the new and old
: Garrett's voice actor is different, & I never saw a good excuse for that come out of
.  The new guy's good but they could've scored easy points by sticking with the original.
is a fair comparison to make regarding stealth.  This is actually a little like playing the archetypal thief role in that game.  Like
, on Thief difficulty the sneak skill renders the player ridiculously invisible to nearby enemies while crouched; it's almost like there's no concern for proximity, line of sight, cover or lighting.
seems to be the frequently cited title for similarities, and aptly so.  Just about everything from characters, theme & story to environments, mechanics & features bear some resemblance to each other in these games.  Developers take inspiration and cues from each other, so really it shouldn't be an issue.  Both IPs are great in my book & deserve to be enjoyed.
Perhaps the only difference between the new and old
games that I genuinely lament is that this lacks the ever present tension of its predecessors.  There was a certain sinister, scary atmosphere & a darkness to the environments & NPCs that isn't present here.  Some areas & missions feel suitably dangerous but the overall experience didn't make me feel like the old Garrett again.
On the upside, the game looks beautiful, sounds lovely and plays smoothly on high settings.  Those aspects of the game live up to modern standards and then some.
The campaign offers plenty to do, but side missions & challenges eventually grow repetitive.  There's an openness to the city that allows you to roam, even with a linear main mission structure.  The menu interface is quickly and easily navigated.  The story & writing is unoriginal but gets the job done.
really is fun.  I would recommend this to literally any fan of the action genre, especially players familiar with the IP.  Temper your expectations where that's concerned & just enjoy!

First off, I'm someone who has played the first game on the original PS2 Release, which was why I was excited for actually giving this game a shot.
Dislikes:
-Multiplayer-
* I didn't enjoy that they didn't manage to incorporate Steam-Multiplayer, which would have made this game 10 billion times better.
This also means that I bought the game twice, when I didn't have to. No big deal as the game itself is only like 10 bucks, but still, it was a bit of a problem for me.
* I didn't like that you needed to re-add player 2 each time a save was re-loaded, either by dying, or what have you. It also doesn't have FULL controller support, as player 2 can't just press start and join in that way. So you need to have a keyboard plugged in even when using controller.
Mechanics:
I  didn't like that the camera was fixed on a single player, even in multiplayer mode, which made this game absolutely frustrating at points.
Some of the individual character mechanics. Corey is damned annoying to play as, I'll just put it that way. The constant mashing of the Y button for him to get up on something or pull people up was a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ I feel similarly towards Shannon's ability because again the need to grind.
Also not the biggest fan of the fact that the wheels you need to turn at certain points were a bit bugged out, especially in multiplayer. I could never get them to turn at a reasonable speed so half the time I was sitting there for 20 minutes wondering how good this was for my controller...
Story:
I didn't like that the story was linear, I definitely thought that I'd screwed up multiple times because of certain events in the game which confused me. Turns out there is only ONE ending, so that was a bit of a gripe.
I also didn't enjoy the "horny teenager" cheesy plot-line related quips between the characters, and the lack of a sense of loss that certain characters had over someone dying.
I disliked that the main cast from 1 was left incomplete, unless you get every chest in the game, and even then it's unclear what happened to Josh.
Also the story is short. Seriously you can beat this game in under 5 hours.
That said, onto the good points.
Good points:
-No More flashlights-
This was good. Obscure was annoying because of how buggy/bad to aim the flashlights were in the original game, this vastly improved on need to use regarding flashlights. Monsters can still be killed even when they're swarmed in darkness. Not having to constantly blast a flashlight at something before smashing it to bits was great.
-Better controls-
This is SO MUCH BETTER. I can't even begin to say, not only do they have an autotarget for monsters, but actually fighting things in this game was a lot easier, and a lot more user intuitive. Great work.
-Better items-
You can get waaaaay better weapons and items much faster than you thought. Being that the game is short, also means that you can get the best weapons really fast.
-better puzzles-
As much as I ripped about character abilities, some of the puzzles were actually really fun to figure out and do in a quick time, also the music made things a bit more tense.
Would I recommend this game?
Yes - If you like cheesy horror movies, and you're looking for a casual horror survival game? Give obscure 2 a shot. Or better yet, play through all of them.

Obscure 2 is a refined example of the good effort turns bad and unsuccessful sequel, which made a big question of any further titles in the line. What we had in the first Obscure game? Old-school TPS "survival horror" ala Resident Evil 3. Fixed camera action, some monsters to beat with baseball bats and shoot with pistols and shotguns. Some not too hard puzzles to solve, some missed keys to find, some really bad big freak to finish in the end... Not perfect, but quite working recipe. As a bonus, there was a unique good soundtrack and overall athmosphere, which was really fitting the setting.
Now, the second game. It seems that developers were really going to make the sequel bigger and better than original.
Fixed camera? No more! Now you can choose the camera angles by your mouse, and shoot the monsters from the FPS perspective!
The characters. In the first game, every one of them had some unique and helpful feature. One could notice items laying around, another could outrun almost anything, third was breaking locks way faster... But, really, you could beat all the game with just one person, while others were sitting on the bench for all the way. Now, in sequel, it's much more intense! Every person still have some useful tricks under the belt, and the game course make you use them all! Some girl solving puzzles, other hacking the electronic locks, some guy is as agile as monkey and always somewhere above the floor level, trying to open the locked door by going some way to the other side of it. Et cetera. And it is working! There are really much more puzzles and other situations, where you need some team work, which feels even better in the coop mode!
The atmosphere is almost the same and maybe even more closely recalls the teens horror movies, which was the plan from the start. The music - goes from the same guy who made the first soundtrack... What could go wrong? The developers are certainly made a good work, so, why do I (and not only I, but overall sales numbers and ratings) think that the second game isn't that good?
Well, there will not be some clear answer. Sure, the plot is way too generic and pathetic - somehow even worse than before. Gameplay is much more versatile than before - and much more clamped all the way. Sure, the battle part, even with more different weapons and enemies - is lacking the using the lights part from the first game, and is clumsy more than could be due to the awkward controls. But hey, it's the same devs! Same story setting! Same and even upgraded coop game, where you really do team work!
Yet - alas - the aftertaste is much, much worse. So, my mark is about 62/100. Worth the interest in case you like the first game, and/or if you were looking for survival horror coop game which is not Resident Evil. For any other interest and especially in case you haven't played the first game - start from it, please.

You are in the Himalayan country of Kyrat and that is a place of myth, faith, secrets, lies, and beauty, and it's one of the best-realized locations I've ever explored in a video game. Kyrat is a colossal, dense, visually diverse place that feels lived in, torn up, and ancient. Far Cry 4 capitalizes on every available strength to make it an amazing open world for first-person action and adventure, while failing repeatedly in creating enjoyable characters within it.
Ajay Ghale, the American son of Kyrati freedom fighters, returns to his Himalayan birthplace to scatter his mother’s ashes, and becomes embroiled in his parents’ revolution. It’s a smart, human premise that justifies Ajay’s rampant warpath throughout Kyrat, but Ajay isn’t remotely as interesting as the things he does.
Liberating outposts is more challenging in Far Cry 4 than in its predecessor, and more satisfying as a result. Take the stealthy approach and you can disable alarms individually to prevent enemy reinforcements, and use bait to attract tigers, bears, and other animals to occupy the enemy’s attention. The hard counter to this is the Hunter, a new, silent enemy wielding a bow and capable of charming animals into fighting for him. He creates another unexpected variable that made me think even harder about how these excellent combat systems worked together. Plus, enemy forces sometimes attempt to reclaim their territory, challenging you to drop what you're doing and fend off waves of ruthless soldiers. Before I start I just want to say that I grew up on Total War games starting at Shogun. Being a diehard strategy fan, the series rubbed me in all the right spots. Unfortunately this one is a blemish on CA and the series. I understand that it may get better and that it’s still in development but oi vay. Anyway on to my review, the good points are that this game has a fun geo terrain aspect to it in which you can alter terrain to move water and rivers around. This can be fun and challenging at times as during flooding season your whole city can be flooded if you don’t know what you’re doing. I also enjoyed the tile aspect of buildings in which you can get different bonuses depending on how you pair up buildings and where you place them. The battles are scaled down obviously as this is aimed for tablet and phone platform. This kills strategy completely as battles come down to how upgraded your troops are and what gear you have purchased or smithed for them. Early on the only way to get good gear is to spend real cash on it, this gear will open up and be possible to craft later on in the game but you have to make it far to be able to do that. This makes the early phases very pay 2 win as you will struggle against even AI w/o gear. And dont get me started on other players, I didnt even mess with PvP after a few tries as the 5 people I tried fighting completly demolished me because all their troops were high end and fully maxed on gear where as I did not spend money and decided to get ther gear the hard way. The other aspect of battles is the charge mechanic in which you dictate when your squad charges the enemy. Your troops slowly start moving toward one another and if you time it right and click on the squad at the right time to charge you can get a damage bonus. This is very basic and has no strategy to it, to me the total war series was all about the battle mechanics. Now I know you can’t make a massive battle game work for touch screen but I feel they could have put more effort into it and included other detail. I do still want to see how it plays on my touch device though. The other downside is the ridiculous wait times to gather resources such as 8 hours for some (which has been mentioned before). I feel as though this game is aimed to take your money and nothing more, hopefully they improve it as it stand now this game was made to take your green paper with little to none fun compensation. For now, I am giving this one a thumbs down.

Depression quest dares to bare all by making depression the main focus of the story. You follow the life of an individual and their significant other, as well as friends and well-wishers, as they tackle this debilitating mental disease. As you progress through the story you will be given choices which will affect future text while constantly giving you updates on your current condition. As your condition worsens the music will get distorted and sound effects will pop in and out which does kind of add to the feeling that comes with depression. Multiple decisions can lead to multiple endings which can provide replay value if you so choose. A game like this may be beneficial not only to those seeking understanding, but it may clearify certain issues within depressed individuals themselves. I, myself, had a bit of an eye opener. Perhaps this could be used as part of presentation or dissertation to individuals that are studying this particular subject as well. Depression is a very serious illness and like all things serious you need to tackle the subject effectively if you expect to reach and/or help anyone and this is where I feel Depression Quest truly fails. Let's start from the top...
For starters, this is marketed as a game. This piece of media is as much of a game as me snapping two lego blocks together and calling myself an engineer. This is a digital book with SLIGHT interaction and dialouge differences based on choice. Call me a gamer snob but there is a difference. In all honesty, I'm a little hesitant to call it interactive, however, I give them props for being up front about this being not fun because it delivers on THAT aspect. You'll spend most of your time staring at black text on white paper. A photo will pop in from time to time and your current condition is in static text. With the morose music, that may or may not get worse, you may nod off, stop caring completely and skip entire chunks of dialougue. Don't worry about forgetting what you are playing or who designed it because 20% of the screen, on the left, is a constant reminder for you. After playing this game I couldn't shake this feeling of arrogance and preachiness that I felt this game was giving off. Perhaps that's MY bipolar depression talking. The real kicker for me, however, was the last bit of text. It read something along the lines of, "not all games have to be fun" and it was at that moment where two semi's collided with each other at top speed.
That is, by far, one the most foolish things I've heard and I'm a university student. The purpose of a game is to be fun. Furthermore, we already have games that aren't fun and they're called jobs. If you're in a bad marriage then congratulations you have quick-time events, too. I understand that you were trying to be poetic but instead you came off as pretentious. This kind of menatality is clearly refelected upon your body of work as I feel as though only two ideals were focused on here: 1. get the story written and 2. make sure it is not fun because depression is not fun. There are many different forms of media that tackle these issues in a far more successful and interesting way. The stylisitc choice that was chosen to display this novel is as unappealing, stale, and bothersome as the disease itself. While I don't have a definitive solution to the personal issues that I have with this game, I would like to reference That Dragon, Cancer. The game is by no means perfect but it also deals with a serious affliction in a far more interactive way. Besides that game feeling closer to an actual game it made more of an effort to connect with its audience with successful results. When you combine all the elements of depression quest you end up tired, listless, and empty. Choosing to be bold puts greater stress on a developer as it requires you to think harder and outside the box because you want to reach an audience about a subject that many would rather choose to ignore altogether. There's a reason why there is no mental illness section at GAMESTOP. I cannot recommend this game because I feel as though this novel is potentially more of a bother than a potential boon but clearly it has its audience and its leaving me a bit perplexed. I know its different strokes for different folks but I can't help but feel as though we are playing entirely different games. Before I wrote this review I noticed that it is the winner of three awards and not one of them is the kryptonian atomic face palm award. Perhaps my problems lie with the fact that I only played, like, 45 minutes but I just can't bring myself to give it another go. I guess I'm just going to have to stay ignorant about it.
I want to make it perfectly clear that I don't mean any ill-will toward anyone but this "game" and certain elements just rubbed me the wrong way. If I've offended anyone, though, I'm sorry. I understand and believe that this game has altruistic intentions but the execution is so off the mark that its not even on the map. If you make games that no one wants to play then who are you helping? Who's the target audience? There is no audience because they're too busy playing fun games.

I don’t have moral objections to Depression Quest for its attempts to bring harsh themes of mental illness affecting many of today’s youth into an interactive element. I have moral objections to the carelessness with which it approached its subject.
I find Depression Quest to be harmful for the cause it attempts to defend. Depression Quest is bad not for depressives but for anyone who would wish to inform themselves about depression by playing an educational game based on it.
I did not initially get very far in Depression Quest, I was actively repulsed by it within minutes and I was forced to come back to it a few times. This is not due to its hamhanded, burdened writing, but because Depression Quest stated in its writing and what little gameplay I was subjected to that it is not interested in educating anyone about depression.
In the introductory page of Depression Quest, the game states that “[Depression Quest’s goal is]… to illustrate as clearly as possible what depression is like, so that it may be better understood by people without depression…”
The player is then introduced by the main character who is represented by “you”. Here is where the game may have needed a deeper examination in the writing stage.
Depression Quest is an interactive fiction, much like a choose-your-own-adventure book. This means that by referring to the character as “you” (which will then be internalized as “me” or “I”), the game necessarily has to be the one telling you how you feel. Consequently, the game saddles itself in the uncomfortable, frustrating space between allowing yourself to feel your own emotions and empathizing with another person’s story. Instead of learning about depression by relating to the experiences of another or by making your own informed decisions based on the situation at hand, “you” are handed thoughts and emotions and forced to make decisions based on what you are told that you feel.
At best, this is merely bad writing and bad game design. To be told that one is depressed without any true sense of context (not that real life depression needs context to exist, but we’ll get back to that) and then limit a player’s options based on said depression is frustrating and unintuitive. The very first choice given to the player has visibly cut off the most positive action that can be taken because of a prescribed emotion that has been saddled on the player. This is maddening because the other three options are extremely negative, depressing options.
At worst, however, this informs a calloused, offensive view of depression. Where the stated goal is to inform others about what depression feels like, the game is not only tight-lipped but dictatorial about emotions. On the surface, this would seem to be what depression means, but when a player is forced to empathize with nothingness, where emotions are prescribed and positivity is blocked off without the slightest hint of context beyond a tedious, menial job, the player who will, by their nature, be fighting against the boundaries of the game will be filled with one thought…
“Why doesn’t this person just cheer up?”
Anyone who cared enough to read the opening introduction to the game will know why this character cannot cheer up, it’s because they have depression, which is a mental illness that prevents cheering up. But I, the player, do not have depression which is why I am playing this game. I am here to learn about depression, but consequently am given a meaningless scenario without context with which one can only hopelessly fight against. Without the buffer and tenderness that empathy to a fleshed out, acting and feeling character can provide, we are only asked to hop into the body of another person, act in their best interests and then be reprimanded for doing so.
So if Depression Quest doesn’t inform its players about depression or allow them to make choices (again: blocking positive answers such as “shake off your funk and go have a good time with your girlfriend” from usage), what is the substance that takes up Depression Quest’s overly long play time?
That substance would be vague, unsatisfactory explanations of the general idea of what it is like, not to be depressed, but to be a little sad. Near the start of the game is a sentence that I would like to conclude this little rant by deconstructing.
Firstly, some context. The main character (again: “you”) are working on a “project” (never explained either, even in its own explanatory page) that is distracting “you” from the tedium and meaninglessness of your nine to five job. It is a freelance project with no backing and is simply a personal creative exercise, possibly made to be monetized at some point. It has no deadline and no collaborators.
When the main character returns home from work hoping to continue their project (Here, unable to “Order some food, grab a drink and hunker down for a night of work.”), a form of vague panic begins to creep up on the “player” and then the game states that “All you can think about is how incredibly far behind you are,[…]” and that the work seems insurmountable.
Let’s take that sentence apart.
“All”, all means entirety. A sum. “You”. Ascribing this entirety to me only after a few pages of contextless description. “Can”, ability to. “think about”. By saying “All you can think about…”, the creator is in fact stating that the player is helpless behind this vague mental blockage (described only as “panic”). The second half of that statement “how incredibly far behind you are” is nonsense. This is clearly not a project with a deadline or true obligation (“You started this project some months ago and have, miraculously, managed to keep at it.”), thus “far behind” is a concept that exists only in the mind of this character who clearly does not represent me.
“All you can think about is how incredibly far behind you are…” is a damning phrase that tellingly states that the player is not only unable to surmount this vague, unnoble emotion that has been forcefully given to them, but also in that submission, they exist only at the behest of complete nonsense that doesn’t exist in the mind of the player or even the main character but rather the creator who believes that simply describing his/her actions and thoughts and not the concepts that inform them is enough to make someone finally understand what it is truly like to be depressed.
Depression is a tough thing. It is not sadness or strife as described by Papers, Please or Spec Ops: The Line. It can come without warning. It can manipulate your life and remove any form of agency from your actions. People who have not suffered depression may not understand what that’s like. It needs to be handled with greater care and understanding than the simple act of describing sadness.
Imagine if I were enacting an emotional exercise with another person. Imagine I told this person that they were depressed, but that taking certain actions may help them become less depressed. This person then tells me that they would like to go out for ice cream to alleviate their depression.
If I told this person that depression simply doesn’t work like that and all they get to do, all they are able to do, without any explanation, is go home and waste away in front of the television, would I not be grossly oversimplifying a state of mental illness?
Would I not be providing a disservice to anyone who suffers clinical depression by trivializing their experiences?
Would that not be a wrongheaded, self-indulgent, callous and hurtful way to describe a serious, harmful psychological state of being?
I am not accusing the creator of being insensitive. I am accusing the creator of being indulgent. Depression, being the bilious virus it is, demands more care than its creator was willing to provide.
That’s not evil or malicious. It’s simply a shame.

Depression Quest is an interactive novel – nothing less, nothing more. It does not have any gameplay nor challenging riddles that will put one's mettle to the test. Moreover, it is not a be-all and end-all guide to depression but it does not claim to be. It is made clear by the authors that the sickness varies from person to person, hence it is an impossible task to describe every type of it. I, for one, believe that the story is universal enough to convey the message well – that no matter how well-off one might be, it can happen to anyone from all walks of life.
The game looks like this: a few photographs at the top of the page, a wall of text in the middle with hyperlinks (additional information in the beginning, going to the next page, and making choices), and three bars at the bottom informing the player about the character's mental state, whether they attend a therapy and supplement it with medication or not. Personally, I am not fond of the bars but they do not get in the way and one can simply ignore them. There's also a monotonous soundtrack with sparse instrumentation and a couple of sounds added depending on the context. The writing is decent for the most part, albeit with minor mistakes here and there, and it is paced rather well. However, I absolutely love one thing they did: many of the options are crossed out, depending on your state. I reckon this is a neat mechanic that illustrates well what depressed people have to go through – they
what is the right thing to do but they lack the energy and motivation to make it happen.
The game has a number of endings and a few ways to get there so there is no one way to "win" it. My only complaints are that the novel ends rather abruptly and there is a major inconsequence one can possibly encounter when exploring one of the ways. Other than that, it is a decent novel,
. However, understanding depression is not an easy task so one has to be open-minded in order to get what the novel is really about.

This is Magic the Gathering in a hassle free format compared to the physical version. It is reflective of the current cards in play. While this game is pretty neat, the constant paywall is still preventing people from fully appreciating the game. It would have been better to just remove the gambling element of MTG and let their fans buy an entire set of cards. The rarity creep is a bane on their game.
Conclusion, Magic Duels is still a Pay To Win Game. The best price is at 7500 gold for $53.48. Each booster pack costs 150 gold each. Since they control the system online, Magic Duels can actually give you non-repeatable cards.
1. The Story
I like playing through the story mode a lot. While I have already read the story of the Planeswalkers online, it was enjoyable to play the story. Since I enjoyed this part, I believe I am a Johnny. I don't memorise the entire card deck, so I can't be a Spike.
2. Neater System
It's all stored online so you don't have a mess. Every bit of nitty gritty is calculated for you and you won't forget actions that are easily forgettable. E.g. Actions that are taken from the graveyard once something occurs.
1. Pay To Win
You still need to pay coins for the booster packs.
2. No Trading
Since you can't trade the cards, there is no secondary market. Without the secondary market, the rares have no value. In real life, the physical copies are plain paper anyway and can be printed by Carta Mundi in the millions.
3. Cut scenes
Very ugly. I would have preferred moving artwork instead. The cut scenes reminded of video graphics of old games like Dungeon Keeper.
4. Rare Cards
Another problem with these TCGs.
5. Minor Bugs
Sometimes, some of the abilities don't show up. I've uploaded screenshots.
1. Completing Campaign Rewards a Starter Box
At the end of a full campaign, you gain a starter box full of cards of that set. While I like the idea, knowing that the pay to win is still existent does not fulfill it enough.

This is a roguelike game, but it doesn't have the bizarre interface, hard-to-learn game mechanics, or ascii-graphics normally associated with the genre, making it very accessible and an excellent introduction to roguelikes.  Some of the jokes appear to be aimed at veterans, though.  There are a lot of jokes and a very strange sense of humour.  This doesn't mean it's a silly game - the game itself is not a joke, but a lot of the flavour text is.
Instead of choosing a class, you choose 7 skills, ranging from weapon skills, armour skills, numerous magic skills, dodging, veganism, geology, archaeology...  so although there's no "warrior" class, you can just make a warrior by choosing all weapon and armor skills.  Or make a mage, or a rogue, or just about anything in between.  Because of the way heavy armor and spellcasting work together (they don't), warrior-wizard hybrids have some problems, but any other hybrid can work well.
There are also crafting skills, and a lot of craftable items and discoverable recipies.  Thanks to some very powerful craftables introduced in the expansion packs, crafting is a bit overpowered.
Modding support is very good - indeed, the free expansion pack is mostly made up of of the best player-made mods.
I have very few complaints.  One is that the final boss is *MUCH* more dangerous than anything that comes before it.  The problem is not the toughness of the boss by itself, it's just that the rest of the game doesn't do a good job of teaching the player how to deal with him.
Also, this is an indie game, made with an indie budget.  Occasionally that shows, like with late-game monsters that look like palette-swapped versions of earlier monsters.  It also comes with an indie price tag, and that makes it excellent value for money.

So I've only logged 1.8 hours worth on this game.
Unfortunately, there's only 1.8 hours worth of content in this game.
I was really impressed with the art direction for this game, and the multiplayer set up is extremely interesting - for 1.8 hours. But the maps are so small, so few, and the game modes so limited, that after a while you wonder what the point of it all is.
Why I can't suggest you download this game now - even if it might be free - is because Motiga thinks that already it can charge you through the nose to buy skins and characters for a very, very unfinished game. So don't endorse that by taking your precious time to download this.
Oh, and by the way, when I say 'unfinished,' I don't mean unfinished in just the lack-of-content sense of the word. There are technical issues as well. I experienced frequent frame-rate drops and hiccups that often were the death of me. (I'm running an i7-6770k + 16 gigs memory + GTX 1070.) When they didn't drop, FPS seemed capped at around 60 fps. C'mon! This is 2017! Unlock that mess, or at least provide the option to uncap it!
Oh, one more thing. Video settings are eye-cancer. I don't know about other players, but I couldn't even adjust my resolution. I guess they thought by removing as many options as possible, they could achieve a simple, user-friendly interface. Some things, though, shouldn't be toyed with.
So yeah. Don't spend your money on this. Motiga needs to humble up and make a name for itself before it charges 100 bucks for a bit of in-game currency. We need to see the potential - the art style is fantastic and I like where the game is going with the lore, but we need more content, more settings, and closure on the technical issues.
So for now, I don't recommend this. Let's give Motiga some time as see if they listen to their community. This game has extraordinary potential. But I will leave it in the dust if it progresses as is.

This is the best 4X game ever made since MoM.
Alright, so a little bit for those of you still reading the review as most people only skim the first few letters.
The game is off to a bit of a rough start. It was released before being ready to be release due to contractual obligations, however the devs are patching the game on a daily basis lmost and are always on the forum keeping a look out for bugs or questions and sugestions.
During early access the devs have been the most responsive and actually using feedback from the testers. So many things were introduced and changed due to feedback which shows the passion of the devs fr this project.
So why is this a great game? It has a great civilisation building depth while not going so deep that it's a headache.
There are tons and tons of spells and you can use many combinations and archieve tactical victories through many means. Either having hordes of empored units or great damaging spells or taking control of the enemy. Just to name a few really... The whole game has a great deal of depth without actually going into the realm of grand strategy depth.
So what are the problems? Well the first one relates to the learning curve. Until you learn what you need to have a good start and what enemy units can do you will find yourself being kicked in the rear time and time again. You will however not have much of a problem if you used to play MoM since it's a lot like it.
Now for the temporary problems. There are a few spells missing. There are a few disciplines missing, sounds are mising (it was outsourced and the guys screwed so it got late to the devs), there are bugs (most not game breaking though), there is a lack of polish and there is some more optimisation to be done. Now for me and many people these aren't really anything that will stop the enjoyment of the game. However, with so much updating and bug fixing coming so quickly, more often than not saves are not compactible so if you don't have a lot of time to play, it's very possible that you won't be able to finish games for a while.
I imagine that it will take it a couple weeks to a month at best to get everything missing and have the game relatively bug free (at least without gamebreaking bugs (there aren't any now but they show up every now and then with an update)).
So if you can't deal with the current state of teh game, hold off in buying it for a couple of weeks or a month. if you can deal with it, it's a great game and it will only get better. Definitly the best 4X made since MoM.

This Game has had mostly negative reviews, but I believe that is due to the miscomprehension of what this game actually is supposed to be. People compare this to other total war titles and, of course, it falls short of expectations. The truth is this really is something different. The only reasons it has the total war stamp is for publicity and because it also has a historical backdrop. However, this is not a bad game.
1st - it is multi-dimensional: There is the aspect of building your land, yes, but there is also the aspect of battles.
2nd - there is change: water rises and lowers; there are floods and droughts, and there are seasons which significantly change the way you play the game, so it stays fresh. Also, there are a lot of combinations of units you can use in battle, and even more unplayable units, for example danes and picts.
3rd - waiting is not crippling: Remember this is a mobile game. Things take time to build, and people have lives. If there was no waiting, a dedicated idiot who played 16h a day would win the game easily. Instead, everyone has a chance if they can actually fight, which brings us to battles. if your units don't lose too many people, you don't have to wait. Waiting is a punishment for losing battles, or a necessary thing for building and collecting resources. Also, people keep saying this game has 8h waiting periods, but most times the waiting is 20 mins or so. It is like that with units and most collecting resources. If you decide to fell a whole forest, yeah, it is gonna take 8h, but that is dumb to begin with. Forests don't just grow back, certainly not when you wipe the whole thing out at the same time.
4th - though gold can help you win, you cannot pay to win after the first few weeks. Once people actually have time to craft some special units, it becomes impossible to pay to win. The only ways you can help yourself with gold is by not waiting (which helps very little) and by getting special units (which you can also craft, though that takes longer), and special bonuses (which, again, you can craft). It is a known fact that, if you spend too much money on a game, you get bored easily and stop playing - too much money, too little reward. So after the first few weeks, older players who stick with it will be mopping the floor with younger players with lots of money.
5th - Again, this is not a proper total war title. This is for waiting rooms, for work breaks, for commuting, etc. If you want a past time for that, this is a good choice. If you want a game to play at home, do yourself a favor and buy rome and/or attila. That's what steam sales are for.
6th - comparison with other mobile games: this game is so much better than any other mobile games i've seen, it is not even fair. Candy crush, farmville, and the like are basically the same thing over and over again. There is very little difference. Also, here at least you get a (very tiny albeit existant) bit of history. You at least learn that there were picts and danes in england. To be honest, there should be more information about that, as well as about the game mechanics. But this is a beta, so I expect that will eventually show up - I HOPE. And you can just enjoy a casual game. If you want something else, something more encompassing, get another game.
Still, not bad. For what it is.

The Sexy Brutale combines the concept of
(the board game) with time travel elements to provide a unique murder mystery experience. For the six of you that played
, you'll feel right at home here.
You play as a party guest in a mansion where the staff are brutally murdering everyone. Your goal is to save all of the guests
with the help of a pocket watch that lets you manipulate time. The core gameplay loop consists of exploring the mansion, gathering information on each character's actions and whereabouts via spying, resetting the day and then interfering at the right moment to prevent their gruesome fates.
The Sexy Brutale sold me on its concept alone. Combine that with a great art style, cool theme and surprising good story, I can definitely recommend it to those looking for a unique time travel murder mystery. But it's not perfect. For one, the pacing seemed slower than necessary, mostly because your character moves at a snail's pace, and the time travel mechanics will often have you waiting for things to happen before you can progress. Additionally, I experienced weird extended loading times and graphical glitches whenever I entered rooms for the first time. However, these qualms shouldn't dissuade people from experiencing this wonderful game.

Running Manhunt on your Steam account is going to take some effort. And a patch. And maybe even a cracked version of the application. Take a look on the community help section before you purchase this game; unless you're running an antiquated operating system, you're going to need the assistance. Patch download links (as well as instructions on how to run and install the patch) are available in the community help section; you can also find a link to a complete file that includes both the patch and the occasionally needed cracked version of the application. You'll also find directions for installing the cracked version in your Steam account. Most of the time, the information you need to run the patches and application replacement are right there with the download links. Sometimes not. I had to experiment for an evening to get the game ready to run. You'll also need a game profiler (like Pinnacle) in order to use a game controller. Otherwise, you're stuck with the mouse and keyboard. Lots of work to get up and running, but Manhunt's gory goodness is worth the effort.

And it was pretty enjoyable. The controls are smooth, the stealth mechanics work, and the enemies are very smart... most of the time. There are occaisions where an enemy will just stand in one spot for about five minutes or so, or where you're following one and they'll sporadically turn around and shoot you but for the most part the enemies are smart and adapt to their situations well.
The game is also good on horror and atmosphere- as both are handled very well. I think in the whole 17 hours I played, I was only jump-scared... three times. The rest of the horror came from the story and how it was developed. The layout of the game allows for numerous possibilities on getting your enemies from the land of the living to Hell, and also can tell little stories of it's own. Like what the locations used to be, before you started killing people in them.
My biggest complaint, however, would be the difficulty. This is probably one of the hardest games I've played. Specifically during the last three or four missions. There are a lot of enemies that are well-grouped and will kill you on sight, and the save points are very thinly dispersed so that messing up a little can lead to some major screw-ups that'll have you start all over again.
If you have a strong stomach, an eye for level-design, and a love of horror- then this game will do very well for you. Because in this game the biggest monster... is you.
