. Let's start with the small gripes most of the negative reviews have to get those out of the way in case those are deal breakers for you.
Yes, the game requires 6 gb of ram to play. Because of that requirement, the game runs like a dream when you meet those minimum requirements. If your computer has less than that amount of ram, I'm truly sorry it prevents you from playing the game, but that doesn't mean the game is bad.
Yes, the game requires Arc to run. It's not as polished a platform as Steam and some of the others. But it's a small hassle to put up with compared to the joy Gigantic brings. There's a lot of history on why it's published on that platform in the first place that makes this a situation that's hard to blame the game for...Microsoft, etc.
Legitimate complaint. But this game is very recently launched and I could easily see as someone who works in the software industry why this is in place and how it might not have the same priority as other needs to unlock it. The game plays well at 60 and I don't know if unlocking that at this point would help improve the experience as much as releasing new heroes, maps, etc.
Coming from a game like HOTS, I've heard a number of my friends complain about how hard it is to see the talents a particular hero can go down outside of the match. Yes, you can go into practice and play around with them fairly quickly, but I do agree it would be nice if they added a screen to the hero page where you could see the talent trees for each hero at a glance instead of having to load a whole new game mode away from the rest of your crew.
There's no way to see how much damage you did, healing, or damage soaked. You get the essentials of kills, deaths assists and an efficiency rating, but that's it. I think Motiga is aware of this and it will get added in the future, but for now it's bare bones.
Everyone watching the streams of this game immediately starts trying to compare it to other MOBAs and hero shooters. But to be honest it's created a game mode completely unique to itself. No minions, no items, no towers, no lanes. The main goal of the game is to get to 100 points before the other team so you get a chance of wounding the enemy's guardian. You get points in various ways, 10 points for kills, 10 points for killing enemies baby creatures, 20 for killing the adult version, 20 from collecting orbs that spawn around the map. Once your team hits 100, it's off to the races to try and do enough damage to the enemy guardian before they recover and become invincible again until your team hits 100 points again.
It's refreshing to play a game mode done this way. Every time I die, I know it was my fault. And that "MY" death gave the enemy 10 points toward their victory condition. Likewise, it's exhilarating to score double and triple kills, knowing you just made a significant impact on getting your team one step closer to the win.
In other MOBA's or Hero Shooters, people "feed" and it's hard for anyone to say one way or the other what kind of impact that had on the other team benefiting from your death. In this game it's super apparent and trains new players quickly you have to play smart because the impact is REAL.
Because there are no lanes, minions or items, the game streamlines the most fun parts of a hero shooter and moba. You're constantly in the middle of the action. More on the maps later, but these are designed brilliantly so it's clear what objectives you should be fighting for and when. You're doing a lot of mind games and making quick decisions on whether you should initiate, sneak around the back of a group, go kill a creature that's left unguarded and more. There's no phase of just last hitting creeps or soaking experience until the "real" action starts.
I know art style is subjective, but this game looks like an action strategy shooter set in the WInd Waker world. Everything is hand painted to look like a world unique to others in genre. On top of this, the maps all have a different feel and strategy to them. In one, you might have standoffs in the center of the map and it's a kill trade game. On another there may be an odd number of control points so big battles tend to occur on those points. Or your team can ignore them and go for some of the further points to get people to abandon their highground strategic points to deal with your threat. You can tell a lot of thought goes into the map design from certain perches for ranged characters to multiple entrances and exits from key control points where line of site can be cut off and spare you a few seconds to regain stamina and health.
This game is going to take much more time to master a hero than Overwatch, HOTS, League or Dota in my opinion. Because of the talent system, each hero can have drastically different builds. Much more so than a talent tree in say HOTS. For example, there's a gerbil like snow yeti named Pako. You can build him very tanky, gaining health and shields as he performs different moves or abilities, or you can turn him into a fat assassin where he bursts down enemies with powerful AOE and damage based on freezing them. Some abilities completely change based on the talent you select. For example, one of my favorite characters named Voden can create a dummy that runs and shoots like the real thing while you stealth so you can get away and recover. I can decide if I want to later take an ability that lets me teleport to the dummy by hitting the button again, or make it so the dummy can do actual damage and help out but lose my stealth ability.
It's things like this that add tremendous depth to each hero. Other mobas and hero shooters have talents too, but most of the time it's a change in making you faster, do more bleed, or crit...not a complete change to the mechanic of how that ability worked. This level of depth makes it super rewarding to master a hero. You'll know exactly when you might branch off your normal path based on the situation you're experiencing in that particular game. Don't have trouble getting away this math? Maybe I'll take a riskier talent that gets rid of my main escape mechanic but lets me do more damage now.
These guys have a model where if you enjoy the game you can unlock every hero now and in the future for $30. Smite is the only other game in the genre I know of that does something like this. I've spent probably $100's over the years on LOL and HOTS heroes so seeing a new game like this flipping that model on it's head is super generous of them. They even go further to allow many of the skins to be unlocked using in game currency. So those looking to support the game beyond the founders pack simply either buy premium skins or boosts. That's pretty much it.
Gigantic is a refreshing and generous strategy hero shooter worth picking up with your friends. It's got a charming look to it along with an addictive gameplay loop. I'm looking forward to where it goes from here. Yes, there are some minor gripes, but nothing some initial learning curve and setup can't fix.

Please ignore my short playtime as of now - I have logged many hours in this game before it launched on Steam and throughout its various stages of alpha and beta testing.
Beware the negative reviews here on Steam - From what I can tell, most people are complaining about 3 things that should really be considered minor points and not make or break for a review. Here's what they are:
1) 6 GB of RAM required to play it.
Okay, okay. I get it. Not everyone plays on a beastly computer. But, we're getting to the point where asking for this amount of RAM is not unreasonable at all, especially for newer games. Read the system requirements before buying, and don't rate a game poorly because your system can't handle it.
2) It uses the Arc launcher.
I'm not a fan of these excessive third party launchers either, but the developers are sort of at the whim of the publisher here, and I can't blame them for that. It's one extra step on your way to playing the game, that's it. I know it isn't much of an excuse, but many other games on Steam have an additional third party launcher and they do not get rated poorly for it. Yes it's a con, but the entire game does not deserve a negative review for it.
3) Monetization.
Yes, you can buy heroes with real money. Yes, skins seem to require real money. However, the heroes can also be bought with in-game currency that you get by simply playing (as is standard with MOBAs and similar genres) and, since the game itself is free, I can't fault them for wanting to make money off skins. Skins don't win the game, and the character design is already solid before spicing up your character's looks so... Who cares?
Anyway, now that those little "cons" are out of the way, let me just say that I love the actual gameplay and mechanics of this game. I think it really took the third person MOBA mechanics from Smite and accomplished so much more with it - you can jump and climb, find vantage points and hiding spots on maps, and strategize on levels and dimensions that most other MOBAs just don't account for.
I also very much appreciate that this doesn't have the typicaly gameplay loop of League or DOTA-style MOBAs where you're just focused on taking down towers to win the game. Instead, you've got to capture and hold points in a sort of tug-of-war, back and forth competition. Add to that the gameplay style and strategy I mentioned previously, and it makes for some really unique experiences and opportunities.
Finally, graphically, this game really holds up. What it lacks in realism, in makes up for in slick and smooth animations and a cast of colorful (both literally and figuratively) characters. While the cast doesn't quite hold up to the level of a game like Overwatch, their attitudes and banter seem a lot less forced and copycat-like than Battleborn.
All in all, if you're a fan of MOBAs or hero shooters, Gigantic is at least worth checking out, especially since it is free. It takes some of the best features from both genres and makes something familiar yet new out of them, settling for a cozy spot right in the middle where victory falls equally upon player skill and using the map strategically.

I really wanted to recommend this game, but I just can't do it. There are plenty of other games out that are far more engaging than Thief. And while I'm not on the "the original Thief games r the BEST!" bandwagon, those games were simply much more fun to play. I still had fun with the new Thief - the game tries hard to be engaging. Stealth is required the minute Garrett steps out of his hideout, interacting with the environment is key to success, and there are multiple ways to accomplish a given task. Sounds good, right?
Except the actual game-play of Thief - thieving and strategizing - happens the same way too many times for the game to carry my interest through to the end (I did get there eventually on my third attempt). The story could have been engaging, but characters are under-developed (some only appear in cut-scenes), show up for no reason, and are blessed with campy B-movie dialogue. The cutscene at the end of the game, while complete, made me think there might have been more to the story, but it was trimmed or cut. Who knows.
The mechanics of the game work well, but as before, there's little variation: put out fires to create shadows, throw a bottle to distract guards, and swoop to the objective. What should have been a thrilling exploration of an open world Steampunk city is instead reduced to a grind-fest for loot in a lot of close alleys. Some of the level designs are great - the house with the moving walls was one of my favorites - but the novelty passed quickly once I realized that most loot would be acquired (yet again) by rifling through the desks and closets for pens, ashtrays, golden saucers, scroll holders...
In a sense, Thief really is Kleptomania Simulator. You scamper around the City, stealing random sh*t. But to me, Thief should be about “the job,” not about stealing random sh*t. There are three kinds of jobs in Thief: Main (story) jobs, client jobs that an NPC will provide, and Basso's side jobs. Story jobs advance the story; yes, there's theft along the way, but even with the massive amount of loot in the Baron's mansion, thieving still feels like an afterthought because there's literally no reason to do it. Client jobs have a minor story of their own, but there are only two clients (each provides three missions). Jobs from Basso are side-quests that give some gold and a notice on screen that it's completed. Even though they're acquired from different sources, they all have a similar feel and execution.
Thief has great graphics and fun mechanics - the archery is especially good - but these positives are betrayed by a very average use just about all other game elements. The setting needed to be opened up. The music creates tension without being memorable. Enemies only come in three varieties. The enemies' AI all behaves the same (extremely predictable). And boss battles - what a joke they are! Grab Thief on sale if it interests you, and hope you finish it before your patience is exhausted and you start just killing all the guards so you can loot in peace.
On challenge mode:
There are three maps (one of which is DLC): the Asylum, the Baron's mansion, and the House of Blossoms (all excerpted from the main game). Collect loot before the time runs out. Every time you gather loot, the count-down resets. It's an arcade-y addition that might help refine your thieving technique (there are enemies present), but with only three maps it's little more than a distraction. And if you don't purchase The Forgotten DLC (the Asylum map), there are actually only two maps...
On the Master Thief edition:
The Master Thief edition is b*llsh*t. You get: the Opportunist Booster Pack, a digital comic book, and the digital soundtrack. The Opportunist booster Pack contains items that can be acquired in-game, you just get them at the start. To get the comic book, you have to take the code provided and enter it into an external website. To get the soundtrack, you have to enter the code you receive into a different external website. BUT THE SOUNDTRACK IS NOT COMPLETE. I only received 10 tracks of the soundtrack this way. The full album on Amazon is 20 tracks. A straight-up cheat, plain and simple. Don't get the Master Thief edition.
On DLC:
Of the DLC, the Booster packs are not pay-to-win, but they are pay-for-an-advantage. The Bank Heist is fun if short. If feels like a left-over level for content that was cut from the game. It's fun, but the value of the loot is disappointing, and it can be beaten in 30-60 minutes. If Challenge mode is something you enjoyed, the The Forsaken challenge map is worth the price - on sale at 80% off, of course.

This game doesn't make you rely on your muscle to win, but simply encourages you to use stealth. In fact the main character in the storyline doesn't believe in killing; I kind of like that.
The character models are a bit dated because of the release date of this game on the console, but the depth of the game as far as storyline and gameplay easily make up for it.
If you are into stealth games (MGS, AC etc..) this game is definitely a good pick for you, but I would have to say that this game is just a little above average. I wouldn't put it in the same class as AC and MSG so easily. This game wasn't made with as much love as AC or MSG, but if you digg dark storylines, I think you will easily be happy buying this game.

This game is aimed at someone who's happiest when sneaking so slowly across rooftops, and as a consequence it isn't fun.  If taking 10 minutes to sneak your way across the city just to start the next mission is your idea of a good time, then buy this... but remember, that's not a one-off.  You'll spend more time sneaking round a boring-as-hell city than you will doing almost anything else.
There's not much character development either - I don't give a stuff about any of them, and the 'save the city from an unknown plague' has been done before (and better) by another stealth-em-up.  You don't even feel properly awesome as Garrett, either.  You're a one-trick pony - and that trick (stealth) is painfully slow that getting from one side of the city to the other is simply dull.
It's a real pity, because there's a great game in here, it just needs a set of mod tools (which aren't going to happen) so people can tweak this into something that's actually fun to play.  And I think that's the real nub of the problem - Thief is a stealth simulator, and simulators may be many things, interesting, challenging, skillful, but they're not fun.

Unfortunately Obscure 2 doesn't hold up to the original (which had plenty of flaws on its own).
Pros:
- The story is better and more involved, characters are more fleshed out, voice acting is a bit better, etc.
- Switching between characters is now not only meaningful, but required to progress.
- Larger variety of weapons
- Unique puzzles (most quite clever, apart from the last one, which is actually confusing if you overthink it...like I did)
- Larger variety of enemies
- Marginally better graphics
Cons:
- The story presentation might be better, but unfortunately, most of the mystery is gone now and instead replaced with some kind of illuminati ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and some (almost) retcons...that don't even add anything to the overall story arch
- The camera is more of a ♥♥♥♥♥ than ever and is a serious detriment to the game
- Melee weapons are pretty useless and only get you killed, however, ammo and healing items are sparse, so you often HAVE to resort to beating a big monster with a hockey stick, which goes about as well as you would expect it to. The result: Frequent use of healing items, because you take unavoidable damage. Melee weapons do almost no damage and monsters can attack through your attacks, meaning even timing is useless. Since they also leap at you from long range, have fun...fighting anything bigger than a standard "zombie" with a melee weapon is a death sentence, so I hope you know how to conserve ammo.
- Weapons are not found anymore (most of them at least), but actually have to be unlocked via chests. These chests can only be opened with 3 small keys found around the area. Miss only ONE key and that also means you can't open the chest in that area, which in turn means, you're going to collect a lot of ammo for weapons you don't have...yay. Hunting for the keys for a reward is fine, that reward being the only way to get a new weapon is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, however.
- The AI is dumb as hell again and will happily either just stand there taking hits, walk into bad stuff, use important items and ammo for trivial encounters, etc. And outside of combat they will ALWAYS stand in your way and not move away. Thanks to collision that is a major pain in the butt.
- Character deaths in-game mean restarting from a checkpoint. Characters now only permanently die as part of the story.
- Saving can only be done at certain save points. Once. There can easily be 20 or more minutes between each individual save point in some areas (I think I counted about 16 or so). This is a major step back to the limited saves system in the original.
- No difficulty option
- Combat still terrible in general, thanks to camera and movement as well as reloading mechanic
- Sound assets also still terrible
- Inventory management is a pain and for some reason it doesn't matter which characters you control, they always retain the group's weapons. This would be ok, if you only switched characters at gathering points, but mostly you don't even have a choice, the game just assigns you 2 characters for a certain part of the game. Now, somehow that dude that got split up from the group has the same weapons my other guys should technically have...
- The levels are for the most part very simple and one way. Compared to the semi open game world of the first game it's a bit disappointing, but then again, the overall area is a lot larger. Still, they could have solved this maybe differently with multiple large "hub areas" to explore, instead of "traditional levels".
- Only about 5-6 hours again. Maybe that's a good thing though. Otherwise the rage meter would be building up too high.
Overall, Obscure 2 is a game no one needs to play. For me the story ends after the first game. It had a definitive ending. This one obviously ends on a cliff hanger with a potential for a 3rd one, which is very unlikely by now. Don't even know who has the license to that series...You may want to pick it up as part of a bargain deal, but don't expect much.

Obscure 2 is a more streamlined experience than the first game. It’s much more linear and more focused which can be both a good or bad thing depending on your preference. In the first game you were given the whole school to explore, while in this game you are always focused on one path and constantly switching between characters in different locations for different perspectives. One thing that I failed to mention when reviewing the first game was the soundtrack, it was really good and it is even better in this game. Another thing that I noticed in this game was how hidden the progression was to the next area or an item you are looking for. Because the game uses fixed camera angles for most of the game it’s sometimes hard to spot a door that has a window that you can break to get through because the door is at the edge of the screen and you can’t see it very well. Maybe if the game was widescreen and it didn’t have black bars on the side this wouldn’t have maybe been an issue but there were moments where I was stuck and the solution was very vague and hard to spot. Some of the puzzles are very cryptic and difficult to solve which got annoying. Story and characters are just as stupid as the first game nothing has changed there. The combat is less clunky, the animations are better and the lock on works much better. But overall I found the first game more enjoyable, I think the level design was more unique in the first game and it just had better moments overall. But this is still a worthy sequel that's worth playing if you enjoyed the first game.

When I was a kid, my father bought a copy of Panzer General by SSI for Christmas. The two of us played it to death. The same thing happened to PGII, PGIII, and People's General after their releases. PG and PGII were my top two favourite strategy games of all time. The right amount of depth and history for my mediocre mind, and I had the time to think about it. God bless you, turn-based strategy category.
I have been chasing that kind of game ever since. A friend of mine bought the whole big package and I looked up reviews for the game. "....the spiritual sequel to the Panzer General series ..."  What? No! It can't be.
Oh. It can be. And it is. Trains, planes, troops, tanks, and automobiles. Hexagons and more theatres of war than you can shake a stick at.
I've come home.

Panzer General reborn!
Ever since I got hooked on the original in 1994 I've wanted for someone to make a remake of it. 20 years later, not only that the remake is here, it's everything I've wanted.
A classic turn-based, hex-based strategy at its best, something that requires thinking and planning of troop deployment and movement, something that is SO different from the modern so-called RTS strategies that are a little more than a click-fest.
I'd reccomend it to anyone new who wants to try a real strategy, the "old hands" don't need to be told that :)

Awesome game. Epic
At first I was expecting something like Unity of Command.
But this game is so much deeper, yet accessible and easy to get into.
Simply a blast to play.
But the game is also very difficult, you have to do everything near-perfectly, especially if you want to get
a decisive victory.
But why? Because depending how you play the game, whether you get a normal victory, or get your objectives done quickly to get a decisive victory, will change which missions you are given by high command.
For example the invasion of Poland; invade Poland efficiently and quickly, and show that you are worthy, and you will be assigned to take on the daunting task of the invasion of Norway.
But achieve a regular victory, and you'll be assigned to take Belgium instead.
Also you have core units which you maintain throughout the game, which can gain medals, have heroes within them recognized (giving a stat boost) and gain valuable experience.
(Hint: Alt-Click on a unit to see it's war history and status)
There's just so much to enjoy here, this is a big game and if you get into it like I have been, will chew through your time.
It took me 6 hours, just to complete the Tutorial.
And as of writing this I've logged 20 hours, and am only on Mission 3.
Though mostly that's because I've had to restart each mission so many times to keep from out-right failing.
It's good to be challenged in the brain area by a game some times.
Also the game may look simple graphically, but non-the-less it draws you in.
The sprites are all HD and well-detailed, the sound effects make you feel like you're in the action,
and even the muzzle flashes and smoke drawn during attacks give the game that much more of a 'feel'.
The downside to the game, if you'd call it that, is the DLC.
Don't get me wrong, the DLC, from what I've heard, is awesome, and adds a heavy dose of content to the game.
But the price-tag is a little steep.
That being said I have only heard good things about the DLC and am planning on buying the lot of it soon.
If you're looking for a realistic, tactical-war turn-based strategy game, I cannot think of a better one out there.
Get it 10/10, epic.

Unfortunately there is one word that easily sums up this game: Boring.
I've been needing to scratch the particular itch that the Lego games do so well, so I was looking forward to getting this title when it was on sale. Perhaps I have been spoiled by modern Lego games, but this one feels utterly soulless and bland - one specific thought I had during my last lession was that it felt like a fan-game; lacking any of the style and polish I was used to. Don't get me wrong, I'm no stranger to the older Lego games, having played the older Lego Star Wars and Lego Batman of the same year, but this one feels particularly shallow and tedious to play.
The characters' faces are ugly, with their facial features floating a significant distance away from the head, which is most frequently seen with Indy's stubble. This game was also before they started using audio clips, leaving every chatacter to mumble nonsense and inanely gesture with their claw-hands during cutscenes, which is both unclear and annoying, as well as depriving you of the one-liners that made Indy charming. The cutscene humor also falls flat, relying entirely on visual gags that wouldn't make anyone over five laugh. And speaking of age, let me remind you that this is based off movies that involve nazis, face-melting, monkey brains, and the main character killing people - it really makes you wonder who this game is supposed to appeal to. Maybe I'm just not a big enough Indiana Jones fan, but I was bored of the whole thing within the first hour or two. What makes matters worse is that there are no acheivements to encourage non-linear behaviour - doing something as a specific character, adding any kind of meaning to the weapons or constantly fighting, anything to make the game feel less like one blockade after another while travelling down a straight path.
However, this game does feature some neat moments. I like the inclusion of actual traps in the game, and at least one level had some optional rooms with a decent amount of thought put into their puzzles. The "True Adventurer" goals (collecting bits) are acheivable on your first run and unlockables seem reasonably priced, which is a nice change from basically requiring the multiplier red bricks (which I assume are in this game). And... I mean, the music is too obvious to mention.
Sadly the largest flaw of the game is the one they put the most focus on: fighting. At points throughout a level you will be swarmed by armed guards, all shooting at you with perfect accurary (at a certain distance) while your default character is far less equipped (Indy has his whip, but that's it). Yes, you can pick up enemy guns, but that takes time: time that you will be taking four hearts of damage and lose a chunk of your studs, then of course respawn without the gun. All you can really do is run up to enemies and take the hits while trying to wale on them, and hope you can pick up all your studs when you die (you probably won't). This might not be so bad, like previous games, if it wasn't for the items you can pick up, namely the wrench and shovel. Having picked up one of these items you cannot drop, your character will use it as their standard melee, which is in fact half the speed of punching and doesn't come with invincible kill-moves. Not only that, but your character will occasionally unequip the item, which will require it to be brought back out to attack, which leaves you incapable of any action for a second, impeding fights but also jumping for progression/puzzles.
I remembered playing a Lego Indiana Jones demo a while ago and finding it fine, but sadly it must have been the second one. This game is a slog, an empty shell, and generally not fun. I will continue and 100% it, but I won't enjoy doing it.

I have the graphics settings as high as they can go (They go from Fast to Good) and it's still difficult to tell exactly what tile does what, even with the little symbols pointing at them. The worst are tiles that become corrupted. I still cannot tell what tiles have this effect unless I hover over the tile specifically, and that's annoying since corrupted tiles give no bonuses. Not to mention the number of times I try to click on an army and wind up clicking the tile behind them, or whenever I accidentaly send my army to a town instead of entering the town management screen like I intended to.
Combat is fine, though there is a wide range on damage, like 17-45 with some units. Big annoyance with flyers is that they're pretty close to the ground, so I tend to forget that they're flying a lot of the time.
City building is fine, though a bit slow at times. Most of your workers will be going to food and gold to support any real kind of army, and you need a few towns to do that. I suppose experts at the game will disagree though.
I can't say much about diplomacy because I barely get a chance to use it. That's really all I can say on that, it just never comes up.
At this current moment, I cannot recommend this game for $40. If you see it on sale for $30 or so though, go for it, it's worth that for sure. I'll watch the updates and I might change this if things improve even more.

I definitely recommend this game, as it is very much an update on the old classic Master of Magic. I have many fond memories playing that awesome game for hours on end. Worlds of Magic is very much an update, and a little sadly, it is still a work in progress. However, given that the dev team are very involved with and continuing this development, I have no reservations recommending this game to hardcore fans of Fantasy TBS games. I am already greatly enjoying the variety and depth Worlds of Magic has to offer, and I know it will only get better. *Disclaimer* I am a Kickstarter backer, so I may be a bit biased. Take that into consideration when determining if this game is for you. I would rate it 6.5/10 at present. I suspect it will be 7.5/10 before summer, perhaps higher. As always, use your own judgement in these matters.

This game is the successor to Master of Magic in ways all the other games that have failed to be aren't.  All the pieces are there. Spellbooks, Sorcerer Skills, a Turn-Based-Combat grid, Overland and In-Combat spells, Heroes, Artifacts, Races that are unique and play & build cities differently from each other, mana nodes, enhanced materials (think mithril/ adamantium for the old MoM men)
In that spirit, the game is unforgiving and doesn't hold your hand in a way modern games and gamers don't seem to understand. There's no story, there's no QTE, there's no awesome custcenes that masquerade as content but really just force you on a path the developers want you to follow.  It's your oldschool 4x game with a fantasy twist.
The game was apparently rushed and has it's rough edges. I'm also not a fan of the artwork.  However, since I still fire-up MoM on Dosbox 2-3 times a year that's not an insurmountable problem.
It feels good playing an updated version of MoM with some new features.  Expanded spell books (circles in this game) a resolution that doesn't give me headaches/ force me to squint and some QOL features like showing how far units can move. Damn good.

A very entertaining game. The gameplay involves repeating a single day over and over to learn as much as you can about the deaths of the guests in this casino mansion and using that knowledge to prevent their murders. A very cool concept that harkens back to the Clock Town side quests in Majora's Mask. The puzzles are creative but I found them to be fairly simple once you've explored and collected all the relevant information. It has a macabre wit to it and a great soundtrack. Definitely worth a look if you like a good mystery.

In short, an amazing puzzle game with an interesting premise, excellent aesthetics, and a well told story.
As priest Lafcadio Boone, you must rescue guests from being murdered by the staff of The Sexy Brutale without ever being allowed to be visible to either the guests or the staff.  The mechanic stopping you does it in a nice way that prevents punishing the player from accidentally being in the wrong spot but also stops you from interacting in the rooms when you are.  Through a groundhog's day-esque mechanic, you repeat the day infinitely until you find the way to solve each particular murder, so it's best to just watch what unfolds once or twice before trying to do too much.
It's not a long game, although there are collectibles that unlock some additional content for those that are interested in being completionist.  Instead, The Sexy Brutale focuses on making the most of the time it does have you, and succeeds at it.  The amount of character and lore oozing from the game shows just how much the developer cared about making it.
That said, I think it should be said that this game is not going to satisfy hard-core puzzlers who like fiendishly difficult or complicated games.  The puzzles are interesting, but intuitive.  The true reward of this game isn't solving the puzzle, it's about exploring the mansion and observing all the particulars of each murder.  There's layers upon layers of stuff to find, and as you get further in the story you can appreciate more of it.  In a sense, getting the full picture of what's going on in each scenario is more of the puzzle than solving the murder.
Its a beautiful story with amazing mechanics. I loved the timeloop aspect, it allowed me to take in the scenery without feeling the need to rush.

It's a grudging "Yes I recommend this game", but not as a Thief game. I didn't think the game was awesome (or even great), but at least it's playable. I suspected I wouldn't like this reboot so I deliberately played at the hardest level I could without perma death and made it as good a "Old School" Thief experience as I could.
I wish they had created a new franchise for this, because this isn't really a Thief game. It's the same city, and the main character is called Garrett, but that's about it. I really didn't like the voice acting, Stephen Russell did a million times better job. But that's sort of OK, it's a different Garrett. The events of this Thief seem to take place some time after the original Thief games, but everything familiar is gone. No pagans, no Hammers (or Mechanists), no Keepers... nothing. On level 3 I briefly got excited when Keeper symbology showed up, then some pagan/trickster glyphs, but that was pretty much it. The old cathedral at the end of the game was a disappointment.
The story was meh, but it kept me going. The ending was absolute utter beyond belief♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
Graphically, it's pretty nice. Of course, it's light years ahead of it's predecessors, although of course those games are nigh on 20 years old. But I did enjoy the graphics.
Audio was disappointing. There were times where conversations would go silent, and environmental effects like fires would stop – even when I was standing right next to a fire. Move a bit, and it would all come back.
I play with sub titles enabled, and these were buggy as hell. Conversations would start that I couldn’t hear, and the subtitles would be printed on the screen. The silent conversations would then magically reset halfway through, and the subtitles would restart. On one occasion where I was poking around part of the city hub, the same conversation about Polly’s perfume/activities were played 7 times in a row, without fully completing the conversation.
To complement this, some conversations would play twice audibly – there was a conversation about bear pits, and each time I heard this conversation, it would start, then as soon as the second sentence was spoken, it would restart and both would play at the same time.
More ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Worse, conversations could be lost – on numerous occasions when playing a chapter level, a conversation would start as I was following people. As I was playing the hardest difficulty level, it meant instant fail if I was ever spotted. On reloading after a fail, the conversation would not start again, including the person not moving about as they had been originally. This happen half a dozen times that I was fully aware of, who knows how many times it happened when I didn’t notice.
One final audio issue, I was poking around the edge of the city at one point and could hear massive fires, the sort of fires you’d expect if you were in a burning city. Later in the game that section of the city opens up – and it’s on fire. Even though the setting on fire bit doesn’t actually occur at the point I started hearing the flames.
Overall, the audio was poor.
Levels seemed well designed, I always had a few routes, and managed to finish the whole game without knocking out or killing anything. Hell, even Deus Ex made you kill the bosses even if you were playing stealth, this Thief on the other hand didn’t require you too – something I appreciated in a stealth game. So a bonus point or two for that.
While the environments tried to be varied, the creatures which inhabit this city were another let down. You had guards and civilians. An invisible ghost. And some strange human like things. **MINOR SPOILERS AHEAD**
The original Obscure shocked everyone when it was released on PS2 and Xbox in 2004. What was expected to be a dime-a-dozen, bargain bin action game was actually a budget horror title with a pretty good story, graphics, and gameplay featuring co-op that you could play with a friend. It was a surprise hit that received critical acclaim across the board. A co-op survival horror experience that was the first of it's kind, and for a price that nobody could complain about.
The story was right out of a 90's teen-horror movie, and greatly resembles the horror film, The Faculty. One character, Stan, even looks exactly like Josh Hartnett. Five high school students become trapped in their school and must survive against deformed creatues who thrive in the shadows. Using flashlights and whatever else they can get their hands on, the students battle their way into the bowels of the school to stop whatever is causing the carnage. Each student has their own abilities. The strong, jock character can run fast and move heavy objects,  the stoner can pick locks, etc. The main objective of the game was the keep the five kids alive to obtain the best ending. If one of the teens die, they stay dead forever. The emphasis of the game was definitely survival.
Obscure II (known in the U.S. as Obscure: The Aftermath) came out in 2007. Three of the survivors from the first game make return appearances alongside several new characters. The core gameplay remains the same, but instead of keeping the teens alive, the concentration is more on the narrative. If one of the teens dies, it's game over and you have to restart. No multiple endings this time around, just stay alive until the end.
Obscure II see's some improvements from the previous game. When readying an attack, the camera switches to a RE4-style camera, and gives you a target marker, making it easier to attack and switch between oncoming enemies. In the first game you just had to aim and hope for the best. The camera itself is slightly easier to control, giving you full 3D control in most areas.
It does have it's downsides. There are save points throughout the game, where in the first game you collected CD's and you could save on the spot. The big downside to this is that you can only use a save point ONCE then it's gone. And the stretches between save points can be long and riddled with enemies. Even though the melee combat is improved, like the first game, using melee weapons is a crapshoot. Getting too close to the enemy always results in unecessary hits. You have firearms, but your instinct is always to save ammunition, and this game isn't too generious with ammo pickups. The enemy A.I. is very cheap and will gang up on you in an instant. Partner A.I. is spotty, and usually ends up wasting precious ammo if you give them a gun (like Sheva in RE5).
Obscure II has to have THE MOST DEPRESSING STORY of any game I have ever played. There is a flower growing throughout a college campus called "Black Lotus" by the students. The students learn that you can inhale it and get extremely high, so it's popularity begins to spread. One night during a frat party, monsters begin to show up and slaughter the students. Kevin, Shannon, and Stan return from the first Obscure alongside newcomers Corey, Mei, Amy, and Sven. Like the first game, they all have their own unique abilites that will guide you through the puzzles and obstacles you encounter. Remember when I said it's more about the narrative? Well that's because PEOPLE WILL DIE. Like Game of Thrones, the people you least expect to go get slaughtered in horrific ways. The fates of some of these characters is gruesome and sometimes heartbreaking, making this story much darker and more depressing than the first game.
If you played the first Obscure, the second is worth your time. LIke the first game it is challenging and entertaining in it's own way. Good story, memorable characters, and decent gameplay keep it interesting for the 6 to 8 hours it will take you to complete it.

Aaah, Obscure 2. You see, the first Obscure game was sort of a hidden gem, a game that was kinda wonky and extremely short, but it had its charm. I remember it fondly, because I play it a lot when it first came out, and I had fun playing local co-op with my friends. The music was interesting, the ambience was pretty good, and even for an old game, the graphics were quite decent.
Then, Obscure 2 came around. I dunno what to say about this one, I feel like I wanna love it, but it's just rather boring at times. Unlike the first Obscure, which was a cult classic among fans of this kind of games, Obscure 2 just kinda went by. None of my friends played it, it seems like it was all in all, an even more "Obscure" game than the first one. I wanted to play it back then, but then I sold my PS2 and I lost the chance. After all these years, they re-released it on steam, and I had to give it a try.
Now, where do I begin? Obscure had charm, and it seems like this game seriously lacks it. The voice acting isn't anything outstanding, and the re-appearing characters got a voice change. This game is really, really cheesy, the cutscenes and the dialog from the characters range from mildly funny to seriously cringe worthy. Then again, they are teenagers, so, hooray for realism?
CUTSCENES
The cutscenes didn't age well at all, the characters are deep in the uncanny valley, and most of the time, it's just painful to watch how their mouths and voices try to sync, and fail. Then again, this is an old game, so, I'm willing to let it slip. But wait, there's games older than this one that had half decent cutscenes, so what's wrong with this one? No clue.
MUSIC
The music is pretty awesome, the soundtrack ranges from choir to stuff with heavy guitars mixed with said choir. Most of the songs are a remix of the main theme (Which is awesome, by the way.), but sometimes, they just don't fit the mood of the cutscene or stage they are placed in. This is a hit and miss, but I personally enjoyed it.
CONTROLS AND GAMEPLAY
In the first game, you could finish the game with all of your characters making it out of the school alive. Death was permanent, so you had to reload if one of them died and you wanted to keep them around. In this game, most of the characters (Except for two of them) are doomed by plot. No matter what you do, their time will come, and most of the time their deaths are a bit underwhelming, I think it has to do with the fact that the cutscenes are rather crude and the voice acting is lame at times.
This seriously hurts the game. The controls are wonky and the camera work feels sloppy at times. I played this with a mouse and keyboard, and in the first game, the camera was mostly fixed, like in old school survival horror games like Resident Evil, with a bit of Silent Hill thrown in when the camera was following you. In this game, you've got "full" control of the camera. And I'm saying "full", because sometimes it's just so unresponsive, that it ends up being frustrating. Your character aims to whatever he or she feels like even if there's a bigger threat in front of you, which can be problematic. Sometimes, you try to aim at something that's off screen, coming towards you. And the game just does NOT let you focus the camera on said threat, so you gotta fire blindly. If there's more than a single enemy, this is quite a problem.
AI
This game was made with local co-op in mind, and that's okay, it's a rather hilarious yet pleasant experience if you play it like that. But my god, the AI in this game if you're not playing with a partner is atrocious at times. When you switch weapons, your secondary character will keep the last weapon you were holding in your hands. The AI will switch weapons depending on how big the threat in front of you is, like switching to a melee weapon if there's small spiders in front of you, or switching to a bigger gun if there's something like a berserker. The problem is, the AI sometimes disregards this, and keeps wasting flares (Rare) on lurkers (Rather weak enemies), or rushing a berserker (A rather dangerous, heavy hitting enemy) with a baseball bat. And they are notoriously poor at dodging enemy attacks. Most of the time they will just stand there and take it, or follow you and get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥because they walk and stop, walk and stop, even if you keep moving. This ends up wasting a lot of your healing items. At least they are plentiful.
ENDING AND REPLAY VALUE
Unlike the first game, this one does NOT have any unlockables after you finish the game. No new game+, no extra items, nothing, so, once you're done with this rather short game (Around 2-8 hours of gameplay, depends on how familiarized you're with the game), that's pretty much it. There's little when it comes to alternate routes, there's no different endings, and there's no unlockables, so there's pretty much no replay value. Now, the ending. It felt quite underwhelming, and it will probably disappoint you if you were expecting something awesome.
FINAL VERDICT
While I actually enjoyed this game, it felt like a step down from the first Obscure. It's quite frustrating at times, and boring sometimes. I wouldn't recommend this unless it's on sale, unless you like campy horror games. If you're the average Joe, you might find this a waste of your time. I'd say give it a try, play this game yourself and see if you like it. This one gets a big maybe?
I'll give it a 6/10 ♥♥♥♥s.

A simple arcade-like top-down space shooter where the only goal is to survive and rack up a high score. Enemies drop ammo and sometimes coins. Coins are used to unlock more ships (8 total), later ships have more initial shields, bombs, manueverability, and rate of fire. There are separate high scores for each ship.
The power-up system is very minimal. Powerups are randomly generated (14 total types), don't stack and collecting one replaces the previous one. This means that you want to be lucky with which ones are generated and once you get a good one, avoid the rest. I would have preferred a system where power-ups were additive (instead of replacing the prior one) or at least if you picked up multiple of the same ones the effect would be increased.
The game has auto-fire on by default, but manual shooting is recommended to conserve ammo. Power-ups last as long as you don't run out of ammo. If you aren't wasting ammo with auto-fire and don't accidentally collect too much, you should have a hoard of ammo floating around to easily replenish your power-up.
Worth a look if you like very simple top-down shooters and like grinding for high scores.

2.  Graphics:  Overall, I like the graphics.  The animations are sometimes a bit stilted but overall I like it.  I particularly like seeing each city on the city screen evolve as I add more buildings.
3.  Combat:  It's turn-based and d20 so you kind of feel like you're playing out an RPG battle at times.  I do feel cheated on occasion by the dice rolls but anyone who played D&D will understand that feeling.
4.  Spells:  There are a ton of these, as there should be.  They run the usual RPG gamut from buffs to DOT's to direct damage spells and are nicely presented.
Overall, you get a nice variety of races that play differently, a ton of fantasy type enemies to battle against, and all the 4X you can soak up.  Are there bugs?  Sure.  Is it perfect?  No.  But I strongly believe in the development team based on their support so far.  If you're looking for turn based strategy, fantasy, or a 4X game, you should definitely give this a try.

Honestly the best Lego game they ever made in my opinion. BUT on Windows 10 it's completely broken, as you will notice game breaking glitches that won't allow you to beat the first level. It works fine on Windows 8 though.

A lot of the game is feature incomplete.  There are placeholders for text, and for art.  Dwarf heroes that look like humans, elf heroes that look like humans, orc heroes that look like humans.  Not to say there aren't ANY unique hero arts, there are some already done and they look fine.
Adamantine doesn't work.  You build an alchemist guild and you don't get any benefit from it unit creation wise in that city.  Meanwhile, it does now show up as a material you can use when forging equipment, but there's nothing special about using it over iron right now either.  On the subject of forging it works just fine you can make magic gear for your heroes.  The cost of adding enchantments is exponential though, which can lead to insane costs.  I also don't find most of the current enchantment options for gear that impressive, which compounds the exponential cost aspect.
Most spells seem to work fine.  Some spells don't seem to work at all.  I used word of recall to return a hero to my summoning circle and then he was invisible on the map screen, I gave him an order to fight an enemy army.  He fought that army, battle played just fine and he was visible in that battle, then back on the main screen he was gone completely.  Not just invisible, gone from my unit roster.  I still had his gear but couldn't put it on anyone else as if it was still being worn.  Many spells are missing descriptions of what they actually do.  "Gives a unit armsmaster" for example, doesn't really tell you what armsmaster does.  (It gives +50 experience a turn to all units in the tile discluding the unit who has it).  Levitate doesn't seem to let units cross water.  Planar travel doesn't let a unit move between planes, or if it does I couldn't find the way to do it via the UI.
Tactical combat is slow, partly due to the revision of MoM system of fighting.  In MoM if two units fought they hit each other at the same time and figures died at that same time.  In this game for clarity's sake a guy swings, damage numbers pop up or it says miss, then the other guys get hit or dodge.  In MoM you saw no damage numbers, so it could be hard to tell what happened at times but at least it was FAST.  At the very least this game could use "Very Fast unit animations" or the ability to turn them off all together.  Auto resolve works about as well as it does in most games.  Sometimes you lose guys you wouldn't fighting it out, but then that's to be expected.
On the subject of the UI I think it's fine, a lot of people are bashing the game over that, I am much more upset at the amount of place holder stuff and general incompleteness, adamantine in particular not working really upsets me.  The UI is very usable, although I will say for battles I often adjust the camera at the start of the fight so I can see and click on everything because the default camera position isn't zoomed out enough nor tilted well.  City wise the UI is just fine, although displays glitchy if you put a lot of stuff in the que.  The UI does a great job with the end turn button however, it willl always let you know about armies you have yet to move or tell to fortify, research a new spell if you forgot, and make sure your cities are building.  Clicking the end turn button when any of these things aren't ready immediately takes you to whatever you need to take care of, and before you click it the end turn button displays a graphic corresponding to what hasn't been handled.
All that said the game is in a far better state already than Elemental was at it's release, and if they fix the broken stuff and fill in the placeholders this will be a great game.  I can actually say that the game is fun for me right now, although I have not personally had it crash on me more than once in my 28 hours of play so far.  I can't recommend it over Endless Legends as of this moment, however, I still think even in it's current state this game is playable and fun.

I have been playing Worlds of Magic since early access began.  As a long time player of Master of Magic, I find it to be similar in many aspects.   If you enjoyed that game, you will likely enjoy WoM.
As an early access player, I able to see the game progress from largely unplayable to an enjoyable experience.  Since the general release, I have played about 15 hours.  The initial release was bumpy, to say the least; however, after an initial difficulty getting the game to run, the recent hot-fix has allowed me to play for a few hundred turns with only one freeze which I was able to recover from using the autosave.
I have few criticisms of the interface... it may be cumbersome at first, but with familiarity, I found it to be not too bad.  Similarly, once you get used to the 3d map, the features become more recognizable.  If you miss a few along the way, well there are lots to chose from anyway, and you see them eventually in any case as play moves along.
I am a little disappointed with the current AI as it does not explore well not expand into other planes... necessary to be competitive.
That being said, from early access to now, I have seen remarkable improvements in AI and am fairly confident that Wastelands will continue to improve it to a state where it is as proficient as any AI in the business.  I can not understate the remarkable progress the designers have made during the course of development, and this gives me confidence that the game we see today will be far outstripped by the one that will arise in the future.  I fully expect various bugs and AI deficiencies to be addressed over the next few months.
As is, I am enjoying playing the game.  I am a builder and enjoy clearing the various goody huts.   Combat with other lords is not my forte or the most enjoyable part of the game for me.  Exploring is really fun and building your forces so that you can start clearing features is rewarding in and of itself.  I expect that as development progress, I will have to face new challenges... I look forward to that as well.
I recommend purchasing this product... if not now, I think that potential buyers should not dismiss the game's potential in the future, and if they are hesitant about purchasing immediately, come back and see the game has progressed in a few months.

Awesome revamp of the original Panzer General!

Cons:
- EXPENSIVE ($80 for a collection !!!)
- Repetetive (click, point, click, point, click, point, etc).
- While overall the graphics are fine, some aspects remain problematic.  Trees are extremely tiny, look like bushes on the map, forests or trees adjasent to forests extend over tiles which are classified as fields making strategic planning often burdensome
- Simplistic.  Units health = 10, what does this mean?, why not show actual numbers of soldiers, equipment?  Supply map is not well explained/shown/integrated/conceptualized by the player, while supply is very important in grand strategy games in Panzer Corp you can be encircled over a wide area and still be fully supplied, how is that possible? Simply run on the map to the marked points (usually cities), knocking out enemy units on the way without worrying much about supplies, partisants or any other side-aspects of a typical 20th century warfare.  Very limited focus on units morale (all units generally have high morale, I guess German morale in Russia in the 1940s was generally good <-- NO IT WASNT, look at historic photographs and battle statistics)
- No understanding what the units actually represent leads me to form a very poor bond with my
units.  Are these units divisions, armies?  What are these formations? (for exmaple, AT gun unit, does this mean its several platoons with AT guns?, but then how can this be when the map streches over 100s of kilometers and there are only about 60 units on the map).  When a unit reaches 0/10 its destroyed (kind of an arcade time count)
- No battle/war statistics displayed at the end of each campaign/war (this is a historic grand strategy game so tables, graphs, performance charts is a MUST HAVE! )
Pros:
- Decent selection of equipment from the era.
- Decent graphics with well visible/recognizable unit icons
- Awards to particular units for bravery or other special achievements
- Simple click, point and click strategy game on a hex-based board layout (this might be a drawback for some, see below)
________________________________________________________________
More about the problems:
The collection is EXTREMELY EXPENSIVE, the game is basically the old Panzer General series, its a simple hex-based board game, with slightly better (its a 2D graphics so you shouldnt expect much in the graphics department), maybe a few new units and mostly just new maps.  I mean COMMON $80 for dozens of new 2D maps for $80, REALLY?  Skyrim with its excellent 3D graphics and a much more complex engine was not even as expensive as Panzer Corps Collection is now.  Yes the developers state that this is a BRILLIANT REMAKE or some crap like that on their website, however they dont justify that argument with neither specific explanations about why its presumably so much better than the old, nor have I experiance anything new playing this game.  Considering that you can get Panzer General 2 for several dollars online and there hundreds (if not thousands) of FREE maps/campaigns made over the last 20 years or so which can be downloaded online, the games price is simply out of norm at the moment.  Also, some aspects of the older games were actually better than in this most recent one.  For example, I actually preferred the terrain in Panzer General 2 over this game (e.g., vegetation type, such as tree cover, was far more pleasent and recognizable in the old one).  Automatic switching between ground units and air units (e.g., when you move an air unit to attack a ground unit) is very clumsy and in some cases does and sometmes it does not result in an attack (you have to execute the command once more after you place the air unit of ground unit to attack).  There are other problems with the game, but these do not neccessarly reflect a sole problem of Panzer Corps but rather a general design flaw with hex-based war games (e.g., AT guns = if these are inf units equiped with AT guns, why are they weaker than regular inf units which lack AT guns?).
Publishers Censorship:
Aside from the game itself, the developer has been known to block/censor people on steam forum who complain about aspects of the game, such as the extremely high cost of the game.  Basically someone posts a message stating that the game price is overblown, then some other users (potentialy someone who works for the developer as this has been repeated numerous times on steam forum) posts a comment criticising the original comment with some unpleasent remarks (not even swear words), then the original poster responds to it with more unpleasent remarks (again, no swear words) and then the publisher quickly blocks the post and bans the original person posting the comment criticising the high cost of the game PERMANENTLY stating that the person has made an unpleasent comment !  Simple corporate scheme to block critique against the buisness strategy of the company.

TL;DR: rated 9/10 dead guests. Buy now if keen, wait for sale otherwise.
Lovely art style & cute character designs offset the brutal tragedy sealed up in the walls of the eponymous mansion/casino. Yes, the game is named after the location where it is set. If this bunches your panties for whatever reason, I'd suggest you have a look at some of Steam's other fine games. Life is too short to get infuriated over such developer choices or suggest lists of banal alternatives.
Gameplay involves sneaking around the sprawling mansion spying on everyone, picking up everything that isn't nailed down and figuring out to use it. Much of the challenge comes from figuring out where you need to be and when, then how to be there at the right time to do your thing, sometimes involving a chain of such planned actions. Feels different and fresh enough to be diverting. The day resets at midnight, giving you as many shots as you need at getting your current task right. Keeping everyone's movements and actions straight isn't too taxing as the game has a built-in system for showing character's movements on the map once you have observed them pass. You can scrub back and forth through the day to see where they're going and when so you can plan your own actions. Gameplay is expanded by obtaining powers from new masks that give you more potential actions and the ability to solve problems that you could not before. Rather like what you'd get in a metroidvania/zelda game.
For me, The Sexy Brutale didn't outstay its welcome, giving me about 13 hours for main game completion + 100% Achievements and miscellaneous messing around stalking characters ingame trying to get every last snippet of dialog (some of which were quite chucklesome). It left me wanting a little more, and I like that a great deal better than dragging out so long I put it on the shelf and never come back.
At time of writing Steam tells me it is priced at $19.99USD, so perhaps this would put it into questionable value-for-money territory for many of you. I feel like it would be better priced at $15 and I'd certainly endorse purchase at $9.99 and lower. If you're on the fence wait for a sale!

The Sexy Brutale is one of the more interesting games that I have played recently. The story telling and world are the definite highlights of the game. The fact that game is basically you replaying the same 12 hours every time trying in order to save the next person/pair, which then allows you to further explore the mansion is definitely interesting. One thing I loved is when you start the game you hear all these sounds and experience certain environmental events that leave you wondering what exactly is going on. By the end of the game you know exactly what is happening at every moment within the mansion. Personally I do think there are some minor issues in the game.
Pros:
+ Story is very interesting
+ Art work and visuals are very nice and clean
+ Music and sound effects are great
+ Characters are interesting
+ The puzzles are unique
+ Very interesting world mechanic
Cons:
- 4 to 6 hours to complete (maybe an extra hour if you want to collect everything)
- No replay value since you know how to solve everything

- Puzzles are relatively simple (I feel this is the case since there is a very limited in game time to do stuff)
Overall, I say this game is very fun and interesting and definitely worth picking up during a sale or if you have some extra money to spend. Though I would say it probably not something I would recommend at the current full price $20 if money is a bit tight.

I do recommend "The Sexy Brutale".
Now a little more detail on why that is exactly. For me it is the charm of the game that works so well. The soundtrack is amazing - the trailer should already give you a good idea of what the music is like.
What I wasn't so sure about at first was the gameplay itself. Especially interacting in those rooms looked like it would be a hassle to me. They are beautifully crafted and all have their own style, but they looked messy to me. They weren't tho. The gamplay is surprisingly clean. Almost too clean actually. The things you can do in a specific room are surprisingly limited. You usually get a bunch of optional things you can click at to get some background or description on the artwork, statue, vase etc. you are looking at and maybe an object that is relevant to the story. Those relevant things are used for puzzles which are pretty linear. The whole story is pretty linear actually. Over the course of the game you get new things you can do. And while you can go back to areas you've been to already to get collectables you haven't collected previously (or couln't), they are usually needed to progress in the story in the first place. So if you were hopeing to explore the mansion freely at your own will, you might be disappointed.
All that didn't really matter to me tho. I was sucked in by the atmosphere and read everything I discovered just to know a little more about the mansion and its secrets. Same goes for the puzzles by the way. They are not really hard to pull off. Once you know how to intervene it is pretty easy to pull off. They get a little more complicated over the course of the game, but It is NOT a hard game at all. But again the story of each of those puzzles is unique to the characters they involve and it was fun to me to explore why something was happening.
So if you want to play this game do it for the atmosphere - otherwise you might be disappointed. Oh and by the way, it isn't very long either. I spend about 10-11 hours in it. And I have 100% in everything. Plus there were moments I just listened to music a little or was reading some lore. So I wasn't in a hurry. For me the price (got it in a sale) was perfectly fine for what I got, but that might be different for other people, so keep that in mind.

right, now that's out of the way...
here's some downsides for your consideration:
oh, and a point of consideration may be to take the system requirements seriously. my computer almost meets the specifications, but drops frames like mad seemingly at random and can feel unresponsive at times.
i have no doubt that this problem is on my end rather than being the game's fault.
now, onto the upsides:
The Sexy Brutale, for as long as it lasts, is an amazing experience. The story is rather great, with a conclusion that i unfortunately saw coming due to spoilers but nevertheless felt almost chilling.
and unlike far too many games with great stories, the gameplay doesn't suffer from it. You start off with the power to reset the day and can gain other less important powers as you save people from their gruesome deaths, all without interacting with them directly.
none of the puzzles are too hard to grasp and the dynamic day is short enough that once you figure out what you need to do (or think you have done) you can act on those plans with haste. Even so, even the simpler puzzles still feel... gratifying (?) to solve.
I bought this game for ~£10 in the summer sales. I'm normally the kind of person who expects an hour of play for every pound (at least), but i didn't even slightly regret this purchase.
as for whether it would be worth it at full price, i'd say that depends on how much you value a good puzzle game and a good story. puzzle games aren't really my thing, which is why i put it in my wishlist and waited for a sale.

What a great roguelike! DUNGEONS OD DREDMOR was the first commercial traditional roguelike that got popular, before-hand roguelikes were mostly free and way too complex for a broad audience. Dredmor came and changed that. Don't give me wrong; DoD still is a traditional roguelike but alot of the mechanics were dumbed down so that most of the people would understand them. DoD simplified a lot of stuff but kept the standard mechanics of a turn-based roguelike. This game still has the most important things:
<> randomization
<> Perma Death (there also is an option to turn that off, again trying to appeal to a broad audience)
<> Crafting
<> Skill Trees
<> Quests
DoD had all that but as I said simplified! And that's what makes this roguelike so great! It's simple yet so challenging and complex. It always keeps this fine balance between "dumb-easy" and "complex-easy". But this game is not easy to beat; not at all!
DUNGEONS OF DREDMOR is pure roguelike-awesomeness, and it also is the perfect game to start for newcomers to the traditional roguelike genre.

I was a huge fan of MOM when it was released. I remember buying the strategy guide, being blown away by its size, and then spending hours reading it and coming up with all sorts of magic/racial combos to try out.  For me, it was a magical game that let me escape from reality and be the powerful wizard that explored mysterious lands while ruling (sometimes kindly, sometimes not so much) a civilization.   Of course, MOM was hardly perfect (unbalanced races and spells, the AI wasn’t the brightest), but it was greater than the sum of its parts…at least for me.  It had that “one more turn” feeling that I loved.

I backed Worlds of Magic during its first kickstarter.  I loved the concept and the developers definitely seem to want to recreate the magic that was in MOM while adding some fresh new ideas to change things up.  I was very excited when the game first came out on early release only to find it to be a buggy mess when I played it at that time.  Disappointed, I decided to wait and see what it looked like when it was finally released.  I would follow the forum from time to time just to see how things were going.  The developers always seemed interested in feedback and also seemed open to constructive comments or suggestions which was encouraging.

Release day came and I almost felt like a kid on Christmas morning.  “Please, let this game not suck because god knows how long I will have to wait for another MOM successor”, I thought.  I fired it up, and you know what?  It was a big improvement over when I played it before.  Is it perfect?  No, there are certainly things that could be better (zoom out further, city UI, and better AI…of course every strategy game in this genre could benefit from better AI).  Still, it has that hook like MOM that pulls me in and won’t let me go, and that is EXACTLY what I have been waiting for.  If you’ve played MOM, then you know what I’m talking about.  This game is not easy, and can be a bit opaque at times, but if you’re patient and take the time to uncover its layers, then you will be rewarded.  If you are on the fence about buying it right now, then I see nothing wrong with waiting for the kinks to be worked out because I’m very confident that they will be.  This game is definitely a labor of love for the developers, and they seem to care very much about it.

I predict that great things are in store for Worlds of Magic, and I should know because I’m Merlin, mighty and benevolent ruler of the grey elves!  Now, if you’ll excuse me, there’s an ancient ruin over there that I need to go investigate…(just one more turn)…What?!?! It’s already 1AM in the morning?! $%#*!!!!!!!!!!
-A satisfied, but very sleep deprived customer

EDIT: Updated from a No to Yes recommendation.
I am not a fan of arcade shooters. However, I bought this game because it was under a dollar (in terms of USD), and I haven't played arcade shooters in more than a decade. So it was more of a novelty.
Bit Blaster XL itself is not very innovative. It's a pretty straightforward arcade shooter, with a grindy unlock system for more powerful spaceships. Ironically I preferred the slower, lower-tier spaceship for its easier control haha.
I find the difficulty ramp-up a little unsatisfying. Some spaceships are mere annoyances, while there's 2 particular spaceships that are a must-kill or the map becomes a dodge-em after than a shoot-em-up.
Ammo and Boost/Brake is a limited resource, though the latter is time-rechargeable. The limited ammo is pretty interesting, though I find it a little on the tough side to conserve ammo given that all the Ammo powerups eat through ammo so quickly.
For its price, Bit Blaster XL is pretty alright for a quick, casual play. There's enough gameplay mechanics and polish inside to give you a few good hours spread over a couple of days.
Each ship has its own music. I think my spaceship choice is somewhat related to my preferred choice of tunes. It's a little refreshing when you switch to a new ship after a couple of rounds/days and you hear a new tune.
I highly recommend using a controller for this game. If you're using controller, you should probably remap the buttons so that you can Fire, Boost/Brake at the same time.
This game has mild performance issues. Keep VSync on. Although VSync off makes the controls more responsive, but it causes random screen stutters. I'm using i7-7700HQ so it's not a spec issue.
* Polish: 5/5
* Novelty: 2/5
* Music: 4/5
* Fun: 4/5
* Replayability: 5/5
* Playtime: 0.2 - 0.5 hour each
Go get the developer's other game as a Bundle: Orbt XL. It's more addictive and fun.

Tired of reboots that are worse than the original? Well... Sorry but this is kind of one of them. I say kind of because of this: if you compare it to the original, it's not as good. It's more linear, it has QTE's, it's just not Thief.
If you forget that this is a reboot, call it "Adventures of a Thief" or something else, detatch it from the series (or if you haven't played the first 3, that works too) then the game suddenly becomes rather good.
The atmosphere is fantastic, the controls feel good (with a exceptions like QTE and not being able to jump or use rope arrows when you want), it is a suprisingly good game! It's even better if you really do try to go for full stealth instead of confronting guards. And there are still some bits from the old Thiefs that carry over, such as using water arrows to take out torches, knocking people out and hiding them, and just generally being stealthy.
The story is good, the graphics and art style fit well with the game and the audio (while unfortunately broken at times) is very immersive.
Would I recommend this game to a hardcore Thief fan? Probably not, unless you can detatch it from the rest of the series. If you're new to the series, and love the stealth genre then yes I'd recommend it. And to anyone else I'd probably recommend it too. Just remember, try not to compare it to it's predecessors and let it become a game of its own.

LONG REVIEW INCOMING:
It is amazing how much love has been visibly put into the game - it has so much personality. It is definitely worth trying out if you like hero shooters and/or mobas. It is a nice and healthy, fast paced mix between games like Overwatch/Paladins and Mobas like Smite, with some additional mechanics that the game throws in. Definitely worth the look because it's just SO fun and the artstyle is just wow. Try it!
Edit: A more and way longer in depth description and review:
The way the game works is that every side has a guardian, represented by a giant creature. Your aim is to build up your guardians power to 100 with your 4 allies before the enemy does the same; once that happens, your guardian starts to battle with the enemy guardian, holding it down and exposing a wound; you then have to attack said wound with your team and destroy it or defend your guardians wound if the enemy was faster. The tutorial explains all that very well. Do that three times and you win.
Matches in Gigantic don't last longer than twenty minutes. The way you build up power for your guardian is by placing one of three monsters you can choose before the match on one of the three summon circles available for your team. Those are strewn throughout the map; 6 in total. Once you summoned a creature, it will defend that circle. Circles automatically generate power regardless of if a creature is placed on it; but if a creature is on the circle, it automatically collects the power essentially continuously harvesting it. If not, you have to go there and collect it yourself.
You can only place monsters on the circles on your side of the map; but you can go to enemies circles, destroy their monsters and thus keep them from automatically collecting power. It creates an interesting and fun clash where many things can happen everywhere at the same time; maps are small and movement fast enough that you can always react or defend. After a few guardian battles, it turns into a clash that changes the entire map, like ravaging mountains and changing terrain and the sort. Really cool.
That's all about the gameplay and it's very fun and engaging; it has that "one more round" feel.
Characters develop throughout the match by a skill point you get every level. You get experience by killing monsters and enemies, defending your own, placing monsters and so on. You can put the skill points in any of your abilities to make it stronger in one of two ways. Depending on which way you choose in which ability, said ability can be improved again next level if you like with two completely different improvements. It's all very clear cut and customizable and just a joy to explore.
The characters are very good looking, the fighting system is active, the artstyle is great and the animations are very fluid to the point where it's just a joy to play and look at the many different characters. It doesn't seem like there is any imbalance in the game; since you don't always need to fight and can be sneaky as well, collect your enemies power etc. There are always enough options. Even if you're not defending your guardian when it's attacked for example and want to just kill people, killing them adds a shield that your guardian uses to fend off the enemy guardians attacks for the duration of the battle. This game thought of everything.
In all honesty this game is what Battleborn should have been and what I expected from it, but what it never delivered. Long story short, if you like multiplayer games of any kind and fun, delve right in; you won't regret it; this is the first game in a long time that I would consider a pretty perfect game.
Personal Score: 10/10 (amazing)
