Obscure 2 is an extremely stupid game.
This 2007 horror game by Hydravision Entertainment (now Mighty Rocket Studio) is a direct sequel to the 2004 survival game of the same name. Obscure 2 is not a love-letter to b-list horror titles, it is a b-list horror title.
Important to note that Obscure 2 is compatible with both Xbox and Dualshock. Like the previous game, I'd strongly recommend using one.
Sequels are a tricky affair in any situation. For all the cries of innovation, a certain degree of iteration is expected of any game with the same name slapped on it - a lesson Mighty Rocket Studio learned when they attempted to reboot Obscure and ended up pressured into renaming it "Final Exam". Obscure 2 is so heavily intertwined with the original that it's impossible to review it without heavy comparison.
There's heavy improvements - most notably, from the getgo, melee is not only tolerable but almost fun. Devil May Cry isn't in danger of being displaced from the top of the food chain, but hitting enemies with the weapons the game throws at you is no longer a nightmare in itself. The characters swinging the bats have received similar improvement.
At the cost of the "anyone can die" gimmick, characters now have variety, depth, story arcs, and dialogue, and aren't just completely interchangeable and forgettable. I almost got attached to some of the new and returning characters during the calmer moments where duos would banter. Calmer moments that are also heavily improved - the puzzles, from the minigames to the environmental work - is leagues ahead of Obscure's, despite the new action focus.
On top of all this, it looks better - character models are respectable and environments much more detailed and interactive (with an insane amount of flavour text in select areas). None of which disguises the hilariously bad plot.
Obscure 2's plot is full of holes, contrivances, retcons, arbitrary character shifts and terrifying CGs nestled comfortably in the pit of the Uncanny Valley. Even if not compared to the first game's flimsy pretext, Obscure 2's plot goes to insane and hilarious over-the-top places, while remaining completely straight-faced, even retroactively turning Obscure's plot into a land of stupidity. And you know none of it is ironic, because the developers are French. It is a joy on every level.
But this came at a heavy cost.
The beautiful level design  that intertwined with pleasing complexity is axed in favour of a completely linear game to almost corridor levels. The slowly filled-in maps are gone, along with maps altogether. The haunting camera angles are gone. The suspense-laden pacing is gone. The flashlight mechanics are gone. The atmosphere is completely brutalized and thrown out the window in favour of an action game with action pacing.
That's without mentioning that co-op is now mandatory - and while the AI is no longer borderline useless, you now get to watch them walk over and over into enemy's reaches while handling ranged weapons and sucking up your extremely scarce resources, and then refusing to get out of the way while attempting to explore.
As many failed attempts at escort missions and multiplayer games have proved - it's not fun to babysit the braindead.
Even with the action horror and better controls, Obscure 2 sacrifices so much of what made the first one special that it feels completely underwhelming as a result. It's no longer surprising that Hydravision went on to make one of the worst-received Alone in the Dark titles. Play it for the camp plot, but if you're looking for more of the well-designed brilliance that was on par with the great Survival Horrors, you're going to be disappointed.
I still recommend Obscure 2 - but it's a lukewarm recommendation.

As stated by other reviewers, this is a revised and updated Panzer General. Great fun (assuming you liked PG or turn based strategy in general), incredible diversity of scenarios if you buy the DLC. Gameplay and graphics are solid, never had an issue of any kind. If there is anything negative it is that the more difficult settings are well balanced in the early years of the Grand campaign (playing as Germany), but once you reach 1943 it becomes nearly impossible to maintain a core force and therefore you will also end up fielding units of old men and middle school kids. Playing as the Allies you will roll through later years of campaign. Of course this is what happened IRL and you might argue that the game reflects the historical imbalance of production/manpower and ultimately hopeless situation of the Nazi's. Either way it is fun, there is some replayability in terms of applying different mix of units to the same scenarios, and I keep coming back to it from time to time to try different strategies and increase the difficulty.  If you buy, get the Grand Campaign DLC and if it is ever in a Steam Sale this is a no brainer for any turn based strategy fans, particularly those who have fond memories of Panzer General or enjoy WWII as a setting.

I finally picked up Panzer Corps a few weeks ago, after waiting for it to go on sale--it's not cheap.  Like many other reviewers, I was a big fan of Panzer General and the Steel Thunder games back in the stone age. On the surface, Panzer Corps seems like a pretty straightforward reboot of those titles. It has a lot more depth, though. The game seems insanely easy to play at first--the interface is as straightforward and clear as anything. There are definitely right and wrong ways to do things, though.  It's rewarding to find out that Panzer Corps responds in the ways you expect it to, though--if you have a reasonable grasp of what the different unit types are supposed to do, it's fun to discover that your dreams of being an armchair Rommel actually work out.
There's a huge variety of unit types, and it's really fun to build up the core of your army throughout a campaign. You really start to care about your units. In one campaign I was invading Sicily and feeling way too confident...I let my prized British commando unit (elites that couldn't be replaced) get chewed up by the Germans when I got cocky. It was one of those slo-mo 'no no no nonooooooooooooooo' moments, hehe.
Oh, and after a bad day at work and/or with the gf/wife/whatever you've got, PC has the perfect solution to your problems.  Start a Wehrmacht '39 campaign on the easiest setting, and just roflstomp your way through the baby seals.

Panzer Corps can be qualified as a successor to the famous and rewarded Panzer General series.
In this game you take command of the German forces in World War II, sometimes assisted by their allies and must complete various objectives such as destroying a target or more often conquer the map. Panzer Corps is a turned-based 2D game which means that you organise your movements, attacks or other strategic action before the enemy does his.
The German campaign will lead you in several theaters of the war such as the invasion of France, the taking of Norwegian's Narvik city, the assistance of Italian troops in their invasion of Greece or the famous operation Barbarossa. The campaign offers a continuity in the various operations which means you will keep your units from a theater to another. That way you will quickly care for your troops as they gain experience, medals and war heroes and you will try to keep the best of your regiments alive. I feel like this game is the mother of the -modern- "roguelike", in that I only remember seeing the extreme popularity of the genre rise after this game was released.  Likely a coincidence, who knows for sure.  In essence, this is THE roguelike dungeon crawler to get if you're looking for this kind of game, complete with its steal of a price tag.
This is about as archetypal as they come:  a(n optionally) perma-death dungeon crawler that is turn-based, randomized floors, a lot of randomized loot, a LOT of surprises, borderline unfair difficulty (which is what makes it so fun) combined with fine balancing, a boatload of skills to make a unique character in a large number of ways, strong overtone of well-executed humor, and then some.  Charming visuals and old-school, catchy music seal the deal.
I once died trying to kick a locked door down.  No, I wasn't actively going for the achievement.  Yes, there's an achievement for dying while kicking a door down.  There is also an achievement for crashing the game.

If you're a fan of traditional roguelikes, you're a bit like a fan of hitting yourself in the knee repeatedly with the pointy end of a claw hammer. Dredmor puts a fun, inviting spin on what is essentially a vicious cycle of internal self-abuse. Losing a game repeatedly due primarily to random chance, but being tricked into thinking it's due to your poor optimization or lack of skill has never been so pleasant! Dungeons of Dredmor, the game that puts a lovable, cheeky attitude to your enternal torment!
If you love roguelikes, you have my condolences. Maybe one day I'll start a support group.

Even at that, however, the game is more than satisfying.

Ok, So my previous review was based on a bunch of playtime in the EA state, and about an hour in the official release, which hadn't really changed all that much from when I played EA. After more time in the official release I will upgrade to a recommended, but I still feel like as a spiritual successor it falls short.
Press N. Thats what changed my mind about this game. The standard map view is too busy and too zoomed in and with the way tiles don't blend very well was very straining on the eyes. Changing the camera to a top down view changed the feel of the game immensely, even if it did cut out some of the nicer graphical touches on landmarks.
Anyway, the bad. The UI is rather unintuitive, I find myself constantly moving units I don't want moved because it defaults the selection to all units in a stack rather than just active ones, the build buttons are off in the middle/top of the city screens instead of down by the build queue where they should be. Sometimes I end up wasting mana when casting spells because rather than cast it when I'm done it gives me a "ready to cast" notification in the bottom that I don't notice until I've ended my turn.
Plus there are just some little things that have been in other 4x games for years that are just odd they weren't included. Such as directing engineers to build roads along a route, instead you have to move them each tile manually whenever they complete building the road on a single tile. When you build cities it automatically names them without any input from you. City borders don't appear to expand, and if you build too close to another the border lines just double up rather than joining. I was also hoping for a better map generation algorythm for release. Although the random mishmash of map tiles definitely brings back Master of Magic, thats not one of the things that should have been brought back. Having some sort of tectonic generation that produces cleaner variations of map tiles would have been nice, instead of having mountains, desert, swamp, forest, and plains all within the borders of one city.
That said there is a lot to like. The team did a great job on building the lore around the factions, and the art in the Sorceror Lord and factions selection screens is top notch. While they couldn't use some of the exact names from Master of Magic, the characters are some pretty obvious references, with some excellent updates. Combat isn't as straight forward as it could be, and with the d20 system sometimes bigger numbers don't always translate to victory. This can lead to more in depth combat strategies, but also to some frustration. Theres a good variety of spells and units, and the factions all feel unique.
Its a closer successor to Master of Magic than a lot of others claiming the title, but  the little things matter. Master of Magic always felt fun, with level up and recruitment annoucements coming with some trumpeted fanfare, the bright colours, and the upbeat music. Worlds of Magic feels very modern by comparison, and not in a good way, with a lot of brown, a darker tone, and just less of a fun feel. That said, it is fun to play, and thats what games are about.

Typos, formatting errors, and placeholders abound in the text in this game. The UI from the stone age makes the game feel like you're actually playing Masters of Magic while you're trying to move and manage your units. The sound effects in the game are comically unimpressive, especially when everything that gets hit makes the same manly grunt whether they be man, woman, beast, or being of pure magic. Worlds of Magic might eventually become a fun game, but playing the 1.0 version, I can say it is laughably unready for release.
Which is a shame really, because underneath all of these superficial yet aggressively apparent flaws is a game with mechanics that do not suck. Each of the game's factions play relatively differently. There is a large enough pool of worlds, spells, monsters, resources, and special events to give you a feeling of exploration after multiple playthroughs. Six hours into the game, I have also found it delightful to explore the strategic and tactical options the game allows you to play with.

An introductory level wargame that skimps on realism to deliver "beer and pretzels", jump right in and conquer the world goods.  You'll be playing the campaign as any individual scenario is not particularly compelling and definitely is NOT a historical simulation of its respective battle.  The campaign is a blast to play, though as you'll be given a core force of Wehrmacht units representing Infantry, Artillery, Panzer, etc of possibly brigade/division size.  IMO, the units have no realistic size as the game is abstracted and for funsies.  As you conquer cities and finish battles, you'll accumulate "influence" points with which you can upgrade your existing units and buy new ones.  In addition, your units accumulate experience when they fight which will make them more effective and randomly generate leaders attached to the unit that gives them special abilities like +1 Movement, for example.  As the war progresses, new units will unlock as your original units become obsolete.  You'll start the war with PzKfw I and end with Tiger IIs.  The campaign has branching possibilities depending on the victory level you achieve, so it is possible to invade England, e.g.  My beefs with the game are few.  The main one being that the base game is short (but replayable) and to properly enjoy the game, one should purchase the Grand Campaign.  The game overall has an admirable level of polish.  Wish there was more animation. Don't expect depth or realism.  This is War lite, playable while drunk.

A modern recreation of Panzer General, a game from ye olde, Panzer Corps plays with the same classic gameplay of the original, kicked into the 21st Century.
Giving the option of a progressive campaign, or both single and multiplayer independent scenarios, the Second World War comes back to life with the renouwned almost chess-like system of balance between Infantry, Armour, Reconnaisance, Anti-Armour, Artillery, AA, Fighters, and Tactical & Strategic Bombers. Each unit has its' own advantages, strengths and weaknesses - a King Tiger is truely a powerful tank, but it cannot win the war alone! With the original prestige system the game forces you to adapt your strategy around the battlefield: if you're taking heavy losses, should I pull-back, give them green reinforcements, or veterans? As you push through the campaign, with a choice of five starting years, your core forces follow through, gaining experience, and eventually medals and heroes.
The flexibility of tactics allow your preferences to come out in your core and mission results. Choices such as those between ground attack and fighter-bomber aircraft: early in the game, you have the Ju87 Stuka and the Bf110. The Stuka is a more reliable source of damage, but more vulnerable to enemy interceptors and anti-air fire whilst the 110 can engage other aircraft, typically used to finish off shattered aircraft or mop up craft that cannot do much back like bombers, as well as faring better in air combat, but at the cost of less performance in ground strikes.
Anti-tank, artillery, or anti-aircraft weapons on a tank chassis make for faster, more reliable defence and offense, but at a higher price and losing out on the bonuses crewed non vehicle weapons obtain - as they are not armoured, they fare better in close terrain and hold better ambush advantages, amongst other things. Sometimes a mix is better - keeping general support weapons with main attacks whilst giving mechanised AA, AT and artillery to tank groups to better support their attacks can benefit both. But now you're dividing your forces into two distinct groups and you have to weigh up whether the advantages are enough!
A range of scenarios are present in the game: relive the humble beginnings in Poland, to the start of the turning point in the Caucauses - from all the major operations in the war, but also covering hypothetical situations - what would be the real outcome of a German invasion of the British Isles, or even an invasion of the American east coast?
A strong variety of units are present. Progressive models of vehicles like tanks and fighters give you the oppertunity to upgrade as history produced each - even the late-war Panzer IV J has it's roots in the D model! Is the cost always worth it for the battle? Much of your choices may reflect necessities found in the real war, such as the shock of heavier armour in Barbarossa! Different types of each group present theirselves - infantry are diverse: light, heavy, mountain, paratroop, engineer, bridge-laying, cavalry, motorised and so on, and this type of diversity is continued in the unit groups. Upgrade your units! Infantry, anti-tank, artillery and the like can be given transport. The first option is the classic Opel Blitz truck, which gets you where you need. However, as a mere truck, it is highly susceptible to attack and as such many choose to upgrade some of their units to use the sd.kfz 251 or 250 halftracks which also benefit from the ability to fire when under attacked (or when the risky commander chooses to engage enemies!) Throughout the campaign, you also have the chance to obtain prototype and unique units, from the tremendous Schwere-Gustav railgun to the infamous Maus.
Finally, if you wish to continue, the devs have bundled up new content in the form of two expansion packs, Allied & Afrika Corps, for a new experience, and the Grand Campaign which allows you to progress through all notable battles in the war: 1939 is now split into fourteen seperate scenarios! Carve your route through the war - your successes or failures will decide factors such as whether your force attacks through the Danzig North or Danzig South corridor in Poland, or whether to obey orders or mount an assault on the Dunkirk evacuation! Many of the scenarios have been bundled with unique objectives. For instance, one scenario in 1940 challenges you to assault positions to extract a French general and take him to the rear of the map, whilst one Polish situation requires you to halt troop trains to gain a decisive victory! Now get out there herr oberleutnant, and turn the course of the war!

So what is Panzer Corps ?
Panzer Corps is an exact copy of Panzer General II updated for mordern computers.  That's it.  Overall this a pretty great classic game.  I can't count the number of hours that I spent playing the original, and there is absoultely nothing wrong with this game.  Would buy again.
The only comment I will make is that if you are looking to see what a modern hex based WWII game looks like, then you should also pick up a copy of "Unity of Command", which was clearly influenced by Panzer General II, but which has its own really fresh take on hex based wargames.

The tried and true formula so familiar to the classic Panzer General fans gets a second wind in Panzer Corps. You get to command a mostly persistent force through a number of historical and hypothetical WWII campaign scenarios that unravel depending on progress and success in prior battles. It's thanks to tactical depth, freedom and replayability as well as an unprecedented scale of campaigns found in both the base game and especially the numerous DLCs that Panzer Corps deserves in my mind the title of the best turn-and-hex based strategy game of 2014.
Accessible for even those players completely unfamiliar with the genre conventions, it's a gem worth checking out even at the current steep price. As far as DLCs are concerned, the Grand Campaign '39-'45 is a must for fans of the genre.
Highly recommended game for anyone that enjoys the genre! A+ wish I had more time to play it.

Ye gods, the pop culture references...so many pop culture references.
Dungeons of Dredmore is your typical roguelike; maintaining the tradition of esoteric skill trees, randomly generated dungeon levels, and optional permadeath (ouch).  The actual gameplay is fun and incredibly engrossing in and of itself, the game could stand on that alone even though that is not what makes DoD truly shine.
The thing that really makes DoD the first among roguelikes, the reason that you should play THIS roguelike is the irreverent, unrepentant sense of humor.  It keeps you laughing through every.last.permadeath.  Nothing is sacred...least of all the protagonist.  The descriptions of the "normal" loot, equipment, skills, etc. are hilarious; and the standard content is just the tip of this iceberg of absurdity.  Then there is the humor inherent in the things that you would never expect from this kind of setting.  Really, though, who wouldn't love a game with skill trees for such things as Veganism, Archeology, Magical Law and Tourism?
Finally, this game will really reach out to you with more cultural references than you can shake a standard-issue 10' pole at.  Really, recognizing all of them would borderline on a superhuman ability.  Not only is the sheer number impressive, but the game creators chose to cast this particular net over a large area of pop-culture and sub-cultures rather than limiting themselves to areas of interest most common to gamers.  It would take a vastly longer review than this to list off all of the fandoms, but rest assured that something near and dear to your heart will be mocked.  It's a tough call, but in the end I think that the cultural references are the funniest part of the game.
There are only two criticisms that I have to offer.  First of all, the mad libs-style random generator for the names of places and artifacts is rather inelegant.  The intent is funny, as are some of the results, but frequently the grammatical issues with the names and titles just gets in the way of the humor.  Secondly, there seem to be specific room layouts that are frequently re-used in the random level generation, making the rooms occasionally repetitive.  I don't know anything about coding, so I have no idea if that is something that is even possible to change.  However, neither of these two issues drastically impact my enjoyment of the game.

Chances are, the only reason you've heard of this game is because of the controversy over the violence, and there's a good reason for that. You know those parts of some games where it suddenly decides it wants to be a stealth game, and it makes you play with poorly cobbled together stealth mechanics for a little while and even if you're a big fan of stealth games it's hard to enjoy it because the mechanics are so poorly designed? Manhunt is like that, except that they forgot to make the rest of the game that's actually fun. It's an extremely simple, basic stealth game where almost every environment is a bland, featureless alleyway or concrete building, and lacks any sort of story beyond what's in the steam description. Along the way you have to deal with other gameplay favorites such as two escort missions and a section where if you get spotted 4 times, the episode fails. It's a game where the only reason to play it is the violence, but even that is pretty tame by today's standards - I could see it being edgy enough to be a decent gimmick in 2003, but in 2015 after you've seen the first two or three strong executions you'll probably just wish they had a skip key so that you wouldn't have to watch any more, since they have barely any variety and aren't particularly graphic. It's just overall an extremely boring game, and I can't recommend it to anyone for even $10 unless you played it back then and are just desperate to relive your 2003 days.

Short version: this is a fantastic premise and art design in need of better writing and scenario design. More of a proof of concept than a satisfying game.
Long version:
I was real disappointed with this. Lost interest 90 minutes into the game and have shelved it for the moment.
They have the great framework for a great game, and they certainly have the artistic talent. The problem is they just don't have the writing or design talent to go with it.
The plot: Comparisons have been made to Ghost Trick: Phantom Detective. The plot in that game managed to make the player give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about the story right from the very beginning. Sexy Brutale...I guess they wanted to go for "mysterious" but they don't have the writing chops to pull it off, and you're given absolutely nothing to care about from the start. You're dumped into playing a mute protagonist with no background, trying to save people you know nothing about from murderers you know nothing about in a setting you know nothing about, and it's all presented not in a sinister tone but a whimsical tone like "Clue" so you're not even motivated by basic righting of wrongs. For all you know, the guests are evil and the servants are heroic resistance fighters. Even the people who have beaten the game say there's no plot to care about, until the very end where you get hit with a clumsy exposition dump.
The puzzles: Are far too simple. There are usually only one or two VERY basic and obvious steps to stopping each murder. The challenge isn't figuring them out, it's sitting through the tedious NPC travel routines waiting for the right time to do something. You quickly figure out the simple solution to stopping a murder, then spend five times as long peeking through doors waiting for NPCs to slowly waddle along and leave the room so you can do something. Worse is that, although you can rewind time, you cannot fast forward it and every rewind point is at least one full minute of real time waiting for key events. Every retried attempt is at least 60 seconds of just sitting there waiting for NPCs to run through the same routine. It gets old very very fast. The puzzles are 20% (very basic) deduction and 80% tedious waiting. This game would be great if they could get the Danganronpa writers who know how to write an intricate murder to solve.
That's not even mentioning the awful PC controls. Hold down right click to move (not right click to move, HOLD DOWN. If you let go you stop moving), left click to open door, then E and space to examine or peek through doors. It might sound simple, but trust me it's super awkward trying to play. It feels like a lazy DS port except it was never designed for touchscreen! There is no reason everything couldn't have been tied to left and right mouse clicks. It's definitely not worth $20. Even at 40% off for the summer sale I feel I didn't get my money's worth for 90 minutes until I lost interest. The only reason I can think of for buying this is supporting the developer enough so that they eventually get decent writing & design talent and release a proper game for this concept in the future.﻿
(for anyone thinking I can't review this after only 90 minutes, just how long should you give a game to give a good impression if the whole thing is only 4-6 hours long?)

A delightful gem, it's hard to know where to start complimenting The Sexy Brutale. The gameplay is fun and innovative, with the reliving of events from different angles providing a challenging but rewarding way of solving a mystery. While some players might feel off-put by the idea of having to hit the resest button  and start the day over again, the game is paced well enough that you will usually find that you've made some degree of noteworthy progress with each pass. The puzzles and gathering of clues to learn how to solve them is fun and never feels like a chore. The characters and writing is a clever blend of humorous and dark, with enough moments to make you laugh while simultaneously shocking you with their brutality. The music is terrific, composed to swell and blend with things that are happening within the plot, and always acting as a treat for the ears. But I think the greatest strength of the game is that it simply offers a good mystery that plays well with the reliving of the day. Things like hearing a gun shot, watching the lights flicker, or seeing something pass a window all tell the player that something is going on somewhere else in the house, and gives incentive to keep progressing if only to find out what is causing the phenomena that you watch each day.
As a whole, I cannot reccomend this game enough. An absolute must have for anyone who lieks a good mystery.

If you liked Master of Magic, and are willing to try it again with newer graphics and a few changes, then you are really going to want to play this game.
Worlds of Magic is a shameless spiritual successor to Master of Magic; the races are there (High Men, Elves, Dwarves, Dragonkin, Orcs, and Undead, so far, with the possibility of more coming along later); the heroes are there; the artifacts that make your heroes monstrously powerful are there; the spells, spell books (circles in WoM), and Wizard Lord perks are there; town management and research and all the strategic features.  WoM is instantly accessible if you know MoM.  But there have been some changes, and I think most of them are for the better.
The magic system is different but makes a lot of sense.  Spells are now part of two distinct schools, and the sum of your proficiency in those schools unlocks them.  So, say you like a particular buffing spell that's part of Biomancy and Life.  If you have enough of either, you are able to research the spell - but if you spread out your spell picks and got some of both, then the total you have will allow unlocking the spell for research.  It's a nice way to distinguish the spells within their MoM types - not all Life spells are equal, after all, so why should they all require the same prerequisites?  The infusion system in Worlds of Magic allows your combat spells to scale in power as you gain greater Spellcraft (like many of the spells in MoM did), so even those starting spells can be of great use throughout the game.
Combat mechanics are handled via the d20 system, which is very easy to understand.  The numbers get a good deal bigger than the Master of Magic nimbers did (a basic High Men spearman unit can end up with almost 100 hit points at maximum level, without special buffs, for example), but the damage keeps up so battles don't slog on.  Healing feels a little weaker (except for Healing Wind, which at maximum infusion turns enormous fights against the undead into a two-turn rout), but that just means that your tactical choices are a little more important.
Races are much better balanced in Worlds of Magic than in the MoM predecessor.  If you've played MoM, you know that Paladins = Instawin.  All races have the ability to dominate, in WoM; the Grey Elves, for example, have probably the most powerful starting unit in the game (Archers), but even an army full of levelled archers can be managed.  Similarly, an army of Paladins in WoM will be powerful, for sure, but not unstoppable - especially if you have an opposing army of similarly powerful units (orcish Manslayers; Elven Faradrax; Draconian Elders, etc).
The economy in WoM is very familiar to anyone who played MoM - with one notable exception.  The undead have been worked to have a different, simplified economy.  This is an interesting option, because it completely changes the feel of the game.  With undead being unable to invade and keep the cities of the living (they are the enemies of all life, after all), playing as the Unhallowed (WoM name for undead) turns you unto a rolling tide of death, and makes the whole expansion part of the game feel faster and inexorable.
Finally, Worlds of Magic takes the Arcanum/Myrror plane aspect of Master of Magic and makes it much more detailed, and much more meaningful.  Now, you have the Prime plane, as well as planes of Earth, Water, Air, Fire, and Shadow.  Each plane offers special strategic benefits in the form of city resources, and thus plays into the strengths of specific races.  Unhallowed start in the plane of Shadow and draw strength from the negative energy sources all around; dwarves will become production powerhouses in the plane of earth, cranking out high-cost units every other turn or earning ridiculous amounts of gold when making Trade Goods.  Because there are so many planes, it is possible to take shortcuts across the map via planar travel.  Can't get across the sea?  Maybe there's a gateway to another place on the coast - go through it, and if you can traverse the land of that plane, you can find another gateway back to your starting plane, and cross the sea (by way of one or more planes) without ever getting wet or building a ship!  The mutiplane design is quite rewarding, and offers a great deal of replay value, since you can choose how many planes to allow in the game world, their size, how much of each is land, and the general configuration of that land (islands, continents, one giant landmass).
Like Master of Magic, on release there are a few things that still need fixed.  There are some bugs, and the on-screen error reporter will tell you exactly what they are, so you can report them in detail and hopefully help get them fixed quickly.  This isn't a flawless game, but it's a shot of nostalgia for anyone who loves Master of Magic and wished someone would make a proper sequel.  Get it; you won't regret the purchase.

This game is completely inspired by the old 90's classic, Master of Magic. So it has the same 4X formula, along with spellcasting at global and tactical level, spell research, and various races to play as. As far as capturing that old MoM gameplay feel, WoM nails it.
The graphics are a mix of gorgeous and merely good. Some of the planes of existence, units and buildings look stunning! Some of the spell animations and the way that persistent spells are displayed could be improved upon. (at the moment, there's no specific animation or effect for a persistent spell that's been placed on a unit; e.g. think of the ice shields in Diablo3).
There are some things I'd like to see change; for example, the enemy Lords could use some extra writing or graphics to give them a but more of a personality (at the moment they're devious opponents but they seem to prefer to keep things discreet. They're not the same type of flashy enemies that MoM had).
The game rules are super solid. Economies are finely balanced, there's a challenging learning curve and high-level magic feels suitably powerful and effective. This is one of those games where you can end up shaping the world you live in to better suit your needs.
Most importantly it has that 'one more turn' feeling that a good strat game needs to have. All in all I recommend it - it's an early access product that will be great at launch and incredible after a few free DLC's have been added.

Unfortunately, unless they have a MAJOR overhaul to the enemy and unit AI, totally redo the HUD and put a goodly amount of work into balancing the different units in the next 3 days until their purported launch, you are simply better off dropping 10 bucks on Masters of Magic at GOG.  It has a wealth more content and fun to offer, as do many of the other 4x games that have come out in the past few years such as Age of Wonders 3, Endless Legend, Fallen Enchantress, Civ V...hell, even Warlock.
As someone who kickstarted this for over a hundred dollars based purely on the idea of a new Masters of Magic game, to say I am disappointed in the direction they took would be an understatement.  I applaud them for their efforts and having the ambition to try, but ultimately this game will fail to live up to even the most gaunt of shadows cast by it's predecessor.

This may be the first positive review...!
In short, it's engaging, dynamic, fairly effortless and solidly immersive. A game to snack into from time to time.
It's Civilization meets Travian meets Total War - and done fairly well.
To be clear, the idea of this game is to be a cross-platform thing you can dip in and out of: Battles are tres petit and your actions generally take several minutes to several hours to complete on the campaign map. With that in mind, it's not a typical Total War game to sit at for 18 hours solid conquering. If you come in  with that expectation, you're going to cry.
Instead it's like so many similar time-based multiplayer online games (Travian, Tribal Wars, Clash of Clans - there may be haters, but they're good fun with work colleagues when you don't have a lot of time on hand). Only difference is that this is so far more immersive and much more fun. Battles are suitably tactical and challenging and deliver a quick buzz (handy for coursework breaks).
So far, the campaign map's relatively well paced and there are plenty of new glossy things getting unlocked to keep me interested. It's a massive hex map that you unlock new theatres by defeating the army there - in each one it's a mix of terra-forming and town-building (lots and lots of little houses), trying to twist streams where you want them to make life more fertile and sustainably milk the land. It was an emphasis I wasn't expecting, but a lot of fun.
I haven't felt at a disadvantage by not buying any things yet either.
Negatives... Haven't found any significant ones yet, other than it's eating too much of my productivity.
Give it a go - just don't expect MTW3.

Spent many hours in the early alpha tests convincing myself that all the potential was here, and that all it needed were a few tweaks to reach that next level. Four(?!) years later, the game seems shallower and less satisfying than ever, albeit with a nice fresh coat of paint. The user interface and the in-game leveling menus are the biggest change that I can see outside of the different maps, and these (so far as I can remember) are nice upgrades.
The game yearns to be competitive and fast-paced, but it controls like an Elder Scrolls game, making movement stiff, clunky, linear and tied to a stamina bar. In a game about casual exploration and story-telling, these mechanics are entirely passable, but not in a genre where these inputs are the very core of the experience.
I tried a character I'd never seen before--a pink girl with a huge sword who looked like something out of Adventure Time. Visually, I have no strong opinon on the character one way or the other. Mechanically, it's the worst-designed character I've seen in a competitive game, so that didn't win me over.
This review is subject to change, but my first (new) impression has largely been one of ambivalence, maybe mild disappointment that things couldn't be brought back around.

Combine a storyline more loopy and incoherent than almost every Japanese anime ever made, a cumbersome real-time item-choosing system guaranteed to make you use those medkits even faster, a save system which ensures you'll have to waste countless minutes at a time getting back to the bit which killed you in the first place, the occasional obstructive "camera angle" almost deliberately designed to ♥♥♥♥ you six-ways-to-Sunday, and some of the ♥♥♥♥♥iest boss fights in all of video game history...and what do you have?
Well, oddly enough, a mostly enjoyable and worthwhile gaming experience...but ONLY if you've already played several dozen other post-Resident Evil third-person "survival horror" games, and are so addicted to such curiosities that you'll endure almost any level of punishment in search of that next elusive "fix".
I recently played and wrote a review of the first Obscure in which I declared it a "pleasant surprise", or words to roughly that effect. Given that I had slightly higher expectations of this one in the wake of its more-than-serviceable predecessor, I wouldn't say that I'm "disappointed" so much as a little bewildered at just how nutty and, well, borderline incompetent this one so often gets.
Don't get me wrong: there's a lot of REALLY GOOD IDEAS here. One improvement it arguably makes over the original are the very distinct "special abilities" which each character has, all of which you will at some point REQUIRE to make progress through the game (as opposed to the "vaguely-useful-but-mostly-inessential" abilities evidenced by most of the characters in Obscure 1). To this effect, much of the puzzle-solving in this game is actually quite clever (though asking the player to pick a tricky lock puzzle in the midst of the climactic boss fight while a monster clobbers you from the side was perhaps pushing the friendship a little)! And the learning curve applied to these mini game-within-a-games is mostly realistic and achievable, even for a certifiable doofus such as I.
The scenery is also frequently interesting and varied. Perhaps a little TOO varied for realistic geography purposes, but never mind (just think of it like one of those epic sword-and-sorcery fantasy worlds where a blazingly hot desert and an icy wasteland are just a hop, skip and a jump away from each other...apparently suburban high schools and spooky, near-desolate islands inhabited by in-bred Texas Chainsaw rejects do much the same thing).
It's also a game with lots of "personality", not least of all within the characters themselves. Plenty of entertaining banter and carry-on whilst the gameplay continues unabated, giving it a convincingly "cinematic" feel and making you actually "care" a little more for the fate of said characters than your average paper cut-out video game personas (off the top of my head, the Walking Dead and Left 4 Dead games are about the only other horror titles so earnestly devoted to giving their protagonists more than two dimensions).
Look, it's pretty clear by now that I have a certain fondness for these games, even if this one in particular infuriated me almost to the point of electronic pulpification. Mostly I'm just relieved there was never an Obscure 3, 'cause you know that I'd feel obliged to play it, and judging by the quality arc this series has evidenced thus far, it would probably be almost intolerably "bad". ALMOST.
In the tradition of the best "trashy" horror films, let's just chalk this one up as a "guilty pleasure"...even if the "pleasure" parts only seem to come in spurts.
Verdict: 8/10.

Mini Metro's distinct levels--all inspired by real-world metro lines--definitely have deep nuances that affect your tactics for each and reward your experimentation and practice.
It's a lot like Flight Control, except more complex.
I love the meditative, minimalist aesthetic, especially with Night Mode enabled. FEZ composer Disasterpeace has crafted a lush, warm, subdued soundscape full of soft sines and small clocks that grows, shrinks, or shifts dynamically in response to your actions based on conditions in the game. Though even at full volume on my laptop, it wasn't loud enough for me.
At their core, simulation and management games are about optimizing a particular workflow or mastering a certain system as best as you can. Mini Metro falls into that category, even loosely--just on a smaller, less permanent scale. I admit, a larger and lasting scale of some kind would be even more interesting here, but it shares these traits of "starting all over" with both score-chaser Arcade games and procedurally-generated Roguelike games.
Yet even with all its depth and variations, the gameplay itself is eventually too simple to be this repetitive, and too repetitive to be this simple. I guess that makes it more suited to being used as a palette cleanser between games or between life, once you've played past using it as a game. Hence the inclusion of a Daily Challenge.
Overall, there is far more praiseworthy about this game than not, and too few games accomplish similar concepts this beautifully. I hope to improve at it regularly and look forward to whatever features and content future patches will bring along!

The premise of this game had me intrigued as I am curious about how metro systems around the world are designed. I though that I was getting a sim-style game that would let me lay out a metro system in meticulous detail, but this isn't the game that I was looking for. I do enjoy the game, but it is a real-time puzzle game, and not a sim.
There are many cities that you can play in, and each starts with three stations of different shapes - a Circle, Square, and Triangle. A station's shape determines the destination of/number of passengers that will spawn there. For example, Circles will spawn the most riders, but few passengers from other stations will want to go there. A station spawns riders in the shape of the station that they wish to go to, and each passenger boards trains that can take them to one of their destination type, and not a specific station. Your score is the number of total passengers delivered to their destination.
Stations spawn periodically and connecting lines to them so that passengers will get picked up in a timely manner before the stations get overcrowded is the goal of the game. In addition to the three main shapes, several unique shapes can spawn as well, which ups the difficulty quite a bit. Passengers choose trains intelligently, so not always by the shortest route, but the one that will likely take the least amount of time.
Each "week" you get a new train and another random reward that could be a carriage (more passengers for a train), tunnels (the number varies), a new line (there is a maximum number of lines on each map, and you always start with three), or an interchange (increases the number of passengers a stop can handle before overcrowding).
You get visual and audible warnings when a station start to get overcrowded, and if the problem isn't resolved in about 45 seconds, the game ends. So planning ahead is vital, but you can't always do that due to the random nature of the station spawns. Sometimes you'll have a nice mix of stations along each line, and can get quite an impressive score. Other times you'll have eight Circle stations isolated from everything else and only one or two lines to service them, which is usually not enough.
Games last anywhere from a few minutes to 30, and scores range from 200 to 2000+, depending on the map and the luck of the spawns. I recommend the game, but it can be frustrating when you have a good game going and three or four Circle stations spawn in inconvenient spots and ruin it. Still, it's great for when you have 10-20 minutes and not too taxing on the brain.

A great premise, consistent artwork, and casual-yet-intense gameplay.
However, don't go in expecting a long-form strategy game. After you bid on a plot of land and go to develop it, you have exactly one day to extract from it before it's gone forever. No matter how much oil you pull out, once you've run out of time it's gone forever. That's a very different game than one where each plot continues to make money as you pull oil out of the ground, or one where you revisit the same plots over and over.
That's not necessarily a bad thing, the game is fun and challenging. But it's perhaps not the game I wanted to buy. This game is less of a meal and more of a snack, meant to be eaten in small portions before being abandoned. It's the sort of thing that feels like it looked wistfully at mobile games and wanted to fit in, but knew it was too complicated to do so.
The only real gripe I can bring up is that the prices of oil fluctuate _completely_ unexpectedly. There is obviously some pattern to when they rise and fall, and at what rate, but so much of the game is built on random chance that you'll be able to sell your oil to someone with a good price that it feels less as if you're getting better at the game, and more that you "struck oil" and got lucky with the RNG.
Again, that may just be how the game wants to be played. But to me the differences in my expectations and reality were enough to make me not want to play more.

Turmoil is an utterly charming little genre-mix with many mechanisms that blend well with each other.
You are an oil tycoon in the 19th century wild west. You have an auction phase to bid for drill plots, you manage your town (which serves as equipment upgrades) and then the real time drilling begins.
The art style and the music aren't top-notch, but they are really comforting. They serve their purpose very well.
The drilling for oil is executed perfectly. Even though it's in real time, I never felt like needing a tactical pause nor did I ever feel it's too slow. The pace is incredibly well balanced. There is a faint sense of urgency, but it never gets hectical.
The money earned from drilling is spent on expanding your town and thus upgrading your equipment for more efficient drilling.
Some mentioned that the game becomes repetitive soon. I was afraid of that as well, but to my surprise I haven't hit that spot yet. I don't feel like I'm going to get there any time soon.

Before you get this game, I strongly advise that you do some research.
Not because the game sucks, it's actually one of the best roguelikes I've played recently, but because of a problem I'll describe.
The game has an auto-save feature that sometimes crashes the game (Runtime Error).
You can NOT remove this auto-save feature, which wouldn't be a problem if it didn't corrupt savefiles, but unfortunately it does.
The developers of this game even acknowledged the issue, but did nothing after 2 years of knowing about it.
The only workaround is to:
1) Turn off Steam Cloud
2) "Save and Continue" in the menu (unavailable if you play Permadeath mode)
3) Manually backup your savefiles from Windows folders every now and then,  so when it happens you can replace the corrupted save
I lost a 28 hours savefile due to not knowing of this issue, and I'm not gonna recommend the game despite it being rather good. I might give this another try someday, but right now I'm stunned.
Do yourself a favor and do some research before you get this game, and you won't be caught offguard.

Is ridiculously deep strategy game with an easy to learn surface, but a million fathoms of strategic depth to uncover.  The game's main feature is the dynamic campaign, each scenario has specific parametres to achieve "decisive victory" these are like "S" ranking a mission in other games and it is actually quite hard to achieve a decisive victory even in the early levels.  I often found myself getting a decisive victory on the last turn.  If you win through any other means it is a mere "marginal victory" and this is where the game gets really interesting.  A marginal victory is cause history to play out normally, but a decisive victory will lead into scenarios like Operation Sea Lion.  Furthermore, your core units (as long as they survive) will persist between scenarios in the campaign, they can also gain medals and have heroes added to them depending on their performance.  If you are a strategy fan this may scratch that itch for you.

I recently went looking for Master of Magic to play, and I ended up discovering what was marketed as the spiritual successor to Master of Magic.  An updated version of the game that I have not stopped loving, regardless of how much time passes and how many other games release?  I was excited, and I was a bit pensive as well.  Were they going to truly capture the feels I felt as a child?
In my opinion, they have.  Admittedly, it's difficult to replicate the feel of nostalgia I get with the game, coming downstairs during the early summer morning and watching my dad's budding Human empire grow slowly day by day before he heads off to work.  Many associates to Master of Magic to me had almost nothing to do with the game itself, though I still loved the game.
With Worlds of Magic, you have a lot of very familiar surroundings.  You can swap the camera to an overhead view that mirrors MoM.  Your city influence is the same fat plus at the start.  You can modify your farmer/worker ratio (and you have another option now, too!), you build armies, you build new cities, you explore caves and towers and magical sources of power around the world, you encounter enemies and fantastical creatures, you summon creatures, cast destructive spells, manipulate an enemy's city, buff your own city.  The Power system feels familiar, but the number of new spells and the way the Battleboard plays with the D20 system really add a lot of additional flavor for me.
It's like loving pizza all of your life, then someone brings you a piece of pizza with ranch dressing, and you're like "Oh wow, this is the same deliciousness, with a nice addition!"
That's how I feel about Worlds of Magic.  In addition, the devs have been borderline-insanely receptive to feedback.  I personally have pointed out early access bugs and quality of life changes that have, within days, been fixed or added to the game.  These devs *love* this game, and they are willing to hear feedback and incorporate it into the game if it sounds like a good idea.
I can't wait to see this game grow over the years, and I can't wait to keep playing it (while also recommending it to my aforementioned dad, as well as my bro!).

Excellent start.
Anyone buying this in Beta, please remember it's beta, meaning it's not finished yet. (Always a danger for a company to market a beta product, but sometimes budgets demand it). All that said, I have to review the product as it is, with some extrapolation as to what it probably will become.
I'm a lifer in this 4x genre, having played just about everything in it for 20+ years. Fantasy 4x is rare, and my favorite. So, how does this game stack up against MoM (the classic)? I'd say it's off to a good start.
Good:
-Very MoM-like, with updated graphics and a similar interface. Possibly, it's a little
, but I like the squares and the randomness of the worlds, etc... Let's be honest, I love them!
-Lots of classic fantasy races (I HATE made up races, or "six flavors of humans" games. Give me an Elf and a Dwarf, dammit).
- You build your own faction/Wizard. Variety and strategy right from the "New Game" screen.
-Create your own items, unit experience, construct your empire city-by-city, tactical combat maps with full control, etc.
Maybe just because its Beta:
-The interface feels rough in spots, but I'm fairly sure that this will be improved. As it is, you might be put off at first until you get used to it. Give it 5+ hours before giving up.
-The AI is a little weak, but they're working on that.
-There are bugs, but it has yet to crash on me.
-Right now, it is a cpu hog. Runs fine on my gaming rig, but not on my notebook (which is an I7 with a vid card).
-No real diplomacy yet.
The Bad:
-The screen feels crowded with stuff. Makes it difficult to read the map especially when a new player is starting out. Possibly some of the 3-d Icons will be reduced in size so they don't stack up into a junkyard-blur in the future.
-The biggest area where it differs from MoM is a critical one: tactical combat resolution. The map and movement, etc, is the same, but when you attack it figures out what happens differently. They went with a D&D clone D20 system, where you have reflex saves and the like. The main problem I see with it is the increased variation of results. Sometimes, a settler will crit and kick your swordsman azz. I would suggest they go thru and tighten the dice rolls, making it 3D6+7, maybe, instead of 5D6 damage. Could even be an option. Also, crits should probably do +50% instead of 2x damage. This matters because things like enchantment spell bonuses are unbalanced in relative value if you can just "get lucky" also, it's annoying to have reload and replay battles due to crits. Could be an option to disable crits (that would take like 10 minutes of programming time).
Overall, I have high hopes. Modding options might help some balance issues, such as the value of various spells, etc. The AI is often a weak spot in 4x games, I'm hoping they'll give it a few more IQ points before release.

Really fun game in first couple chapters, that gets repetitive, boring and in some parts annoying while you move on. Stealth element is nice, sneaking around, looting everything that shine, uncovering people secrets, all that is interesting and fun. Visually game is decent, with somewhat poor animation in form of character actions and movement. Character AI is very basic and easily fooled. Voice acting is also poor and in some places you can barely hear what people say.
You are very dependent on your arrows, if you run low, you must travel to the merchant. A lot of arrow variations and not enough interactions by hand, to turn off lights, extinguish flames, etc. Why we can't put out torches or fires, lamps by hand or some other method that doesn't involve arrows is beyond me.
Learning skills, buying tools, equipment is done through gold, so more you steal, more you can learn/buy. In my opinion game has great and dark mood of old "London", or should I say fiction London. Level design is very hectic and navigating through all the areas tied with loading screens gets really old, really fast.
You don't see clear transition points from area to area in the same level, and often just stumble on a random window that loads you to other area. Levels are closed, instanced small to medium size areas often filled with a lot of buildings and narrow pathways, with a lot of apartment access points from roof.
Story is just not there, you blindly steal different stuff for each mission with almost no explanation on why or what for. If you like to loot shiny things, be sneaky and stealthy, do a lot of climbing all around the city then you might like this game.

TLDR - If you pick this game up for less than 10 bucks, I can recomend it. More in depth - I'm going to start of by stating YES, I'm a fan of the previous games.  In fact, they were my favorite games of all times.  But I went into this knowing it was a flawed product, and played all the previous ones again to get a fresh perspective so that my comparison to the previous games would not be biased by nostalgia.  I came into this with the flaws and good points of the previous games fresh in my head.
In straight comparison, the pros and cons in terms of Genre....
PROS
- They were kind enough to give appropriate nods to the previous games with symbols from the Mechanists and Hammerites present in the game
- It was nice to see some of the old locations in the previous games present.
- Basso is a riot.  I honestly wish we could of seen more of that guy.
- I found the voice actor for Garret to be close enough in most cases.  While the dialog wasn't spot on, I took it from the standpoint of "gawd I'm tired of having to keep saving this city".
- While the factions that generally represented Chaos and Order were not present, the game still held onto that conflict as one of it's core vibe's.
CONS
- They completely dumped the made up curses of the world (Shut up you Taffer!) in favor of real curses.  Bad move - not only loses some of the flavor of the previous games, but turns of your previous playerbase.
- Use of the Rope arrows - while it was nice to see them back their use was too restrictive in a series that generally allowed it where you felt like it.
- Straight up fights were more like a quick time event than a real fight.  Made me miss the sword play of the first two games.
- Where the hell were the Pagan's?  The Hammerites?
Now.... the game itself lifted elements from other games such as Dishonored, Dues Ex, Batman, and Assassin's Creed.  This in itself does not bother me.  Indeed all of the above can trace their stealth roots to the original Thief - so it seems appropriate to me that the grandaddy of stealth games would borrow some of the best of it's grand-children to make itself better.  Some of it was great for the game such as the drop knockdowns, upgrade system, and the takeouts were very appropriate.  But other parts such as the pipe and ledge climbing felt tacked on and were terrible in execution.
Taking the game by itself without judging it against it's predecessors I can give you the following pros and cons
PROS
- Running on normal settings, I had zero issues with graphical lag and stuttering.  Impressive given my computer is 5 years old.
- The asylum level was very well done and scared that absolute crap out of me.
- Character always responded as I wanted to once I understood what I was doing wrong in the controls.
- The world itself was gorgous.
- I loved trying to find hidden switches in books and in picture safes.  I wished there was more varients of this.
- some people may of found it tedius, but I enjoyed having to open drawers to find all the loot.  watching my hands work helped in the immersion.
- Final Boss fight was appropriate and a breath of fresh air - even if it was a bit easy
CONS
- Lock picking system is unintiative and quite frankly garbage. 2nd worst lock picking system I've ever experienced.  Took me most of the game to realize it works best if you work the mouse in a circliar motion - and even then the audio-visual feedback is terrible.
- Guard personalities were very flat and uninteresting.
- Erin... well I hate her and so did everybody else apparently.  Terrible character.  You're supposed to care about her, but they do a terrible job making you give a rip about her and her past.
- Sound... omg the sound positioning in this game is absolutely aweful!  It's really hard to tell where sounds are coming from or how far they are from you.  This is absolutely unacceptable in a stealth-based game!
- Control system is made unnecessarely complicated and unintiative.  Why is there a separate key for drop down and crouch?  Why doesn't jump work if you just want to jump down?
Overall?  I give the game a Solid C.  it's an okay game in it's own right, but was never worth 60 bucks to anybody with half a brain.

The Sexy Brutale is a puzzle game focusing on observing folks in order to get information and working out how to save your fellow guests at the mansion. Admittedly, I found the puzzles a little too simple: in earlier cases I accidentally solved the puzzle just messing around with things, thinking there'd be more to it than that. Instead, the challenge comes from gathering the information you need and sidestepping everybody (as you're not allowed to be in the same room).
Also, it's short: You'll have the game finished in an afternoon, maybe two if you go hunting for all the collectables.
With that said, the attention to detail is absolutely incredible. Almost every room in the mansion is unique and characters are wonderfully animated. The audio too is absolutely brilliant. Each area of the mansion has its own tune, and the way the chipper or serene songs build tension as the clock ticks closer to a guest's impending doom is amazing. When it came to presentation, The Sexy Brutale spared no quarter.
Despite how short it is, the puzzles and story are interesting, the characters are entertaining and the nuances in the audio bring the world to life. It's the little things that come together to make it a solid gem that shows plenty of polish.

Rarely, if ever, have I been so certain that I would enjoy a game as quickly as I was with MacGuffin. Inside of two minutes I had already purchased a copy for a friend, and we were both laughing our donkeys off!
The concept of MacGuffin is that you must break into a crumbling Japanese nuclear plant and find an item known as a “MacGuffin”. (Many of you are already in on the joke, right?) The puzzles are silly easy, and not intended to interfere with progress. Clearly, MacGuffin is a satire of the satirical “The Stanley Parable”, but infinitely funnier (which is in no way a criticism of TSP.) If you liked “Stanley” for the humor, you’ll LOVE MacGuffin for the same reason. (BUT, if you are unable to laugh at yourself, you may find it hard to laugh at MacGuffin as much as others might.)
Pop culture references have perhaps never been as ever present as in MacGuffin, from Nixon and what I believe is the song Funkytown, to the dead-solid best uses of the international NO symbol ever created. This game is simply hilarious, and worth more than the pittance being charged. Much of the humor is hidden or subtly sophisticated(?), and is well worth your time to find.
I only have two issues. One is that there is no SAVE feature, and there are SO MANY hilarious screenshots to be posted that I found myself starting over repeatedly (which is maybe the BEST problem ever!) The other is that the gameplay locks at various points (but not menu access. This would lead me to believe that is was intentional, except that the locking has occurred in three places, one quite early.) But since the game is actually the journey rather than the destination, the locking takes away rather little from the experience.
And while MacGuffin is a short game (how short can’t be determined until more info about the locking is shared by the DEVs), but for this rock-bottom price and its high degree of replayability, it’s well worth your time and money.

Gigantic is a MOBA/shooter, cell-shaded game packed with strategy and action. While it may be easy to miss the more subtle nuances of strategy (what abilities to take to combat the other team, what creatures to summon where, or when to go for or hold off on a creature kill), the game itself plays smoothly when it comes to character control.
There are downsides, and I'll cover them right away. There are some complaints about being capped at 60 fps, and some about the 6 gb RAM requirement for the game. While I don't have a problem with either of these, I do have a problem with the requirement of the 3rd party launcher, Arc. All-in-all it's small and out of the way, and not nearly as bad as UPlay, but it shouldn't be necessary. Sadly, it doesn't seem like it will be going away.
What are the real positives? The game DOES run smoothly, though it is clear more optimization will come down the line. There are new MOBA elements, such as stamina, that make the genre feel more fresh. Combat is fluid and fun, and experimenting with different builds can be rewarding.
Perhaps the game's biggest asset comes in the form of communication from the developers. Check out the Gigantic subreddit. There's constant developer posts. Most avid gamers have seen some sort of exploitation from developers in regards to their founders, but not from Motiga. Supporters of the game had their products upgraded upon Steam Release, and got bonuses beyond the expected.
tl;dr:
Cons:
-60 fps cap (make sure this is actually an issue for you before you shun the game)
- requirement of a third-party launcher, albeit lightweight and unobtrusive.
-6 gb RAM requirement
Pros:
-Action-based, responsive MOBA with Third-person shooter elements
-Diverse playstyles and creative characters
-Responsive and communicative Dev group committed to honoring their backers
-Positive and supportive community
-Creative art-style, if that's your thing
-Different than a simple "lane push" or "cart push" playstyle.
-Subtle forms of strategy that separate players on a tactical level
Overall, I would recommend this game, despite its flaws. For just-released title, it's some of the most fun I've had in the genre for quite some time.

As for the game itself. It is pretty slowpaced but steadily gains velocity as you progress. You start off with 1 of 6 regions and you have a restriction of how many buildings you can mantain within this region. This restriction gradually decreases the more regions you liberate and castles you upgrade within each region. Effectively increasing your playtime each session. I do not want to venture any further into the building system and the little tricks therein, because a little trial and error doesnt hurt.
is rather short and gives you the basics of the basics but not all the vital information you desperately need. In my opinion this is a bad choice of tutorial, instead of having tutorial pieces pop up when you need them, say changing seasons, new buildings, new units, new regions, small events etc. they leave you out to fend for yourself and figure it out on your own.
Along with the tutorial
also lack information as well as numbers.
Tooltips need a desperate overhaul and the tutorial needs to be more than just an introduction to the basics of basics. To counter a lack of information a compedium of such would have been a nice way to make wating somehow enjoyable.
is a squad based rock-paper-scissors system (if that makes any sense). Every unit consists of multiple soldiers and counter or is countered by another unit. Lance > Rider > Shield > Archer > Lance > and so on. Additionaly armor is a factor Mace > leather + chain , Axe > Plate.
If that wasn't enough, in the beginning the two facing units charge each other to engage in close combat depending on your timing, you do heavy charge damage before the brawl begins or none at all (pre-emptive strike).
Every unit can get one of two abilites purchased through experience acquired through battle. Making your units more diverse and useful in certain situation. For example switching your shield units with a your mounted units which are engaged with lance units (rock-paper-scissors, remember?) to avoid certain death for your horsemen.
To top it all of you can have in your 9-squad army up to 3 and at least 1 siege unit. Ranging from ballistaes, trebuchets or mangonels. Ballistaes hit only enemy units for moderate damage, instantly killing weak armored targets. Trebuchets hit all units for a good amount of damage. Mangonels leave the area they hit burning and damaging any and all units that remain in this area. Every siege unit act as an ability with their own innate cooldown before you can use them again. But if you have 3 siege units and 6 fighting units and on the other hand your oppenent has 9 fighting units which disperse your 6 quite fast you have lost even with the siege units still intact und unscathed. (I don't think you can actually damage / destroy siege units)
Quite the arsenal and not as simple a battlesystem I dare say.
After every battle your units need time to recuperate depending on how wounded they are 10 to 20 min. or if unscathed not at all. However you cannot engage in another battle while a unit in your army is still recuperating. Yes, you can skip waiting with a little bit of moneyflow but if you are eager to fight battle after battle it can become very expensive and you should play another Total War game.
The experience your units gain can be used to either upgrade the unit itself thus adding more soldiers to this unit, upgrade melee damage, range damage, armor rating or charge damage. Or as already mentioned purchase one of two abilites for this unit which may turn the tide of battle.
TL;DR: It's a F2P inbetween-games-(tablet)game with no content locked behind a paywall (no paying user exclusives). Paying players cannot exceed the limits of a non-paying player. Slowpaced at the start with steadily increasing session lengths. Lack of information may result in uneffecient use of terrain, buildings or units. Not a game for the impatient.

Mini Metro's distinct levels--all inspired by real-world metro lines--definitely have deep nuances that affect your tactics for each and reward your experimentation and practice.
It's a lot like Flight Control, except more complex.
I love the meditative, minimalist aesthetic, especially with Night Mode enabled. FEZ composer Disasterpeace has crafted a lush, warm, subdued soundscape full of soft sines and small clocks that grows, shrinks, or shifts dynamically in response to your actions based on conditions in the game. Though even at full volume on my laptop, it wasn't loud enough for me.
At their core, simulation and management games are about optimizing a particular workflow or mastering a certain system as best as you can. Mini Metro falls into that category, even loosely--just on a smaller, less permanent scale. I admit, a larger and lasting scale of some kind would be even more interesting here, but it shares these traits of "starting all over" with both score-chaser Arcade games and procedurally-generated Roguelike games.
Yet even with all its depth and variations, the gameplay itself is eventually too simple to be this repetitive, and too repetitive to be this simple. I guess that makes it more suited to being used as a palette cleanser between games or between life, once you've played past using it as a game. Hence the inclusion of a Daily Challenge.
Overall, there is far more praiseworthy about this game than not, and too few games accomplish similar concepts this beautifully. I hope to improve at it regularly and look forward to whatever features and content future patches will bring along!

The premise of this game had me intrigued as I am curious about how metro systems around the world are designed. I though that I was getting a sim-style game that would let me lay out a metro system in meticulous detail, but this isn't the game that I was looking for. I do enjoy the game, but it is a real-time puzzle game, and not a sim.
There are many cities that you can play in, and each starts with three stations of different shapes - a Circle, Square, and Triangle. A station's shape determines the destination of/number of passengers that will spawn there. For example, Circles will spawn the most riders, but few passengers from other stations will want to go there. A station spawns riders in the shape of the station that they wish to go to, and each passenger boards trains that can take them to one of their destination type, and not a specific station. Your score is the number of total passengers delivered to their destination.
Stations spawn periodically and connecting lines to them so that passengers will get picked up in a timely manner before the stations get overcrowded is the goal of the game. In addition to the three main shapes, several unique shapes can spawn as well, which ups the difficulty quite a bit. Passengers choose trains intelligently, so not always by the shortest route, but the one that will likely take the least amount of time.
Each "week" you get a new train and another random reward that could be a carriage (more passengers for a train), tunnels (the number varies), a new line (there is a maximum number of lines on each map, and you always start with three), or an interchange (increases the number of passengers a stop can handle before overcrowding).
You get visual and audible warnings when a station start to get overcrowded, and if the problem isn't resolved in about 45 seconds, the game ends. So planning ahead is vital, but you can't always do that due to the random nature of the station spawns. Sometimes you'll have a nice mix of stations along each line, and can get quite an impressive score. Other times you'll have eight Circle stations isolated from everything else and only one or two lines to service them, which is usually not enough.
Games last anywhere from a few minutes to 30, and scores range from 200 to 2000+, depending on the map and the luck of the spawns. I recommend the game, but it can be frustrating when you have a good game going and three or four Circle stations spawn in inconvenient spots and ruin it. Still, it's great for when you have 10-20 minutes and not too taxing on the brain.

One of the games I return to quite often. A simple to play, complex to master dungeon crawler with so much vairation. The most important thing is that the player can custom-create the character's class, which is one of the most important things in creating variance between play-throughs.

The short version: It's fun.  Build character, collect loot, be a god on one floor and die to a piece of vegetable on the next.
The long version:
This game is a turn-based, dungeon crawling, rogue-like-power-fantasy.
That last bit may sound contradictory but in the same game I slaughtered an entire room of 50 something+ monsters without batting an eye and ran like a baby carrot panda from a stupid corn thing.
The character building is fantastic as the player can choose a handful of skill trees which creates a lot of different character builds. Progressing down different trees in different order can create a new experience for the playthrough.
The rogue-like aspects are tweakable so the player can choose how difficult or easy a playthrough will be. They can even turn off perma-death and load a save when a character dies. Along with the built in options, this game is moddable with Steam Workshop support for easy browsing/installation.
Combat is turn-based and depending on how you setup your character it can range from flinging fireballs and running away until things are recharged to teleporting into the thick of things and slowly laying the smack down on every living thing in the area.
Crafting is a little clunky. It has a lot of depth and that can be a blessing and a curse. The player has a limited inventory space but the amount of crafting materials is a little overwhelming at first. In general, there is a crafting material for each craft (smithing, tinkering, etc) and for each crafting material there are multiple levels (copper, silver, brass, etc). Inventory can become cluttered unless the player is not a hoarder (what's wrong with you?) and they know exactly what they want to make and how much of a certain material is required.
On the other hand, the depth allows for a lot of customization and there are even recipes to be found on bookshelves to create even more things.
The humor and flavor text in the game is a bit of hit or miss. While it can be funny, at times it gets in the way of figuring out what exactly a skill does. This can also be half the fun for some.
As for the story, something something evil something something you are the one panda to save them all. Yeah, game's about loot and poking things till they're puddles of goo.
It's a great game for people who like to experiment with builds and go dungeon crawling/loot collecting through randomized levels. If you don't like the rogue-like element, you can turn it into a rogue-lite. Mods extend the fun.
