The steam hubs and/or google will provide a player with everything they need to get Manhunt up and running.
The widescreen resolutions stretch the game screen, distorting a 4:3 image into a 16:9 image. This is my only complaint.
The game plays well and with solidness.
Hand-to-hand combat is tough and relies on quick reflexes as well as knowledge of how to fight. The game's primary point is in stealth, and it works.
Cash (the main character) can use "Stealth mode" to quiet his footsteps and stalk the enemy with convincing animations. He can also hide in dark places, rendering him invisible to his foes.
The executions are gory and satisfying, which follows as sometimes the set-ups for these moves are the trickiest part. Cash can also hit the walls with his fists or weapons to draw enemies away from their posts and cause them to become more vulnerate.
The storytelling is effective, and the voicework is good. Buy this game if you've got an urge to kill that just isn't satisfied by the typical fare.

The original Thief series is my favorite game franchise ever, and as a longtime fan of the classic series, I was originally concerned and saddened by the departures from the original games - No more mention of the Keepers, the Hammers or the Pagans..  The narrative style and art in the cinematics is gone, Garret has a new voice actor (He's still very good, and sounds similar... but to those of us longtime fans there is only one "real" Garret)  And...  they hardly use "Taffer"   That said....  Holy crap does the city look good!!  It was always central to the games, with it's specific feel, and more than ever it seems like a living, breathing organism and full of secrets and intrigue.  I have found myself delving around every corner and alley, and trying every door and window just to see what I can discover.  I love this town!  It's atmosphere is slightly more modern than before but it feels very much like the proper home of Garret, and is rife with immersive character in it's own right..  My one quibble here would be that it sort of reminds me of Dunwall from Dishonored with the updated feel and the ever present threat of plague...  But, it's still it's own town and feels very right for Thief.    This is a successful reboot - even with no Hammers chasing you around and no Keepers trying to vainly counsel you out of trouble, this is legitimately Thief to me.   I'm not taffin you here, its real as a bear pit fight.

So I was reading reviews and people (in 2015) were claiming there were game breaking bugs and they couldn't finish individual levels. I have played every level twice and am at about 90% completion so I don't quite see what was unfinishable about the first level.
I feel this game is part of the Golden Era in the LEGO games alongside Star Wars Complete Saga and Batman 1. After Star Wars I where they've refined everything and figured out what works, but before they started expanding with overworlds that are part of the story or the horror of voice acting. The charm comes from them telling the story you already know through slapstick mime. I know Batman was an original story but I won't go into that because this is about Indy not Batman.
Gameplay wise: It's incredibly simple.
If you can push things into a position, push them into place then proceed.
If you need a certain type of character to proceed, tag them then proceed.
If you don't have that character on you, then you either need to steal a hat or it's something intended for Free Play mode.
If you need a certain item to proceed, obtain it and then proceed.
If you cannot find the item you need, you are either trying to go into an area intended for Free Play mode, or you haven't smashed enough things that the item may be hiding behind/inside.
I know it's simple, but it's fun. Except the Bridge Battle on Temple of Doom. That is the only problem I have with this game.
I will admit there were two bugs I encountered - but both were easily overcome. One was the intended solution for posting one of the parcels doesn't seem possible. But there's another solution that really wasn't hard to think up myself, and given it's a puzzle game I don't mind them forcing people to actually think about their solution, deliberately or not.
The other is on one level, it mistakes having thrown a sword at a green piece where you're meant to attach something for the actual something, and so it won't let you attach it but it also won't respond as though you have attached it. So just be careful when throwing swords in Last Crusade.

You'd expect more from a LEGO game. The theme of the game makes it easy to overlook the flaws. Everyone loves Indiana Jones, right?

From the perspective of someone who both studies in this field and experiences depression, quite honestly this feels like it was written by someone with minimal understanding of depression and how it works. yes it has some basic symptoms down, but it also seems to perpetuate the notion that those with depression are not in much control of their action. Beyond the beginning where it states to call a suicide hotline if you are feeling suicidal, this does nothing to encourage seeking out proper help--it continues to push the notion that trying to get help is pointless and will never really work. It appears to hold tightly onto the belief that opening does not help and will result in some form of resentment from others or some kind or patronization (though this is far from true).
All this game does is further stereotypes and push further on the negative feelings one experiences. It pushes the idea that getting help isnt worth it or is pointless.
This pushes the concept of helplessness.
Some of the senarios also seem to be more closely related to social anxiety as opposed to depression. All in all this just looks like one persons experience with depression. It holds a claim that it hopes to make others with depression feel as though they are not alone, however, given how little variability there is, it leaves out many people who suffer from depression; people who may see this and feel they either overreact too much, or people who may feel their diagnosis is invalid because they do not percieve themselves as having it as bad.
This "game", if it can even be called that, is not helpful. It shows one example of how bad it can get, but it is not accurate, nor does it give any notion of encouraging getting help. It does not show how help and understanding can make things better. This game will not help those with depression. It will not help those who dont have it understand it. It was not well written.
As someone who has experiences with depression and studies in this area, not only would i reccomend people NOT play this, I would also wholeheartedly recommend it be taken off of steam. This "game" is dangerous. it pushes stereotypes, negative thoughts, and all in all does nothing to really encourage help seeking.
I would rate it 0/10. Do not "play" this "game". It helps no one. It educates no one. And it pushes too many negative stereotypes and ignores too many situations and possibilities. Putting a disclaimer to call the suicide hotline at the very beginning does not take away all of the harm that this "game"/"simulation" can do.

Drilling for oil is an interesting process, filled with high stakes risk-reward decisions in a competitive environment with never enough information when commiting your resources.  There's a lot of room for awesome gameplay in this space.  Turmoil... doesn't really deliver on it though.

Geologists study local surface rock formations to decide where to survey, and then analyse those surveys to determine likely spots to drill  Skill at both steps determines the value

Pick a spot on the board at random, or near previous finds.  Hire a unit that tells you there's a deposit below a specific spot.  Infallibly, although the amount of oil is completely random.

Even M.U.L.E. had assaying.  Geographic information is a closely guarded corporate secret, with scanning technology and the ability to put various public and proprietary data together into a useful whole to determine a good drill spot provide game play, upgrade paths, and player differentiation.

High stakes negotiations with landholders to determine lease costs.  This includes clauses such as minimum production targets, as well as land use restrictions  (can't drill near the farmhouse)

Buy land for a set rate, or 'outbid' another player by paying the current rate + X$  (remember, you're doing this largely blind.

Players are currently bidding on the next property based on identical costs and perfect information.  There's no risk/reward, no 'I know something you don't' about bidding, and no 'my tech means I can get oil out of this property better than you'  Even delaying the announcement of total oil on other players land by a turn (and/or limiting that information to what they actually got) would create a more interesting bidding space.  Is that low number a sign that the other player is bad, or that there wasn't anything to find?  Did they get lucky and find all the oil early and close to the surface, or is it a good spot to drill?

Complicated process involving drilling long distances while monitoring a variety of readouts to determine the status of a drillbit 1000s of feet under the surface, including where exactly underground you are and what you're drilling through.

Click to drill your pipe to a specific location, including twists and turns

This one isn't so bad, although exploratory drilling could be more interesting/informative

Lots of stuff comes out of the ground.  It needs to be managed, processed and routed correctly.  Wells are either pumped or naturally flowing based on positive pressure.  Should the well be produced (oil extracted) or shut in to build up pressure (for greater flow later).  Water or gas can be injected to increase pressure.  Pumped wells often burn oil or gas coming from the well to power themselves.  Lease requirements mean a certain amount of production must be maintained.

Wells flow until empty, but make sure the oil is being hauled away or else it'll blow!

Risk/Reward for maximizing a well's production, the value of production now vs. over time.

This one may be anachronistic, but in addition to price differentials, different purchasers have different quantities they'll accept on a given day.

Time management game determining which to sell to vs. cost of storage.

I really like the cost of storage vs. sales now, except so far as it is a timed map and you've got to sell everything at the end.  That seems just silly.  Making sure the wagons go to the higher price, though, is time management in the worst way.  Anachronistic, but the cost of a pipeline (faster, cheaper movement of oil) vs trucking (or wagons) is another good decision point.

All wells continue to produce as long as it is viable to operate them.  This involves balancing ongoing costs with the perception of a wells future profitability.  Lease requirements play into this, and there is a significant cost involved in shutting a well down.

You have a few months to a year to drill for oil in a spot.  Regardless of your rigs, your lease is up at the end of the year, and you lose anything that's left unsold.  Risk/reward is entirely based around 'will I have time to make this back if I spend it now'

This is the weakest part of the game (imho).  It turns the game into a rush rush rush time management sim rather than allowing the player to focus on serious risk/reward decisions, like if I drill here, how much oil will I get, and will that be enough to pay for the drilling.  Is it worth drilling another well to maintain the lease, even if the well isn't likely to produce much?
Basically, this is a time management game.  The risk reward decisions are all there, but they are forced by artificial and silly time limits rather than likely profits.  In addition, several opportunities to allow players to develop unique strategies (find the best oil fields,  produce the oil efficiently, manage land efficiently, etc) are missed.
I'd like to see this game improve, but as long as it's leaning so heavily on time managment tropes, I'm going to stay away.

Though you WILL need a patch to get this working properly, the pc version is the best version. I don’t really care about graphics, though the original ps2 version is really muddy and grainy and low res, whereas the pc version is cleaner since it can be ran in your native resolution so it’s much cleaner especially when you turn of that grainy camera filter, and they also upgraded the textures. However the aspect that really propels the pc version is the control scheme, since you can change it to however you want. Whereas on the ps2 the controls are very stiff and clunky with awkward button mapping; most games its left analogue stick to move, right to rotate camera, whereas in manhunt its left to move forward, back, and turn left and right, right stick to go to first person mode, and l2 and r2 to  strafe left and right. Also when using guns with ps2 version you have to lock on and you can only go for headshots when close enough whereas with the pc it’s free aim.
The story is that you play as a death row inmate called James earl cash, who was meant to be executed but it turns out it was only a sedative and a man only heard through an ear piece called “The director” has gotten the city overrun by gangs of criminals and forces you to participate in a snuff film.
Manhunt is a third person stealth game where most of the time you go from point A to B or have to complete a certain objective. The stealth mechanics are that you hide in shadows to avoid being seen which you will know when it’s dark enough by a contact sensitive icon of Cash will turn blue. The only time an enemy will know where you are hiding is if they see you going into a shadow or if they bump into you. Sound is also another huge part of the stealth: if you run, bump into something, slam doors open, or fire a gun, that will create some noise and the amount of noise is determined by how large the red circle is on the radar. One way to lure enemies out of their spots is to use a lure object being either a brick, a glass bottle or a decapitated head, or by hitting a wall. When an enemy hears you they will start searching for you, if you wait long enough they will give up and go back to their spots or patrolling as normal, if they see you they will attempt to kill you. There are two types of combat in this game: melee, and fire fights, for melee combat you have quicker attacks and heavier and you can block though the melee combat is tricky and difficult since you aren’t a close combat power house and the enemies will call the rest and group up on you and you will most likely be beaten to death, so melee combat is best to be avoided and its only worth doing it if you have a good enough melee weapon and it’s a loan enemy and you have no other choice. Gunplay in this game is half cover based and the other half is using tactics such as the old round the corner murder cue trick, you get a fairly small range of weapons in this game being, pistols (revolvers, locks, and desert eagles) submachineguns (an Uzi) assault rifles (an m16) shotguns (sawn off and a spas 12) and a sniper rifle. Most of the time you will be aiming for headshots though body shots are good if you have a shotgun or a machinegun. Even though you have combat the main focus is using stealth by sneaking up on enemies and murdering them with any kind of sports equipment, kitchen appliance, garden tool and sometimes objects such as plastic bags, glass shards, and barbed wire. There are three levels of brutality with the stealth kills which you increase by holding the attack button down when behind an enemy. The three levels are: white, yellow, and red. White is meant to be quick and clean, yellow is meant to be more violent, and red is meant to be the most violent you can do. The violence in this game is quite realistic, they have realistic sounds for beating, stabbing, slashing, blood spurting, skull cracking, and the choking and cries of pain from the enemies. It isn’t that bad or uncomfortable to watch (Manhunt 2 is way worse) but that’s coming from someone with a lot of experience with video game violence, I’ve played the worst of the worst.

This is also a very difficult game and the difficulty increases with each new gang and set of enemies you will come across in the next few chapters; the AI becomes smarter, they search for you longer, they start getting better at working in groups, they get better at melee combat, they are more accurate shots in gunfights they will have quicker reactions in gunfights and they are better equipped.
This is also a horror game, it uses horror in a somewhat unique way since this game is highly grounded in reality (there are no super natural elements) the environments are unsettling in terms of how close to real life they are in terms of how rough it is, they are fairly creepy, there are a lot of disturbing sights such as ripped and torn body parts, hanging bodies, body parts used as decoration, and just gore lying around. This game also has an extremely dark, grisly, and gritty atmosphere which is aided massively by the music. I just love the atmosphere in this game, the only game which I can think of that has a similarly dark, gritty and grisly atmosphere is condemned criminal origins. And the last mission which I won’t spoil.
There aren’t really any outright problems with this game, one chapter near the beginning can get a bit boring due to the fact that you usually only have one melee weapon and you’ll see the same kill animations over and over and that the environment in that section is the most dullest in the game (it’s a junk yard).  This is also a very unappealing game and the violence, tone, and subject matter can be a huge off putter depending on what kind of person you are, and you might end up in an argument arguing whether this game is completely sick and should be banned worldwide!!
The one thing this game will be most remembered for is the controversy: this game created tons of controversy because people thought it was so violent and gory and the fact that you use everyday objects and in this country (the UK) the game was blamed for inspiring a murder, this case remained controversial for years after even though the Police at the investigation clearly stated that it was a drug related robbery and not the game and it was the victim who owned the game. Now the only thing that is gory in this game are decapitations and cranial explosions. Many people around the world think this is the most violent game ever made, it's far from that, even for the time this is nothing when it comes to how violent a game could be, this came out in 2003, the same year postal 2 came out which is quite possibly the most violent game to date and the previous year soldier of fortune 2 came out which is quite possibly the most realistically violent and one of the goriest games to date.
This is a great game in my opinion and you should try it if you’re not the kind of person who protests “BAN THIS SICK FILTH!!!”

This is the quintiessential modern rogue game.  You have all the essentials:  procedural levels, turn-based combat, deep customization, perma-death, punishing but fair gameplay.  What really sets this apart for me from a lot of faithful rogue games is that unlike most rogue games that have tiny tiny sprites or ASCII graphics, Dredmor has big, beautiful sprites.  I cut my rogue teeth on Azure Dreams so I just got used to the idea of having a normal sized character on screen.  When I started getting into rogue games on PC, I was really disappointed to find so many had teeny tiny little sprites for graphics.  It made me feel more like I was looking down on an overhead map, it made it hard for me to get immersed in the game.  Dredmor solves that problem, has a normal sized character and enemies but in my opinion sacrifices nothing.  The UI is a little weird but not bad and you get used to it quickly.  My one complaint is that after dozens of runs, you do start to get tired of seeing the same enemies, but the expansions are cheap and great and I highly recommend buying all of them right off the bat.  It also adds more classes to the game, making the character customization possiblities go from large to astronomical.  Permadeath is optional but as far as I'm concerned, the only way to play.  The risk of death keeps you always on your toes.
TL;DL:  If you like Rogue, Azure Dreams, any Mystery Dungeon game, buy this, you will love it.

This is a largely beautiful and stylish game to look at, with one of the best soundtracks I've heard in a game. Gameplay-wise, it plays a bit like Ghost Trick, but solving each puzzle is less about trial and error (and is far less complicated), and instead focuses on exploring your environment, learning everyone's movements and actions, and figuring out what you need to do.

I know some people may not be enamored with some of the story beats, but I really enjoyed the story myself. It runs a bit on the short side, animations are sometimes a little janky (but only for a few frames) and if your vision is bad you may  have a hard time seeing some items - the circles around interactables are definitely your friends. If Clue and Majora's Mask had a child, it would be The Sexy Brutale.
You're Lafcadio, a guest in a lavish mansion where all guests are killed in one way or another via the hosts and servants. You quickly find yourself a pocketwatch that can rewind time and reset the day. If you've played Majora's Mask you know the drill, though, think of The Sexy Brutal as single day that goes by very quickly and you're in a dungeonous version of Clocktown though a bit bigger. There's 7 "missions," where you have to save a guest (or pair) but figuring out how to can be time consuming so there's a decent chunk  of content.
The Clue aspect is basically the film, but in reverse. First you have to find the person you need to save and how they're going to die and by whom, finding that out is the easy part. There's a minor stealth aspect in that you can't be in the same room as anyone else, everything goes dark an their mask will chase you down and out of the room. With that said, you can peer through keyholes and listen in on conversations to figure out where people have been and or what they're doing. You have to piece together all this information, in reverse, to find the key points where you mess with a plan or item that changes the course of time.
Once you save a guest you'll get a new power that will open up more of the mansion and the day will reset, all of the guests you save are still living out the same day, actually all guests are living the same day over and over and you can hear them all happening as well throughout the day. So for instance the first guest you save, the tutorial guest, is killed via a gunshot and at the same time everyday you'll hear that gunshot and you know he's died, yet again. Your task into the save them again, but to press forward.
At 5 hours I'm pretty much at the end of the game, I'm on last pair of guests I need to save before the final, single guest, so I can say I'm close to the end. It seems like the game can be done in under 8 hours easily which might seem short, but there's optional collectibles and the game has a great charm to it that makes it short and sweet so it adds a lot to the replayability for me.
So maybe, just like the game itself, I'll play it again... and again... and again... because it's really fun. Highly recommended.

This game touches a subject that most games don't: the lives of civilians during war. And I have to say, it does the work brilliantly. You'll feel the bleakness of the atmosphere and the despair of your survivors. And more often than not you're forced to take meaningful moral choices: when you really need supplies, do you try to sneak around a warehouse full of patrolling bandits and risk getting shot, or do you barge in a small house owned by an elderly couple and rob them blind? Whatever you choose, the game won't blatantly tell you if you're right or wrong, but your characters (and you) will remember your actions.
One of the best parts about this game is the survivors. Each of them has their own story and personality, so they feel like real, believable people instead of machines. You'll
them to survive, and you'll feel terrible if one of them dies for whatever reasons. In addition, the endings for your survivors are cleverly built in as well. Even when you've survived the war, you may find that you just haven't won at all, as your people fail to find their families and friends, live an unhappy life, or even commit suicide out of guilt. The moment when each of your characters earns their happy ending is the most heartwarming moment ever.
Even when I've completely mastered this game, I still found myself coming back to it over and over again. I'm not exaggerating; this is a game that everyone should play at least once.

Panzer Corps is a turn-based strategy or ‘wargame’. Each scenario you are tasked with deploying your troops and taking a set number of objectives across the map. Units earn experience and can be upgraded during the deployment phase with any new equipment unlocked. This is done using prestige points that you acquire by completing objectives and are also used to reinforce units during battle when they lose strength. Prestige points are persistent throughout the campaign meaning spending all of your points in one battle may not be wise as you are effectively depleting your resources for the next engagement; although you do receive some at the beginning of each scenario, what you have carries over.
The graphics of Panzer Corps are fairly basic although nice to look at with each type of unit distinguishable from each other. Sounds can also said to be somewhat basic as each unit type has a single sound that is played during movement and attack. This may sound repetitive however after 18 hours of playing Panzer Corps I can say this has yet to bother me. The interface is effective at doing the job and gives you access to all of the information you need without being intrusive.
Panzer Corps strikes a great balance between depth and accessibility and offers a great entry point into wargames for the uninitiated. The gameplay is addictive and the visuals and audio serve the game well, while the multiplayer uses a play-by-email method so multiple games can be played at once over the course of a few or more days.
Panzer Corps has quickly become one of my favourite games and I would happily recommend it to anyone.

Wasting already over 30 hours, alone on the main campaign, i feel the need to write a recommendation for this really impressive strategy game.
If you´re in this kind of strategy and maybe played games like Panzer General and the many others in the "General" series (i for one also would still like a modern version of Fantasy General) from good old SSI, you already know, what to expect.
A deep and challenging campaign throughout the WW II time, with many varied unit types from each time of the war. The way you take is partly based on your success in the battles, if you manage to overtake the enemy fast enough, you can also change the course of history and get interesting hypothetical scenarios like invasion of GB or USA.
Beside the well thought out maps and unit strengths/weaknesses your motivation is also to keep your core units alive, which stay with you and get experience/heroes/medals with your victories.
To lose your trusty reconnaissance unit after five years, truly hurts.
Surely it could use some comfort functions and the steam integration is still a bit lacking, but without question Panzer Corps is a must have for fans of this type of game.

Disclaimer: This is a highly subjective review, it covers a topic many will find very emotional, including me.
This "game" is surprisingly good.
It's a text based, slice of life, rpg where you play a not very relatable character.
But as I said in the beginning it is suprisingly good. It's well written and the situations the player's character finds himself are relatable, even if the character's reaction often are not. If you do not struggle with depression yourself this game will not be of much value to you. But for me the game was able to stirr some emotions. That's a feat in and off itself. I made me go from "this guy is whiney b***h" over laughter at situations involving a cat that might not have been that funny, but I laughed anyway, to legitimately making me cry.
As with all games of this genre it's meat and bones are the supporting cast of characters. And this game has some.
Alex, the main character's girlfriend stands out in particular. To me at least. She is a well written, loving girlfriend. Even though she comes of as being an idealised version of one, never the less she hit just the right emotional spot for me.
But that might have to do with me having gone through a rather bad break up a few months ago.
The older brother Malcolm is another great character. He is the kind of older brother I strive to be, again just the right emotional spot.
I don't use numerical rating systems, and I don't think this piece of work might even be able to fit one. So all I an say is: Feel free to try this game out for youself, it's freeware after all. I don't think you will get the same emotional reaction out of it but you might find something enjoyable in it.

(TLDR: It's not a game, it's an experience, and it's amazing. Go on and play.)
First and foremost, I would like to tell those considering downloading Depression Quest this: Depression Quest is not a game. Depression Quest is an experience, aiming to help people understand the trials and tribulations that come with depression. At this, it does an incredible job. In all the stories I've read, all the games I've played, and in all my experiences watching someone try to explain what depression is like, Depression Quest is one of the most realistic representations I've seen.
The music used sets a somber tone, that pulls you into the lethargic, dreary state that the protagonist is in for most of the "game" (depending on how you play.) This only furthers it's ability to connect you to the protagonist. In this, mixed with the simplistic, yet elaborate backstories of nearly all the charcters and the seemingly devastating amount of stress placed on each decision, the creators have made a beautiful piece of art.
Many people, as I have seen in the reviews and online forums, have spoken about it sometimes being "dramatic," or "over-done," but it's really not. Depression is different for everyone. What could seem dramatic in Depression Quest, would be paradise to someone suffering from extreme, heavy-set depression.
So in the end, I implore you to play this. It's an amazing experience, and you will not be disappointed afterward.
You might not by happy. You might even be sad, or upset. Certainly, though, you will not be dissapointed.

The Sexy Brutale is an intriguing, clever, and stylish story-driven puzzle game which makes excellent use of its time travel mechanics, and it's absolutely worth picking up and playing through. The biggest complaints I have are the sound design being somewhat subpar, a slightly dodgy translation, and the lack of any real, definable difficulty curve. These are all very easy to overlook in the face of both the imaginative nature of the scenarios on display, the game's slick presentation, and the quality of the plot, which uses a superb third-act reveal to tie everything up in a neat little bow and provide a very satisfying emotional payoff.

The Sexy Brutale feels somewhat like real-time Clue meets Groundhog Day. The longer I played the more evident their attention to detail was in crafting the connections in this game.
You'll restart the day whenever the clock reaches midnight. One by one you follow and scope out the villains, eventually solving (and preventing) each individual murder. I had a blast sneaking around, listening to conversations, and manipulating time.
The in-game map automatically records the whereabouts of anyone you've seen at a particular time, you can fast forward and rewind the map to figure out where you need to be and at what time.
If you avoid guides and read the lore, The Sexy Brutale will take around 10hrs to complete. I highly recommend this game, it's worth whatever price you find it at when viewing this page.
Special thanks to the friend that gifted this to me, I may have missed this gem otherwise.

There is much to be said about manhunt. If you do not already know, this game was surrounded by tons of controversy, this is the singular game your soccer mom does not want you to play. If you do not know the story behind the controversy, grab a drink and get comfortable, because this is a long and interesting story. When the game was first released, nobody really paid much attention to the game, critics gave it mixed reviews and the game almost fell into the category of overlooked. But of course this did not happen, on July 28th 2004 14 year old Stefan Pakeerah had been brutally murdered by his best friend Warren Leblanc. Now, when something like this happens, we as humans go through what I call a “moral panic”, meaning when we have been wronged in some way it is so much easier for us to find a boogie-man to pin all of our problems on, so that way we don’t have to take responsibility for these tragic actions. And in this case Leblanc’s parents had their own moral panic and rather take responsibility for not noticing their kids dwindling mental stability, they found their sons copy of Manhunt, a perfect boogie-man to go to court with. Fortunately the 50 million pound (or 81,156,500 dollar) lawsuit was dropped, however the controversy never went away and has since then followed Rockstar Studios to this day.
Now on to the game itself. The gameplay is very violent, and you will be murdering in systematic and unique ways. Honestly, in my opinion, it’s really not that bad. There are so many other violent and brutal games out there that make this game look like Super Smash Bros. in comparison. It is a stealth based game so you will learn to work on baiting your enemies into a trap where you will slowly pick them off 1 by 1, engaging head-on will get you absolutely nowhere. The AI can be a bit frustrating with their dead on aiming and their ninja reflexes, but bear in mind this is a very old game and the AI is very simplistic by our standards. Don’t let that be a turn off, the plotline mysterious and ominous.
Overall I would highly recommend this game to anybody who is looking for a fun and plot oriented action game. This game really did not deserve all the controversy it received and I think it’s a real jewel that has slowly faded out of the spotlight.
Yet another example of Rockstar's uncanny knack for delivering compelling gameplay and story to a game flooded with controversial mechanics the mainstream media will never look beyond.

Manhunt is a Educational E-Rated video game which is fun to play with the whole family and is recommended for all ages.

Known to be one of the most, if not arguably, "The" most controversial game of all time due to its extreme and realistic form of violence. Manhunt's game structure is based straight off a cat and mouse game where running is most of the time your only option to survive. And if the hunters don't murder you, you murder them. Oh and during the whole process you're being recorded and monitored for entertaiment by a deluded director who saves you from your own execution in prison.
The praised concept regarding this game is simple. Kill, run, or die. It's like the SAW movies only with all the traps being replaced with uneducated, disturbed, bad-mouthed criminals bribed to murder you in any way possible. And this game made   headlines due to how realistically players dispatched the enemies set to hunt them. The execution style killings you commit with each weapon, which by the way have 3 different stages each, are brutal and very detailed. Manhunt was one of those rare titles where its M rated content was not generated by violent interaction with monsters or creatures but purely between human characters.
If you're a fan of stealth, violent, suspenseful games, Manhunt is a must-play and one controversial gem you shouldn't miss.

Below you'll find a written and video impression on the game.
To break Turmoil down quickly, it's a business oil tycoon simulation, that distills sim mechanics to the basics.
In Turmoil, the game feature upgrade options to better your oil drilling business while competing with other tycoons for land and resources. The goal is to make as much money as possible, as you would expect from these kinds of games.
The mechanics are simple enough. You have a town phase, where each tycoon get an opportunity to upgrade and buy new equipment, get loans from banks, and even do some underhanded business dealings, bribing prominent members of the community. Once that's set, each tycoon will bid on their plot of land, each tycoon can out bid each other, if there's a valuable plot available, adding an extra layer of competitiveness. Once all the pre planning is complete, you'll head out and start digging for oil.
Digging for Oil is very simple. Just hire some dossers to find hidden plots of oil, then lay down some drills to start digging. Hire some horse and buggy to transport your oil to what ever company is paying the most. The strategy is a mix of hide and seek, as you look for more oil plots, and business management, as it requires a delicate balance of profit, time, and costs.
Turmoil's visuals are definitely bright and cheery, but it does have a distinct frontier look, with an audio to match. It's of a fairly simple design, with a minimalist art design. It might not be appreciated by all gamers, but I found it to be charming.
Turmoil is fairly addictive, and found there to be a decent amount of content to play through, but I did find it a bit repetitive. Each excursion plays almost exactly the same, with only your purchased upgrades making any difference. Once you find a groove, a set of actions you find most efficient, you'll be sticking to the same strategy through out the game.
Turmoil overall was a pretty fun romp. A great little simulation game to break away from other main staples of the genre. Though the game can get repetitive, it does offer a decent serving for the player.
Pros:
- A decent size game
- Simple and easy to learn
Cons:
- Repetitive

The base management is awfully silly, with only one real production chain.
The difficulty... What difficulty? I've reached the ceasfire on the first try with no idea what I was doing (no lets plays, spoilers, nothing). Played four different stories and I haven't lost... ever.
There's much annoyance in the game (e.g. in the winter you have to keep your heater full of wood, so you can't end the day early even if you have nothing else to do - the temperature will drop and people will get sick). The stories that intend to be more difficult (only one survivor, or two really bad ones) achieve this by being even more annoying.
You can't go for any kind of sustainability, cause everything is tied to components (or otherwise arbitrarily limited, like you can only have two traps) - which take a lot of carrying space when scavenging and are otherwise very limited when trading. I always have enough goods to buy more components, I always want more components, there's never enough components. It's not just for building, it's for everything. To grow food you need water. To prepare food you need water. How do you get water? With a filter made with components. And it serves no real purpose, since there's only one production chain (so you can't adapt by switching what you were doing) and there's nothing else to do (so you just sit on your♥♥♥♥♥and wait for more components). On the other hand, even with unlimited components, just feeding that one silly chain would be tedious and boring.
Speaking of arbitrary restrictions, you can't have more than one person scavenging. Apparently the city is not big enough (although I've had a bug once, where the game claimed two people brought supplies from scavenging).
Basically it's a glorified tamagotchi in a war setting. Built like a free to wait game, except your credit card won't alleviate the waiting. I was more attached to the tamagotchi than the characters here. First playthrough is like 6-8 hours and the second part of that already gets annoying and repetitive. The immersion is easily killed by bugs, that are quite common (although not gamebreaking - but you might lose one of your survivors to a bug, not get a very important loot item due to a but etc. It's not a huge problem considering the overall difficulty).
Apparently war is buggy, easy to survive and rather boring.
I'm not crying, there's something in my eye. If your at least half human this game will elicit some sort of emotional response.

Love this game, I am biased as I've been an alpha tester since 2014, but damn I'm so happy its finally launching. Plain and simple its a hero shooter/moba hybrid, as compared to Paragon it leans more towards hero shooter as there are no creep waves, but instead you can summon creatures to guard points/destroy your opponents to try to gain power, which allows you to get an opportunity to attack the enemy's guardian.
Every match is action packed and honestly very back and forth when two teams of similar skill duke it out. Due to the mechanic that your Guardian has 3 smaller health bars that have to be destroyed during seperate attacks, it prevents a team from instantly ending off one good "push" but also allows for a team from behind to pull some strong comebacks if they can outplay their opponents. Matches are also a fulfilling 10-20 minutes of very solid gameplay with essentially no downtime other than 5-15 second death timers.
Probably one of my favorite things about the game though is the lack of snowballing. A team can definitely gain some incremental advantages as they 'ace' the enemy team, but its far from the kind of feeding that occurs in traditional mobas. Your character is not going to be twice as strong as the enemy just because you took a lead in the early game. It will be slightly stronger as you will unlock some skill upgrades, but usually not enough added power to let you flat out overpower the game.

I did have to think quite a lot about whether I could recommend this game and while it’s not a bad game per se it certainly isn’t a good game at the moment ( I appreciate it’s still in beta and a lot could change) . In fact to be fair to this game as a free-2-play it’s not too bad and miles ahead of Stronghold: kingdoms in both art style and mechanics.
On the positive side I thought that the building and settlement creation were quite well done though they are a little basic. Kudos to the team for pretty excellent terrain height, excavation and water mechanic programing, it really helps to create this felling that the world itself can be shaped to suit your needs. The time required for building and resource gathering was pretty good, not obscenely long as in most free-2-plays (read as free-2-wait). On top of this you can even find and mine premium currency allowing any player no matter how stingy to gain some of the advantages. In fact if the game was purely the build section then I would actually recommend it.
There are however massive issues with the battle system. And by massive issues I mean JESUS CHRIST WHY DID YOU THINK THIS WAS A GOOD IDEA? Yeah that level of bad. I do have to admit that most of my issues with the combat are simply that it is difficult to accept calling this a total war game. I am a die-hard fan of the series (hell I even like empire) and like many total war fans I love the complexity of tactics one can to utilize to win. The battles of Battles: Kingdom seem to have stripped all this away to be replaced with clicking to charge at the right time….what?..... WHAT?.... HOW HAVE YOU TURNED YOUR COMBAT INTO QUICK TIME EVENTS? QTEs in total war now, along with day one dlc you’d be forgiven for thinking EA had bought CA. That said Sega aren’t much better look what they did to sonic. I have't played Shogun 2 Battles but i see that the combat in that is turn based, why didn't they keep that? sure its not total war but at least it's still tactical not ♥♥♥♥ING QTEs!!! But my issues with the battles don’t stop there. I have a few other problems with it as well like why is there a cool down for ordering archers to fire? One unit fires on one enemy unit and I have to wait a good few seconds before I can order an entirely separate unit of archers to fire on an entirely separate unit of archers. The orders system is a nice idea but I don’t think it is well realised. The unit special abilities and general abilities from Rome 2 would’ve been a better style of system and each ability has advantages and disadvantages meaning that they are a tactical choice. The orders on the others hand you just spam every time the cool down timer is over.
How did they mess this up so badly?

Caveat; This will be a very short review, mostly due to the fact that the game is only in alpha testing yet and many things are yet to be implemented and tweaked upon.
The developers of this game openly advertises that their main inspiration is the old Microprose/Simtex game Master of Magic
.
As a fan of said game, who has wasted countless hours playing it, both when it initially came out, and still today, I can safely say that Worlds of Magic hits many, if not all, of the sweet buttons Master of Magic did.
The inspiration is clear, especially in how cities are developed and how magic is handled.
In the case of the former, there are build trees for the cities. You need certain buildings to be able to build others down the same line. And if you wish to produce a certain unit, you'll have to first build the prerequisite buildings in one of your cities. For instance, to produce the Crossbowmen unit, you need to have both a sawmill and an armory in your city. The sawmill in turn requires a builders hall, and the armory requires a smithy. So you cannot immediately start to produce Crossbowmen in a newly settled city.
The magic is handled very similar to Master of Magic. You have a certain pool of power available. You invest that in three possible spheres;
1; To increase your spellcasting power, said power dictates how much mana you can channel each turn, and as such, how many/powerful spells you can cast. For overland spells, you can cast any spell, but if your power is lower than the total mana cost, it'll take more than a single turn to cast. For a combat spell, you need to have a spellcasting power at least equal to the mana cost to be able to cast a spell.
2; To research new spells. You start out knowing a set number of spells, dependent on how many and which spell spheres you've chosen to know from the beginning. To learn new spells, you need to be eligble (have the required spheres for said spell) and invest the power to research them.
3; To increase your mana reserves. Without mana, you cannot cast new spells, and you cannot maintain already cast spells including any summons.
Considering this is still just in alpha, I've already sunk more hours into playing it than I'd expected. It just keeps sucking me in. The "one more turn" vibe is strong here. The appeal to me, is clear. It FEELS like Master of Magic in a new skin, even if the underlying mechanics have changed (to an adaptation of the D20 rules set).
I can heartily recommend the game. I don't regret backing it when it was just a kickstarter project.

I don't recommend the purchase YET (mid Sep 2014).  I was very excited by the screenshots and other reviews; I love turn based strategy games; I've been an avid Civilization fan for years (up until they nerfed the franchise with Civ V).  The gameplay is kind of like a basic version of Civilization (city management) with turn based 4X battles and a healthy dose of RPG magic.  Although I think the game has promise, at $40, I was very disappointed; I would have returned it if I could have.  Lots of bugs; gameplay still clunky and not smooth.
My main criticisms are two fold:
(1) The in-game information is severly lacking, leading you to kind of guess at what you're doing, especially without a tutorial.  For example,
*In the world creation screen, you have to select spells, but they never tell you what the spell actually does, e.g., +1 damage, or +1 health.  You have to pick them based on a vague description (or prior knowledge).
*During gameplay, certain tiles offer "bonuses" like Civilzation, but you have no idea what they do or why you would need them.
*When in a tactical battle, you don't know how many action points are left for any given unit or the mana cost of certain unit spells.
*On the info screen for all your cities, data would be much easier to access if displayed in a big table: cities in rows and data types in columns, instead it's displayed in a cumbersome graphic.
*Before you build units, you don't know what their attack/defense powers are.  There's no in-game tech tree, so I don't know what researching one spell will lead to.
*Upkeep cost on spells is buried in info screen; it should be on the spell graphic somewhere easily accessible at a glance.
*The city view screen is a nice view of the town, but doesn't give me any useful in game info: I'd rather it take up less screen real estate and make it easier to access what my city can build.  I don't need a "producing" and "queue" tab in city screen: collapse them and offer the number of turns till finished on same screen.
(2) The actions and/or information you're typically going after are buried beneath too many button clicks or hard to manage sliders.
*You can convert gold into mana on the Alchemy tab, but it needs a + and - button to increment by units and not just drag back and forth, or be able to type a number.
*You are able to convert "power" generated by temples/shrines into mana/research, but shifting between mama/spellcraft/research is SO annoying: trying to put extra power in specific spots isn't easy.
*This game NEEDS keyboard commands.
*When in the city build screen, I have to click on a button to see that buildings I can build in a pop up screen, and yet antoher to see what units I could build.
Finally, there are some elements of the game they haven't quite thought through: For example, in character creation, you can chose a "bad trait," such as a gold storage cap, that will give you more 2 skill points; however, you can also chose the "alchemist" trait which allows you to freely convert mana into gold and vice versa at a cost of only one skill point.  Since you can convert for free, you might as well "store" your gold as mana and get the free skill point in the beginning.  Of course, if you can freely convert between the two "currencies," why have two of them?  It's just annoying.

Lego Indiana Jones: Original Adventures is sort of a sequel to Lego Star Wars, this time taking three original Indiana Jones movies and turning them once again into casual 3D Platformer in world where everything is made from Lego. It came out in 2008. It also had another Indiana Jones game in 2009, which takes all 4 movies as a basis. But from what I heard, it changed levels layouts and such, so Original Adventures is still worth getting.
EDIT: Finally played Lego Indiana Jones 2. It's completely different. Like taking same basic idea of the first three movies plot, then changing it up and building up a "in a nutshell" levels from scratch. So yes, Original Adventures is still worth it.
From technical side, it has a very nasty bug: you can't jump off the stuff that you built. It gets fixed easily, just turn on VSync. Yea, strange. But works. Lack of knowledge how to fix it is the reason why this game has mixed reviews right now, by the way.
I also have trouble in Fullscreen mode in my Windows 8.1 where I have to alt-tab once for game to start to actually load after launching it. Otherwise you will be staring at the black screen forever.
I also would recommend getting controller in this case. Didn't try it with keyboard, but there are some bridges and such where you want to have something more precise than keyboard.
So, when it comes to Traveller's Tales LEGO games, I only played Lego Star Wars and Lego Indiana Jones. And I can tell you that: While Indiana doesn't change core gameplay much, still being casual platformign where you can't run out of lives and more focused on collecting studs, it has much better pacing and game design to it. In second half of Lego Star Wars I wanted it to end already, while with Lego Indiana Jones I enjoyed the whole ride. It helps that Indiana Jones is shorter, so it doesn't outstay it's welcome. That, and sure it could be because I don't like Star Wars settings much. But hey, Indiana Jones feels more fitting to this game. At least because you don't travel with 3-5 characters who's AI ignores enemies. Or slow "just to open door" ones.
It takes storyline from movies, but does them in completely silent way, Just characters gruntng and making moves during cutscenes. There isn't even text that explains things like in Star Wars. And well, it still was enjoyable for what it is despite me never seeing a movie. I checked movie plots after playing these and also noticed that some scenes were changed a bit. So yea, movies fans will like comedy there. Well, if they like slapstick.
Platforming was improved, addings ledges and ropes for your adventuring. It takes a bit more spotlight at times. There are even parts in the game where you got ledges on circullar pillars that turn around and you have to time your jump. Quite enjoyable and simple.
Puzzles are still nice too. You still have to use individual characters for some things, like Short Round can crawl into tiny entrances, heroine of second movie can scream so high that grass breaks and Indiana Jones is qutie a hero, using whip effectively to grab something or swing over pit. It's fairly stdandard pushing and pulling, along with taking some items and bringing them to other helps. Having to find tools for some actions also help to break monotomy. Heck, there even were at least two spots where I had no idea what to do next and had to actually think. It's still quite casual otherwise.
Fighting got improved too. Well, since game isn't about fighting, you can't truly die, it's just a better distraction now. Enemies don't appear as often for one. Indiana can do a nice kill animation (well, as much as you can say that for kids lego games) if he attacks in same time as enemy does.Whip can be used there too. To vary things up, most of main characters can only melee, punching and slapping. Instead, they can take and grab additional weapons, whether it's throwable sword, a chair or a huge rifle. It once again helps to break up monotomy, even though game is a bit less fair thsi way. But hey, seeing how fighting isn't punishing and isn't focus, it's just nice not just mashing same attack buttong while watching character avoid everything as well.
There are still cases when waves of infinite enemies will annoy you while you are thinking what to do next in puzzle, sadly. Enemies with explosives are frustrating to fight against too.
And yea, you still collect much studs. Breaking stuff and doing things, explorign levels for treasures to collect statue out of 10 of them on each level. Plus, one red post per level that unlocks extra bonuses, mostly cheating ones. They are still fun to find. It's just that Free Play where you can freely select needed character during gameplay is the way to go when you want to collect everything. And it's a shame, since you may feel that collecting anything during Story Mode is somewhat pointless by comparsion. There are some treasures that require thinking to get in Story Mode but easily picked up in Free Play, and some you can get only in Free Play. I would had liked if there were treasures for Story Mode only too.
So, it's nicely done Lego game, which gets pacing down, so even normal players will not get too bored. Well, at least not will feel like it should end already. I would recommend picking this one over Lego Star Wars for sure. Though it's still casual game, so depends.

My Thoughts:
A clever, unique and very charming murder mystery with a fantastic art style that involves you working out enemy paterns and movement, then manipulating time to save their victims. Awesome stuff!
Game Details:
The Sexy Brutale — a never-ending masked ball featuring intrigue, murder and the (quite possibly) occult! Relive the same mysterious day where the guests at the casino mansion are being murdered by the staff over and over again.
Worth it

I bought this game based on the soundtrack and a small glimpse of the gameplay. I didn't know what to expect other than an amazing soundtrack. What I got was a work of art. While the puzzles themselves are not overly difficult and the replay value may not be high given the nature of a puzzle game, the entertainment I received was well worth the money.
The Sexy Brutale flips the idea of a murder mystery on its head. You know who the killers are, you know how the victims die, and you have to use time travel to prevent them. The art style is beautiful, the atmosphere macabre. The deaths are creative outside of the tutorial murder. The world feels alive with each guest and each murderer moving about the house. The music is excellent - the main theme is something I could listen to for hours.
I highly, highly recommend this game.

Pros:
++Smooth movement, rarely get hung-up and terrain is well defined.
++Stealing is fun, as you must be quick and careful to succeed.
+Interesting levels and enviroment, even if it is stereotypically gloomy.
+Spooky asylum level would've been right at home in a horror game.
+Rewards the completion of challenges based on different playstyles, similar to Mark of the Ninja.
Mixed:
~Main character lacks depth, he's just a guy who steals stuff with your average merc-style "I like money" mixed with the Batmanish "I'm a lonely nocturnal guy who doesn't have very many friends." Does have some good dialogue, however.
~A great many similarities to Dishonored, including: special magic vision, an oppressive leader with full authority over the city guard, a disease killing all the citizens, rescuing the girl, a ♥♥♥♥♥house level, and the creepy old blind lady with special powers. Also,
~Game is linear, which seems to make people poop their pants. If the ride is a good one, why complain? That being said, only some deviation is allowed beyond sidequests.
Negative:
--Story is lame and unimaginative, generic save-the-girl story but with even less story sprinkled in than other games. Magic occult spooky stuff and whatever.
-Level design can be very confusing sometimes. I got stuck on the stupid staircase puzzle longer than i'd like to admit.
Overall, if you can get it for $15 bucks or less, it's worth it. I'd give it a 7.5. It's enjoyable, has a good amount of content, and even has replay value.
Rating: 7.5
Value: ~$15 or less.

Comparing it to Dark Project, Metal Age, and Deadly Shadows is somewhat pointless really, as the developers themselves hardly decided to take their predecessors amazing talent and creativity into account and ask "Is this really what Thief is about?"  As a passionate fan of the series, I was incredibly disheartened to see major elements removed that made the games what they were- everything from full freedom of movement to the City itself, along with all of its inhabitants. This reboot, whether it belongs in a parallel dimension or in the future, or wherever the developers intended it to be, is unfortunately a hollow shell. Sure, you're a Thief, in a City, Stealing.  However, that isn't what made Thief the beloved series that it is.  Having the untethered abilility to climb almost anywhere or shoot a rope arrow into any wooden surface- and thus allowing unparallel choice, is what made Thief incredible. The games felt alive- all the way from the poorly scribbled maps to the various written correspondance that you crept upon.  The reboot just feels lifeless. Garrett is dull, the menu-generated maps and letters are a pain to read, and the progression is forced.
In the end, there is hardly any way to compare this game to the first three.  Of course, the classic ones had plenty of flaws of their own; however this Reboot did not attempt to evolve from its predecessor in any way besides graphically.  In some cases, it's even a step back like in level design, creative direction, and most importantly, freedom of movement.
So lets talk about Thief without comparing it to the other games in the series.  Right away, if you've played Dishonored, you'll feel like this is some strange spinoff.  The environment looks the same. The story sounds similar.  There is even this blind enigmatic woman.
While the city is fun to explore for the first few jumps and crawls, it gets repetitive quick, especially since you're forced to go through the same locations constantly.  There is hardly any dynamic changes to the guard patrols as the story moves on.  The main level here is the city- it's the hub between missions and locations. You'll spend most of your time here, buying expensive arrows to reach inexpensive treasures or constantly tapping your keyboard to jimmy open a window- a function that becomes infuriating once you realize that its a key "feature" of interactive design.  The actual missions become more challenging and sometimes offer multiple options of progression, often making the difference between "Ghosting" which means not utilizing any resources and basically leaving no trace, or being an "Opportunist" and snuffing candles, using vent shafts, or rope arrows.  While it's nice to have different routes based on playstyle, you usually end up in the same exact location, no matter the playstyle.  The illusion of choice is there, but when your only choice is to go into the same room, does it really matter whether you go through the back door or the window that's right next to that door? Not really.  Lastly, everything in the main hub resets when you complete a mission. All doors need to get unlocked, all vent shafts need to get unscrewed.  It's nothing short of repetitive, especially when you have to see the same action over and over again.
The audio is very erratic- sometimes people talking next to you are very muffled and other times you hear guards or other voices talking through multiple walls.  You constantly pass by conversations that are supposed to occur behind closed doors or windows but it sounds like they are right in front of you.  Speaking of conversation, you'll be hearing the same lines of banter over... and over... and over.  Sloop sellers here, sloop sellers there.  I didn't really get an ambient feeling- the music was pretty forgetful and sometimes overpowered the audio, especially in dangerous situations when I was attempting to listen to footsteps. Speaking of footsteps, there was hardly a difference on what surface you stepped on, whether it was noisy glass, metal, or water.  As long as you move slow, you won't be heard. Even though I'm hearing the glass being crushed clearly beneath me, Benny the guard can't, despite being right behind me.
As I mentioned, most characters are boring.  Even Garrett.  He isn't some "master thief"- he's a clumsy brigand that relies too much on his tools rather than his wits. I've had to do massive amounts of reloading soley due to him missing a rope that was right in front of him, or falling off a rail for no reason.  The context sensitivity is ridiculous on all accounts.  Regarding his tools, its amusing how in the prologue, Garrett scolds his protege for relying too much on the grappling hook, yet as soon as he takes possession of it, he can't survive without it.  For a city that is supposed to be alive, it looks and feels dead. You either talk to the same three questgivers who say the same things, or to some blackmarket vendors who all look the same. The guards look no different than the criminals who replace them later in the chapters.  Despite the detail and hardwork put into the city, the appearance and dialogue of the NPCs seem more of an afterthought than anything.
Bland. If you haven't played the previous games, you'll uncover a gleam of possibility in the muddy cracks of this city.  Unfortunately, it ends before you get anywhere.  If you've played the previous games, at the least, you'll be incredibily disappointed at the writers for missing an opportunity to re-establish some beloved factions.  At most, you'll probably feel a bit insulted that they attempted to make some subtle references to the city of the past and left it in the shadows.

This game touches a subject that most games don't: the lives of civilians during war. And I have to say, it does the work brilliantly. You'll feel the bleakness of the atmosphere and the despair of your survivors. And more often than not you're forced to take meaningful moral choices: when you really need supplies, do you try to sneak around a warehouse full of patrolling bandits and risk getting shot, or do you barge in a small house owned by an elderly couple and rob them blind? Whatever you choose, the game won't blatantly tell you if you're right or wrong, but your characters (and you) will remember your actions.
One of the best parts about this game is the survivors. Each of them has their own story and personality, so they feel like real, believable people instead of machines. You'll
them to survive, and you'll feel terrible if one of them dies for whatever reasons. In addition, the endings for your survivors are cleverly built in as well. Even when you've survived the war, you may find that you just haven't won at all, as your people fail to find their families and friends, live an unhappy life, or even commit suicide out of guilt. The moment when each of your characters earns their happy ending is the most heartwarming moment ever.
Even when I've completely mastered this game, I still found myself coming back to it over and over again. I'm not exaggerating; this is a game that everyone should play at least once.
Sure I haven't played This War of Mine, but once you get into it, everything feels real, almost as if you are stranded and stuck in a society lost in war. Highly recommended. Good Luck!

This is an iconic game and, perhaps, not for the right reasons.
Beyond the post gammergate fuss it's worth assessing this game as a stand alone experience, as a game in it's own right not as an exercise in either alt-right baiting or alt-right propagandising.
As such this game stands up as a worthwhile experience.
The game mechanics are simple: you have a list of options available to you each time a decision is made. you begin with most of these unavailable as you fall into depression and then as you are offered options such as speaking to loved ones and seeking professional help more options become available. if you choose not to the options narrow again, if you choose to open up to others and seek help more options become available.
This is a simple but effective game mechanic and is effective in mimicking the path depression may take.
No, the game is not 'fun' but why should games be fun and why are the mainstream games which offer you opportunities to do nothing but kill 'fun?'
This is a game about emotional states and it is a work of art. if this is not what you are after from a game then don't play it and don't review it but don't trash the game the same way i would not trash a FPS.

Step 2. Steam Support

Easily my favorite war game on PC was the SSI classic Panzer General (1993).   PG went on to have 4-5 sequals and generally was a fan favorite for a decade.   Luckly for us Slitherine decided to dust off this classic with a bit newer graphics but the same old fun gameplay.   If you loved PG then stop reading this review buy the game and play.  If you are new to the series lets go over what makes it fun.  First unlike many other war games its very easy to pick up learn and enjoy.  Most gamers should be able to pick up most of what they need to learn in under 30 minutes of play.  Next for those of us who like detail but dislike horrible interfaces Panzer Corps has an easy to use interface that is nearly perfict.  Finally the depth of the historical missions are fun and exciting.  Eventually you will get attached to some of your brigades and be pitching a fit if one gets nailed in a bad spot.   Now for the bad....
One area that really could use some help is music, its ok but after awhile you wish you could just turn it off.  Its not cheep but its not well done.  Also while they were faithfull to the old PG game they really didnt try to bring in something new that would wow the audience.  Perhaps a research element, perhaps better naval options, perhaps better ways to manage air cover who knows but they really didnt change any core gameplay.  Yes this isnt necessarly a bad thing PG was a darn good game but that was 20 years ago.
All in all the game is easily worth 50 without the DLC.  If you are a wargamer this is a must buy if there ever was one.  If you are on the fence or just havent played a war game before I would say there is no other game that could possibly be a better game to try.

Still, the game is well worth it IMHO.

What a disappointment.
I honestly was excited for this game's release. I thought, "Ooh, a free Magic: the Gathering game. I hope it's better than the crummy "Duels of the Planeswalkers" games." I downloaded the game on launch day...and was completely let down.
I was initially disappointed by the anemic tutorial which (barely) teaches you how to play...
But then the AI got CHEAP.
The opponent AI in the campaign mode is the single cruelest...thing ever devised. Your opponent will always manage to get their best cards before you can respond. The biggest example is the Jace vs. Alhammarret fight, where if your starting hand doesn't have the TWO Cancels that your deck runs at that point, you WILL lose to a brutal mill deck.
This leads to problem number two, the premise decks SUCK. Seriously. Why did Chandra's deck have two Young Pyromancers in a deck with next to no instants or sorceries? Why does Liliana's deck have terrible creatures that can't do anything useful. No reanimator strategies?
The only way you can get a decent deck is through custom building one, and the biggest problem shows here...the free-to-play business model. This game rewards players who pay lots of real-world money on packs, giving them large numbers of cards to choose from. By contrast, a completely free player has a strict collection to choose from, and a lot of these cards are unplayable. You can get lucky and pack something like a Liliana in a gift pack (Envy me, ♥♥♥♥♥es.), but most people can't compete with paid players. Compare this to Hearth stone, where new players not only have a chance against more experienced ones, they actually have a shot at winning.
So, no. I cannot allow this game a free pass because the concept is good. This is one game that I will never install again.

This is my favorite "early" Lego game. Now, with LOTR, POTC, and Batman 2, these games have complex "hub worlds" and hundreds of collectables of different sorts.  This game, Star Wars, and Batman (1) were the original Lego games with a bunch of characters, 10 minikit pieces per level, and not much else.  They seem basic compared to games like Lego LOTR, but this game, Indiana Jonse 1, was the best of the original lego games.  It has the best level design, a broad selection of the characters you'd want, a great soundtrack, and a general sense of completeness.  It has everything you'd want in a Lego Indy game (if you are not a big Crystal Skull fan--which I am not).  Some things about this game that are different from other early Lego games: You can pick up weapons (a fallen foe's scimitar, a native's spear, a Nazi's rifle).  It adds variety to mashing the fight button.  The game makes good use of Indy's whip.  It also reminds you of how great all three individual soundtracks were, and the difference between them.  Highly recommended for the casual player or devoted collector-type. :)

Games like this is why I love indie developers, they are the only ones brave enough to try different games and personally I had more fun in the 7 hours 100% completing this game than I have in more expensive AAA titles.
The game has an extremely cool premise where you have to stop a series of murders from happening by observing the murder take place and then tracing the steps back before the murder of both the victim and the perpetrator.  Its super clever and really fun to witness everything going on.
The story is great, the mystery of why you are stopping these murders unravels as you get further on and by the end I felt completely satisfied, I wouldn’t change a thing in regards to the story.  Although the game has a puzzle tag the actual puzzle solving aspect isn't particularly difficult, it's more important to getting your timings right and observe the characters and how they interact with each other.
The design of the environment is truly great, the individual rooms are beautiful to look at and the whole place is amazing to wander around.  As you solve murders you gain new abilities that let you explore other parts of the mansion, it's always good to revisit earlier parts of the mansion with the new abilities.
The music is completely on point, it changes depending on the area you are in and appropriately sets up the mood for what is to happen next.  I particularly liked the music in the entrance of the casino :)
People say that the game is short but personally I think it's perfect in length, any more and it would be become stale, any less things would have felt rushed.  6-7 hours to complete and find all the secrets is perfect for me.
My only complaint with the game is there is little to no penalty for not being stealthy, I know it's not really a stealth game but being able to walk into a room whilst people are taking and just walk straight through and out the other side without any really impact to the story or characters is disappointing, personally I would have rather it changed the outcome of that particular day to which you need to rewind time to fix your mistake.
Overall though this game is exceptional, so far it’s the best game I've player this year (2017) and I would highly recommend it to anyone.

The Puzzles are a bit simple, although the charm is in how you obtain the clues and sneak around, and get a bit more from each area as you progress. Overall, I really hope that the developers expand on the game a bit: it would be very easy to have some form of a "New Game +" mode, with greater player risks, and an altered "day" to play through. At any rate, I'd definitely recommend this game to anyone who likes a game that plays as a good story and experience. There's much annoyance in the game (e.g. in the winter you have to keep your heater full of wood, so you can't end the day early even if you have nothing else to do - the temperature will drop and people will get sick). You can't go for any kind of sustainability, cause everything is tied to components (or otherwise arbitrarily limited, like you can only have two traps) - which take a lot of carrying space when scavenging and are otherwise very limited when trading. I always have enough goods to buy more components, I always want more components, there's never enough components. It's not just for building, it's for everything. To grow food you need water. To prepare food you need water. How do you get water? With a filter made with components. And it serves no real purpose, since there's only one production chain (so you can't adapt by switching what you were doing) and there's nothing else to do (so you just sit on your♥♥♥♥♥and wait for more components). On the other hand, even with unlimited components, just feeding that one silly chain would be tedious and boring.
Speaking of arbitrary restrictions, you can't have more than one person scavenging. Apparently the city is not big enough (although I've had a bug once, where the game claimed two people brought supplies from scavenging).
