I've been a part of this game's Beta and Alpha for a couple years, watching it grow since its announcement a few years ago. It hasn't gained the fame and popularity I had hoped, drowned out by both hero shooters and MOBAs alike. With a difficult development cycle and near closure of Motiga, this game went through a lot of rough times to get here today.
Basically it is a very fast paced 3rd person shooter, with MOBA like elements. While it lacks the minions/creeps of traditional MOBAs, it still focuses on map/lane control, and taking out your enemy's core... which in this case is a gigantic (hah) guardian that is capable of already destructive power.
Gameplay: Third person action shooter with emphasis on mobility, strategy, and accuracy. It doesn't feel quite as streamlined as hero shooters like Overwatch, Paladins, or Battleborn, as you still need to focus on gaining map control, gathering power for your guardian, and upgrading skills. Yet it is much faster paced and gives more player control than MOBAs like League, DOTA2, and Smite. If you're looking for a nice middle-ground this is a fantastic game to check out.
Art Style - Visually gorgeous, with cell-shading that is reminiscent of games like Wind Waker, and character designs unique and cool to look at. Unfortunately, visuals can be a bit too abundant at times, with effects dominating the screen and creating a bit of a distraction to the gameplay, making it hard to focus sometimes. Better though than what it was in the beta and alpha.
Sound - Booming voices from guardians, with overall okay voice acting from the heroes. Some shine, while others falter, and overall kind of shows the limited budget as compared to getting highly talented voice actors in other games. Plus voice actor strike hasn't helped.
TLDR
Pros
Middleground gameplay between Dota 2, League, and Overwatch, Paladins, Battleborn.
Fast paced action gameplay.
Very colorful visuals.
Free with no Pay to Win model attatched
Cons
Arc launcher, but I mean come on, it's not like most other competitive games on steam have a 3rd party DRM attatched at this point.
Voice acting for some characters not so great
Visuals in large scale team fights may get distracting for some.
Overall: As a F2P game, it should definatley be checked out

Nostalgia is a funny thing. I played Icewind Dale when I was younger like many people and when I saw the EE edition I was thrilled. As a young boy I was terrible at the game and as an adult I was only slightly better! I would avoid Icewind Dale for several reasons but the game is still strong for certain players.
What I didn't like:
- Now I'm not an RPG isometric nut ball and I certainly don't know the DnD world that well. Character creation was fun when I was younger but it was a chore this time around. Making a decent party of the right amount of members was very trial and error for me. I'd advise a guide for this.
- How many bloody enemies? Now maybe I'm terrible but the amount of enemies the game would sometimes surround you with was beyond a joke. It didn't matter if you kited them or fought them up front, you'd die. The game often made me exploit it by firing random fireballs into the dark to kill/damage enemies before they saw me. Doesn't seem very balanced.
- Bugs or maybe a feature. In some areas you would return and the whole room would be repopulated after loading a quick save. This often put me in a tricky situation of getting out of an area to head back to heal. Keep an eye out on the game pulling this fast one.
- Backtracking. Now I'm sure this comes down to my inexperience of having a terrible cleric or whatever but having to backtrack each time I need 1000x health potions or to revive at a temple was beyond a joke. Backtracking is never fun and Icewind forces you do to it...a lot.
Things I liked:
- Blast from the past, it was great to see a game that I adored when I was a child on steam. I can't say it was worth it for the nostalgia but I gave it a shot.
- Spells - The different spells of the mage was a great feeling, I didn't use them much when I was younger so it was nice to experience this character.
- Environments, there we're plenty of different areas to explore that felt different in their own way. This tied into the story which I enjoyed even though the fighting part of the game took a way from it.
Summary:
I would only buy Icewind Dale if you want a blast from the past or you're seriously into your roleplaying games and understand different elements of character creation. This would probably make the game pretty easy but I found is very hard but luckily made it to the end. Give it a shot if you have the patience.

Icewind Dale itself is a marvelous game (subjectively of course).  As the Enhanced Edition sits currently, I do not recommend it.  To clarify: Enhanced Edition is not the original and there are changes.  Some of the additions are fun (I'm not going to reiterate them here), but there are downsides that will catch your attention if you've played the original.
The enhanced editions are built from the Baldur's Gate 2 engine using CRE V1.0 and CHR V2.0.  What many do not realize is that because of this some content from the original Icewind Dale has been removed to bring it into line with the Baldur's Gate 2 engine.  I stumbled across this fact in my playing of Enhanced Edition.  I couldn't quite seem to figure out why the gameplay seemed more monotonous than in the original.  And then I discovered that the number of sounds your characters make had been greatly reduced (from 40 to 22).  What this means is that the variety of remarks and sounds your characters make as you command them to move, they take damage, you tell them to attack an enemy, etc. is reduced by almost half.
I'm not sure if there are other aspects of the game that had to be similarly altered in creating Icewind Dale Enhanced Edition.  And for some this may be inconsequential or outweighed by some of the neat additions.  But for me, losing original content is significant.  I'll be playing one of my copies of the original with a mod to make it full screen (find mods easily doing any internet search if you're interested).  Icewind Dale is fantastic.  Just know that if you go the Enhanced Edition route you are going to be missing out on at least a couple authentic elements.  Personally I feel these losses should've been listed with the additions in Enhanced Edition's description so one could properly compare it with the original, but I guess that wouldn't help Beamdog's sales.  I can't help but wonder what else may be missing...
PS  During my playing of Enhanced Edition I had a number of crashes occur (playing the Steam version in Windows).  One would normally report these at the Beamdog forums in the hopes of a fix, but apparently Steam does something that renders crash reporting useless to the developers at Beamdog (as one of them informed me).  Crashes suck.
Edit 2/25/2016:  As of this edit 128 people found this review helpful.  I didn't think it'd get that much visibility.  With enough urging we could actually make a difference.  It is possible, should they determine it worth the effort, for the developers at Beamdog to create new file structures and restore these missing sounds in a future patch.  If you would like to see this happen, visit the feature request section on their forums and let your voice be heard.  The more of us that indicate a desire for such action, the more likely it is to happen.  I've already made such a request here (
) if you'd simply like to login in and give a +1.

This is not a Total War game, it is just a pay2win mobile game. By hearing the title Total War I expect three things, a campaign map, epic scale battles and extended use of strategy. Unfortunately,I saw none of those main features in this game. Instead, it is mainly a city building game.
There are the main resources that you use for costructing buildings and recruiting units. However, some processes take hours to be finished and you have to use gold which can be collected by two ways, or by completing missions and objectives, (which are just to build a number of specific buildings ,fight battles or to conquer new parts of the map, ) or by spending real money. The only thing that I personally liked was the teraforming feature because lakes and rivers can affect both positively and negatively the production of some resources.
The battles are just a huge dissapointment because they are not huge and they have no strategy at all. Furthermore, you have to deploy your units on three lines , with maximum three units per line, they march towards the enemy and you have to just order charge at the right moment to have some bonus and there are some special abilities that give advantage to your units for a short time. Except from that, your units cannot move on a horizontal axis to help their fellow soldiers, they can attack only on the units that are in front of them. And the worst part is that the battles last for a few seconds.
The visuals are great for a mobile strategy game. The map and the battles are 3d and generally the game does not look ugly. Instead, it looks quite beautiful. The audio is decent except from one part, the voice acting of the soldiers is the same from Rome II and no matter the fact that the British used to be christians back then you may hear them say "praise the gods". It's not a fun game, but it's not intended to be. This is a brave attempt to broaden the purpose of games, and to broaden the genre. It's a storytelling game that gives insight into what living with depression can be like. So this can be used to help people who have a depressed friend or loved one understand a little of what they're going through, and maybe give them some talking points to broach difficult subjects.
I suffer from anxiety/depression myself.  I'm 45 years old, but had I played this game earlier in life, I can see how it could have positively influenced me.
My only criticism is that it's a text adventure format.  I think it works for this subject matter, though.  Also, it's important to consider that there was a lot less funding for experimental games when this one was being produced.  Consider it a pioneering game in the indie field.
All in all, I applaud the effort, and hope that people find it helpful. I also hope that we continue experimenting with therapeutic possibilities of games.

This game serves as an excellent example of how something can be "dinky" and still good. There are all sorts of "rogue-like" and "rogue-lite" games on Steam nowadays, and this is certainly among the best.

Everything around you kinda looks vomit-colored and some of the monsters blend in with the scenery so well that they look like furniture. If it weren't for the fact that items "sparkled" when on the ground, you'd really have no way of knowing the difference between a new pair of boots and a corpse. Dob't get me wrong; it's not the worst looking game in the world by any means, but it could easily be made better.
In short, this game is cheap and goes on sale a fair bit. It's perfectly for when you've got some spare time at work and things are slow, so you should look to add it to your library when you get the chance.

Signal Ops is a game by independent developers Space Bullet Dynamics. Set in a retro-futuristic 1940s, this bureaucratic society is governed by two feuding organisation, the military and the church. You play as an agent of the church, tasked with carrying out missions involving spying and espionage. However your character never actually enters combat but instead issues commands via video and radio links to the operatives in the field.
The game is a first person shooter and you control 3 operatives, at the same time, via these links in single player or cooperatively. This concept is very original but is also the games greatest achievement and weakness. The controls can be frustrating and take time to master. They require lots of patience, organisation and multitasking to pull off, even minor mistakes can lead to panic and mission failure. The gameplay mechanics are also very retro and rather basic when compared to more mainstream tactical espionage games.
However, once you are accustomed with the basics this charming game, with it's stylized oil painting graphics, simple plot, humorous narrative and nods to cult film classic "Brazil", combine to form a really interesting tactical espionage action sandbox where objectives can be tackled in any number of ways, alone or with friends. 7/10

Well this game is definitely different.  It's the only game I know of where up to 6 view points (the player and up to 5 characters controllable by the player) are utilized at once.  It is also the first I've played that uses a radio mechanic to limit where players can go.
I should make it clear right away that there are two fundamental things you need to know about this game:
1) Radios: on Easy difficulty, all of the Radios are enabled and you don't have to worry about this.  On Normal, you have a "bolt" soldier which carries a radio to power boxes, sets it up, and then that power box becomes a permanent radio so you can move your portable radio to another box.  On Hard, the radios are not permanent which effectively requires two players to advance the game.  If a character leaves, or gets left out of, radio range, they effectively become deaf and blind.  This is the first time ever I experienced this in a game and at first, I have to say it is quite frightening.  In situations where you have to do this, you learn to rely on other characters to be the eyes for the one out of range.  This is a very unique mechanic and it serves its purpose well.
2) FPS: Make no mistake that at its core, this is a shooter.  The only thing that's really different on this end is you can switch between up to five different shooters.  The shooting mechanics, after turning up the mouse sensitivity, are good.
That said, I really only have two complaints:
1) I got stuck for hours, repeatedly, and Google/Bing were no help.  Searching Steam forums was so if you run into problems, don't bother with search engines, just search the Signal Ops Steam forum.
2) Switching between perspectives isn't as easy as I'd like it to be because the game is set up to command first (hold that perspective's key), control second (push perspective's key 2-4 times--it should just be 2 but often find myself smashing it to change).  I really wish it was control first, and command second because it was really, really rare that I commanded and very, very frequent that I controlled.
That said, I enjoyed the game and recommend it.  I'll probably replay it sometime in the future.

Probably one of my favorite games, but it's not for everyone.
It's in its own unique niche in terms of skill, so nothing you learned from other games carries over really. Infact this game reminded me what it was like when I first started playing video games, because it was so out there. It pretty much took me until 3/4ths into the game before I felt completely comfortable with the controls and gameplay, and the missions are very replayable both in design (large various paths) and with the fact that you can use different combination of agents.
I feel though that anyone saying it's badly designed and clunky isn't really justified. This game relies a ton on strategy and positioning, so the most I would say is if you get caught completely out of position with your pants down it can
clunky because you have to on the spot deal with pressure which is difficult when you have 2-3 sometimes 4 units in first person perspective. So being caught off guard can be really punishing at first when you're adjusting to the micromanaging, although it is a strategic game so it's fair.
Combat is kind of a non-option in this game unless your idea of combat is flanking enemies and not having an open firefight. A lot of the guns aren't really effective on more than one guard (minus sniper and shield), however it is extremely forgiving defensive wise as your agents have a lot of health and you are given ~10-11 lives per level. Dying can be a pain though as the new agent is parachuted in at a certain point with nothing but a melee weapon, so you need to retrieve your items or just leave them and steal a guards guns (as long as you didn't lose a valuable item like the radio)
All in all, this game is 95% positioning and tactics 5% shooter, and it makes it really interesting and fun to play after you get use to having to micro 4 first person cameras.

I ran into this at PAX and was smitten immediately. It is so hectic and yet Zen and peaceful. Like many of my favorite games, it's more about what's happening in your head than what's on the screen.
This is a traffic routing game where you draw subway lines to take little shape people to the matching station shape. People appear in real time, but you can pause and redraw your map at any time. You use little rectangular trains, a few colors, a few bridges to cross rivers.
The art is straight out of the classic London Underground map. But you get to make the map, in a stylized but real world city with its geography (eg London, Paris, Berlin, New York).
As you deliver more passengers, you meet the challenges of growth. New stations crop up in outlying areas, forcing you to take apart the ingenious system that worked so well before and think again. New shapes of passenger and station appear, making it impossible to service all shapes with any one line. But they will transfer along the shortest route, which means you want your trains to meet at some stations. Mix in a long haul train line? Maybe you want to add a passenger car to accommodate all the people that build up as it makes its slow way.
The stations and demand are randomly placed every time. The gameplay is the same every time, but the random map constantly challenges your understanding of these systems.
I'm having a great time with it.
A fun little distraction. _Much_ harder than it looks

As of today, sept. 4th, 2015, Mini Metro is still in development. But it's already a fully playable (and enjoyable) game.
Mini Metro is a minimalist game, in the sense that:
- the goal is simple (keep your metro network working as fluidly as possible)
- the gameplay elements are simple (as time goes on, you gain more lines, train, tunnel...)
- the ergonomics are simple (draw a line between two stations and you've built a new metro line ; click and drop a train on a line and it'll immediately work on its own schedule)
- the look is simple (as you can see, the visuals are inspired by subway maps you can find all around the world)
But a minimalist game isn't a simple game. Each station has a specific shape. Imagine that a circle represents a residential district and that a triangle represents a business area. Passengers will then tend to go from a circle to triangle. And back. But as time goes, new shapes appear. And it really feels like if a city was blooming before your eyes. Again, imagine that a square is a commercial district, a star is a tourist area,  a diamond is an airport... Some of the shapes will appear in large numbers and close together. Others will be scarce but will be a favorite destination from all around the map. Again, just like in a real blooming city.
Add to that the fact that a dozen of real life cites are present in the game, each with a different feel, different tools, different obstacles.
To put it simply, the game is already perfect as it is. But it's still quite hard to explain and you really have to experience how it works, for it's both a very stressing and demanding game
a most contemplative and artistic pice of work.

This game looked like another case (or victim?) of the zombie fad. However I was always intrested in this title, as it's openly stated that it's a puzzle game. A zombie puzzler game. This is either really meh (zombies instead of coloured blocks) or pure sh*t (because noways you can sell anything, that has zombies) or something original.  For me, it turned out to be the third option.
The game itself is really simple. It's kind of a falling-block game, but instead of the most usual match-3 system you need to surround a group of zombies with similar "coloured" units (Policemen, armymen, vandals or scientists) and depending on the size of the zombie group, you can get a bonus unique to the faction you used to contain the zombie group.
It's very possible that this isn't the first game with this mechanic, yet it was new for me. Some additional mechanisms actually contributes to the "zombie game" feeling. Sometimes zombies charge your group, turning people on the borders to zombies. The zombies are alive, and will attack neighbouring humans and turn them. And with this, we reached the most intresting part of the game. Imagine the situation: you try to surround a group of Zeds with policemen, and another group with vandals. However you're unlucky, and both groups attack two people who are neighbours - and the two hordes became one - but you possibly don't have enough character of the same type to surround them. You'll either lose, or you should kill smaller groups in the hope of bonuses (like molotov cocktail) to divide the big horde into smaller, managable sizes.    This threat is kinda non-existant at early levels, but at middle-late campaign you should be very wary about how do you deal with Z groups fastly and efficiently.
A small list about the game's different aspects:
Game mechanism: traditional puzzle's mechanics (2-hit blocks and 1-colour-only blocks as well appear) with reasonable and well executed zombie mechanism
Game graphics: well, nothing intresting. I won't rate this with numbers, it's just average - nothing too ugly now nothing exceptional to an indie puzzler game. You won't have trouble identifying anything on the screen.
Game music: If I remember well this was actually really good, atmospheric zombie-music. However I think it's quite short, becomes repetitive after a while (played and finished the game a few weeks ago, please forgive me for my leaky memory)
Addtitional note: Campaign is quite good. Starts easy, becames harder as new enemies are introduced. It's learning curve is very reasonable, only bossfights can be difficult for the first few tries. I also have to mention the campaign's narration - it's visible on the road as you move from board to board - it's really well written, gives quite an atmosphere :)
As the game's base price is low, and also usually appears in bundles, I do recommend it. Gives a lot of fun for low price if you enjoy puzzler games.

This game has a short "campaign" which is basically a drawn-out training module for the more (too) grueling survival mode. It tries to be quirky with some of the monster types (shielded wizard zombies and super-zombies), but this only succeeds in ruining the immersion. The primary mechanic is "surround the cell"; this would be great except for the RNG and the fact that it is paced poorly; the exponential growth of enemies eventually cannot be overcome. You really need the power-up items, but the game is stingy and mysterious in their application. With only 3 slots for single-use power-ups, one might think there would be some strategy in their application but they only instead act as a bottleneck, forcing the player to cycle through collected power-ups in order to avoid wasting new ones waiting for pickup. You could dedicate months to perfecting your timing - or just find another game to play because there are so many out there to choose from.

Another zombie game, you're thinking? Well, no, not really. At least, not a TYPICAL zombie game by any means.
As the title states, it's a puzzler - no hybrid zombie shooter♥♥♥♥♥puzzler. Just a puzzler.  So why the zombie inclusion? For the most part, it's not relevant really at all. It could be anything that takes the place of those zombies, but the important thing is it's a pretty good puzzler.
It's based on the "match 3" style of puzzle, and you start with a full grid of objects/zombies (a bit like Bejeweled) - and just like Bejeweled, once you clear a group, the spaces are refilled. That's about where similarities end.
Your basic aim is to clear the zombies on the board, and the way you clear a group is to surround them with a colour-coded group of your little guys, doing their utmost against the contagion (go little guys!) As the game progresses, slight variations and hurdles are introduced to up the ante. Difficulty is kept nicely linear, and paced just right. I could go into deeper description of these hurdles, but I think doing so would rather spoil it for you. There's not much else to say about the mechanics - it does what it should rather well indeed.
The levels are tied together in a "story mode" format, and to be frank, the story is pretty rubbish, and terribly amateurly written. However, as this is in the form of text on-screen, there's no awful voice acting to listen to, and it skims along quickly enough, so that you soon progress onto the next level with a minimal of fuss. In short, you can easily ignore it, and it impacts the game in no other way than this.
So, even if you've completely had your fill of the over-used zombie craze, this is a worthy purchase, especially if "matching" puzzles are your thing. I picked it up in an indie bundle and was pleasantly surprised - so much so that I replayed it as soon as I'd finished the story mode. It's not exactly very graphically intensive either, so a moderate/low PC should run it capably too.
All in all a pleasant little puzzler that very much does it's own slant on a formula, and well worth the purchase. As always my metric is price, and I'd say this is worth a good £6-7. If you aren't so into puzzles, then I'd still recommend it, although you should adjust the price accordingly.

First of all - addressing most of the negative reviews of this game: Do not treat this as a total war game. It may have the name Total War on it but it was never meant to be compared to the standard TW games. I started the game up expecting something similar to Tribal Wars and nothing more and that is exactly what this game has offered. A highly polished cross-platform casual game with fast (but fun) real-time battles.
As with all games of this genre there is an option to pay for gold to speed up your progress and recruit different (not overpowered, just a slightly different role) units. You can still earn gold in-game but unless you intend on playing this game for long periods of time in one go then gold is not neccesary. The Kingdom building is fantastic, you can terraform the land to your liking, build it how you like focusing either on your military to capture enemy (AI) settlements or on your economy to buy them out.
The PvP multiplayer aspect I haven't yet reached but I'm assuming so far it is for 1v1 army duels only so I can't comment on this.
You can customise your coat of arms with a variety of options which will then show up on the shields of your units, loading screens, and various other places.
Despite looking rather simple, the combat actually does have a lot of depth to it. In fact compared to any other casual-like game of this genre it has the most depth I have seen. There are 9 unit slots and you can build your army as you wish, individual-stat / ability progression per unit, special  ability-activated buffs you can earn from building churches and so on. There is more to the combat than this - try it! It seems mind-numbingly simple at the beginning but as the army sizes begin to grow and as you gain more abilities the game reveals more and more depth which was a very pleasant surprise.
Overall unless you buy gold with real money (you do get A LOT of gold for a small amount of money!) apart from at the beginning this is not a game that you can play for more than an hour at a time due to the nature of the game, but for playing half an hour or so every now and then it's brilliant. A fun, casual game. I highly recommend it!

Do I want to bulid a shovel to clear rubble, or a knife to defend myself?
But if you take the time to examine everything the game offers, you will find that This War of Mine may be one of the best war stories ever told. Each character has a backstory which is only revealed slowly, agonizingly, as you forge through the uncertain days, and the treacherous nights. At no point are you even forced to confront the history of the characters. You must choose to invest in their identity and struggle, but if you do, you will experience the game as it was meant to be played.

Using the same engine as Deus Ex: Human Revolution, the Eidos Monreal team has the Thief franchise thrust into their lap by the publisher in order to make a once-dead franchise profitable again.
So what's good?
>you feel like a thief, stealing whatever isn't nailed down and skulking about trying to avoid detection.
>It's almost entirely in first person, save for a couple places, which harkens back to the first 2 Thief games.
>The city is quite large, which was a missing aspect of the 3rd Thief title.
>Lots of weapons/items to use, which a modern game would obviously have.
>RPG elements add a progressive element to the game, making you feel like you're improving as the game moves on.
>The world has a dark, shadowy forboding feel do it, so I feel like I'm in the world of Thief. Wonderful graphics/atmosphere.
>Lots of random places in the City for you to break into and do your thieving tasks, which was practically missing from Thief 3.
>TRAPS! About time!
>Thief Vision is kinda cool, I guess... but it rips off the Batman games.
>Dodge mechanic is kinda cool, if you A) practice at it and B) aren't in an enclosed space, which you will be nearly all of the time.
>When you steal an item, you immediately get gold for it rather than taking it to a fence, so that saves on time/effort, I guess...
But there's a lot to dislike...
>Erin is pointless, pointless, pointless, pointless, pointless, pointless, pointless, pointless, POINTLESS!!!!!!!!!
>None of the original voice actors are present, not even the guy who played Garret!
>Light Gem has been greatly simplified to just 3 levels: hidden (sort of), kinda hidden and visible.
>None of the original factions are in the game! No Hammerites, no Pagans, not even the Keepers, the very group Garret was once associated with! WHAT?! Not even Heartless Perry! (there's an Oxheart Perry in the game, but he's just some faceless schmuck you steal from in a mission)
>Story is WEAK! The ending is TREMENDOUSLY DISAPPOINTING!!! One of the worst endings to a video game I've ever seen!
>You don't take your stolen goods to fences and get paid. Instead you're instantly rewarded when you steal something, which may simplify things, but it takes away from the whole theft aspect of dumping your ill-gotten goods to a shady underground thief consortium.
>AI is, at best, predictable, and at worst, buggy. On plenty of occasions the guards would be walking along when they suddenly start spinning in place! This gives them 'omnivision' and you can't get past that area without distracting them somehow.
>Missions are very linear with little infiltration variety, and the side missions are microscopic in comparisson with almost no variety to them at all. You could literally run through them in a couple of minutes, tops, and sneaking through them would add about 5 minutes or so if you know what you're doing. There's even one with NO PEOPLE AT ALL!!!
>Some missions have a 'no escape' design, i.e. once you pass a certain point you can't return the way you came or leave the area without going through the entire mission. Good job at that whole 'open world' feel, Eidos!
>No dagger. All melee is with the blackjack, so you can't be a ruthless murdering jerk.
>Flash grenade blinds you as well as the enemies!
>The old eye that had sorta-night vision and could telescopically zoom in on things? GONE! Replaced with 'Bat Vision' that reveals stealable objects/interactives. Total ripoff of Batman.
>While opening drawers and cabinets in realtime is realistic, why is it that everything is empty unless it has one valuable thing inside it? Do people in this world just not put anything into drawers unless it's monetarily valuable?
>Other than 'special' items, the things you steal are stupid/pointless. Pens, ink wells, perfume bottles, ASHTRAYS! F___ING ASHTRAYS!!!
>The mace-thing Garret uses to climb stuff... completely pointless. Coulda been replaced with parkour and natural agility.
>There's no main threat. The game is basically 'the government is bad! fight the powah!' Well, there's the thief-keeper guy, but he's about at much of a concern as a fly that SOMEONE ELSE swats.
>Garret has been reduced from a snarky sarcastic slickster who just wants to make a living into a brooding emo loner who involves himself in things 'because he has to', i.e. Batman.
>The girl who you're after the whole game? Replace her with a puppy/kitten and you'll actually have more attachment and drive to save them than you will for this b*tch you're required to 'save'. That is until she turns on you in the typical Hollywood fashion. *SPOILER*
>The original dialect, i.e. 'Taffer' dialogue has been replaced with common swears to make it 'edgy'.
>game has a bad habit of hanging, i.e. you're walking along and it suddenly freezes for 5-10 seconds to load areas/textures, and I have a 6-core CPU and 2 7970's. Inexcusable.
>most of the weapons you're given aren't used unless you don't give a lick about stealth, which defeats the whole purpose of the game. Reminds me of the Tenchu games...
>Even when completely hidden, the baddies will still find you just by being in front of them long enough, which betrays the original games outright.
>the map is so confusing and very poorly designed. What looks like one huge area is actually divided into sections with no indication at all as to where 'doors' to the other areas are located. Sometimes you can go through doors or alleys, sometimes you climb through windows, sometimes you climb ropes... and you can't tell the difference between a window to someone's home and a window to a whole other part of the map! Shameful!
>You can't set your own map markers. While having the game provide you with mission markers is nice, being able to set your own markers would be really helpful.
>You have to find important people first (particularly suppliers) in order to have a map marker for them appear. This may be 'realistic' with people you know nothing about, but wouldn't a thief, whose stock and trade is thieving, already know where thieving suppliers would be located? Thief 3 was better at giving locations than this game.
>Finding people who can provide you with additional side missions is entirely by luck! If you find them, they get an icon on the map, but the game gives you no other clues on the whereabouts of other mission givers, so be ready to scour every inch of the map looking for them all.
The only ones who should play this game are those who've never played any of the previous Thief games or anyone who's looking to have their stealth itches scratched. Were you to have no prior knowledge of the series, or if you could somehow tell yourself that Eidos Montreal didn't do any research and decided to make their own Thief-like world from the ground up, you could play this game and get lost in it for a while. If you've played ANY of the previous games, you might be entertained for a bit, but the omissions and betrayals of the original games will constantly pound at you like a 2-year old hitting your head with a squeaky hammer.

Impressive strategy game. You command either the Soviet or German forces on the European eastern front of WW2. The game is accurate to history reagarding the sequencing of Stalingrad, and a perfect way to carry out the battle as you may seem fit. But remember the game is just that: Stalingrad with surrounding skirmishes, and nothing but that.
The combat is comparable to Civilization V's: hexagons with finite movement for units. The main difference between Unity and Civ's combat systems, however, is the logistic behavior. Units have supply gauges that change with the availability of resources, toggled by supply line efficiency. Of course, if the enemy captures a section of your supply line, it will not be efficient for you! So a main component of the game's objective is supply line management, a category of logistics.
One might think that this game is simply strategy combat, and therefore boring. Within an hour of gameplay, that person can testify otherwise. The dynamic weather/landscape and intelligent AI kept me engaged for sure; the enemy always has something brewing in the pot. You can notice its strategy, often focusing on your weak and vulnerable units to find a path to your supply line. Other times it makes deliberate retreats when you do that same thing to them. It's truly captivating.
If you are interested in a microcosm of Civ V's combat and then some, this is the game for you. Nothing daunting, just casual strategy fun.

It's kind of like Sam and Max mixed with Majora's Mask with a dash of the investigative moments of Phoenix Wright. Your job is to witness a murder, take note of who does it, who dies, how it's done, and what YOU can do to stop it without getting DIRECTLY involved. The solutions are usually easier than you might initially think, but the act of realizing "Oh, THAT'S what I have to do!" is where the victorious rush comes in. One murder required me to screw over the perpetrator in a way that left me laughing like a gremlin, which is always fun.
PROS:
+Fascinating series of murders that tie in well to the victims' personalities and pasts.
+Lovely art style
+Fantastic music that swells at the more tense moments
+Gloriously dark sense of humor
+Bittersweet ending
CONS:
-Your character moves rather slowly, making running throughout the mansion a bit of a chore
-The flaming doors that you can't pass get a little old the further you get into the game
-It's fairly short - I was wishing to have more murders to solve/prevent.
-(Nitpick) Characters look better... WITH their masks than without.
BOTTOM LINE: A brief but great experience, mainly carried by characters with a surprising amount of depth behind their words and actions.

If you enjoy matching games like Bejwelled, the zombie theme, and moderate difficulty levels, then you should really enjoy this one.
The aesthetics are nice, the different zombie types and character models have a decent amount of detail. The different item/environmental hazard effects are good, and the setting (urban) is repetitive but still slightly different for each section. The music and sounds are good, but I usually play with all of the sounds muted and use my own - especially since the random quotes from the characters can get annoying when you've played this game for a while.
The learning curve is minimal to moderate - you have to completely surround zombies with units of the same color in order to kill them. The tutorial is very helpful and an appropriate length. The ability to hit ESC and replay a "block" (there are 3 Acts, each having 5 levels with a certain number of blocks within) before you are about to lose makes the game very, very easy; however, if you have a decent enough reaction time, you really won't have to resort to this. Personally, I only found the 20-level survival mode to be slightly difficult.
Besides campaign mode, there are 3 survival levels (20, 10, or 7 levels respectively) you can play. When you kill a large number of zombies and/or "chain" combos by having your survivors set up so that zombies are killed consecutively, items will most likely drop. These items can be things like a sniper shot, bombing run, molotov, etc. You can hold and carry over 3 items, however, items that drop will stay at the bottom of the screen until you progress to the next block. One useful item is the armor vests, which will turn a horizontal line of up to 3 survivors into "armored" units. These units can take one zombie hit (they'll revert back to their original color), and count as a rainbow (all) color.
There are 4 unit colors - blue, orange, pink, green. Later, a special zombie type will require you to use a specific color to kill them, and this adds to the difficulty; however, you can always save and use items specifically for these enemies. There are 3 other zombie types besides the regular enemy, and 3 bosses (one at the end of each Act). In between blocks, the story is given in the form of text on the streets/ground - the story is average, but is still nice to have.
There are also environmental pieces you can interact with, which usually glow red/white. Examples are gas tanks, garbages, etc. Red hazards usually help you by killing an area of the game map; and white items can yield items, more zombies, or nothing. On the side/background, lingering zombies can slowly walk to and join the game map. Periodically, red x's will indicate incoming zombies that may drop/dig into play. If you take too long to kill a zombie, it will eventually attack a nearby character, turning it into a zombie. In survival (and the last few levels), the zombies have a shorter attack cooldown, and being slow can cause you to easily be overwhelmed (and lose).
For any achievement hunters, many of the achievements for this game are easy to get, however, there is quite a bit of grinding for the zombie kills (5000 and 10000) ones. There is an exploit for this, if you cannot be bothered to do it the regular way, but that will still take a bit of time.
Overall, the game is a nice match-style game, and uses the zombie theme well. If you are interested, give it a try.
Recommend.

Seeing quite a few negative reviews I was hesitant to try this simple game. Is it a total war? Well.. Technically yes, but only at the bare minimum of comparisons. Is it a good game? Yes for a simple slightly more advanced "facebook" style of game, it is.  Is it worth all the negative reviews? Well that depends on if you were ignorant enough to go in expecting a Total War Attila style facebook game or not. If you don't like Facebook games, you won't like this. It's a good game to just manage when you're bored, or sitting waiting for something on your mobile.
Alot of reviews are claiming this is just another usual facebook game with nothing new. Obviously they didn't spend any longer than a few minutes in the tutorial. There are quite a few interesting things in this game.
Of course it is a pay to win setup, as all facebook like games are, however that doesn't mean there aren't alternative ways to getting gold. There are 2 currencies in the game, Gold and Silver. Gold being special currency to buy advanced soldiers or upgrades for soldiers. The main way to get Gold is through paying money. Silver is used to buy everything else, and is gained through Blacksmiths, Markets, etc. ingame by waiting for the timer to loop like most facebook games.
This doesn't mean paying Gold is the only way to get gold however. Linking several Taverns together can net you some Gold, as well as Mining. Mines can uncover Gold deposits as well. Chopping down tree's and uncovering ruins can also net you surprises including Gold. Completing Quests and Objectives will net you Gold as well.
There are other unique features as well, such as being able to raise and lower the land, fill land in, or use mines to dig land out gaining Dirt. Or simply raise and lower it. Why would you want to do this? Besides being able to sculpt the land to your liking for cosmetic reasons, there is water on the maps. Dams can be made to stop water flow, and make usually unuseable land, useable and buildable.

The battles are pretty basic. With special skills gained from the churches you build, your soldiers are lined up 3 x 3. Like most Total War games, the basics are there. Swordsmans vs Spears, Spears vs Horses, Horses vs Archers or Swordsmans.
Choosing the correct time to charge as well nets you bonus's.

I mentioned this can be compared to other Total War games at the very basic and most minimum. The only real comparisons are the fact that soldier types are rock paper scissors at the basic like other Total War Games, and that you are essentially building up multiple towns to upkeep your armies... yea.. not really much comparisons, you can still argue it's not a Total War game at all, and I wouldn't say you are wrong. This is a facebook game however, so expecting more is lunacy.

I have to agree with other reviewers. This game has very little, if anything to do with the Total War series, apart from its name. This game is nearly identical to other pay to win phone games, where you do something, and then wait for it to be done, or pay for it to be done faster. This type of system is ridiculous on ANY PLATFORM, let alone PC. Why companies continue to try to extort their fans with this sort of trash is beyond me.

Holy crap is this game great!
My party consisted of:
A Fighter - Main tank, dealt mega damage, and could take a lot of punishment. He got a nifty throwing axe in Chapter 4 that worked like a boomerang. Making him decent at ranged combat.
A Palladin - Secondary tank, had a few off heals, could cure disease but was mainly a melee fighter, almost as good as the fighter with a few utility moves to compensate. Got a helmet in Chapter 5 that enabled him to cure paralysis once per day, god damn was that useful.
A Cleric - Also used as an off tank, heavy armor, clubbed things with a morningstar, and had such an array of healing and support spells, some later spells enabled him to temporarilly fight with the effectiveness as a fighter.
A Theif - used for scouting, trap detection and disarming, basic ranged attacks, but could also duel wield and do mega damage if attacking an enemy from behind. He got a lot of gear that increased his ability to hide in shadows, so by chapter 5 he was in a permanent form of semi stealth, which made it so enemies rarely noticed him and made his attacks all the more powerful.
A Ranger - Crapped out the most damage with the longbow, and later a crossbow. She could also do great melee damage later on when I found a powerful halbred for her. Both her and the theif could not take much damage though.
A Druid - Had a large array of offensive and healing spells, one of the most useful characters. Got a ring in Chapter 6 that enabled her to cast extra level 1 and 2 spells.
That is what I love about the classes in this game, they are so versatile that you can fight in so many ways. There is so much strategy to the game its unreal, and the gear you get just feels so empowering for your party. Even then the game is hard as nails, and I wouldn't have it any other way.
There are a few annoying things about the game though, most of the bosses are immune to ranged weapons, forcing my Ranger and theif to go melee, no matter what the hit rating was of my ranged weapons, the arrows just had no effect. Even if I used the special arrows that you can only get my killing certain enemies in the game, which you have to get identified before you can even use them; those are still not good enough to harm the bosses. And the last boss is immune to magic, so many boss fights just come down to either tank n spank, or kite and spank as most of the bosses will rip even my fighter a new ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ if you go toe to toe with them.
Bare in mind, the game does not explain a lot of what the stats do, so let me just warn you:
If you want anyone to do melee combat, they need dexterity to incrase their armor, or else they will be too easy to hit.
Many ranged weapons have a strengthing requirement, make sure your ranger has atleast 15 strength.
In anycase, the game is freaken great, and it will take a long time to beat if you've never played it before, I played the original until my computer broke when I was on chapter six, which took maybe 70-90 hours to get there, but I beat in now in 28 hours or so because I knew so much about the game.
Replayability is moderate, there are a million ways to play, but its basically the same game over and over.

Fun game if you prefer combat over roleplaying when it comes to D&D.  Lots of replay value, customizable icons and a remarkable number of strategies you can employ to win battles based on your characters' classes.
Far from perfect though.  The pathfinding is truly awful.  Basically every second of the game you''ll be herding your party like an electric sheep dog.  If you hate escort missions, don't play this game: your dimbulb team will walk over traps, into clouds of gas/webs/firestorms, you name it.  And that's when they aren't wandering off alone into mobs of hungry monsters.
Gear has to be micromanaged, so when you're not a sheepdog, you're an accoutant tallying arrows and bullets.  I bet out of the 250+ hours I've played, a solid 75 have been spent sorting and selling gear.
The expansion pack is totally worthwhile, expanding your spells and gear significantly.  Make sure you do every subplot, and buy every good toy in the expansion before going after the last boss, though: once you beat it, it's a one-way trip back.
It's also very linear, and with one notable exception, you'll never have to go back to any completed dungeons.  Essentially, to enjoy this game you'll need to love carefully crafting characters and using them to inflict all manner of pain on the hordes of enemies in your way.
Which I do.

I love RPG games, and i missed this one when it originally came out because i use Linux exclusively. When the EE came out on Steam with Linux support, it was my chance to finally play this classic.
After spending 2 hours on carefully building a team, setting the skills points, selecting classes/races; i die on the first battle. Obviously this game is hard and shows you how much games have changed. Even modern games which try to capture the spirit of the old RPG games (for example, the excellent 'Legend Of Grimrock') don't come close in difficulty level compared to Icewind Dale.
If you're looking for an easy game, you're not going to find it here. But it doesn't matter, it's a good game and soon enough you'll get the hang of it and slay monsters and solve puzzles as if there is no tomorrow (hang in there and keep trying). But you need to get into it for sure, after i came out vacation i had to get into it again, because i got defeated at the first battle. Modern games would be much more forgiven.
Somethings could be better, for example pathfinding is not always optimal, this causes a character to choose a really weird way to get to the marked destination, sometimes with undesirable effects. And don't be fooled with the word 'Enhanced' in the title. It is still very much the same game as it was originally released, no rerendering of the gfx/movies for example, doesn't make the game look that great at certain points.
There are no issues with the game on SteamOS, not once did it crash, slow down or give problems.
It is a massive, great game and you should check it out if you are a RPG fanatic or a retro game player.

If you're looking for a strong competetive or skill-based experience pass over this game.
As someone with lots of hours on games like Overwatch, League of Legends, TF2, Battleborn and other class based objective games this game just really isn't up to par in anyway.
Its visually very pretty but from the short time I've spent playing the game that's about all it has going for it. I would have played it more but the gameplay and matches were just unbearable.
Group up or die is essentially the style of the game. You physically can't take objectives on your own because they do more damage than you and no amount of skill or accuracy will allow you to survive a direct 2v1.
Most reviews I see boast of the games high skill cieling but really each character has such an overloaded kit that chaos takes over and any sembelance of skill is thrown out the window.
Measurement of skill in this game is following your team around and landing attacks, that is all.
The games that went badly were because everyone split up and ignored objectives and there was nothing I could do about it.
The games that went well were just grouping up and killing the objective monsters until we won as an unstoppable gank squad.
I played a lot of a character that was described as a high mobility assassin, but all of his mobility was tied to the same stamina bar that every other character has and abilities with incredibly long cooldown. For an assassin his damage was very low even landing most of your abilities on squishier characters and his mobility was hindered by a stamina bar that depleted even after jumping or utilizing his basic attacks.
I have decent net and there are no ping trackers in-game so I wasn't able to tell what the problem was, but every ability and attack had about a full half second delay to a whole second, this is not okay for such a high mobility character and does not work at all with the combat system of the game.
There are so many things going on in a fight that its incredibly easy to just fall victim to the chaotic nature of the game and die very quickly with no indication of how you died until you read the death logs.
This game would benefit so much more if it were simplified but the combat system is so overly complicated and characters have so many annoying mechanics that unless you've sunk about 50 hours into the game you'll have no concept of what other characters can do and therefore be unable to counterplay appropriately.
This game is hilariously unbalanced and over-complicated in so many regards that any kind of competetive atmosphere goes out the window.
It works well in some aspects though.
The combat is very fluid and its pretty straightforward for a MOBA. It works well as a fun, free experience to jump and and have a bit of fun with. The character I played mostly had a really genuinely interesting mechanics where he lunged when attacking immediately after a dodge, but again, the lag, lack of polish and mindlessly chaotic gameplay just renders any kind of creative gameplay useless.
If you want a similar game with more polish, play Battleborn. They play almost identically except battleborn's match progression makes much more sense and has much more rewarding gameplay.
fun to play sometimes, but that's about it, if you're looking for anything deeper than flashy combat and constant spam-fests, do yourself a favor and pass on investing much time into this game.

I DO reccomend this game however, this game is FAR from perfect in my eyes. There are a decent amount of bugs. A lot. Be willing to deal with that. There are a few times where the bugs in this game have made me ragequit. Expect this game to play like FC3, but not nearly as smooth. There are a few new vehicles, helicopter/hoverboat that i have come across in my first ten hours, but they're not super helpful. They seem a little gimmiky.
The bugs that i have encountered have been mostly random deaths. The AI sometimes will just plow through you walking down the road. Sometimes if hit head on by AIs while in a vehicle, i find that even though the vehicle and I are on full health, you might die. So be careful where you're driving.
Another AI bug i found is that friendlies will not always move out of the way enough like in FC3. Such as accidentally slamming into another friendly vehicle could get you chased after by a truck with a machine gun. That being said the only way to un aggro them is by escaping, because killing them lowers your karma.
The Karma system is interesting, positive actions gain +150xp and negative -50xp. The gun for hire tokens seem kind of useless, (especially on a stealth playthrough), but that being said i haven't touched the story that much, and they may be more useful later.
The wildlife, is ♥♥♥♥ing annoying as hell. I've upgraded my healing bars twice now and the stupid eagles (which you can shoot down, but good luck when you're playing with a bow) come out of nowhere and attack you, knocking your health signifigantly. It does really increase the difficulty, Im playing on normal and it really pisses me off.
The radio towers, the puzzles are decent, but not super intuitive, so you might need to try it from some different angles. Nothing too terrible so far.
Enemy ai is much more observant than FC3, stealth playthrough seems a little more difficult, but makes the gameplay a little more engaging.
The story seems ok from where i stand. I have played around 3-4 story missions and it doesn't seem to drag me in like FC3 would, take that with a grain of salt though, because I have barely touched the story. The first couple missions really engaged me, so I'm hoping the story will improve soon.
The content: There seems to be a large amount of gameplay content, like FC3. The wanted and path of the hunter quests have been replaced with alternatives, and there seems to be a little bit of extra on top of that.
Map is huge, autodrive was added, but I wouldn't reccomend using it much unless you're playing without fast travel as the ai driving tends to mow down people in the way.
All in all it seems like a pretty good game, I'm enjoying it even though i've barely skimmed 5-10% of the content. Like Far Cry 3 i'm sure ill get my money's worth.
Runs smooth on high ultra settings with R9 270x and Fx6300 + 16gp of ram (my aprox 700-900$ build) so most decent desktops should be able to handle it.
UPLAY IS CRAP, RUN THIS GAME WITH UPLAY IN OFFLINE MODE IF YOU ARE NOT USING ONLINE, GREATLY IMPROVES FPS + PLAYABILITY.
Ultimately if you liked FC3, you'll like this, though im still hoping for a few patches to improve the couple bugs i've found.

It would be odd if they weren't there but they are also not that interesting right at the moment. Kind of like the books in an Elder Scrolls, they might be useful but not all of them. They add, but not very much. But the overall impression along with the characters which you are to save add quite a bit to them all.
There is no voice-acting but that might actually be a plus as most things are easy to interrupt and avoid the repetition. No need to hear how many arrows you have taken to your knee as it were. The music is in the background most of the time and changes with the game events. The main music is kind of upbeat but non-descript as well. It's kind of reminds me of an old 8-bit midi track that some games had to fill the soundscape and it reminds very much of Ms. Fischers Murder Mysteries main theme, which is kind of fitting.
The normal sound follows the same as the music. Effective but sparse for the most part. It's not bad quality, just not a lot of sounds.
The artstyle is very stylised and cartoony. Very distinct which helps with the feel of the game as well. It is very reminicent of Monkey Island and such click based puzzle games where most things were exaggerated to a degree.
The one bad point is the interaction. Extremely reliant of left click to get into stuff but also get out of dialogs which will get annoying quite quickly as you move by right-clicking on the screen. You kind of expect to move right away but a dialog is up and you don't notice it all the time. A trvivial thing but the one annoyance actually.
Not a lot of options are available but what is there suffices. This game could easily be playable on a tablet as well.
Overall this game is a gem, well worth the price in my opinion.

Mini Metro is a minimalistic optimization game where you are presented with various symbols representing metro stations with commuters represented by smaller symbols. Your job? Connect the station with coloured lines representing metro lines,  allowing metro trains represented by rectangles to transport the commuters to their desired destination. You lose when too many passengers are waiting on a station. And that's it!
The art style and the soundtrack are minimalistic and very clear: the game uses bright colours and clear shapes so you can clearly see the current situation. Meanwhile, each event produces a sound: communers appearing make a *plop* sound, each train plays a section of a sound file when travelling, and a ticking noise is heard when too many passengers are waiting. I was pleasantly surprised that this didn't make a cacophony, but a pleasant almost melodious arrangement of seemingly random sounds. It is very relaxing, and now you don't only see that you made a good working metro network, but you can hear it too!
The difficulty lies of course not in solving the puzzle, but in optimizing it. Everyone can make a good functioning metro system, but creating a well optimized network requires clever thinking combined with trial and error. You can compare your scores to that of the world and friends, giving you the motivation to perform better. This game is easy to learn, but hard to master.
Tl;dr: Optimize a metro system, represented by minimalistic vectors and melodious sound effects. Buy it now, because a price increase is coming soon! (see news)

This is a really fun puzzle game. It's basically a block-matching game. Zombies and citizens are in a grid. To kill the zombies, you you need to swap citizens among cells until you surround the zombies with people of a single color. If you take too many turns, the zombies spread to neighboring cells. You'll also occasionally get attacked from the sides of the grid. You have a variety of special weapons - sniper rifle, grenades, air strikes, gas masks (which create wild card citizens that serve as all colors), and others. The game is not hard, and the campaign is short (~2-3 hours), but the levels are randomized so there is plenty of replay. There is also a survival mode, though it is just like the campaign but without the ability to continue on if you lose (you have to start over in survival mode, but can replay a level in campaign mode). I wish the game got a bit tougher on later levels, or for a way to increase the difficulty, but the game is quite a lot of fun as is. Overall, a really nice and fun game. I highly recommend it.

1.- Magic Duels is an interesting Game of Magic The Gathering that also provides the excitement of opening new boosters.
To get the boosters, you earn coins fulfilling part of the story of the Multiverse of Magic, from the Magic Origins expansion and so on.
I really like how the game is presented, although there are several important differences between this game rules of deck building of the paper card game.
2.- Except for the basic lands, you can only have 4 cards in the deck with the same name if they are Commons; 3 cards if they are Uncommons; 2 if they are Rares; and 1 if it is Mythic Rare. In the proper card game you may have 4 cards of the same name in the same deck.
3.- The good thing about purchasing boosters is that you will get, at most, those many cards, so you can manage to get a collection complete if you purchase enough boosters. One booster is 150 coins. You will not get too many copies of a card and you will not get to use them. From Time to Time, there are boosters "on sale". So dsaving coins for those moments can be useful. They cost 1000 coins on sale.
4.- The way to earn Coins is interesting: Complete the story mode.
Then, you have several quests to do while playing games. you get a new quest each day if you have completed the ones you have, so you can play each day to get more coins.
You can also play the computer to earn small amounts of coins.
If you win online against another human opponent, you get more coins than against the AI; so that encourages facing people online.
5.- You are usually paired with people with the same rank you have (Rank is obtained by the games you win minus the games you lose online), so you should face people with the same skill as you have. You can also play against your friends.
6.- There are many cards and you can make interesting decks, although not that many. And Tribal decks are not that much supported.
DOWNS
1.- The bad thing about the game is the VERY HIGH requirements for a card game. It does not require that much 3D acceleration or anything, I can only play this game on my main computer, but not on my laptop. It crashes. It should require less power for this kind of game, from my point of view. Why does it need that much memory? For the AI?
2.- This encourages new Deck Building skills, and that is interesting in some way.
3.- It is quite slow to obtain the boosters. You have to win coins each day from the quests, you usually have too many quests if you do not play each day. The booster sale is not that often, and it does not promote getting coins more often, because you do not know when you are going to get boosters cheaper.
4.- Most of the Times, quests require to play online. But you have to play in a non-optimal way to fulfill those quests.
5.- The pair system only pairs you with people in the "Win - Lose" ratio, even if they have many cards and you are starting. So it is difficult to balance.
You have to WIN to get coins. That does not encourage playing online. Sometimes, you get so many lost games you do not want to keep playing.
I believe that, to encourage playing with anyone, you should get coins even when you lose. If you win, you get 30 coins. Then, if you lose, you should get at least 5 coins. That would encourage you to play with other people online, people you do not know.
Also, playing with a friend of yours is not encouraged. You do not get any amount of coins for either wining or losing against your friend.
I believe that you should get some coins from that, from playing with your friends. Get, at least 5 coins each. And, if you wih another 5, making a total of 10 coins. Then, you should play a game with your friends 30 Times to get a booster if you do not win any game. THIRTY TIMES. Ok, maybe that it seems that it is too much Time to get one booster... But you earn something from just playing your friends, and that encourages you to play the game, and get more friends into the game.

This is one of my favorites games. It seems complex at first, but it's essentially just a race to 100 points.  There's a great mix of melee and ranged combat that works fluidly.
TIPS:
- For new players, treat 50% missing health as your gauge for backing out.  You'll slowly learn how long you can stay in a fight.  Staying alive > Getting kills.
- Team fights can get chaotic; If you find yourself in the middle of a big throwdown, learn to back up a few steps so you can parse it and look for opportunities to re-engage.  Don't just stand in the middle -  die - and then say "this game sucks, it's too chaotic."
- Most of the heroes have relatively high skill caps.  I thought Wu sucked when I started playing because nobody ever did well with him, then I got out of super low MMR and realized that he's actually devastatingly good and can carry.  It's best not to base your impressions of a hero on only a few games.
- The only negative reviews I see on here stem from people complaining that they don't meet the system requirements for 6GB free RAM (which is a strange thing to leave a negative review over).  If you're one of the less fortunate folk who hasn't been able to get a computer or RAM in the last 8 years, just remember that Windows uses part of your RAM so you need *more* than just 6 to actually meet the requirement.
Anyhow, I hope this game gets a large, dedicated user base, because it's got that "something" and deserves it.
Oh, and please don't summon both neutral points on Sanctum Falls unless your team is really rofl-stomping.  It's hard to hold both, man.
GG.

Here's my thoughts on the controversy over Total Wars Battles: KINGDOM.
After playing about 1 hour of the game, I got through the basic tutorials and I eventually made it to around level 4 or level 5. From there, I unlocked a few new buildings which gave me access to new units, the ability to build homes on sand, etc. Although I do sense some browser game elements along with a mesh of facebook game elements, this game does have potential to be something good. There are some p2w elements within the game, such as how you need Gold to buy specific troops and gold can only be gained at small amounts (5-10 gold per special quest, 1 special quest per level) or you can buy a whack-load of gold very quickly. This tends to be a bit tedious as there are wait times for just about everything in the game. (Getting stone, chopping wood, etc.)
Pros:
- Fairly nice graphics
- Hexagonal grid works well
- Good potential to be something different
- Can gain gold without buying it
- Interesting, seemingly non-linear missions system
- Somewhat interesting water system, flowing water, crops only grow near water, dams can block off water steams and water destroys buildings.
Cons:
- Major P2W elements (you must spend gold to buy ______ troops)
- Long wait times for most things in the game
- Microtransactions
- Feels like a browser game
- Gaining gold without buying it is tedious and takes a long time
- Limit to 9 troops per battle, with extremely small troop sizes
- Doesn't feel like a total war game
- Total War engine isn't evident - it's more turn-based
- Wait times, even in combat.
- P2W elements in combat (buy mercenaries before combat, other upgrades)
Overall:
Overall, I would rate this game a 4/10. It does have some nice elements but if you look at the list above, there is just too many cons for the game to seem good in my shoes. If issues like the ones above got fixed, then the game would be more interesting to me and I would most likely spend more time on it.
Do I Reccomend It?:
No. This somewhat feels incomplete, like a browser or a facebook game, and those styles are extremely evident with the microtransactions, small battles, wait times, and many other features that just make it feel like you're playing a cheap browser game where you have to wait 8 hours to mine a single block of stone (where you'd only get 10-40 stone...) It is also quite difficult to level up, considering how the starting area (unless it's not a pre-generated starting area) is surrounded by water and forest, you get little options to expand and thus little options to build buildings which are required for majority of things. Although you might start with 150 gold, it tends to run out. With the one hour I played, I was already down to 84 gold because I was so tired of waiting.

The missions are nice and varied but sometimes leave very little leg room for stealth without arresting or killing guards. One puzzle I hated in the game was the pipe puzzle in the second mission. I love this game, but it should be made clear that it is NOT a strategic or tactical combat simulator like games such as Panzer General. I think that many users dislike the game because they have mistaken it for a tactical combat simulator, which is just not the case.
It is instead an Operational warfare simulator where the destruction of enemy units and control of the map are less important than creating and exploiting breakthroughs in enemy lines, disrupting the enemy's and protecting your own supply lines and sparingly deploying your reserve forces. Because the game focuses on the Operational level of warfare, it is entirely possible to win a decisive victory without destroying the enemy's army if you pay attention to maneuver and logistics. You will actually be punished for throwing your forces into a full blown assault in an attempt to destroy their forces or control the entire map because the AI prioritizes logistics and maneuver, and because the scenarios have a very short turn limit.
I recommend this game but do NOT mistake it for a tactical combat simulator. This is not Panzer General; winning takes careful planning and attention to factors that other strategy games downplay or leave out all-together.

The units are set up in predetermined positions. The AI is extremely passive and just reacts to the very few outcomes you can do by scripting. The AI stands absolutely no chance in a fair fight. The only reason why the campaign is so hard is because you are usually extremely outnumbered, you have a limited number of turns to get your objective and the supply line mechanic is designed so you are at a disadvantage as an attacker. Combined with the extremely closed scenarios, the AI just reacts to your predictable movements with strategies scripted by the designer. I frankly do not find any fun in that.
TL;DR This is not a strategy game. It is a puzzle game where you play against the level designer to beat a level in a few turns with an overwhelming disadvantage. If you like that and pretty graphics, try this game. Otherwise stay clear of it.

The heart of this game is stalking the guests (victims), and staff (killers) through the mansion to piece together the story of each murder, and then using what you learned to find the one thread which unravels each murder. The Ground Hog Day time-travel mehanics (or Majora Mask mechanics if you perfer gaming metaphores) are brillantly implemented to give you all the time you need to investigate, and all the trys you need to stop the murder in time, while adding a undertone of tragic futility, as you hear all the murders you couldn't prevent because your time is spent saving the one (or pair) you are working on now. The game's use of sound is brilliant, with music that is both catchy and encapsulates the timing and feeling of the murder(s) happening in that corner of The Sexy Brutale; and each murder carries with it its own sound that echos throughout the house, like the first gunshot,
. The game is relatively short, and my 12 hr play time, is probably about as long as you could spend, seeking out every collectable and reading all the lore, while piecing together as much information as possible as early as possible.

The Sexy Brutale is a stylish murder-mystery, wrapped with point-and-click-esque puzzles (sans moon logic) and crossed with time travel.
The mansion is filled with over the top furnishings and rooms, both fantastic and occult. Quite fun to just explore, especially if you're a completionist who has to touch all the things. I loved following the different guests and staff around, watching them interact and eavesdropping on their conversations. The world is very well built and written, and the way the character paths weave together over the time line make the time travel quite satisfying. Most of the murders are creative and fun to foil, some are just weird.
There are a few rough patches. Some animation and audio transitions are jerky/sudden, and during my second play session some of the rooms took a noticable two or three seconds to load. The main character also controls poorly when near walls or obstacles, or even doors. Usually the game is generous enough with time that it doesn't cause you to fail, but it can be frustrating when you're trying to get to a closet to hide just before someone enters a room. May take you out of the experience for a moment, but the game will pull you right back in.
Played with a 360 controller. Beat the game 100% in a little over 8 hours. There's an alternate ending if you collect all the things. Decent length for the price, and doesn't overstay its welcome.
Recommended if you like a good story and some light puzzling.

this game is lovely.
it's very straightforward: you're given a city, and you're in charge of keeping it connected. there's nothing else to it. no complicated sim elements, no bulky unnecessary content or visuals. everything from the gameplay to its cutely metro map-inspired visual style emphasizes cleanliness and efficiency. overall, mini metro is extremely minimalistic, but it doesn't feel lacking. it makes for an oddly soothing, hypnotic experience. it's just you and your lines.  the recent addition of musical elements (courtesy of disasterpeace) improves it dramatically - the music builds organically from the ground up, gradually becoming more and more complex as your lines become busier and busier, and it creates a nice sense of progression.
though the core gameplay never changes much, it does serve a healthy amount of challenge, with each successive city being more busy and populated than the last. over time the game becomes a bit like watching a machine at work, making slight adjustments, waiting for the inevitable moment it breaks under pressure. for those who prefer darker color schemes (like me), a softly-colored night mode is included, and for those who are colorblind, they've included a colorblind mode as well. everything you need to know about how to play can be understood through visuals alone, and the only thing you need to worry about is how long your design will serve its purpose. if you enjoy peaceful puzzle-ish games with a bit of strategy, it's definitely worth the price.

First off is the choices when making your character, some sound normal and make sense such as Dual Weilding and Blacksmithing, and then you find the lower end which are just as useful if you know how to use them, Tourist where your camera flash stuns surrounding enemies and the fungal arts, unleashing the power of mushrooms within the dungeon.

Its a bejeweled style game where you get to kill zombies. You win by turning all the avalible tiles into survivors.

Essentially it is a flash game, an enjoyable variant similar to the Candy Crush type game if you've ever played it, that will provide around 5-20 hours of fun.  Graphics are functional, while the soundtrack is very basic.  At its core its a puzzle game with strong elements of strategy.
The premise of the game is that you have to surround groups of zombies with the same type/coloured survivor to remove them from play.  Survivors consist of the soldier, the policeman, the cheerleader and the thug, each providing a different voiceover when a group is cleared which is quite nicely done. There is one 5 act/20 level campaign which should take you around 5 hours to complete.  The learning curve is very well done which is good as there is only one difficulty setting.
A range of harder zombie types provide the bulk of the challenge is this game as you progress through the campaign.  The simplistic gameplay is added to with environmental hazards that can kill off survivors or block more of them from coming through to reinforce the game board.  Additionally you can have up to three power-ups to blast away groups of zombies when in a tight sequeeze.  There are around 6/7 each individually adapted to provide a unique destructive effect when used.
There are three additional survival levels that you can play if you get hooked. If you are an achievement hunter it should take you between 14-20 hours in total to get the last one, as its a grinder!
Overall Id say the game does what it says in the store page.  Its nothing special but it is enjoyable if you like this sort of game, as I have.  If you are a hardcore gamer then this is probably not for you unless you like a dose of casual on the side!
