A very accessible text adventure. If you've played any text adventures before, you won't find this one very difficult. It's easier than Eric the Unready (do play Eric the Unready if you haven't yet). Unlike Eric, Thaumistry is text only, except for the map.
The game doesn't overload you with pages of text, there are no long expositions, no long dialogs, no books to read, not too many active objects.
The story probably isn't its strong point. The character has his "Nothing is the same anymore" moment on page one and sets out to perform bizarre tasks right from the start. It doesn't feel very plausible, and the story doesn't go anywhere after that. Progressing through the game just means gaining access to new areas.
It doesn't have any particularly memorable character stories either, and I wouldn't exactly call it a comedy adventure. It's often amusing though. And always quirky.
There are a few subpar puzzles, like fetch quests or obtaining common everyday objects in very contrived ways.
Mostly you'll need only a very basic set of actions. Move, look at active objects, talk to NPCs about them, cast spells on objects/NPCs/yourself. How to use an item with something is almost always obvious.
On the upside, that means you don't struggle with the parser, and the level of difficulty is never high. The downside is that you get much less of what is unique to text adventures. Using the items just as well could be done by clicking a "use" icon. Several graphic adventures use spells as a way to extend the "verb list". But puzzles where you have to get creative with what kind of action is required (hold your breath? stand on one leg? turn your clothes inside out?) -- that's what makes text adventures special.
But there are still plenty of puzzles where it's really enjoyable to instruct the player character what to do.
The game is very good with its "diegetic" hints, and also it has a separate multi-level hint system.
The tagline for Thaumistry can be "A text adventure how you remember them, not how they were" (unless the other guy has already copyrighted that blurb).

No spoilers. My cred: I've been playing text adventures for long enough that back in the 1980s, I used to wait for Infocom to come out with new games. This is a new game by one of the authors who worked for them then. I backed it on Kickstarter and I've been playing it off and on for a week. I moved the install over to Steam just recently, so don't let steam tell you I've only played it for 5 minutes.
For an old Infocom fan like me, this game feels like coming home. Thaumistry is fun, funny, and at times infuriating (in a good way). I've put the game down when I've been stuck, walked the dog, and come back to a new way of thinking about it that got me to the next hard one.
I love the dialog and the humor; the characters feel well-drawn and comfortable. You're interacting with interesting people, not just the environment.
Highly recommended.

This is my first text adventure game, and I'm loving it! Thaumistry has no graphics (except a map): you type commands, and read the response. And just like with a book, you use your imagination to visualise characters, locations and events. It feels very refreshing in 2017. And it's guaranteed no pixel hunting!
Thaumistry has a well written, tongue-in-cheek story involving crazy inventions, conspiracies and magic - with sparks of tasteful humour here and there, and reminds of Legend Entertainment games. The puzzles are logical and balanced. It's tailored to modern gamers in that it's much more forgiving than old-school adventures - no random threats or deaths, no one-time opportunities. Overall it's a friendly, delightful experience that I can recommend to anyone who enjoys the adventure genre and is not afraid to type and read. Or just curious to discover how a computer game can be entertaining and captivating while having no graphics or sound.
Also, although game is tagged as Indie, it is written by an industry veteran Bob Bates. So while being an independent production, it's by no means amateurish.

The thief series have long been my favorite game series of all time.
Thief - The Dark Project was a masterpiece with a wonderful engrossing story to it, that starts small but then drags you into an epic conclusion.

Thief - Deadly Shadows is a bit different than the first two games, but I loved it. It brings all the games together, making a full circle. Kind of Zen/taoism touch to it all, how the balance shifts due to your actions through the games.
Sadly... the fourth game, this one, is a letdown. I haven't played through it yet, I admit, the story might be as good as the other games. I don't know yet.
But then there's the reason I haven't played through it yet... and that's the controls for starters. It's made for consoles. you have few buttons to press, and those few buttons are supposed to do everything the keyboard did in the earlier games. If you for an example want to crouch behind some crates, your game might decide that you want to climb up on them instead. the same button is used for everything.
Needless to say, if you want to hide, standing on top of well lit crates is a bad idea.
I could live with that, but then there are annoying bugs aswell. I play the game as a thief not an assassin. There's a bug that requires you to kill people to move on. I hope it's a bug, because you're in a vent. someone passes below you, and you get the option to kill them. if you don't, they move on, and you can't get down from there. Ever.
There are more gamebreaking bugs I've found aswell, but i've ranted enough.
I want to love this game, but I can't.

I know at the time of writing this I only have a few hours of gameplay into Thief, and I will probably add more over the next few days, but there are things about this game that I find let down lovers of the original Thief series.
To be honest, I'm not even sure why this title was "rebooted" another time after Thief: Deadly Shadows.  The answer is probably out there, but I'm just too lazy (and I honestly don't care) to find it.
The first thing I noticed when even starting this game is that it feels very much more like a reboot... far from the roots of the originals.
The world, although they would like you to think it's "open" leads you by the hand down the garden path.  Practically every Thief game prior to this one is very much more "open" to exploration than this one.  In those prior installments, you could at least wander around a bit... find other marks, find other points of interest, find little nooks and secrets that you can explore and loot to your heart's content.  This game seems very restrictive by comparison.  You can't even jump up on walls or buildings.  For a minute there, I was wondering why the game would practically highlight everything that could be climbed or held onto, but now I guess I know why.... because you can't jump up on, climb, or hold onto just anything anymore.  It even tells you to "find a way into <insert building here>" but then puts a freakin' marker on your screen to point out exactly where to go.
The next thing is the dialog.  I honestly can't explain why developers think that adding profanity will somehow lead to a better game.  The originals managed to do excellent without it.  Personally, I find it a sign of a weak script if the developers think they have to sprinkle curse words throughout just to give it some body (which curse words alone can't do).  It's getting that I have to ditch my computer speaker system and start using headphones because NOTHING is able to be played around my family anymore.
That said, one of the tiny nitpicky things I found was that the lipsyncing sorta was hit and miss at times.  There were a few points where the dialog was done but the character kept flappin' their gums.  Other times, the character would speak but their mouth would not move at all.
However, even having said all that, I'm still finding the gameplay OK... yes, merely OK... not stellar, not horrible... just OK.  I do have to admit that the environments and texturing are well done and they actually are one thing that shines in this game.  At least it still LOOKS like a Thief game.  But even then, it doesn't fix what's wrong with the game.
I wish Steam had a sideways thumb... I don't really want to recommend this game for anyone who came from the original Thief series, but it's not entirely a bad game as such.  It's just not as immersive as the previous games.  So, that being said I will still give it a thumbs up, but it should actually be pointing sideways.

There have been a lot of mixed reviews of Thief, and the main reason for this is that this reboot had a LOT to live up to. The original Thief and Thief 2 (and Thief 3 to a lesser extent) are classics. They DEFINED the stealth genre for years. So any new stealth game is immediately compared to them. And if your going to reboot the Thief franchise, and claim the Thief name, you need to be amazing to get past the nostalgia of those who remember the originals.
Does this Thief, live up to the old Thief? In atmosphere - yes. In the charachter of Garrett - yes. In the fun of exploring the city, and doing side missions - yes, yes, yes! In the story and plot - yes and no. Are the controls and gameplay perfect - unfortunately not always. Is it as much fun as the originals - my subjective answer - YES.
The game captures the feel of a city on the brink of revolution perfectly, Garrett is dark, brooding, witty and a delight to follow. Exploring the city and completing side missions are an absolute joy. The storyline is dark, (even disturbing at times), and assumes a level of adult comprehension to understand. The story is best enjoyed if you do your best to read all the documents in the missions, as so much of the extra details are included here and not told out front in people talking to each other or even in the cutscenes. The game assumes a level of willingness to explore and find everything in order to get the most from it, but isnt that why we play Thief games anyway?
Not everything is perfect though - the linking between city sections is annoying, the crippling of the rope arrows to only being able to be used at designated points is a step back, and the single button for swooping and jumping is at times frustrating. Also, if you like someone to hold your hand with story telling (i.e. no loose ends, no implied outcomes, no subtle finishes (such as wet footprints) which are not pointed out with a big sign to bring them to your attention), then you probably wont enjoy the way this story is told. But if you enjoy subtle story telling then this is a great version of it.
I highly recommend this game. I found it extremely enjoyable, and can say that if you take the time, explore the world, find all the notes, discover the secret areas, and piece together the takes you find, then you will discover yourself immersed in a gameworld that feels alive, and with a dark adult fantasy setting that is rare to find these days in the gaming genre.

I really don't get the Hatred of this game from the Community. Amazing what Nostalgia can do huh?
First off, let me introduce myself. I've played every single Splinter Cell title so far. I have played Hitman: Blood Money and Hitman: Contracts. I understand how dangerous names can be when attached to games; especiallly if the name is that of one of the most successful game franchises in history. I personally didn't like Splinter Cell: Conviction and Hitman: Absolution for the same reason, though on several replays, I actually kinda enjoyed them.
I have never played a Thief game before though, even though half the gamers on earth seem to have. I have read enough reviews about the game to prepare me to, so to speak, turn my brain off during the story cutscenes and treat the game as a series of increasingly difficult and structured challenges.
Having done so, I can honestly say that I enjoyed the story and the setting in this game. The game literrally reeks atmosphere. The story so far has given me a reason to continue playing, which is all I ask for games (Not that more effort in that department is unappreciated). Garret himself seems to be a pretty likable character, with appropriate quips at appropriate times.
The best thing about the game is that it accomplishes what it set out to do in the title. The stealing part of this game is absolutely fan-tas-tic. Everytime I spot some loot somewhere across the map, I feel like: "That's mine". This feeling isn't exactly quantifyable, but it is the one thing about this game which I have not felt in any other game I've played so far. Except maybe Deus Ex.
Which then leads on to the second thing about the game which is great. I felt the need to explore each level within the game, looking for loot to pick up. The game rewards you with loot. That's it. You get a small reward for completing main and side missions, obviously, but its a lot smaller compared to the loot you get through simple exploration. There's also some special, rather beautiful looking loot in some areas of the game which are an absolute joy to get.
Level Design in the game sometimes remind me of the first few Splinter Cell games. You're usually provided with a reasonably-sized area guarded by a couple of NPCs with multiple ways of getting past them. Some levels are much bigger. Without spoiling the game, there's one level within the game which is bigger than any level I've seen in any game which I've played so far.
The design goals seem to put Challenge and Atmosphere above things like Choice. Solutions to each stealth puzzle do not seem to be particularly organic. The smaller size of each level lead to greater challenge through intelligent placing of guards. Thankfully, the Quicksave mechanic in the game removes most of the frustration usually caused due to such designs.
Garret is not a particularly atheletic character by modern game standards. He cannot navigate ledges. He is sometimes quite snotty about which bits of furniture he would and wouldn't climb onto. I recommend turning the display for contextual button presses on to remedy this issue. Pretty soon though, I was able to recognize which areas in the game I could navigate and which I could not. It's quite simple really.
This gets me back to another often-repeated complaint about the game which really grinds-my-gears. The complaint is that the game world is absolutely littered with pathways you cannot use that are differentiated from other pathways you're can use in no meaningful way. Pathways in the game world were incredibly clear to me. Traversals in the game feel like platformer challenges (eg. there's only one way to get up on the roof of that building). Once you start treating rooftop traversal in that fashion, the game becomes much more logically structured.
AI in the game is not particularly bad. Throwing noisemakers and using Water Arrows acheive the desiered effect. AI reactions are convincing enough to enhance gameplay. Though, a couple of times, I did wish they were better at searching for me once I rasied the alarm. Bottomline: they get the job done. I assume, however that the AI was much worse at lauch and was patched to this level.
The city is one more part of the game which I think deserves special mention. It is designed quite well. As soon as you figure out the means of traversal about the city, you feel a bit like Garret, i.e., the way he can just sprint around the city and get to where he wants to go rather easily. It seems to be divided into several smaller segments, each connected to other segments by a loading screen. Note that its not a linear connect-the-city-segments network. There are several means to get to a particular segment from another segment. This city was not designed by the lead designer of Hitman: Absolution (that game had some seriously awesome doors).
Overall, the game is more than the sum of its parts. If you buy this game, I recommend not paying really close attention to story. Explore a lot. Read every letter that you find in the game world. Enjoy the game for what it is, and not what you want it to be. You might be surprised by what you get out of it. I sure was.
To the developers: I have no clue of how you feel right now, having put so much effort into making a game that was badly rated (in my opinion) mostly due to nostalgia. You guys have done a pretty good job with the game, which so far, has robbed over 25 hours of my life. I'm sorry about what happened to you guys. Don't lose hope. Make a new stealth game based on the ideas you had when you developed Thief. Just don't name it Thief this time.

So I have not played much of this game yet. I can say I was very excited about it when I first signed up and when I got my beta key. Now, well... not so much. The game itself is a lot like a mix between civilization and clash of clans with the battles being much like the total war battles: shogun except without all the buildings you can build in battle. So as a sequel to total war battles: shogun, it is ok. As a Total War game, I do not recommend it.
Positives:
Graphics and terraforming are pretty cool
The simple strategies may appeal to less serious strategy gamers
I enjoy building my town
The tutorial is helpful
Although they are simple, microbattles are pretty cool to see because each unit is fighting against individual enemies
Orders are cool as well as they give different bonuses to units and orders are attainable from churches
Not everything is pay to win as some things you cannot use gold to get
Login is good and not buggy (which tends to happen in many beta games)
I like the medieval feel of the game
There seems to be an unlimited amount of "workers" or "builders" which is great!
The peasant and craftsman systems (your workers) seems useful.
I enjoy having to build multiple barracks and stables that each field one unit as this makes the town bigger and cooler-looking.
Negatives:
Fighting is too simple (see above positives)
Not at all what I expected from a total war game
More or less pay to win (strong units cost "gold", aka money) You can of course earn gold but it takes a very long time (I guess it makes sense because the game will be free so they need a way to make money)
Some buildings are not available until much later in the game
Upgrading buildings seems to take a lot of grinding and upgrading castles (main building) seems to require having multiple castles and towns and having a certain amount of buildings in your town.
I personally think that the lord (basically, you) should be more customizable as right now there are only a few different options for hair color, bacjground of profile, etc.
So overall this is a fun game although not at all what I expected or wanted to play from Total War,
I RECOMMEND IT TO JUST PLAY A CLASH OF CLANS/CIV MIX BUT NOT AS A TOTAL WAR GAME!
and because of the pay-to-win aspect of this game, I will not recommend it overall.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

What can I say about Dungeons of Dredmor? Well, for one, it's one of my favorite games on Steam. I could spend countless hours playing character after character looting and exploring dungeon after dungeon, and never have the same experuience twice. I'm not kidding. Not even once have I found a room exactly the same. Talk about Procedurally Generated.
The joy of this game does not come in any one category. There are parts of this game that, if anywhere else, would make for a horrid experience. The combat isn't that complicated, but it can be difficult, and it's always fun. Wearing a piece of clothing or weilding a specfic weapon doesn't effect your outward appearance, only adding (or subtracting) from your stats, so for people who like to see your appearance change it's a problem.
Dungeons of Dredmor isn't like most other games out there, as you may have already guessed, but it is ery entertaining, and hours will go by without you even knowing it. There is so much content in this game, and of all the hours I have played so far, I have not made it past the second dungeon. Is this because it is difficult? Maybe a little. But the real reason is that the game is really really big. Too many different types of monsters to count, as many weapons, more items than I've ever seen in a game, and interesting text on everything.
This game has a lot of pop culture references and stuff like that, so for people who hate that with a passion, this game probably isn't a good choice for you. But if you want a game that can make you laugh, that's really fun, and can let you waste away hours of your life, then this game is perfect for you.
I highly reccomend this game.

I keep comparing this game to Panzer General, the real classic. Definately it's much simplier, but still realistic. You won't have your core units anymore, nor alternative history scenarios (you just have to keep winning). You can't also chose from different types of units - you only have infantry (may be mechanized), cavalry and tanks (although you can add specialized step to each like artilery, enginers or recon). There is no fog of war and the scenerios are much shorter (half an hour is usually enough). No navy and air support is very simple. Still I like the game for the way how supply routes are treated. This is a thing that Panzer General really suffered at. You had to supply your units sometimes, but rarely, so they didn't really feel bad in encirclement. Here it is different. Your units even after one turn of lack of supplies will suffer and after second turn they can't attack. After third turn they are so easy to kill. Therefore in you offensive you really aim at a blitzkrieg - fast advance and encirclement. This adds another dimension which PG lacked. I would really like to play PG with this system implemented, but would I still find time for that? I'd like to play this alternative histories with my core units again - this game lacks a lot of stuff compared to PG but still is extremely fun to play!
Definately if you loved PG and don't have time for it's enormous scenarios anymore - this is a game for you. Highly recommended. If you have time - why not install original PG on dosbox instead? If you never tried PG and you like hexes then you will be probbably amazed with the game.

This review is spoiler-free and doesn't discuss any particular puzzles or scenes.
So far I'm about two hours into the game, and judging by the number of unlocked achievements and score I've reached the halfway point. Of course, the game will likely ramp up the difficulty later on, so I don't expect to be done in just another two hours.
It's been a very entertaining experience until now. This is a pure text adventure with real, honest-to-goodness puzzles in it. It's not an interactive story with just some minor decisions points, nor is the focus on storytelling. If you've played earlier Legend Entertainment titles, like Spellcasting 101, TimeQuest, or Eric the Unready, you'll have a good idea what to expect.
The descriptions are well-written and interspersed with humor that doesn't go over the top with breaking the fourth wall. There are some references to past works of Bob Bates. I particularly enjoyed talking to a certain Mr. Vettenmyer.
The puzzles have been logical so far, and the way they are designed invites the player to experiment. I don't think there are any dead ends. I managed to die at one point, but the game gave me ample warning beforehand. There is a hint system in the game, but I didn't have to use it yet, as I never got stuck for more than a couple of minutes. The world gradually opens up and doesn't overwhelm the player with a lot of new locations at once.
The (typing) interface uses standards that were establish during the Infocom days, with handy abbreviations like "x" for examine and "g" for repeating the previous command. Moving around can become a bit cumbersome if I need to go from one location in Manhattan to another. As far as I know, there is no fast-travel option, probably because skipping rooms could circumvent events that are supposed to happen if the player passes through.
Naturally, there are no graphics, except for a diagram that shows the current room layout and a (weirdly stretched) map of Manhattan. Sound is completely absent as well, but if I wanted to, I could just start a music player in the background.
All in all, this has been a pleasant two hours. The central game mechanic (which I won't spoil here) offers interesting ways of interacting with objects and people. At one point, I found a method to learn details about the NPCs, which added more depth to their personalities. That was a nice touch.
If you are looking for an old-school adventure game that harkens back to the days of Infocom and Legend, Thaumistry gets my recommendation.

I've played all of the Far Cry games so far, and this is the most polished yet. All of the Far Cry games essentially throw your character in a large, sprawling "sandbox" map with gorgeous vistas, and allow you to defeat enemies in any way you see fit. You can choose which weapons you want, and how you approach your targets. Will you silently sneak into the base? Will you be a sniper and pick them off from a distance? Will you throw mines and bombs into the camp? Will you fire at them up high from a helicopter?... or will you just go in guns blazing, driving a truck through the gates, and start blasting everyone from a mounted turret? The choice is yours!
There are plenty of vehicles left lying around for you to use: cars, boats, bajaj (the three wheel motor taxis), gyrocopters, hang-gliders (a Far Cry staple), and this time around, even elephants! In this release, you can even fire from inside vehicles - a very welcome addition.
The map is huge and there's plenty to explore - although the scenery feels a bit samey. You can even climb up and swing on ropes in the installment of the game. You'll find loot all over the place, herbs to make medicines, prayer wheels to spin for karma, and evils masks to destroy. There are wild animals to hunt, and skin to make holsters to increase your carrying abilities. There are radio towers to climb that expose more of the map. There are also letters scattered around the map - finding them will give you the backstory, and could prove to help guide your choices later on in the game. In short, there is a lot to do!
As a sandbox game, it excels when random elements that come together to create memorable experiences. A few times I'd be camping outside a base quietly to spy on the enemies inside, only to be attacked by a leopard and blow my cover. Then the entire base came out to get me!
The story campaign will throw you a few curveballs including "stoner" levels (you'll see), and sidequests into the mystic world of Shangri-La which are absolutely gorgeous (If not ripping off Elder-Scrolls Oblivion just a little bit!)
In addition to the story campaign, and an arena deathmatch.... so you are not spoiled for choice here in gameplay options. There is co-op multiplayer as well, so you don't have to play alone if you don't want to.
To top off an impressive package, there is a map editor.... so when you've completed the game, you can design your own outposts, or play hundreds of other players' maps off the internet. You'll be getting endless replay value from this alone.
The "Escape from Durgesh" DLC is yet another take on the sandbox, and is a supreme challenge for expert players. Much more replay value than the yeti DLC.
Now the negatives:
If you've played previous Far Cry games (particularly Far Cry 3), this game isn't going to feel much different. In fact it almost feels ripped right off, with a new coat of paint and a new antagonist. It only has some tweaks on the already successful formula. In addition the story feels tacked on an a bit hokey and stupid. The plot only starts to become coherent towards the end - but you might be initially turned off by it. I certainly was. Perseverance is recommended, even when it gets stupid and you have some mad idiot NPC right up in your face, invading your body space and rambling on about some nonsense. FarCry 2 at least tried to be intelligent.
If you overlook the story though, the game is really great, especially if you haven't played a Far Cry game before.

I cannot recommend this to any determined completionist. Bugs will be plentiful.
To everyone else, this is a pretty solid game.

Explosion sound not going away: happens when you die and restart just afterwards, sound can stack many, many, many times; fix: exit the game
Unable to jump: happens when you die or restart in an area where you aren't allowed to jump; fix: go into a no-jump area and come back out
Immediately hit as mission starts: just happens sometimes; fix: get onto a small ledge (like the island of a roundabout) such that the limo is angled and restart
If you can deal with a few annoying, unfixed bugs, then I recommend this. Determined completionists will probably find the bugs too annoying to deal with.
EDIT: After completing the game, I can say that completing the game is definitely very fun. But, unlocking all of the achievements wasn't so fun. Compellingly frustrating gameplay, a relentlessly catchy soundtrack, and hilariously cheesy fully acted cutscenes guiding you through a story of loss, love, strife, and a spinning limousine.
I was originally going to nominate this for the "suspension of disbelief" award in the Steam awards 2017, because after the first tutorial mission, you just take it for granted that yes, the car rotates. There's no attempt to explain how or why, but you just go with it as you attempt to negotiate the streets to complete missions, progressing the amusing storyline, or simply exploring to pick up special tokens, including bundles to cash, that allow you to mod your limo, or buy real estate around the city.
Ultimately, however, I nominated it for the "Whoooaaaaaa, Dude! 2.0" award, as that seemed far more appropriate overall.
For such a cheap and seemingly simple game, there's a surprising amount of depth, and even replayability - while you only need to mosey your way through any story quest once to progress, you can go back and repeat the missions as much as you like to attempt to improve your standing against your friends and globally.
All in all, I'd say that this game is fully worth the price even if it's not on special. When it's on an absurd sale, it's truly a no-brainer.

It crashed partway through picking all of the completely obvious "what you are supposed to do" options. I do not have depression but from others' descriptions, this is nothing like it. Maybe it was a programming error that made it crash, my computer, or done on purpose. I don't care. Does that make me depressed now? That's pretty much what this game taught me.
This game lets you choose how to make your life suck more. Sadly, playing Depression Quest was not one of the options.
This game is nothing like how actual depression is or how you'd logicly deal with it.

I saw the many negative reviews, read some of them, and knew what was going on.
The fact that there are so many negative reviews is indicative of the very thing that is one major cause of depression. Things like complaining that not all reaction options are available or criticizing an allegedly clichée or cheesy or pretentious writing or how the music is dull and repetitive shows a horrifying lack of empathy, a refusal to see and experience a situation from someone else's viewpoint or to even look at it; upset of not being handed an I-win-button, annoyed by discomfort, by the game tucking at things suppressed in the psyche.
I suspect that at least some of the negative reviewers who claim they have been through depression themselves and this game is no good for portraying that have merely been 'successfully' conditioned into dealing with an uncaring world by becoming more uncaring themselves. Because if you can't stand the pain anymore, you have to become the pain. But everybody just becoming as egotistical as the society that affects them is not a solution, but the very expression of the problem.
The general emotional experience of the player character I can relate to a lot, while many situational elements not, but that doesn't matter. This game is art in that it conveys an experience to the player, so I guess it is only natural that all those who are fueling the problem will not like it. This game is like an enactment, through showing the mirror and making people attack their projection or focus on evasion points.
Its high negative review ratio is like a representative for the emotional distance and uncaring that depressed people might have to deal with every day.
It was easy for me to come to a very positive outcome, just by choosing what I would have chosen in a real situation, not even the supposedly strongest, ideal decisions (if there even is one, because everything has up- and downsides). The player character is relatively lucky. Other people might not have any of the potentially positive influences available to tap into. For them it might be a losing game from the start. Unless we change that.
If the negative critique points mentioned are your grievances, too, then take that as a sign that you are not helping with your current mindset. And maybe I shouldn't even say mindset, because as this game conveys quite well, the mind alone cannot solve problems of the heart. It is caring and the will to make an effort for a better world, to accept inconveniences based on empathy for others, that solves such problems. And that requires a certain amount of courage. Not so much the kind of courage that makes the warrior wield a sword against a foe, but the kind that makes him cut out a parasite from his own body.
All the mind can do is square the circle, but it can never remove the sharp edges that cause injury.
True caring hurts.
That's why it's unpopular.

It pains me slightly to give this a negative review, but it just isn't quite good enough to justify the endorsement. It's not a bad game by any stretch, more mediocre than anything else - and it may appeal to big fans of the genre. I just wasn't particularly taken by it.
Although it's an iOS port, Tiny Troopers is far from poor and the dev deserves props for patching in some additional control options to overcome teething problems left over from the initial touch interface. A small thing, but always good to see. The game plays exactly as you think a casual topdown shooter would - you track through relatively simple missions with your squad, following along in a string ala Cannon Fodder. Unfortunately, the similarities pretty much end there.
There are quite a few missions in the game and trying to get three stars on all of them would be a reasonable challenge by the standards of an iOS game, even if they do get samey fairly swiftly. The zombie defense mode is also surprisingly fun for a little while. The graphics are cute and the humour is there, at the very least - the game seems reminiscent of the 3D Worms games in both senses.
Ultimately though, what's fun for an hour or two quickly gets stale - and that's why I can't recommend this game. Worth picking up on sale if you like the genre, but otherwise this one seems destined to clutter bundles. Tiny Troopers, I salute you for your efforts but I can't banish Cannon Fodder from my mind. Perhaps that's on me and I shouldn't be making so many comparisons, but that's just how I feel. It suffers the same fate as the numerous Lemmings clones have over the years - even today, they suffer by comparison to the original.

Let's get this out of the way: I'm a Thief fan. I even liked Deadly Shadows (that was supposed to be bad or at least worse than the previous installments), a lot, played so much my disk cracked. And since the serial code was not accepted by steam (no wonder, old retail purchase) I'm stuck without it. And honestly, that game was better than this.
Now, before I start my rant, I will obviously mention the best parts first.
-Visuals
This is maybe the only strong point in the game. The city, the graphical effects (I personally like parallax occlusion a lot) are gorgeous. End.
Yes, that's all I like. I couldn't even get into the story much so that might be fine if read in a book. In the game however...
So the bad comes now.
-Optimalization. The game looks gorgeous at first glance. However even on high settings, it's surprisingly ugly close up. Textures look washed out a lot, especially on lower settings - while even on these lower settings the game eats the resources of my rig like it's nothing. Loading times are... out of this world. Someone mentioned I should get an SSD - then I mentioned if I need an SSD to play a game properly then I might not need that SSD after all (since that game is not worth buying/playing). Also SSD for playing?
Let me make it more simple - compared to how much this game needs to run, it's ugly. Essentially means it's not optimized well. Maybe a bad port. Who knows, who cares...
-Characters. I miss the old times so I'm not going into this one since I can't produce an objective opinion. Wouldn't be so bad I guess?
Now on to the more technical/gaming parts.
-World.
While the design revolves around the "usual" dark/steampunk/middleages theme, which I love to Hell and back, the maps are incredibly tight and empty. Others mentioned this before me but even compared to Deadly Shadows, the city feels empty even when it's supposed to be in chaos.
-Lack of freedom.
The game feels scripted. My hand is constantly held and even when I'm supposed to plan/decide how I want to approach a problem, the "use rope arrow here" object, oil miraculously spilled at the right spot etc. will kinda give it away that the game does not really think I'm capable of making my own choices. In fact you are not even allowed. Feels like Assassin's Creed with the perfectly well placed haycarts under the "Leap of faith" spots. Not that such a cart would save anyone but I would so move one just a little. Preferably right before the guy lands...
What's worse than the deliberately provided "paths" is that you rarely have the opportunity to deviate from those.
I never could get into playing this particular Thief game much and they can easily blame that on Dishonored. That game does a so much better job that it hurts. The moment I see it on sale I'm buying it on steam - should stop bothering others to let me in the seat and play it :) I already completed that game and I can safely say it's worth buying - so much better than Thief that it hurts.
Freedom of movement, gorgeous, painting like, big maps (sometimes really huge), barely any loading.
If you are thinking about buying Thief, go and buy that instead. Seriously. I tried this game before getting it and while hoped it got patched to the point it might at least get rid of it's ridiculous engine problems, I had to be disappointed (hence the low game time on steam). Do as I did if you must try it and play at a friend's house a bit :) Then do the same to Dishonored and you will see what I mean.

I've played all of the Far Cry games so far, and this is the most polished yet. All of the Far Cry games essentially throw your character in a large, sprawling "sandbox" map with gorgeous vistas, and allow you to defeat enemies in any way you see fit. You can choose which weapons you want, and how you approach your targets. Will you silently sneak into the base? Will you be a sniper and pick them off from a distance? Will you throw mines and bombs into the camp? Will you fire at them up high from a helicopter?... or will you just go in guns blazing, driving a truck through the gates, and start blasting everyone from a mounted turret? The choice is yours!
There are plenty of vehicles left lying around for you to use: cars, boats, bajaj (the three wheel motor taxis), gyrocopters, hang-gliders (a Far Cry staple), and this time around, even elephants! In this release, you can even fire from inside vehicles - a very welcome addition.
The map is huge and there's plenty to explore - although the scenery feels a bit samey. You can even climb up and swing on ropes in the installment of the game. You'll find loot all over the place, herbs to make medicines, prayer wheels to spin for karma, and evils masks to destroy. There are wild animals to hunt, and skin to make holsters to increase your carrying abilities. There are radio towers to climb that expose more of the map. There are also letters scattered around the map - finding them will give you the backstory, and could prove to help guide your choices later on in the game. In short, there is a lot to do!
As a sandbox game, it excels when random elements that come together to create memorable experiences. A few times I'd be camping outside a base quietly to spy on the enemies inside, only to be attacked by a leopard and blow my cover. Then the entire base came out to get me!
The story campaign will throw you a few curveballs including "stoner" levels (you'll see), and sidequests into the mystic world of Shangri-La which are absolutely gorgeous (If not ripping off Elder-Scrolls Oblivion just a little bit!)
In addition to the story campaign, and an arena deathmatch.... so you are not spoiled for choice here in gameplay options. There is co-op multiplayer as well, so you don't have to play alone if you don't want to.
To top off an impressive package, there is a map editor.... so when you've completed the game, you can design your own outposts, or play hundreds of other players' maps off the internet. You'll be getting endless replay value from this alone.
The "Escape from Durgesh" DLC is yet another take on the sandbox, and is a supreme challenge for expert players. Much more replay value than the yeti DLC.
Now the negatives:
If you've played previous Far Cry games (particularly Far Cry 3), this game isn't going to feel much different. In fact it almost feels ripped right off, with a new coat of paint and a new antagonist. It only has some tweaks on the already successful formula. In addition the story feels tacked on an a bit hokey and stupid. The plot only starts to become coherent towards the end - but you might be initially turned off by it. I certainly was. Perseverance is recommended, even when it gets stupid and you have some mad idiot NPC right up in your face, invading your body space and rambling on about some nonsense. FarCry 2 at least tried to be intelligent.
If you overlook the story though, the game is really great, especially if you haven't played a Far Cry game before.

This is a game in which you play a limo driver whose limo literally spins around.  In the daily course of your job, you meet a mechanic who promises to help you get into the big leagues, fight a French-Canadian ripoff, hallucinate a talking skeleton, and fall in love with a spotaneous young woman.
If that doesn't already sell you on this, I don't know what more I can tell you.  I guess I'll try, though.
Georgio Manos is a revolving limo driver who comes to the city of Roundabout in 1977 with the intention of acquiring fame, fortune, and hopefully very little nausea.  The game plays like a combination of Kuru Kuru Kururin and Crazy Taxi - your goal in each mission is to drive the passenger to their destination via a series of checkpoints while collecting coins, mowing down pedestrians, and avoiding obstacles.  It's simple to learn, challenging to master, and a whole lot of fun to watch.
As the game progresses, you unlock more powerups for your limo, such as the ability to slow down time, reverse which direction you're spinning, and fire traffic cones out of your trunk (no, really).  Between missions, you can explore the overworld to purchase properties around town, collect cash bundles, attempt special mini-game challenges, and unlock new horn noises for your limo.
The gameplay is plenty of fun on its own, but what really makes Roundabout stand out is the story.  Every cutscene is presented as something out of a cheesy 70s B-movie, mixing stock footage with actors so amateur that it's actually pretty adorable.  Georgio Manos never speaks a word, but it's not necessary - the facial expressions she gives the passengers is all the communication you need.  The eclectic cast of characters ranges from a nervous guy going out on a date, to an anarchist art enthusiast, to a hallucinated talking skeleton.  (Seriously, I can't emphasize the talking skeleton enough.)
My one major complaint is that trying to 100% the game can be incredibly frustrating.  Each mission has a series of bonus objectives which range from fairly doable (collect every coin) to nearly impossible (complete the mission in under 12 seconds), and picking up all the collectibles in the overworld is sure to drive you insane.
Additionally, the game is fairly short - you can probably complete the main story in just 6-7 hours.  But this is a more minor complaint, because the game fits everything it needs to into that time.  Any longer, and it would probably just feel like overkill.
All in all, Roundabout is a great game with a quirky sense of humor and a whole lot of creative heart.  If you're looking for an indie experience that unapologetically goes balls to the wall and never takes itself too seriously, this is for you.

Admirably, but again the game isn't trying to win any technical awards so good performance is a requirement at this point. The music and sounds are about as good, with nothing to complain about nor speak of in particular. Of course, the cutscenes are great at the end of the day they'll be what you remember most of all.

If you're not looking for a puzzle game, for a short game or for a game that's not very challenging, then I'd recommend avoiding Roundabout.

At $0.99 (or cheaper if on sale), you can't do much better for a retro-styled arcade shmup. The game plays much like Asteroids except you can't cross the borders of the screen and the enemies only come from the left and right sides. The game starts off with simple asteroids to pick off and gradually introduces enemies of increasing complexity as your score increases. Initially, there is only one ship to play the game, but as you gather coins from random drops from destroyed enemies, there are seven additional variants to unlock (but only in order). The late game ships are generally more capable, so most players will probably be sticking with Ships 6-8. I personally prefer Ship 8 because it has the best capabilities, but at 100 coins to unlock (in addition to needing to using coins to unlock the previous ships), you'll have to play for a while to get it.
There are a multitude of powerups to collect during regular gameplay, but I think most will find that only a few are actually useful and the others are quite terrible. Now, it is tempting for me to just write off the offending powerups, but it does make for interesting gameplay in that you are trying to dodge enemies and bullets in addition to powerups that are likely to ruin a good run. It can be agony waiting for the right powerup to appear sometimes though (especially near the start, I tend to start over if a powerup I don't like appears first). After you get a powerup, you have it as long as you don't run out of ammo. It can be really difficult to conserve ammo with auto-fire enabled, but quite simple to do firing manually.
Two of powerups have rather odd behavior though. There is a homing powerup that seems to go after ships you are aiming at (otherwise targeting closest ships), which is fine, but this often means that you'll have a homing shot going after a small asteroid in the distance while completely ignoring actual threats nearby. You can still fire manually with the homing powerup, but it is frustrating to watch the homing shot completely pass more dangerous enemies. The other powerup that I feel has issues is magnet, a powerup that draws in ammo and coins on screen. There is really no need for this powerup in manual firing mode, but the thing I really don't like about it is the lag it seems to introduce with firing inputs (which is hard to tell if it's intentional or not). I have accidentally collided with a number of enemies due to a lack of firing from this lag that the magnet powerup seems to introduce. Though again, this just adds to gameplay in giving me an incentive to avoid collecting the magnet powerup altogether.
Aside from powerups, my only other real gripe is that sometimes the hitbox seems bigger than it should be, but otherwise gameplay is about what you can expect from an arcade shmup styled in way that feels like Asteroids. There are a number achievements with the game that most will find are appropriately difficult. I still haven't gotten the 75K in a single run achievement, but will as I try to improve my high score.
And on the topic of high scores, this is a gripe that is unrelated to the game itself. When I first played the game, the Version 3.00 patch was relatively new and the leaderboards had scores that appeared achievable. However, I recently checked and the top scores are now clearly the work of cheaters. The main way you can tell is that they unlocked all the achievements in the game within an hour (most within fifteen minutes) which just reeks of foul play. On a game worth $0.99, come on, really? Is it really that important to you to cheat to get the highest score on the leaderboard? I mostly play to improve my own score, but it is sad that not even this game is immune to cheaters unfairly getting the top positions on the scoreboard. Unfortunate, but I think most will be able to see where the real leaderboard starts. EDIT: Most recent check has the blatantly cheating scores removed, so at least for a moment there is a proactive effort going on to keep the leaderboard clean.

I was an avid PS Home user since 2008 and see a lot of the spirit of PS Home in Atom Universe (AU). The creators of AU, Atom Republic, previously created content for PS Home, but after PS Home was shut down in March 2015, they asked the community what they should do next and the overwhelming response was to build a new virtual world as a successor to PS Home and hence the idea of Atom Universe was born. Atom Republic had a Kickstarter campaign for the game in April 2015 to help fund the development of the intial release which was successful. Atom Republic has partnered with several former 3rd party developers for PS Home such as Engine Giant, Game Mechanics, JAM Games, PS Talent (of which I am a long time member), and more to come. Patrick O'Luanaigh, CEO of nDreams, was also made the AU team's non-executive director during the summer of 2015. He has referred to Atom Universe as "the successor to PS Home." Since PS Home's closure, many former PS Home developers have created their own game, but Atom Republic is the only one to have partnered with others. The game is developed with Unreal Engine 4 and features amazing realistic graphics and supports cross-play between PC and PS4 with the potentional to be supported on other platforms (Mac, XBoxOne, etc.), including future ones, e.g. PS5. The game will also support Virtual Reality with such headsets as PlayStation VR for PS4 and Oculus Rift for PC. Atom Republic has been very responsive to feedback from its community and IMO done an excellent job with this project. As a reward for my donation level to the game's Kickstarter that I mentioned, I was given the opportunity to test the Alpha version of the game, which I have been doing for several months now. During this time, I have seen a lot of progress made on the game's development as new features have been added and various bugs fixed. The Early Access version was just made available to backers of the project this past Saturday, February 27, which includes a space which we have not seen in the Alpha called Arcade Plaza. Here's a promotional video that shows what the Arcade Plaza looks like:
The Early Access version will later be made available to the entire Steam Community but until then, backers like myself will continue to test it. Whether you are looking for a successor to PS Home or a new realistic social game/virtual world in which to play then Atom Universe is for you. I HIGHLY RECOMMEND THIS GAME!!!

I'll address some comon complaints and list Pros and Cons.
Common complaints
Snipers- Snipers have a very "Soldier Front" feel. They have perfect accuracy. No scope sway. Very fast target aquisition. Can be fired accurately during fast movement including jumping. Can be quick scoped. Instant kill to head and chest and fully tuned will one hit anywhere else (bolt action anyway, semis dont seem to). HOWEVER if you don't like them you can ban them from your lobby. Also they are very satisfying to play as its quite rewarding when you begin to get better with them. Easy to flank or outplay those that use them.
Pay 2 Win- NO! It is not P2W. There is no advantage to buying with real cash other than to have things faster, or to have cosmetics. Buying permanent weapons is expensive, but you dont need them to do well and can easily play well with default or free lease items.
PROs
- Weapon tuning, it is awesome thank you!
- Powers, Skills, enhancments. Very rewarding to use and drastically effects gameplay and strategy. Also theyre not forced on you can simple choose to play in matches that has all or a combination of them.
- Movement. it is not slow or clunky and has a very real effect on your play. you can sprint, run, crouch, jump. No prone and No lean.
- Game modes. Free For All, Team Deathmatch, Domination, Search and Destroy, CTF, Survivor, Duel, Defense. A wonderful variety.
- Not published by Nexxon.
- Daily, Weekly, Monthly, and Ranking Rewards!
- 3 switchable loadouts in game.
- Can do knife fights and pistol battles. Great control over your match settings.
- Quickly see which fights have your pals in them.
- Large maps and Small maps.
Cons
- Permanant Weapons are super expensive about 30 hours playing if you hoard your gold.
- Servers down often though for short times, to be expected and I believe they'll be on it.
- Small glitches like abilities randomly not working or like the hatchet not melee unless you aim at the legs.

Far Cry 4 is easy to dismiss, if you're so inclined.
"It’s just more Far Cry 3!" Well, yes, in a way, you're right. No wheels have been reinvented here: Kyrat, a mountain nation nestled in the Himalayas, is a sprawling piece of land for you to hunt, kill and climb your way through. There are outposts to conquer, towers to climb, a near-infinite supply of valuables to filch.
But this convenient yet misguided shorthand becomes instantly less useful once you actually find yourself submerged in Far Cry 4: This is a bigger, better, braver version of an already fantastic thing and that’s awesome.
So what's new, different and better? A lot of it tracks back to Ajay Ghale, the young man making his first journey home to Kyrat, which he fled as a child during a civil war.
Far Cry 3 got a lot of heat for its reliance on the problematic "white savior" trope, but I found myself far more distracted by the fact that Jason Brody was sort of a chuckleheaded♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Ajay isn't. He's got ties to this land — his father founded the rebel group The Golden Path, which attempts to overthrow despotic king Pagan Min — and he's returned with the noble goal of spreading his mother’s ashes in the country she loved.
Perhaps the best thing about Ajay (and this shouldn't be such a rare compliment in a game made in 2014) is that he actually sounds like a human being. That extends to all of Far Cry 4's characters actually; I cannot tell you what a relief it is to hear lines being delivered in a naturalistic fashion that don't sound like they were squeezed out right before the recording engineer took his union-mandated break. Some superlative performance capture also helps Kyrat's inhabitants feel like real, actual people.
This is true for no one so much as Pagan Min, the stylishly monstrous yin to Ajay's yang. He's plenty evil, but in such a fun, seductive way that I’d be lying if I said I wasn't a little tempted when he invited me to go "tear♥♥♥♥♥♥up" with him in the game's opening moments.
"But … you do get to tear♥♥♥♥♥♥up, right?" I hear you ask worriedly, and let me put those fears to rest. Yes.♥♥♥♥♥♥is torn up. It's torn in multiple directions and with near-infinite variety. If you can think of a way in which♥♥♥♥♥♥can be torn, Far Cry 4 lets you tear♥♥♥♥♥♥in that precise fashion, and probably gives you a unique shotgun if you do it five times.
As I mentioned, the basics from Far Cry 3 are all here. Much like Brody, Ajay can scope out enemy encampments with binoculars, highlighting enemies for elimination and executing a precise, stealthy strategy to eliminate his opposition undetected. Alternately, he can stroll in the front door, ignite his flamethrower and secure an unconscionable amount of overtime pay for the staff of Kyrat General’s burn ward. Both approaches are valid, and both are a singular treat, especially when circumstance forces you to pivot from one to the other.
This is the same loop that Far Cry 3 already nailed so well, but the increased verticality provided by Kyrat’s mountainous terrain helps to liven things up a bit. While you can still sneak around a base’s perimeter to try to gather your intel, you might be able to use Ajay's grappling hook to scale a cliffside and get a perfect view of all your targets.
That grappling hook deserves special mention. In so many games, the grappling hook is a mechanical way of getting from A to B, but it's so much more here. Use it to swing like Tarzan, use it to rappel into an otherwise deadly crevice, use it for daring clifftop escapes; there's a ton of flexibility, and it’s a delight to play with. It’s not Far Cry 4's best new toy (that honor goes to the one-man gyrocopter), but it's a close second.
The gadgets and gizmos aplenty are, of course, ostensibly provided to help you take down Pagan Min, and the missions that form the path to that point are excellent. What they lack in the open world's flexibility, they make up for with variety and pyrotechnics. One minute, you’re scrounging for oxygen tanks in the Himalayas as you hide from enemy soldiers in a blizzard, the next you’re stunting an ATV off an airstrip so you can soar into a plane with your wingsuit.
Straying from the critical path a little provides even more outlandish scenarios for Ajay, like a series of drug-fueled hallucinations with loquacious stoners Yogi and Reggie, or traveling to Shangri-La to inhabit the body of an ancient warrior who bids a spirit tiger do his killing for him. Far Cry 4 is many things, but it is never boring.
If anything, there’s perhaps too much to do. Beyond the missions and side missions, there are side-side missions like destroying Pagan Min's propaganda centers for pirate DJ Rabi Ray and hunting rare animal skins for flirtatious clothing designer Mumu Chiffon.
Then there are more generic side-side-side missions where the people of Kyrat beg you to avenge a family member, rescue a friend or deliver supplies. These are distinct from à la carte objectives like outpost takedowns (excellent) or liberating radio towers (fun, but more mechanical).
And then there are the collectibles: propaganda posters, treasure chests, plants used to make stat-boosting syringes, diaries, letters, masks and probably a few I’m forgetting. It's staggering.
Whether or not that's a knock against the game is really a matter of taste. I’m typically a completionist, but when faced with the utter infestation of collectible icons on my minimap, I balked. Once I had decided I wouldn't be catching them all, they became more distracting than desirable.
FAR CRY 4 DOESN’T NEED TO ARTIFICIALLY INJECT ITS WORLD WITH DIVERSION
The funny thing about it is that Far Cry 4 doesn't need to artificially inject its world with diversion; it's organically being created all around you. Perhaps the most captivating, yet least obvious evolution from its predecessor is the way Far Cry 4 uses roaming soldiers and wild beasts to make the world feel alive. Who needs to go poster-hunting when a tiger and a bear just got into a fight 10 feet in front of you?
These unpredictable threats can be frustrating, like when you turn from your comfy sniping perch to find a pack of wolves ready to tear your throat out. But even when it turned a perfect plan sideways, Far Cry 4's unpredictability did a fantastic job of drawing me in.
It's a world I was delighted to lose myself in and moments after my last confrontation with Min, I was eager to hop right back in and finish all those side, side-side and side-side-side missions I had left hanging.

Even at this early stage, the game has depth, fun, and challenge. The concept of a transportation network game isn't new. Still, the lean abstraction of Mini Metro makes it gives it an urgent Minesweeper/Tetris time puzzle quality without taking away from the satisfying game idea of building an infrastructure to serve people's needs.

As a casual Tales Runner player for the last seven years I wanted to give an actual review for this game of which most of the other steam reviews are not.
Tl;dr: Overall Tales Runner is a very fun game that offers a large amount content for players to enjoy.  It is a game that rewards skill much more than having the best gear. It can be played either hardcore or casually and its microtransactions only offer convenience.
The Review
Tales Runner is primarily a social game. It is a very difficult game to enjoy if you are looking for a single player experience as the game revolves around racing with and against other players. It is also a game that can be played and enjoyed casually due to the lack of a need to maintain gear in order to win races.
The game was originally released in 2005 on its native Korean server and as such has relatively dated graphics when compared to more modern games. The graphics with its anime inspired design, however, has allowed the game to age much better than many of its contemporaries. The game, unfortunately, only supports a 800/600 resolution so if it is not played in windows mode the graphics may be stretched and distorted. I personally would recommend playing in windowed mode as the difference in overal graphic quality is significant.
The game features numerous maps to race in and is adding more with every patch. As such there is enough content that it is rather difficult to become bored with the game. Certain maps, however, are preferred by the community much more than others as such certain maps are nearly completely unplayed such as the animal racing and 20 player co-op maps. There are farms which function like your standard mmo housing system, and a park that features various minigames and offers a place to socialize with other players. There are also various missions for those who are looking to challenge themselves or prove their skills.
Despite what many of the other reviews may say the game is not pay-to-win. All characters and most items are available for purchase using ingame currency that is earned by playing the game. Those items that are only available as microtransactions only offer convienence that may lessen the grind for the ingame currency and experience. There is no gear that is only available for purchase though microtransactions that provides a large enough advantage over the free options for the game to be considered pay-to-win. Despite that I must say that the early grind for in-game currency and alchemy cards is immense but if you are patient and invest in gear that boost your earnings per race the grind diminishes greatly. It should be noted, however, that if a player wants to maintain a large amount of gear without spending money on microtransactions the grind will will be significant and potentially overbearing. Though if a player is willing to spend money to maintain their gear only about $5 a month is necessary which is less than many subscription based MMOs. Finally, having good gear is completely unnecessary to enjoy the game or to be able to win races. A player's skill is a more important contributor to winning races than having the best gear.
The game has daily events that offer players a chance to obtain those items that are only available for real-world currency for free. These daily events function much like a lottery except that there are daily play-time requisites that helps to reduce the number of entries and improves your chance of winning those.
Currently the game is having problems with server stability due to recent DDOS attacks. While overall disconnections are infrequent, there are periods of frequent disconnections that can become an inconvenience. Based upon former server performance I expect this issue to be fully addressed soon. Somewhat related to this, the customer service for this game is rather slow and I hope this will be improved in the future.
The community is average. There are those who are completely unenjoyable to be around and those who are eager to accept and help a new player. Depending on the game mode (mostly cooperative maps) it is likely to be frequently kicked from a room if you are low leveled. This is by far probably the worst aspect of the community for the new player experience. Other issues with the community involve those who are fequently looking to cause player-player drama but they can be easily avoided.
Overall Tales Runner is a very fun game that offers a large amount content for players to enjoy.  It is a game that rewards skill much more than having the best gear. It can be played either hardcore or casually and its microtransactions only offer convenience.

Talesrunner is a unique, DIFFICULT, fun, but old  foot racing game enjoyed on servers around the world. NOTE: There was an old US server on gpotato that died many years ago, some players have played the game since then on other servers.
Also it can be a very amusing social experience where many players share accounts, because they've logged 1000s-10,000s of hours on the game and trust each other completely. Not many games other than WOW and Runescape can accomplish feats like that.
Warning: This game is a racing game at it's core with a HIGH difficulty curve. You WILL be terrible compared to good players for MONTHS, even if you have BETTER equips than them, if you do not learn the tricks to going faster, like dash jumping, and don't route out the maps/look at videos of routes.
2nd Warning: The point of this game is to try and get good times on maps and win races. That means that the equips in the game are not important to skilled players unless they're competing with other highly skilled players. I say this because some new players believe this is Pay to Win just because it takes a LONG time to get a lot of good equipment when lvl 1 players can buy many of the good equips with money (not ALL). Yes, it takes a long time to buy equipment and there are some things that can only be bought with real money, like pet resources. HOWEVER, it takes long because it wants you to master that 90% skill part before getting the 10% equips part and because there would not be much else to do.
ALSO, the in game real money currency, called Astros, is frequently and easily obtained by trading for the normal in game money you can earn and is NOT against the rules to do so.
TL;DR: Try it for a couple days, if you didn't quit already then look up some tutorial videos on youtube or something and set yourself in for the long haul for a game you will never quit forever. (Recommend looking up Dash Jump Tutorial videos and buying 2 new characters, Troy and Kai preferably, before spending in game money on anything else).

It's an easy to understand turn-based strategy game. The ressource management is boiled down to gathering gold via conquering ground and to place various buildings the most efficient way on the newly won space. Each fight you start costs a bit of gold. There are offensive (fleet, army) and defensive units/buildings (forts, villages, universities). The universities give you research points, which you can use to upgrade said units, but also occupy precious space you might need for other purposes (to gather money for example). So it's constant cost-benefit analysis, which i like. The game is randomly generated and comes with pre build 75 maps, but you can generate some on your own. I imagine the local multiplayer mode to be great fun, but I haven't had the chance to test it yet.
I think the game is fun to play, if you are not into micromanagement in strategy games. If you are, don't touch this game and rather blow the dust of some old SSI classics.

I'm another person who suffers from depression, and while the game didn't capture all of that feeling, it did resonate in creating scenes that I certainly recognised from my own life. In that it was successful, although this also led to some trepidation before playing - as a sufferer, I didn't feel the need to revisit what I already experience, especially as it was very likely to remind me of my own difficulties.
I gave it a shot, mostly because I'm at a point where I felt I could explore this theme, and I wanted to see how others have handled expressing it. For me, in my play through, I was pleasantly surprised. I started by making the choices that I knew I would make in real life, and that led downward. But then I started doing what I knew I should do - seeing the therapist, taking medication, confiding in friends - and as you do that, the game rewards you by showing you that those choices can help. It was oversimplified, but close enough to real to be encouraging.
With that said, I'm not sure that this is a game that will help sufferers, but I gather that wasn't its intended role. I remain nervous that choosing the wrong options could lead you to the conclusion that you are stuck with depression, and accordingly I think I'll remain with this one play through for a bit. However, the settings are close enough to real that it might help non-sufferers to understand a tiny bit of what depression can feel like, and maybe help everyone understand that there are ways out. And this seems like a very good thing.
Overall, after months of being wary, I'm glad I finally found the time to play it through. I'd recommand it, but with the proviso that it won't be for everyone.

Okay so real talk from someone who has had clinical Depression since they were 9.
Depression sucks. Big time. A lot of the thought processes, situations, and dialogue that are used in this 'game' are somewhat relatable to some of my own experiences. The not feeling good enough for your partner, being emotionally exhausted, having to pep yourself up for menial activities...It's a lot more difficult than people realize, and I will give some credit to Depression Quest for trying to shed some light on that, for the small hints of it that are there.
However, while I understand what this was trying to accomplish, there are better ways of doing so. This is not a game. It is an interactive journal essentially. It is trying to be a new-age look into a 'deep' soul that ends up sounding very pretentious. I just know most people do not want to sit and read walls of text(s) of sad things, which is probably one of the major reasons Depression Quest has been so negatively received. There's also the fact that the story overall really isn't even that engaging. I started skipping over entries after the seventh one and just clicked the most positive options to get to the end. I also can't stand the title. As another reviewer stated, Depression is not a 'quest' where you get a nice little reward for making it to the end. It's draining and exhausting. It's learning how to cope and when you think everything is fine and figured out, the rules change again for no reason. Basically, it's not nearly as straight-forward as this 'groundbreaking game' claims to be.
I read a bit on Zoe Quinn and her desire to create a more straight-forward game because all the ones dealing with Depression are more metaphorical and about symbolism (which I prefer personally). Well, congratulations Zoe. You created your snorefe-masterpiece!

Ok this is very annoying some of the reviews of this game so I've decided to make a review and give this game the respect it deserves.
I want to make 1 thing very very clear at the start. This game has no P2W element. Any guns you can get from the random (lotto) box are IDENTICAL in stats to their counterpart. This has been said by the GM's in NUMEROUS discussion threads. The only difference is visual.
And for anyone complaining about "cheaters" there are people already putting tons of effort in this game and I would like you to show me some examples of hacks you can find from this game. Battleeye is not a bad anti-cheat, infact it has a better track record than VAC itself.
Now onto the game review, I'll list some pros, cons and possibly some neutral points
Pros:
-This game can run on a toaster (and most people who play put the settings to minimum to reduce map clutter)
- There is already a competitive scene for this game on ESL if you are into that sort of thing with their own rulesets and everything.
- If you want to play with upped graphics the game can look pretty decent but imo it suffers from aliasing issues
- Gameplay is very fluid although there is an odd bug when it comes to jumping in some cases where you will vault instead of jumping normally (pls fix).
- Lobby system, the lobby system is very nicely organized and you can clearly see what lobbies are restricted and to what.
- IF YOU DO NOT LIKE THE "ABILITIES" THERE ARE CLASSIC MODES WITH THEM DISABLED (ESL HAS THEM DISABLED ALSO)
- Mod purchases are cheap and permanent
Cons:
- Servers are unstable but in the recent couple of days I haven't had an issue and hopefully they keep progressing in a right direction with their server stabilities.
- Clan ladders and Ranked ladders are not very populated and it could be a very long time before you can find a game.
- Cannot invite friends to a lobby, they have to find it themselves.
- When inviting people to a matchmaking party sometimes it bugs out and requires a restart to work.
Neutral:
- GP System. You earn an OK amount of GP per game and it is suggested to buy guns as a rental and not try to save for permanent purchases. The developers said they are working on changing the prices or the amount of GP earned to help with purchasing of guns
- Gem System. Gems purchase you visual items (
UPDATE: I did some proper searching about characters and infact they are cosmetic updates and infact one of the characters you can purchase is slower and has worse options for their armor vests. ) but no guns you purchase have a stat boost over their normal counterparts. You can use gems to purchase guns before you unlocked them. You can also purchase gems in game by using steam wallet if you so wish.
TL;DR All in all I do recommend this game and yes it does require a little bit of time investment to get used to their gunplay, movement and to really learn the maps and contact points. Community is friendly and is more often than not willing to answer your questions.

If I could, this would be a neutral review.
Honestly, it has potential: The guns are detailed, feel responsive, and, as advertised, brings a LOT of customization. However, it has several major drawbacks which can really ruin the game for some people:
1. Everything is expensive as♥♥♥♥♥♥ Even some of the earliest guns you unlock will take a long time to own. Attachments are expensive too, and most cosmetics you will never be able to purchase.
2. Unbalanced guns. My very first match was in a sandy temple-esque set of ruins, and it was nothing more than a glorified shooting range. Every single person had a sniper, and 9 times out of 10 a bullet would somehow find its way into my skull, regardless of where I tried to run. One player in particular had a 'Random Box' weapon- AKA the guns that rarely drop and are also OP as hell. Which brings me to point 3.

TL;DR: Play it, it's free, but don't get in deep until (if) balances arrive. On the other hand, if you have tons of money to throw at the devs, pick it up and go hog wild with your one-shot-kill sniper or 30000 RPM LMG.
